title: Dihua Street & Dadaocheng: Tea, Textiles & History
excerpt: A complete guide to Dihua Street and Dadaocheng, exploring historic Baroque architecture, Yongle Fabric Market, Lunar New Year festival streets, traditional dried fruits, tea houses, and boutique craft shops.
content:
Located along the banks of the Tamsui River in Datong District, Dadaocheng (大稻埕) and its famous central artery, Dihua Street (迪化街), form Taipei’s oldest commercial district. Stepping into Dihua Street feels like walking straight into a living museum of Taiwan's rich trading history.

Here, red-brick Qing Dynasty shophouses stand alongside ornate 1920s Japanese-era Baroque facades, housing traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) merchants, dried seafood wholesalers, tea masters, and Taiwan's largest textile market. At the same time, a modern cultural renaissance has swept through Dadaocheng, filling renovated historic courtyard buildings with boutique craft shops, third-wave coffee roasters, art galleries, and vibrant riverside container bars.

Whether you are coming to shop for custom fabrics at Yongle Market, pray for romance at the Xiahai City God Temple, sample dried mangoes, or soak up the electric atmosphere of the Lunar New Year Festival, this comprehensive guide covers everything you need to know about visiting Dihua Street and Dadaocheng.

The History of Dadaocheng: From Tea Port to Commercial Hub

Dadaocheng (which translates literally to "Large Rice Drying Field") began as an agricultural plain inhabited by the indigenous Ketagalan people. In 1853, violent clan feuds in nearby Bangka (modern-day Wanhua) forced Fujianese merchants to move north along the Tamsui River, establishing a new trading post at Dadaocheng.

The district’s golden era arrived in 1860, when the Qing Dynasty opened the Tamsui River to international shipping under the Treaty of Tientsin. Foreign merchants, particularly Scottish trader John Dodd, quickly realized that northern Taiwan produced world-class oolong tea. Dodd set up tea processing plants in Dadaocheng and exported "Formosa Oolong" directly to New York and London, turning Dadaocheng into an international shipping hub.

During the Japanese colonial era (1895–1945), wealthy local merchants built grand multi-story shophouses featuring intricate Western Baroque relief carvings, classical columns, and Japanese Art Deco patterns. The architecture of Dihua Street is famous for its long, narrow shangwu (shop-residence) layout: a front retail shop opens to the street, leading through a open-air central courtyard to private living quarters or warehouses in the rear.

Yongle Fabric Market (永樂市場)

At the center of Dadaocheng sits Yongle Fabric Market (永樂市場), Taiwan’s largest and most famous textile market. Established during the Japanese era as a wholesale cloth bazaar, Yongle Market remains a paradise for fashion designers, cosplayers, craft lovers, and tailors.

  • 2nd Floor (Textile Haven): Hundreds of densely packed stalls sell every imaginable fabric—from traditional Taiwanese floral printed cotton (Hakka floral patterns) and Japanese kimono silks to linen, lace, denim, synthetic furs, and canvas.
  • 3rd Floor (Tailors & Custom Sewing): Professional seamstresses and tailors can turn fabrics purchased downstairs into custom Qipao dresses, curtains, tote bags, or tailored suits within days.
  • 1st Floor (Traditional Food Stalls): The ground floor operates as a vibrant traditional wet market famous for legendary local eateries, including Lin's Oil Rice (林合發油飯店)—famous for its savory sticky rice with mushrooms and pork—and fresh sashimi bowls.

Dihua New Year Street (台北年貨大街)

If you visit Taipei in the two weeks leading up to Lunar New Year (usually late January or early February), Dihua Street hosts the legendary Taipei Lunar New Year Festival (年貨大街).

During the festival, Dihua Street turns into a pedestrian-only sea of red lanterns, upbeat traditional music, and cheerful street vendors wearing traditional outfits. Tens of thousands of locals flock here to stock up on New Year essentials:

  • Festive Sweets & Candies: Tables overflowing with bulk candies, nougat, winter melon sugar, and jelly beans.
  • Delicacies & Premium Gifts: Dried sea cucumber, abalone, dried scallops, bird's nest, and Taiwanese sausages.
  • Free Food Samples: Vendor clerks stand on stools offering free samples of roasted peanuts, pistachios, beef jerky, dried squid, and warm herbal tea to passersby.

Local Food & Traditional Snacks

Dadaocheng is one of Taipei’s premier foodie neighborhoods, blending century-old traditional food stalls with modern artisan bakeries and tea houses:

Walking along the arcade sidewalks, you'll encounter huge sacks of freshly roasted nuts and traditional snacks displayed directly outside wholesalers:

  • Dried Fruits & Vegetables: Dihua Street is famous for natural dried fruits—thick slices of dried Irwin mango, sweet dried guava, pineapple rings, and crispy vacuum-fried taro and okra chips.
  • Pork Paper (豬肉紙): Paper-thin, crispy pork paper flavored with almonds and soy sauce, made famous by shops like Kuai Che (快車肉乾) and Jiang Ji (江記華隆).
  • Peanut Soup & Mochi: Stop by Dadaocheng Peanut Soup (大稻埕花生湯) for hot, velvety sweet peanut soup served with crispy deep-fried dough sticks (Youtiao) or fresh handmade peanut mochi.
  • Traditional Pastry Shops: Historic bakery shops like Lee Huajiah (李亭香) serve traditional mung bean cakes, turtle-shaped peanut cakes (Ping-an-kueh), and pineapple cakes made from hundred-year-old wooden molds.
  • Herbal Teas & TCM Blends: Traditional Chinese medicine shops sell freshly brewed herbal tea, sour plum drink (Wu Mei Zhi), and nourishing ginseng broths.

Boutique Shops & Modern Tea Houses

In recent years, urban revitalization initiatives (such as the URS - Urban Regeneration Station project) have transformed Dadaocheng into a hub for Taiwanese design, independent fashion boutiques, and artisan craftsmanship:

In recent years, urban revitalization initiatives (such as the URS - Urban Regeneration Station project) have transformed Dadaocheng into a hub for Taiwanese design and artisan craftsmanship:

  • Hakuba & InBlooom (印花樂): A Taiwanese lifestyle design brand creating hand-printed textile bags, stationery, and home decor inspired by Taiwan's native birds and vintage tile patterns.
  • A2G & Art Studio Courtyards: Many shophouses feature hidden multi-tier courtyards containing independent leather craft workshops, handmade pottery studios, and antique shops.
  • Historic Tea Salons: Visit South Street Delight (ASPO-TEATOOT) or Watsons Courtyard Tea House to sample high-mountain Formosa Oolong tea paired with delicate Taiwanese sweets inside restored 1920s interior chambers.
  • Craft Beer Taprooms: Stop by Mikkeller Taipei, located inside an elegant historic corner shophouse, featuring 24 craft beer taps alongside Taiwanese brews.

Free Vintage Costume Rental (Dadaocheng Visitor Center)

One of the most unique cultural experiences in Taipei is dressing up in authentic 1920s–1940s vintage Taiwanese attire—including traditional Qipaos (cheongsams), retro suits, traditional waistcoats, and period accessories. The Dadaocheng Visitor Center (大稻埕遊客中心) offers a free vintage costume rental service where visitors can transform their look and step back in time.

The 2nd and 3rd floors of the Visitor Center feature beautifully recreated historical photo sets—including a 1920s traditional Chinese pharmacy, a tea merchant salon, a vintage tailor shop, and a traditional courtyard balcony—providing authentic backdrops for memorable photos in costume.

How It Works & Key Terms

  • 100% Free Rental: The costume rental service itself is entirely free of charge.
  • Online Reservation Required: Due to high demand, you must reserve your time slot in advance online via the official Dadaocheng Vintage Clothing Reservation System. Bookings fill up quickly, so reserve as early as possible.
  • Refundable Deposit & Identification: Participants must present a valid personal ID (passport or national ID card) and pay a refundable cash deposit of NT$1,000 per person upon check-in. The deposit is fully returned when costumes and props are handed back undamaged and on time.
  • Rental Duration & Limits: Each reservation allows 1 outfit and 1 accessory per person for up to 2–3 hours. You are free to take photos inside the Visitor Center's themed rooms and stroll through Dihua Street's historic arcades.
  • Visitor Tips: Wear a thin undershirt or tank top underneath for comfort and hygiene. Cancellations must be made online at least 2 days prior to avoid booking privileges being temporarily suspended.

Taipei Xiahai City God Temple (台北霞海城隍廟)

Located on Section 1 of Dihua Street, the small but hugely famous Xiahai City God Temple (霞海城隍廟) was built in 1859. Despite its compact footprint, it houses over 600 deities, making it one of the densest deity populations per square meter in Taiwan!

The temple is world-famous for its Yue Lao (月下老人)—the "Old Man Under the Moon" or Matchmaker Deity. Thousands of singles from across Taiwan and international tourists visit the temple every week to pray for true love, red threads of fate, and happy marriages.

Dadaocheng Wharf Container Market (大稻埕碼頭)

Just a 5-minute walk west of Dihua Street lies Dadaocheng Wharf (PIER5 / 大稻埕碼頭貨櫃市集) on the Tamsui River. Once the busy docking port for tea junks, the wharf has been converted into a vibrant riverfront container park.

It is one of the best places in Taipei to watch the sunset over the river while enjoying food trucks, craft beer, tacos, and seating on rooftop container decks. It's one of several good spots for drinking outdoors in Taipei. You can also rent a YouBike here to cycle along the riverside bike paths all the way to Tamsui.

Practical Information & Getting There

Dihua Street & Dadaocheng Visitor Guide

  • Address: Dihua Street, Datong District, Taipei City (台北市大同區迪化街一段)
  • Nearest MRT Stations:
    • Beimen Station (Songshan-Xindian Line / Green): Exit 3 (7-minute walk north along Tacheng Street).
    • Daqiaotou Station (Zhonghe-Xinlu Line / Orange): Exit 1 (5-minute walk south to northern Dihua Street).
  • Best Time to Visit: 10:00 AM – 7:00 PM for shops and tea houses; 5:00 PM – 9:00 PM for Dadaocheng Wharf sunset container market.
  • Admission: Free

title: Best Time to Visit Taipei: Month-by-Month Guide
excerpt: Deciding when to visit Taipei? From cherry blossoms in spring to autumn hiking and winter hot springs, here is a complete month-by-month breakdown of Taipei weather, festivals, and annual highlights.
content:
Deciding when to visit Taipei depends on what you want out of your trip. Whether you're looking for comfortable walking weather, vibrant cherry blossoms, colorful cultural festivals, or relaxing hot spring retreats, Taipei offers a distinctly different charm during every season of the year. Whenever you come, it's worth sorting a SIM card or eSIM and somewhere to stay before you fly.

Overall, autumn (October to December) is widely considered the absolute best time to visit Taipei due to warm, dry days, clear blue skies, and low humidity. However, spring brings spectacular flower blossoms, while summer offers buzzing night markets, shaved ice, and thrilling dragon boat races.

See the full 2026 Taipei Annual Events Calendar

Seasons Overview: Quick Summary

  • Autumn (October – December): Best Overall. Mild temperatures (18°C–26°C / 64°F–79°F), minimal rainfall, and crisp air. Perfect for sightseeing, night markets, and mountain hiking.
  • Spring (February – April): Best for Flowers. Cherry blossoms bloom across Yangmingshan and Neihu, followed by Calla Lilies and Azaleas. Temperatures are pleasant (15°C–25°C), though occasional spring drizzles occur.
  • Winter (December – February): Best for Hot Springs & Culture. Cool and damp (13°C–18°C / 55°F–64°F). Excellent for soaking in Beitou and Wulai hot springs, experiencing Lunar New Year markets, and seeing the Lantern Festival.
  • Summer (June – August): Hot & Tropical. High temperatures (28°C–35°C+ / 82°F–95°F+), high humidity, afternoon thunderstorms, and typhoon potential. Great for indoor museums, iced desserts, and late-night street food.

January: Hot Springs & Lunar New Year Prep

January is one of the coolest months in Taipei, with average temperatures ranging between 13°C and 19°C (55°F – 66°F). While it rarely drops below 10°C, the damp humidity can make it feel crisp, so packing a warm jacket and layerable clothing is recommended.

Key Events & Highlights in January:

  • Taipei Lunar New Year Festival: Historic Dihua Street turns into a red-lantern-draped market in the run-up to Lunar New Year.
  • Yangmingshan Camellia Show: Thousands of blooming camellias at the Floriculture Experiment Centre.
  • Maokong Camphor Trail Flower Carnival: Golden lupine flowers along the Maokong Gondola tea hillsides.
  • Shan-Tseng-Chi Flower Festival (Beitou): Taipei's "Mini-Furano," with colorful terraced flower fields.
  • Peak Hot Spring Season: The best month to soak in Beitou or Wulai's natural thermal baths.

See exact 2026 dates for January's events →

February: Cherry Blossoms & Lantern Festivals

February brings mild spring transition weather with temperatures averaging 14°C to 20°C (57°F – 68°F). This is one of the most celebratory months of the year in Taiwan!

Key Events & Highlights in February:

  • Cherry Blossom Season (Peak Bloom): You don't need to fly to Japan to see cherry blossoms! Taipei's sakura season peaks in February:
    • Yangmingshan National Park: Head to Pingjing Street Lane 42 (Egalitarian Lane) or the Yangmingshan Flower Clock for stunning pink cascades.
    • LOHAS Park (Neihu): The LOHAS Cherry Blossom Festival lines the Neihu riverbank with cherry trees lit up by night spotlights.
    • Wulai Mountain Village: Pink blossoms framed by mountain streams and waterfalls.
  • Taiwan Lantern Festival & Pingxi Sky Lanterns: Illuminated lanterns across the city, plus the famous mass sky lantern releases in the Pingxi valley.
  • Taipei Game Show: East Asia's major gaming convention at the Nangang Exhibition Center.

See exact 2026 dates for February's events →

March: Calla Lilies & Temple Celebrations

March marks the arrival of true spring in Taipei. Temperatures warm up pleasantly to 16°C – 23°C (61°F – 73°F), making it fantastic for outdoor walking tours and temple exploring.

Key Events & Highlights in March:

  • Zhuzihu Calla Lily Festival (Yangmingshan): The misty mountain valley of Zhuzihu bursts into sea-of-white calla lilies. Visitors can put on rubber boots and pick their own flowers directly from the misty fields.
  • Taipei Azalea Festival: Daan Forest Park and the NTU (National Taiwan University) campus fill with vibrant pink, white, and magenta azaleas.
  • Baosheng Cultural Festival: A month-long temple festival at the UNESCO-awarded Dalongdong Baoan Temple - lion dances, opera and fire-walking rituals.

See exact 2026 dates for March's events →

April: Spring Blooms & Firefly Watching

April offers comfortable, warm spring weather with temperatures averaging 19°C – 26°C (66°F – 79°F). It is a fantastic month for hiking before summer heat sets in.

Key Events & Highlights in April:

  • Firefly Season (Late April – May): As evening falls, thousands of glowing fireflies appear in the damp forests surrounding Taipei. Top viewing spots include the Muzha Tea Gardens, Wulai, and the Yangmingshan trailheads.
  • Urban Music & Craft Markets: Outdoor craft fairs pop up around Huashan 1914 Creative Park and Songshan Cultural Park.
  • Qingming Festival (Tomb Sweeping Day): A national holiday for honouring ancestors and spring picnics.

See exact 2026 dates for April's events →

May: Hydrangeas & Early Summer Vibes

May transitions into early summer with warmer temperatures averaging 22°C – 29°C (72°F – 84°F). May also coincides with the arrival of the Meiyu (Plum Rain season), bringing intermittent rain showers, so keep a compact umbrella handy!

Key Events & Highlights in May:

  • Zhuzihu Hydrangea Season: Right after calla lilies fade, Zhuzihu on Yangmingshan transforms into stunning terraced hillsides of blue, purple, and pink hydrangeas (ajisai).
  • Taipei International Tourism Expo: A massive travel exhibition held at Nangang Exhibition Center featuring travel deals, food, and culture.
  • Fresh Summer Produce: Mangoes, pineapples and lychees start filling night market stalls.

See exact 2026 dates for May's events →

June: Dragon Boat Races & Mango Shaved Ice

June kicks off official summer in Taipei. Temperatures average 25°C – 32°C (77°F – 90°F) with high humidity and sunny mornings followed by occasional afternoon thunderstorms.

Key Events & Highlights in June:

  • Dragon Boat Festival (Duanwu Festival): Dragon boat races along the Keelung River at Dajia Riverside Park, plus sticky rice dumplings (zongzi).
  • Mango Shaved Ice Season: Fresh Taiwanese mango shaved ice at Yongkang Street or Smoothie House.
  • Taipei Film Festival: International and independent Taiwanese cinema.

See exact 2026 dates for June's events →

July: Summer Night Markets & Fireworks

July is peak summer in Taipei, with high temperatures averaging 27°C – 35°C (81°F – 95°F+). Days are bright and hot, making air-conditioned malls, cafes, and night market food crawls popular after sundown.

Key Events & Highlights in July:

  • Dadaocheng Summer Festival: Weekly Wednesday-evening fireworks over the Tamsui River at Yanping Riverside Park.
  • Taipei Children's Arts Festival: Family-friendly performances across theatres and public plazas.
  • Late-Night Food Culture: Escape the heat with late-night dining in Ximending or at Raohe and Ningxia night markets.

See exact 2026 dates for July's events →

August: Ghost Month & Evening Festivals

August remains hot and humid (27°C – 34°C / 81°F – 93°F). August also falls right in the middle of typhoon season in the Western Pacific, so while sunny days are common, occasional tropical storms can bring heavy rain.

Key Events & Highlights in August:

  • Hungry Ghost Month (Zhongyuan Festival): A month-long Taoist tradition - expect food offerings and incense burning outside shops, temples and homes across the city.
  • Dadaocheng Valentine's Day Fireworks: A fireworks show and live music around Qixi (Chinese Valentine's Day).

See exact 2026 dates for August's events →

September: Mid-Autumn Moon Festival

September brings welcome relief as the intense summer heat begins to break. Temperatures average a pleasant 24°C – 31°C (75°F – 88°F), with drier air toward the end of the month.

Key Events & Highlights in September:

  • Mid-Autumn Festival (Moon Festival): Families gather for street BBQs, mooncakes and pomelos under the full moon - one of Taiwan's best-loved holidays.
  • Taipei Arts Festival: Contemporary music, dance and theatre at venues including the Taipei Performing Arts Center.
  • Sunset Hikes: Evening climbs up Elephant Mountain for Taipei 101 views against clear autumn skies.

See exact 2026 dates for September's events →

October: Ideal Weather & Taiwan Pride

October is universally regarded as one of the single best months to visit Taipei. The weather is perfection: comfortable temperatures averaging 20°C – 27°C (68°F – 81°F), low humidity, low rainfall, and clear blue skies.

Key Events & Highlights in October:

  • Taiwan LGBT+ Pride Parade: The largest Pride celebration in Asia - over 150,000 marchers through central Taipei, ending around Ximending Red House.
  • National Day (Double Tenth): Military parades, flag ceremonies and cultural performances outside the Presidential Office Building.
  • Taipei Jazz Festival: Free outdoor jazz concerts at Daan Forest Park.
  • Nuit Blanche Taipei: An all-night arts festival - light installations and performances from 6pm to 6am in a chosen neighbourhood.

See exact 2026 dates for October's events →

November: Crisp Days & Autumn Foliage

November continues the glorious autumn weather with crisp, comfortable days averaging 18°C – 24°C (64°F – 75°F). It is the prime month for outdoor trekking and exploring historic mountain towns like Jiufen and Shifen.

Key Events & Highlights in November:

  • Shilin Residence Chrysanthemum Show: Thousands of sculpted chrysanthemums in the historic Chiang Kai-shek Shilin Residence gardens.
  • Golden Horse Film Festival: Taiwan's equivalent of the Oscars, celebrating Chinese-language cinema.
  • Autumn Grassland Hikes: Silver grass turns Qingtiangang Meadow on Yangmingshan into golden waves.

See exact 2026 dates for November's events →

December: Christmas Lights & NYE Fireworks

December brings crisp winter air with temperatures averaging 15°C – 20°C (59°F – 68°F). The city gets into full festive holiday mode with light installations and year-end celebrations.

Key Events & Highlights in December:

  • Christmasland in New Taipei City (Banqiao): Taiwan's largest festive event - 3D laser light shows, giant Christmas trees, rides and markets.
  • Taipei Marathon: Thousands of runners race past iconic landmarks from Taipei City Hall.
  • Taipei 101 New Year's Eve Fireworks: Over 100,000 revellers watch the world-famous fireworks launch off the sides of Taipei 101 at midnight.

title: Taipei Nightlife: Clubs, Bars, KTV & Night Tours
excerpt: Experience the best of Taipei's nightlife, from glitzy nightclubs in Xinyi and hidden speakeasies in Daan to late-night KTV, night sightseeing buses, and lively pub crawls.
content:
Taipei is widely known as one of the safest and most energetic capital cities in Asia, and its nightlife is no exception. Whether you are looking to dance the night away in glitzy mega-clubs, sip craft cocktails in award-winning speakeasies, sing until dawn in a private KTV room, or explore night markets and scenic mountain viewpoints, Taipei has something to offer every type of night owl.

Click here to see all my ‘best of’ lists

Best Districts for Nightlife

Before diving into individual spots, it helps to understand the geography of Taipei's nightlife scene, which is clustered around a few key districts – worth bearing in mind when choosing where to stay:

  • Xinyi District: The glitzy commercial center directly beneath Taipei 101. It is the heart of Taipei’s upscale clubbing scene, rooftop hotel bars, and high-energy lounge spots.
  • Zhongxiao Dunhua (Daan / Eastern District): An eclectic neighborhood that comes alive at night, boasting the city's premier collection of speakeasies, high-end cocktail bars, local Izakayas, and a wide array of popular nightclubs.
  • Ximending (Wanhua): The colorful center of Taipei's youth culture. Behind the historic Red House is the city's premier LGBTQ+ nightlife plaza, featuring an open-air courtyard with highly social outdoor bars.
  • Maji Square (Yuanshan): A casual, open-air complex in Expo Park. Popular with international students and expats for its laidback craft beer stalls and alternative vibes.
  • Linsen North Road (Zhongshan): Taipei’s historic "adult" entertainment district. Known for its distinct neon-lit lanes, this district has a more adult-oriented character, filled with Japanese-style hostess bars, piano bars, cabarets, and love hotels.

Top Nightclubs in Taipei

Taipei's nightclub scene offers top-tier sound systems, spectacular laser shows, and sets from international DJs. The main commercial venues are concentrated in Xinyi, specifically in and around the ATT 4 FUN building.

WAVE CLUB Taipei is a staple for a high-intensity night, famous for its open-air balcony that sits directly in front of Taipei 101. WAVE is also popular for its "all-you-can-drink" (open bar) ticket offers. Nearby, AI Nightclub features a highly futuristic interior and plays heavy EDM and hip-hop to a young, high-energy crowd.

For a more premium experience, OMNI in the Eastern District features a massive, award-winning 360-degree LED screen and high-end visual design. If you prefer hip-hop and R&B, KOR Taipei functions as a sleek "lounge-club" hybrid with tiered seating and a world-class sound system focusing on premium whiskey and cocktails.

If you're looking for a casual, friendly vibe without Xinyi's glitz and dress codes, Triangle at Maji Square is a fantastic foreign-friendly spot that spins everything from 90s hits to house music. For underground techno and house heads, alternative venues like Pawnshop and FINAL cater to the city's late-night subcultures with strict no-photo policies.

If you are traveling solo or with a group of friends and want to experience Taipei's clubbing scene while meeting fellow travelers, joining the official Taipei Pub Crawl is a fantastic, highly social way to kick off your night.

World-Class Cocktail Bars & Speakeasies

Taipei has earned a reputation as one of Asia's mixology capitals, regularly sending multiple venues onto the Asia's 50 Best Bars rankings. Speakeasies are a massive trend here, with bars hiding behind all sorts of inconspicuous storefronts.

At Le Kief (菱玖洋服) in Daan, you enter a classic, wood-paneled English tailor shop. To gain entry to the bar behind the wall, you must pick up a vintage telephone and dial a secret code. Ounce Taipei hides behind a secret door inside a café and offers a bespoke experience: there is no menu, and bartenders mix drinks tailored specifically to your flavor preferences. Alchemy Speakeasy Bar sits hidden behind a bookshelf in a restaurant, offering a classy, prohibition-era jazz lounge vibe.

For award-winning mixology, check out Bar Mood, celebrated for its unique botanical cocktails that blend local Taiwanese teas and ingredients with classic spirits. To Infinity & Beyond features a retro-futuristic space capsule design and molecular cocktails, while AHA Saloon offers an old-school record lounge aesthetic with complex tea-infused drinks.

If you prefer a casual evening of bar-hopping in the historical lanes of Zhongshan, grabbing the Taipei Taio-Tong Pass is highly recommended, as it unlocks excellent drink promotions and removes minimum spends across several local establishments.

For a quick, standing-room cocktail before the night begins, Draft Land serves high-quality craft cocktails directly on tap. The vibe is social, and crowds routinely spill out onto the pavement on pleasant evenings.

The Private Room KTV Experience

In Taiwan, KTV (Karaoke Television) is a major social institution. Unlike Western karaoke bars where you sing on stage in front of strangers, the Taiwanese KTV experience is entirely private.

You rent a soundproof private room equipped with comfortable couches, dining tables, dynamic lighting, and private bathrooms. KTV halls operate like fully functioning restaurants; you can order hot Taiwanese food—such as beef noodle soup, dumplings, and fried chicken—and beer directly to your room using a touch screen. Because these buildings are open 24/7, they are the go-to spot for locals to continue singing and eating after the clubs close at 4:00 AM.

The largest and most professional chain is Cashbox Partyworld (錢櫃), famous for its excellent food menu and extensive song selection. Holiday KTV (好樂迪) is a popular budget-friendly alternative that is very popular with students.

Safety Warning: While mainstream chains like Cashbox and Holiday are completely wholesome, family-friendly environments, visitors should be aware that many smaller KTVs around Linsen North Road operate as hostess clubs. In these establishments, companions are paid to sit, drink, and sing with guests. To ensure a standard, fun-focused singing night, stick to the major, well-known chains.

Taipei Nightlife Travel Deals

To help you get the most out of Taipei’s night scene while saving money, there are a few excellent experiences and passes you can book in advance:

  • Taipei Taio-Tong Pass (Tiaotong Pass): Perfect for bar-hoppers wanting to explore the historic Japanese-style bars in Zhongshan's Tiaotong district. The pass provides excellent Buy-1-Get-1-Free drink deals and waives minimum spends at participating venues.
  • Taipei Night Sightseeing Buzz Tour (Tipsy Bus): A unique 2.5-hour mobile social party and bar crawl on an open-top double-decker bus. Starting at ATT 4 FUN in Xinyi, it features a live onboard DJ, music, drinks, and stops at iconic nightlife spots in Yuanshan and Xinyi District to party with new friends.
  • Taipei Pub Crawl: A guided social tour that takes you to multiple local bars and finishes at a nightclub. It includes free welcome drinks, admission to a popular club, and is a fantastic way to meet fellow travelers and expats.
Klook.com

Late-Night Food & Alternative Activities

If you don't drink alcohol, Taipei is still an exceptionally lively place to explore after dark. The city is packed with late-night options that have nothing to do with bars or clubs.

Sharing a steaming hot pot in the middle of the night is a beloved local pastime. Establishments like Mala Hot Pot, Ding Wang, and the ginseng-infused Elixir Health Pot (Wu Lao Guo) serve boiling spicy broths and stay open until 2:00 AM or 4:00 AM. If you are out even later, you can join the queues at 24-hour traditional soy milk breakfast joints like Lai Lai Soy Milk to eat savory danbing (egg crepes) and dip crispy shaobing dough sticks into hot soy milk.

Taipei is also home to the world's first 24-hour bookstore. The flagship Eslite Spectrum Songyan Store operates around the clock, providing a quiet, beautifully designed space to read, browse stationary, and drink tea in the creative park. If you want a peaceful mountain escape, you can travel up to Maokong, where several traditional tea houses remain open late so you can brew hot oolong tea while looking down at the glowing Taipei basin below.

If you want to experience the city's nightlife from a completely different perspective, joining the Taipei Night Sightseeing Buzz Tour is an absolute must-try. This open-top "party bus" rolls through the city with a live DJ and drinks, making it a great way to sightsee and socialize before hitting the clubs.

Essential Practical Tips

  • Carry a Physical Passport: This is absolutely non-negotiable for clubs and high-end bars. Digital photos or scans of your passport on your phone are not accepted by security guards.
  • Subway Closures: The Taipei MRT shuts down at midnight. After this, you will need to rely on yellow taxis or the highly reliable and cheap Uber app to travel.
  • Dress Code: While bars and lounges are generally relaxed, clubs enforce dress codes for men. Avoid wearing sandals, open-toed shoes, or athletic tank tops. Smart-casual is always the safest option.
  • Tipping: There is no tipping culture in Taiwan. Most commercial bars, lounges, and clubs will add a standard 10% service charge to your bill automatically.
  • Safety: Taipei has exceptionally low crime rates, making it one of the safest cities in the world for late-night exploration. However, always keep an eye on your personal belongings in busy areas.

title: Taiwan Visa & Entry Requirements (2026)
excerpt: Who needs a visa for Taiwan, how the 90-day visa-exempt entry works, and how to fill in the online arrival card before you fly so you skip the queues at the airport.
content:
Perfect For

  • First-time visitors
  • Pre-trip planning
  • Checking visa-free eligibility
  • Understanding arrival procedures

Most visitors to Taiwan don't need a visa at all - but the rules depend entirely on your nationality, and it's worth double-checking before you book flights. This guide covers who qualifies for visa-free entry, what you need at the airport, and how to extend your stay if you decide not to go home on time.

💡 The Quick Verdict: Visa & Entry

  • Most Western nationalities: no visa needed for stays up to 90 days - just confirm your specific country on the Bureau of Consular Affairs site.
  • Everyone must complete the TWAC (Taiwan Arrival Card) online up to 7 days before flying - paper cards no longer exist, and doing it in advance avoids a slow kiosk queue at the airport.
  • Not visa-exempt? Apply for a visitor visa at a Taiwan representative office well ahead of your trip - it can take several working days.

This page is a general overview, not immigration advice. Entry requirements change and vary by nationality, so always confirm your specific situation on the Bureau of Consular Affairs website or with your nearest Taiwan representative office before you travel.

Visa-Exempt Entry

Taiwan has one of the more generous visa-free programmes in Asia. Passport holders from a large number of countries - including the US, UK, most of the EU, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Japan and South Korea - can currently enter Taiwan visa-free for up to 90 days for tourism purposes. A smaller number of other nationalities are eligible for shorter visa-free stays (commonly 14 or 30 days).

Because the list of eligible countries (and the number of days granted) changes from time to time, don't rely on second-hand summaries, including this one, to make a final decision - check your eligibility directly on the Bureau of Consular Affairs site linked below before booking.

Typical visa-free stay90 days (tourism)
Applies toMost Western nationalities - always verify your own
Extendable?No - visa-exempt stays generally cannot be extended
Where to checkBureau of Consular Affairs

Passport Requirements

A few basics that catch first-time visitors out:

  • Your passport should be valid for the duration of your stay in Taiwan. Some airlines and immigration desks are stricter than the official minimum, so having at least 6 months of validity remaining is the safest bet if you can.
  • You'll usually be asked for proof of an onward or return flight when checking in or at immigration.
  • Make sure you have at least one blank passport page for the entry stamp.

Online Arrival Card (TWAC)

Since 1 October 2025, Taiwan has done away with paper arrival cards altogether. Every foreign visitor now has to submit a Taiwan Arrival Card (TWAC) electronically - there's no paper form handed out on the plane anymore, so don't wait for one.

You have two ways to do this, and the difference matters:

  • Fill it in online before you fly - takes about five minutes from your phone or laptop, any time in the 7 days before you land.
  • Fill it in at the airport if you haven't done it in advance - you'll be pointed to a QR code at the immigration hall and have to complete the whole form on your phone standing in the queue, or use one of the kiosks. It works, but it's slow, fiddly on a small screen after a long flight, and holds up the queue behind you too.

Doing it in advance is the difference between walking straight up to the immigration desk and standing in the arrivals hall filling in a form on your phone with everyone else who didn't.

How to Fill It In Online

  • Go directly to twac.immigration.gov.tw - this is the official National Immigration Agency site. The NIA has specifically warned about fraudulent copycat sites that charge a fee for what is a completely free government service, so don't just search and click the first result.
  • You can submit it any time from 7 days before your flight up until you land.
  • Have these ready before you start: your passport, flight number and arrival date, and the address of where you're staying in Taiwan (your hotel confirmation email has this).
  • You'll start by entering your email address and verifying it with a code sent to your inbox - do this first, the code expires after about 10 minutes.
  • Most of the form is standard passport details, but a few fields are easy to get wrong: your Date of Entry and Expected Departure Date for Taiwan specifically (not your home country), and your Visa Type - most tourists should select "Visa-Exempt (include TAC)" unless you've actually applied for a visa in advance.
  • You don't have to type your passport details manually - there's a "Retrieve Passport Data" option that lets you scan or upload a photo of your passport's biographical page, and it fills in your name, passport number, nationality and dates automatically.
  • Once submitted, you'll get a confirmation. You don't need to print anything - at immigration, the officer scans your passport and your TWAC submission is pulled up automatically. It's still worth keeping a screenshot as a backup in case of any system issue.

Travelling as a group? You don't need to fill in a separate form from scratch for each person - click "Add Travelers" to add more people to the same submission. If there are a lot of you (or you visit Taiwan often and want to keep the details on file), you can download the Excel template, fill in everyone's details offline, and use Import to add up to 16 people at once.

What Happens at Immigration

Arrival at Taoyuan Airport is generally quick and straightforward:

  • Follow signs for Foreign Passports / Non-ROC Nationals at immigration.
  • You'll have your photo and fingerprints taken as part of standard entry procedures.
  • Have your passport and onward flight details ready to show if asked - your TWAC submission is pulled up automatically when your passport is scanned.
  • Customs after baggage claim is normally a walk-through unless you're carrying something to declare.

Once you're through, see the Airport MRT guide linked below for the quickest way into central Taipei.

Extending Your Stay

This is one of the most common points of confusion: most visa-exempt stays cannot be extended. If you want to stay in Taiwan longer than the visa-free period allows, you generally need to either leave and re-enter (rules on how soon you can do this vary), or apply for an actual visa in advance of your trip rather than relying on the visa-exempt programme. Don't assume you can simply visit an immigration office locally and add extra days - policies here are stricter than in many other countries.

If You're Not Visa-Exempt

If your nationality isn't covered by the visa-exempt programme, you'll need to apply for a visitor visa at a Taiwan representative office (there's no embassy, so look for a "Taipei Economic and Cultural Office" or similar in your country) before you travel. Processing can take at least several working days, so apply well ahead of your trip.

Useful Links

  • Bureau of Consular Affairs - Visa-Exempt Entry - the official, up-to-date list of eligible countries and stay lengths.
  • Taiwan Arrival Card (TWAC) - the official site to submit your arrival card online before you fly.
  • National Immigration Agency - for visa extensions and stay-related questions.

Once your entry is sorted, you might find these useful for the rest of your trip:

title: Taiwan SIM Cards & eSIMs - 2026 Price Comparison
excerpt: Airport and Klook prices compared for 4G, 5G and eSIM, from 3 days to a year. Which to buy, what you need to bring, and where the cheap options stop.
content:
Having travelled to Taiwan on many occasions, I've used many of the pre-paid SIM cards here and believe I'm well placed to write a guide on them.

💡 The Quick Verdict: Getting Connected

  • Just want internet? Buy a data-only eSIM online before you fly. No passport, no age limit, no queue – and for trips up to about two weeks it's the cheapest option by a wide margin. You'll be connected the moment you land.
  • Want a Taiwanese phone number? Then you have to collect a SIM in person and show your passport plus a second ID. That's true of Chunghwa's carrier eSIM as well – despite being an eSIM, it can't be installed until you've registered at a counter. Buy at an airport booth, or at one of the designated city stores if you land after the booths close – not every phone shop sells these tourist plans.
  • Staying a month or more? Buy at the airport. The counters give volume discounts that overtake the eSIM at around 30 days, and beyond 60 days they're the only option.

SIM Card Requirements

These requirements are for a physical tourist SIM card and the Chunghwa carrier eSIM.

If you're getting a data-only eSIM, none of this applies – there's no age limit, no passport check and no cash needed, since it's bought and activated entirely online.

  • Age: usually 20 or over for physical airport SIMs, though some plans are sold from 18 – check before you book. The Chunghwa carrier eSIM is 18+. Data-only eSIMs have no age check.
  • ID: a non-Taiwanese passport – these are tourist deals – plus a second document, such as a residence permit, visa, international driving licence, visa-exemption stamp or e-GATE clearance stamp. Chunghwa will also photograph you at the counter.
  • Payment: Chunghwa is cash only, in New Taiwan Dollars. Taiwan Mobile also accepts credit cards, UnionPay and Alipay. Don't assume you can pay by card.
  • Unlocked phone: your handset must not be carrier-locked, jailbroken or rooted.
  • Limits: one eSIM per person per carrier; a maximum of two physical SIMs per person.
  • Visa length: your plan cannot be longer than your permitted stay.

Worth knowing: completing real-name registration gets you an extra day free – so a 3-day plan runs for four.

Taiwan SIM Card Airport Price Comparison

Both terminals at Taoyuan airport have a number of booths with SIM card offers, or you could order one from Klook and pick it up from one of their booths in the arrivals halls.

Songshan airport is more limited, and only has a Chunghwa Telecom booth. This can also be used to pick up Chunghwa Telecom SIM cards and WiFi routers ordered on Klook.

Pre-ordering the same Chunghwa plan through Klook saves a flat 8% on the counter price – the same plan, the same call credit, the same collection desk. The Klook counter also opens earlier and closes later than the carrier booths, which helps if you land at an awkward hour.

If you don't need a Taiwanese phone number, a data-only eSIM is dramatically cheaper for short trips – around half the counter price for three days – but the saving shrinks the longer you stay, and past about two weeks the airport counter wins outright.

Prices verified August 2025 from the counter boards at Taoyuan Airport, and cross-checked against three further boards and Chunghwa's published rates. Klook prices checked August 2026.

The first thing worth knowing is that all three carriers charge the same at the airport. Chunghwa Telecom, Taiwan Mobile and FarEasTone are identical at 3, 5, 10, 15 and 30 days.

So price is not how you choose a carrier at the airport. Coverage and queue length are.

Which to buy

Under a week – buy a data-only eSIM before you fly. Around half the airport price, and no queue.
One to two weeks – near enough a coin flip. Take the eSIM for convenience, or the counter SIM if you want a phone number.
A month or more – buy at the airport. The counter's volume discounts beat the eSIM by 30% at 30 days.
Two months or more – airport only, and choose Taiwan Mobile.

If you specifically want 5G, the data-only eSIM undercuts the counter at every duration up to 30 days. 5G costs roughly 50–100% more than 4G at the counter, and the premium narrows the longer you stay.

Tethering

If you want to use your phone as a hotspot – to get a travelling companion online, or to connect a laptop – be aware that 5G plans limit hotspot sharing to 1GB per day. It will simply stop sharing after that. However, 4G lists no limit at all.

If several of you need to get online, a portable WiFi router comes with unlimited data of its own and connects up to five devices.

eSIM Options for Taiwan

If you have a modern, unlocked phone that supports eSIM technology, an eSIM is usually the most convenient option – you download a digital profile instead of swapping a physical SIM.

Not all Taiwan eSIMs are the same

There are two quite different products both sold as "Taiwan eSIM", and the difference matters more than the price does.

The catch: the Chunghwa carrier eSIM cannot be installed before you arrive. Taiwan's real-name registration law means the QR code is only issued after you present your passport at an airport or Chunghwa counter in person – where they will also photograph you. So it removes none of the queueing that is usually the whole reason for choosing an eSIM. If avoiding the counter is your goal, you want the data-only eSIM.

What "unlimited" means here: 15GB per day at full speed, then 1Mbps until the next morning. Most travellers won't get near it. Tethering is supported, on Chunghwa's 5G network.

Who Can Get an eSIM?

  • Unlocked Device: Your mobile phone must be carrier-unlocked, and not jailbroken (iOS) or rooted (Android).
  • eSIM Compatible: Most iPhone XS or newer, Google Pixel 3 or newer, and Samsung Galaxy S20 or newer support eSIM. New models are added all the time, so check Klook's full compatible device list before you buy.

A data-only eSIM needs no ID and has no age limit. The Chunghwa carrier eSIM does – see SIM Card Requirements.

Do You Need a Taiwanese Number?

Most travellers never need a Taiwanese number. Maps, messaging, translation, ride-hailing and calls over WhatsApp or LINE all run on data alone, so a data-only eSIM is enough.

You'll want a real number if you plan to:

  • book restaurants or clinics that only take phone reservations
  • register for local services that send an SMS code – food delivery, bike hire, some ticketing
  • be reachable by a hotel, tour operator or landlord while you're out

If any of those apply, get a physical SIM or the Chunghwa carrier eSIM. Otherwise save the money.

Choosing a Data-Only Plan

This eSIM runs on Chunghwa Telecom – considered the best in Taiwan for speed and coverage, including in more remote and mountainous regions, so you're not trading network quality for convenience.

How to Activate a Data-Only eSIM

This is the flow for a data-only eSIM. Setup takes about five minutes, and you can do it from home before you fly – your data and validity period won't start until the eSIM actually connects to a Taiwanese network, so there's no downside to installing it early. (The Chunghwa carrier eSIM works differently – see below.)

  1. Buy your eSIM on Klook. You'll get a QR code (plus the manual activation details as a backup) in the Klook app or by email.
  2. Install the eSIM profile. Easiest way: open the Klook app, go to your booking and tap Add eSIM to device – installation happens automatically. Or manually, go to your phone's Settings > Cellular/Mobile Data > Add eSIM and scan the QR code.
  3. Leave it alone until you land. The plan stays dormant until it detects a Taiwanese network, so installing it days in advance costs you nothing.
  4. Turn on data roaming for the eSIM once you land. In Settings, switch on Data Roaming for the new eSIM line (keep your home SIM active for calls/texts if you're running dual-SIM) – you should be connected within a minute or two.

Having trouble? You can reach Klook's support straight from the app: Account > Bookings > your eSIM booking > Contact merchant.

Get the Data-Only eSIM on Klook

How to Activate a Carrier eSIM

The Chunghwa carrier eSIM cannot be installed in advance. Under Taiwan's real-name registration rules, the QR code is only issued once you have registered in person, so the whole process happens after you land.

  1. Book online and get your voucher. This is a booking confirmation only – there is no QR code yet, and nothing to install.
  2. Go to the counter. Klook emails your exact pick-up point when you book – it will be one of the pick-up locations below, a Chunghwa Telecom service centre or a Senao store. Bring your voucher, your passport and a second form of ID. Staff will also take your photo.
  3. Staff complete the registration and install it for you. They activate the eSIM on your handset at the counter.
  4. If you have no connection afterwards, set your APN to Internet.

The profile can only be downloaded once and is tied permanently to that handset – you cannot move it to another phone later. The voucher itself has no expiry, so it can be collected on any date.

Activate early in the day. Validity is counted in calendar days, not 24-hour periods – activate at 23:59 and that still burns a full day. If you land late at night, you may be better off collecting the eSIM the following morning.

If you're travelling as a group, a pocket-sized WiFi router shares one connection between several devices – and unlike a SIM, it comes with its own unlimited data, so there's nothing else to buy.

Stock is limited and offers like this come and go, so treat it as a bonus rather than a reason to book.

i-Taiwan

i-Taiwan is a free indoor wireless hotspot scheme set up by the Taiwanese government.

With over 5,000 locations all over Taiwan (although mainly in urban areas) it's a great way to get connected for free.

If you already have a Taiwan mobile number, then registering for it simply a case of entering your mobile number, then entering the code shown on the text message you receive.

You then need to find one of the i-Taiwan hotspots and follow these instructions to complete the process.

If you don't have a Taiwan SIM, you can still register for the service, although it's slightly more complicated:

  1. Register for the service. You'll need to enter your country, passport number and date of birth.
  2. After going through immigration in Taiwan, connect to the airport's free WiFi (or any i-Taiwan hotspot) and activate the service. You'll need to re-enter your country and passport number.
  3. Present your passport to the Travel Service Center at one of the following locations and say it's for the i-Taiwan service.
    • Airport
    • MRT
    • Train Station

Then you're registered and can enjoy free WiFi for 30 days!

Conclusion

For most trips, a data-only eSIM is the answer – cheaper for anything up to about two weeks, no passport or cash needed, and working the moment you land.

If you want a Taiwanese phone number, or your phone doesn't take an eSIM, buy at an airport counter – or pre-order the same plan through Klook and save 8%.

Landing late isn't a problem: the Klook counter runs until 01:00, and failing that Chunghwa's city stores sell the same deals as the airport.

title: Taipei Annual Events Calendar 2026

content:
Taipei is a vibrant city with events happening throughout the year. From ancient cultural festivals and temple celebrations to world-class sports, music, and art events, there is always something exciting to experience in Taiwan's capital.

Here is your complete guide to the major annual events in Taipei for 2026, organized by month.

Not sure which month to actually book your trip for? See my month-by-month guide to Taipei's weather for a broader look at temperatures, blossoms and crowds alongside the events below.

January

  • Taipei Lunar New Year Festival (Dihua Street Market) – Festive holiday market selling traditional snacks, dried fruits, teas, and red decorations along historic Dihua Street in Dadaocheng – January 31 – February 15, 2026 (leading up to Lunar New Year Eve)
  • Pingjing Street 42 Cherry Blossoms – The earliest cherry blossom bloom in the Taipei area, located in Yangmingshan – Late January to Mid-February 2026
  • Presidential Building & Guest House Open Days – Rare opportunity to tour the historic Japanese-era interior of the Presidential Office Building – Check official schedule
  • Beitou & Wulai Winter Hot Spring Season – Peak season to relax in natural sulfur and sodium bicarbonate hot spring baths – All January

February

  • Lunar New Year (Year of the Horse) – Taiwan's biggest annual holiday. Expect family reunions, temple incense offerings, and festive street vibes – February 17, 2026 (Festivities Feb 16–22)
  • Taipei Lantern Festival – Spectacular light installations, giant themed lanterns, and cultural shows around Ximending and the North Gate – Late February to March 8, 2026
  • Pingxi Sky Lantern Festival – Thousands of glowing sky lanterns released over Pingxi – February 21 & March 3, 2026 (Lantern Festival Day)
  • LOHAS Park Night Cherry Blossom Festival (Neihu) – Illuminated pink cherry trees along the Neihu River trail, open for evening strolls – February 2026
  • Yangmingshan Flower Festival – Cherry blossoms, azaleas, and camellias blooming across Yangmingshan National Park – Mid-February to Mid-March 2026
  • Tianyuan Temple Tri-Colour Cherry Blossoms (Tamsui) – Hundreds of cherry trees on the hillside behind Wuji Tianyuan Temple, lit up in the evenings during the festival. Free, and the rear garden opens from 06:00 – January 29 to February 11, 2026

March

  • Taiwan Baseball League season begins – Watch the Lamigo Monkeys and the rest of the CPBL at grounds across the city – March to late September
  • Taiwan LPGA golf championship – One of the best women's golf events in the world, about 90 minutes from Taipei – March 12–15, 2026
  • Taiwan Lantern Festival 2026 (Main Festival Day: March 3, 2026) – The official nationwide Lantern Festival peak celebration on the 15th day of the first lunar month – Late February to March 8, 2026
  • Zhuzihu Calla Lily Festival – Sea of pure white calla lilies filling the volcanic fields of Zhuzihu in Yangmingshan, offering hand-picking experiences – Mid-March to Late April 2026
  • Taipei Azalea Festival – Celebrating Taipei's official city flower with concerts, picnic markets, and floral art around Daan Forest Park & NTU campus – March 2026
  • Tianyuan Temple Yoshino Cherry Blossoms (Tamsui) – The second, later bloom at Tianyuan Temple, with Yoshino cherries surrounding the round Tiantan hall. Busiest at weekends and worth going early – Mid-March to Mid-April 2026
  • Dalongdong Baoan Temple Cultural Festival – Traditional Taiwanese temple rituals, folk opera performances, and lion dances – Late March to April 2026
  • Taipei International Book Exhibition (TIBE) – Major international publishing fair held at the Taipei World Trade Center – Early March 2026

April

  • Qingming Festival (Tomb Sweeping Day Holiday) – Spring public holiday with traditional family outings and spring hikes – April 4–5, 2026
  • Wulai & Muzha Firefly Festival – Guided evening walks to observe thousands of bioluminescent fireflies glowing along mountain trails – Mid-April to May 2026
  • Zhuzihu Calla Lily Season – Continuing peak season for picking calla lilies in Yangmingshan – All April 2026
  • Urban Spring Hiking Season – Ideal mild spring weather for hiking Elephant Mountain, Four Beasts, and Xiangshan trails – All April

May

  • Zhuzihu Hydrangea Festival – Breathtaking fields of blue, purple, and pink hydrangeas blooming across Yangmingshan's mountain terraces – May to June 2026
  • Baosheng Emperor Cultural Festival – Grand temple procession, fire-walking rituals, and traditional performing arts at Dalongdong Baoan Temple – May 2026
  • Taipei Outdoor Live Concert Season – Spring music events and outdoor acoustic sessions across Taipei Music Center and Huashan 1914 – May 2026

June

  • Dragon Boat Festival (Duanwu Festival) – Thrilling international dragon boat races along the Keelung River at Dajia Riverside Park, accompanied by traditional rice dumplings (Zongzi) – June 19, 2026
  • Fresh Taiwanese Mango Season – Peak harvest season for sweet Irwin mangoes served atop mountain shaved ice bowls across Yongkang Street – June to August 2026
  • COMPUTEX Taipei – One of the world's leading global technology and hardware expos at Nangang Exhibition Center – Early June 2026

July

  • Dadaocheng Summer Festival – Weekly Wednesday night fireworks displays over the Tamsui River, gourmet food trucks, and live music at Yanping Riverside Park – Mid-July through August 2026
  • Taipei Film Festival – Premier summer film festival highlighting independent cinema and Taiwanese filmmakers – Late June to Mid-July 2026
  • Summer Water Park Season – Water activities and splash events at Taipei Water Park in Gongguan – July to August 2026

August 2026

  • Ghost Month (Hungry Ghost Festival / 中元節) – Traditional month-long folk festival with temple incense offerings and spirit rituals – August 13 – September 11, 2026 (Ghost Festival Main Day: Thursday, August 27, 2026)
  • Qixi Festival (Chinese Valentine's Day / 七夕) – Evening celebrations and romantic events – Wednesday, August 19, 2026
  • Dadaocheng Summer Festival Fireworks – Weekly Wednesday fireworks along the Tamsui River, with the Grand Finale Weekend Fireworks on Sunday, August 30, 2026
  • New Taipei River & Ocean Music Festival (新北市河海音樂季) – Free outdoor indie rock, reggae, and beach concerts along the waterfront at Tamsui Fisherman's Wharf – Early to Mid-August 2026
  • Creative Expo Taiwan (臺灣文博會) – Taiwan’s premier design, illustration, character IP, and cultural goods exhibition at Nangang Exhibition Center – Mid-to-Late August 2026
  • Taipei Fringe Festival (台北藝穗節) – Indie theater, music, dance, comedy, and performance art across non-traditional venues – August 22 – September 6, 2026

September 2026

  • Jam Jam Asia Music Festival (亞州音樂節) – Major Asian pop, indie, and electronic music festival featuring top performers from Taiwan, Japan, Korea, and Southeast Asia at Taipei Music Center – Saturday, September 5 – Sunday, September 6, 2026
  • Taipei Night Market Festival (台北夜市嘉年華) – City-wide street food celebration featuring voting for top food stalls and discount vouchers across Ningxia, Raohe, Shilin, and Huaxi markets – September to October 2026
  • Mid-Autumn Moon Festival (Zhongqiu Festival / 中秋節) – Major national holiday famous for street BBQs, mooncakes, and pomelos – Friday, September 25, 2026 (Long Weekend: September 25–27, 2026)
  • Confucius Birthday & Teachers' Day (教師節) – Authentic 6:00 AM dawn ceremony featuring traditional 8-row dance performances at Taipei Confucius Temple – Monday, September 28, 2026

October 2026

  • Double Tenth National Day (國慶日) – Flag ceremonies, cultural performances, and parades at the Presidential Office Building – Saturday, October 10, 2026
  • Taipei International Beef Noodle Festival (台北國際牛肉麵節) – Major annual culinary festival at Taipei Expo Park where top chefs compete for best traditional braised and creative beef noodles, featuring public tasting stalls – Friday, October 9 – Sunday, October 11, 2026
  • Taipei Jazz Festival (台北爵士音樂節) – Free outdoor live jazz concerts under the stars at Daan Forest Park Main Stage – Friday, October 23 – Sunday, October 25, 2026
  • Art Taipei (台北國際藝術博覽會) – Asia's premier international art fair at Taipei World Trade Center Hall 1 – Friday, October 23 – Monday, October 26, 2026
  • Taiwan LGBT+ Pride Parade (台灣同志遊行) – The largest Pride celebration in Asia, marching through central Taipei to Ximending – Saturday, October 31, 2026

November 2026

  • Nuit Blanche Taipei (白晝之夜) – All-night 12-hour white night arts festival from 6:00 PM to 6:00 AM across a chosen Taipei district – Saturday, November 7 – Sunday, November 8, 2026
  • Taipei Hot Spring Season (台北溫泉季) – Celebrating Beitou's thermal bath culture with Japanese Mikoshi shrine parades, cultural tours, and hot spring pass discounts in Xinbeitou – Late October to Early November 2026
  • Taipei Wine & Spirits Festival (台北國際酒展) – Taiwan’s largest beverage expo featuring international wine, craft beer, and sake tastings at Nangang Exhibition Center – Friday, November 13 – Monday, November 16, 2026
  • Ultra Taiwan (Ultra 台灣獨立電子音樂節) – Massive international EDM festival featuring global top-ranked DJs at Dajia Riverside Park – Mid-November 2026
  • Christmasland in New Taipei City (新北歡樂耶誕城) – Massive 3D light projection show and holiday markets at Banqiao Station Plaza – Friday, November 13, 2026 – Sunday, January 3, 2027
  • Golden Horse Film Festival & Awards (金馬影展) – Asia's most prestigious Chinese-language film festival – November 5 – November 22, 2026 (Awards Ceremony: Saturday, November 21, 2026)
  • Standard Chartered Taipei Marathon – Charity road race through Taipei city streets – Sunday, November 8, 2026
  • Shilin Residence Chrysanthemum Show (士林官邸菊展) – Grand floral topiary and outdoor music at Chiang Kai-Shek Shilin Residence – Friday, November 27 – Sunday, December 13, 2026

December 2026

  • Christmasland in New Taipei City – Full month of holiday light displays, pop concerts, and winter markets – All December 2026 – January 3, 2027
  • Shilin Residence Chrysanthemum Show – Continuing floral exhibition – November 27 – Sunday, December 13, 2026
  • Taipei Marathon (台北馬拉松) – Taiwan's flagship international marathon race – Sunday, December 20, 2026
  • Taipei Illustration Fair (台北插畫藝術節) – Annual contemporary visual art and illustration fair showcasing independent prints and zines at Songshan Cultural Park – Mid-December 2026
  • Taipei 101 New Year's Eve Fireworks & Countdown Concert (台北最High新年城) – World-famous countdown concert at City Hall and midnight fireworks off Taipei 101 – Thursday, December 31, 2026

title: Some Different Options For a Tasty Lunchtime Meal
excerpt: Some lunchtime options to help you decide
content:
Whether you're looking for a quick bite to eat or somewhere nice to dine, there are some nice options in Taipei for a lunchtime meal.

Lunch is also a good time to try some of the more popular restaurants, since they're generally less busy (at least during weekdays), while others offer some good deals during lunchtime.

My suggestions below include child-friendly meals and those suitable for vegetarians. If you're after something specific, we also cover the best Indian restaurants in the city.

Click here to see all my 'best of' lists

Food Courts

Food courts are usually my first choice for lunch. With dozens of malls spread across the city, you're never too far away from one, and almost all malls have food courts found on one of the basement levels.

Serving mainly Asian cuisine, each food stand will have a menu next to their counter so you can just point if there's a language barrier. They'll give you a buzzer which usually takes around 5 minutes - that should give you ample time to find a seat (although some malls do become very busy during peak lunch hours).

Prices range from around NT$140 to NT$220 and the meals are generally very tasty.

There are loads of options for drinks and desserts, and there are also a few restaurants including sushi belts found in these.

My favourite food courts are Q Square, Shin Kong A13 (probably the only court above ground), Taipei 101, and all Eslite malls have excellent courts.

Click here to read more about Food Halls

Quick Lunch

Aside from the food courts, Taipei has a plethora of small places for a quick yet hearty meal.

Miss Energy have a few branches dotted around the city which offer delicious, healthy yet filling bento boxes. These are only open between 11:00 – 14:00 and closed over the weekend.

There are also some nice Hawaiian Poke places that serve up some tasty yet healthy bowls with either sashimi or cooked meal/fish. My favourites are Haloa Poke and Yu Poke.

Very Thai Noodles specialise in Thai/Vietnamese inspired ramen dishes while offering dry noodles and rice dishes too. Service here is fast, and the bowls are consistently delicious.

American Restaurant Chain Deals

These American restaurant chains offer discounts and deals during lunchtime to attract customers:

  • Texas Roadhouse (2 branches)
  • TGI Fridays (6 branches)
  • Gordon Biersch (4 branches)

The deals usually include discounted menu items or combo meal/drink deals. While these deals can be good value, it's worth noting that these restaurants tend to be on the pricier side. However, the quality of the food, including both savoury and sweet dishes, is generally excellent.

One particularly unique TGI Fridays can be found in the Breeze Songgao mall in Xinyi, which has a retro style and serves different food from other branches. There is also a nice Texas Roadhouse located next to this. Another TGI Fridays branch, which has outdoor seating, can be found near the City Hall MRT station.

Hip Restaurant Chains

For vegetarians, Miacucina has several branches in Taipei and has probably the most extensive vegetarian menu found anywhere. This includes Open Sandwiches, Soups, Mini Platters, Salads, 'Budda' Bowls, Pasta, Burgers, Panini and Flatbreads. All the branches are modern-looking and nice places to dine.

Toasteria have two branches, one next to Yongkang Street and one in the heart of the Daan district, and an equally large menu including Panini, Pasta, Arabic (hummus/pitta, shakshuka), Cheese Tables and Salads.

Gonna is a cool Mediterranean restaurant with a large menu consisting of healthy and not-so-healthy meals, categorised as Greens & Grains, Good Protein, Panini & Burger, Hearty Pasta and Snacks.

Finally, The Diner serves breakfast, brunch and lunch meals all day and makes some of the best burgers in Taipei. There are 3 branches found in Taipei.

All these restaurants have extensive drinks menus, including a large wine list.

Fast Food

Apart from the usual western fast food chains such as McDonalds, Burger King and KFC, there are some decent Japanese fast food restaurants including Mos Burger, which has some burger buns made from compacted rice instead of bread.

If you're in the mood for hot dogs, Jimmy's Hotdog offers a variety of hot dogs that can be purchased individually or as part of a meal deal.

Din Tai Fung

Taiwan's own Din Tai Fung has a few branches in Taipei, although these can all get very busy. However, lunchtimes are normally much less crowded than dinner, so it's a good opportunity to sample some of their exquisite dishes including their famous xiaolongbao.

You can view the waiting times for each branch on their website, which I would advise doing before you visit one - see my post for further details.

Click here to read more about Din Tai Fung

Klook.com

Pub Lunch

If you're seeking some pub grub, I would recommend checking out:

Brass Monkey's menu is extensive and varied, and the food here is well-portioned and usually excellent.

Buffet Lunch

Eatogether offers a buffet-style dining experience where customers can choose from a variety of dishes including appetizers, main courses, sides, and desserts.

With multiple locations around the city, they offer a range of cuisines including international and local options, so it's a good choice for those with big appetites or for people who want to try a variety of dishes.

Vouchers for these can be purchased on Klook for either weekdays or weekends (which cost slightly more) with dining hours between 11:30-14:00.

Klook.com

IKEA Canteen

Whenever I'm craving some western food but don't want to pay a small fortune, the IKEA canteen is usually my first port-of-call.

Much like any IKEA found throughout the world, the canteen serves a variety of western-style dishes including their famously delicious Swedish meatballs.

Prices here are in-line with western IKEAs and there are plenty of seating and standing options, although it can become rather crowded during peak lunch hours, especially at the weekend.

Worth being clear that this one is for expats rather than visitors. If you are in Taipei for a week, spend the meal on Taiwanese food instead – this earns its place for anyone living here who occasionally wants something familiar and cheap.

Local Places

Lunch is a good time to visit some of the more popular local restaurants in Taipei, since they're generally less busy then.

Jin Feng Braised Pork Rice is one of the most popular in the city, since their Braised Pork Rice dishes, vegetables, tofu and soups are all delicious.

Yong Kang Beef Noodles, found near the famous Yongkang Street, is usually much less busy for lunch than dinner, and offers many dishes including their famous beef noodles.

Finally, Ay Chung Flour Rice Noodles is a very popular food stand in Ximending which serves wet bowls of rice noodles mixed with pig intestines, which tastes much nicer than they sound.

title: The Best Expat Bars in Taipei (Happy Hour Times Included)
excerpt: Whether you're in need of a refreshing pint or some western food, these are some of the best western style bars in Taipei.
content:
Whether you want to socialise or simply enjoy a nice quiet pint, Taipei has some great expat bars to choose from. If you're looking to enjoy some western-style ales or food, or prefer to sample some of Taiwan's best craft ales, these are some of the best expat bars in Taipei. Happy hour times and prices included below.

Click here to see all my 'best of' lists

On Tap

The most authentic English bar in Taipei, On Tap has a huge range of food and drink, whilst boasting the largest number of screens in Taipei showing live sporting events. The basement has a free pool table and dart boards, and there's plenty of outdoor seating available - if you can bear the humidity. The clientele at On Tap is a good mix of locals, expats and holiday makers, and the atmosphere here is usually very lively.

Happy Hour

Mon-Fri from 17:00 - 20:00
Sat-Sun from 14:00 - 20:00
Includes draft ales and ciders for NT$150 and bottles for NT$100

Best For

  • Live Sport
  • Cheap Drinks
  • Atmosphere

Click here to read more about On Tap

Revolver

Located close to the Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall, Revolver is a small but great place to enjoy a pint or two. With a music venue upstairs hosting some quality alternative bands, many people will come here to drink and socialise in the street outside the venue. It's extremely popular with expats, who flock here to enjoy a craft ale or take advantage of Revolver's amazing happy hour deals - probably the cheapest drinks in Taipei!

Happy Hour

18:30 - 21:30 every day
Some pints, bottles and basic cocktails for only NT$80

Best For

  • Cheap Drinks
  • Socialising
  • Live Music

Click here to read more about Revolver

The Brass Monkey

A popular bar in the north of Taipei, The Brass Monkey is an American-style bar which serves some well-portioned western food, real ales and great cocktails too. It also has many screens showing live sport, with a large projector and pool table in the back room. The Brass Monkey is a popular destination for expats and business people.

Happy Hour

11:00 - 20:00 every day
Many draft ales, bottles and spirits from NT$100
Further reductions between 17:00 and 18:00

Best For

  • Live Sport
  • Food
  • Happy Hour

Click here to read more about The Brass Monkey

The Three Lions Inn

Co-owned by the people behind On Tap, The Three Lions Inn is situated within Maji Square, an outdoor covered area found in the Taipei Expo Park. With many outdoor seats, this English-style pub serves much the same food and drink as On Tap and has some nice happy hour deals during the day.

Happy Hour

Mon to Fri from 11:30 – 19:00
Sat & Sun (inc. national holidays) from 11:30 – 18:00

Carlsberg draft 500ml for NT$145; many spirits, bottles and wines for NT$100.

Best For

  • Outdoor Seating
  • English Ales

Click here to read more about The Three Lions Inn

Driftwood

Located within the very hipster Papa Whale hotel in Ximending, Driftwood is one of three Taihu bars serving their own unique brand of craft ales. While the Taihu Craft Ale Tasting Room bar has a larger selection of ales and better food, Driftwood generally attracts a more western crowd of expats and holiday makers due to it's beach-hut style interiors.

Happy Hour

Mon to Fri from 17:00 - 21:00

Buy 2 beers, get the third free

Best For

  • Vibe
  • Craft Ales

Click here to read more about Driftwood

Beer Geek

The Beer Geek micro-pub is a friendly and cosy bar that's a little out of the way but definitely worth seeking out. Serving a good selection of Taiwanese and international ales, and some great comforting food, Beer Geek has a darts board and video game machine and shows some live Premiership Football games too.

Happy Hour

18:00 - 20:00 every day
Includes Taiwan 18 day tap lager for NT$100; house cocktails for NT$150

Best For

  • Craft Ales
  • Friendly Service

Click here to read more about Beer Geek

Locations

Click here to see some more of the best bars in Taipei

title: Best Western Restaurants in Taipei
excerpt: The best restaurants that serve western-style food in Taipei
content:
If you're searching for some western-style cuisine, Taipei has some great restaurants serving many dishes you've probably missed – from Mediterranean to American brewpub fare.

Gonna

Now with three city branches, Gonna describes itself as a Mediterranean restaurant and has a large menu of mainly healthy dishes. Their salad and pasta dishes are some of the best we've tried, and the dining environment has a great modern/urban feel to it.

Click here to read more about Gonna

Toasteria

Offering a wide variety of western (and some middle-eastern) cuisine, Toasteria has a meal for any time of the day. With two branches to choose from (Dongmen/Yongkang Street and Fuxing), the Dongmen branch is the nicer of the two – a three-floor space, much bigger than the Fuxing location – but both serve up some memorable dishes.

Click here to read more about Toasteria

The Diner

Although many people come to The Diner to enjoy some of the best brunches in Taipei, their huge menu has meals for any time of the day. It's the oldest western-style brunch spot in the city, with the original branch in Da'an since joined by others in Xinyi and Nangang (plus a fourth all the way out in Hsinchu City). With some very well portioned dishes that will satisfy most people's hunger, The Diner shouldn't be overlooked.

Click here to read more about The Diner

Gordon Biersch

A German-inspired American restaurant chain originally from California, Gordon Biersch have four branches found around the city, which serve some of the best western food in Taipei along with some fine craft ales and deliciously indulgent desserts.

Click here to read more about Gordon Biersch
