title: Taipei Fun Pass: What's Included & Is It Worth It?
excerpt: Explore Taipei like a local with the Taipei Fun Pass. Enjoy unlimited access to top attractions, convenient transportation, and exclusive discounts
content:
If you're coming to Taipei to see many of the top attractions, a Taipei Fun Pass is a great option.

💡 The Quick Verdict: Is the Fun Pass Worth It?

  • Doing Taipei 101, the National Palace Museum and the Maokong Gondola, plus riding transport a lot? The Unlimited pass covers free entry to 30+ attractions, unlimited MRT, bus and Tourist Shuttle travel, and a set of free local experiences - it can pay for itself in a single day.
  • Travelling with children? There's a cheaper Child version of the Unlimited pass, which is easy to miss.
  • Skipping Taipei 101 and happy to pay your own fares? The Exploring pass covers 20+ museums, parks and family attractions for a fraction of the price, and doubles as an EasyCard.
  • Only after cheap transport? Get a regular EasyCard or TPASS instead - the Transport pass only wins if you're using the Tourist Shuttle Buses.

Click link to go to the appropriate section on this page.

What is a Taipei Fun Pass?

A Taipei Fun Pass is a contactless smartcard with three variations, offering free entry to many top attractions both in and around Taipei.

Two of the Fun Pass types include free use of public transport, which include the tourist shuttle buses that travel to attractions outside of Taipei.

All of them also include discounts for many shops, restaurants and other attractions.

The passes now stretch well beyond Taipei itself – between them they cover attractions in Taipei, New Taipei, Keelung and Taoyuan.

Taipei Fun Pass Types

Here's how the three types compare:

The Unlimited pass is the only one that includes Taipei 101 Observatory, the National Palace Museum and free public transport. Almost everything else – including the Maokong Gondola, which used to be Unlimited-only – is now on the Exploring pass too.

These can be purchased for use during a fixed number of days:

Prices checked August 2026. The Unlimited pass is often sold below its NT$1,500–2,200 list price, so check before assuming the higher figure.

Taipei Fun Passes can be ordered online and collected in Taipei or at the airport. See Useful Information below for the full list of pick-up points.

Unlimited Fun Pass

The Unlimited Fun Pass offers substantial savings if you intend to visit most of the attractions available (see below for complete list). The official line-up is valued at NT$7,150 for the 1-day pass, NT$7,780 for 2 days and NT$8,410 for 3 days – so against a NT$2,000 three-day pass, visiting even a third of the list puts you ahead.

Realistically, doing Taipei 101 (NT$600), the National Palace Museum (NT$350) and the Maokong Gondola (NT$300) alone comes to NT$1,250, and that's before a single MRT fare.

Travelling with children? There's a Child version at NT$1,100, NT$1,500 and NT$1,700 for 1, 2 and 3 days – roughly NT$200–300 less than the adult card. It's easy to miss on the booking page.

The age bands are strict:

  • Ages 6–11 – buy the Child pass. Bring your child's passport, as staff do ask for proof of age
  • Ages 12 and over – full Adult pass, no discount
  • Under 6 – no pass needed at all. Children under 6 (or under 115cm) travel free on the MRT and city buses when they're with a fare-paying adult, and most of the attractions on the list let them in free too

The free travel isn't unlimited per adult, mind – on city buses each paying adult can take two children free, and on the MRT up to four. So a family of two adults and three small children is covered either way.

One quirk worth knowing: the child card doesn't always work the same way at the gate. At the National Palace Museum you collect a paper ticket at the counter rather than tapping in, and at several museums staff scan the card manually after checking ID.

Klook.com

Click here to order the Unlimited Taipei Fun Pass on Klook

Exploring Fun Pass

The Exploring Fun Pass leaves out the two most expensive attractions – Taipei 101 Observatory and the National Palace Museum – and doesn't include any free travel. What it does cover is 20+ museums, galleries, parks and family attractions across Taipei, New Taipei, Keelung and Taoyuan, including the Maokong Gondola and Taipei Zoo. The line-up is valued at NT$5,230, so a 4-day pass works out at around NT$263 a day.

This is the one I'd point families and museum-lovers towards. It also arrives as a special-edition EasyCard that you can top up and keep using afterwards on the MRT, buses and in convenience stores.

Click here to order the Exploring Fun Pass on Klook

Transport Fun Pass

I would only recommend the Transport Fun Pass if you plan on travelling a lot, while also making use of the Tourist Shuttle Buses. Otherwise, getting an EasyCard will work out cheaper.

Note: Calendar-Day vs. Hourly Passes: The Transport Fun Pass is a calendar-day pass (it expires at midnight on the final day, regardless of what time you first tap). If you are arriving late in the day, you should instead consider the Taipei MRT 24h/48h/72h Travel Passes, which run on a rolling hourly basis from your first tap.

Unlike the Exploring pass, this one is not an EasyCard – it can't be topped up and carries no stored value.

Klook.com

Click here to order the Transport Fun Pass on Klook

Click here to order the Hourly Taipei MRT (24h/48h/72h) Travel Pass on Klook

If Klook is out of the length you want, all four durations are sold directly on the official Fun Pass site.

Taipei Fun Pass Attractions

The attractions covered by each card are listed below. I've separated them into 3 sections for each area:

  • Taipei City - Found in the centre or within a few stops, and easily accessible by bus or MRT
  • New Taipei City - Outside the city, but still reachable on the MRT or a short train ride
  • Beyond the City - Needs a Tourist Shuttle Bus or the Pingxi railway line. See this section for more information

Click here to see everywhere the Fun Pass gets you in for free, or click any attraction in the tables below to read about it on its own.

Taipei City

New Taipei City

* Also requires a ferry ride to Bali District from Tamsui

Beyond the City

** Daxi Tea Factory, Tomita Garden Farm, Hengshan Calligraphy Art Center and Shu Shin Bou KIRIGAKURE. Exploring cardholders also get a discount at Xpark and Window on World.

Free Experiences & Souvenirs

This is the part of the Unlimited pass that most guides miss, and it's genuinely good value. As well as the attractions, the card gets you seven free local experiences – each one would normally be a paid activity:

  • Dadaocheng FunLAB – decorate your own Taiwanese gaji tote bag, plus a voucher for small gifts at 10 shops around Dadaocheng
  • Pingxi four-colour sky lantern – including a set of blessing stickers, at Shifen Old Street
  • Jiufen red lantern blessing – a lucky lantern and blessing card
  • Jiufen A-Po's taro balls – the four-generation shop on Jishan Street
  • Maokong tea-sealing – write a letter and seal it with tea, at the Red Wooden House
  • A pineapple cake or taro pastry from Master A-Tsung, redeemable at Taipei Main Station or the Yongkang store
  • Beitou Marshal Zen Garden foot bath – white sulphur springs at Zhang Xueliang's former residence, with garden access

You also get a free set of two "Taiwan LONG HO" night market glasses, collected from the Ximending Visitor Center or Dadaocheng FunLAB.

Careful: redeeming the glasses or the pineapple cake counts as activating your card. Don't pick them up on the day you land unless you intend to start using the pass.

Other Discounts

All of the Fun Passes will also get you discounts or free items for certain purchases.

The types of places that have these deals include:

  • Restaurants
  • Gift shops
  • Massages & Spas
  • Museums & Theatre
  • Hotels

There are also gift bags for the Dadaocheng, Yongkang, Maokong and Ximending shopping districts, and discounts at the Ever Rich duty free store in Neihu.

Click here for a list/map of the stores participating in this scheme

Tourist Shuttle Buses & the Pingxi Line

The Unlimited and Transport Fun Passes both include unlimited rides on six popular Tourist Shuttle Bus routes running from Taipei to the north and north-east of Taiwan – scenic spots like Yehliu Geopark, Jiufen, Pingxi and Yangmingshan.

The newest of the six, the Jiufen–Jinguashi (965) route, is the useful one: it runs direct from Ximen and gets you to Jiufen Old Street and the Gold Museum without changing at Ruifang. The stop is about 160m from Exit 2 of Ximen MRT.

The Unlimited pass also now includes a Taiwan Railways Pingxi–Shen'ao Line one-day pass, giving unlimited rides on the branch line that serves Shifen and Pingxi – the sky lantern villages. Present the card at the ticket exchange machine in the main hall of Ruifang Station to swap it for a paper ticket first.

Click here for my full guide on Tourist Shuttle Buses, including all the routes, a map, and how to combine them.

Pairing It with the Sightseeing Bus

Worth being clear first: the Taipei Double-Decker Sightseeing Bus is not included in any Fun Pass. That's a separate ticket. The free travel you get covers the MRT, city buses and the Taiwan Tourist Shuttle only.

That said, the two make an unusually good combination. The sightseeing bus stops directly outside Taipei 101, the National Palace Museum, the Shilin Residence and the Fine Arts Museum – NT$1,080 of admissions, all four of them free on the Unlimited pass. The bus handles the awkward journeys (the Palace Museum in particular, which is a nuisance to reach otherwise), and the pass handles the ticket queues.

See my full sightseeing bus guide for both routes, the stop-by-stop timetable and the discounted ticket prices.

Useful Information

  • Download this very useful PDF file, with information about each attraction, suggested itineraries and maps
  • Taipei Fun Passes are valid for the number of days after first use. E.g. a 2-day fun pass will be valid on the first day of use and the next day until midnight. So make sure you first use it early in the day!
  • The pass is not registered to you. There's no deposit, and if you lose it there's no way to cancel or replace it
  • The Unlimited and Transport cards are not EasyCards – they can't be topped up or used to pay for anything. Only the Exploring pass includes a top-up-able EasyCard
  • Free transport excludes the Airport MRT, the light rail (LRT) lines, four-digit highway coaches and Taipei City shuttle services

title: Take a Grand Tour of the Presidential Palace
excerpt: Free tours of the Presidential Palace on weekend mornings, plus the annual full-access open days. Bring your passport — here is what to expect.
content:
The Presidential Palace is partially open to the public on weekend mornings. It is fully open (and the Taipei Guest House) on certain dates each year - see Opening Hours section below.

You will need to bring your passport the gain entry to the building.

Although the front exterior is currently undergoing some extensive renovation, it still looks grand. You'll need to walk towards the rear to access to the building.

After going through a thorough security check, you'll gain entry to the impressive baroque style building.

Access is restricted largely to two floors. You'll begin in the main hallway and work your way through to the reception hall. With only a select few presidential rooms view-able, it's a shame you can't get to see more.

You'll then make your way to the ground floor where there are some exhibitions. To celebrate the 100th anniversary of the building, they've commissioned an exhibition called 'Power to the People', which focuses on the relationship between the building and the people.

Further exhibitions show the history of the building, while you're free to explore the courtyards, gift shops and small markets. During some of the weekend openings, they'll also have some live music performances.

To mark the 100 year anniversary, a spectacular projection and light display was commissioned by the government. It is also tradition for people to visit the building early on New Year's Day, when they'll be a ceremony and will then open to the public.

The Presidential Office Building is undoubtedly the most impressive out of all the grand buildings in the Zhongzheng district of Taipei. With it's very limited full opening hours, you'll need to be lucky to visit it however.

Why not see it as part of a route I've devised?

Pros

  • Presidential rooms very grand

Cons

  • Only a few rooms open to the public
  • Only fully open a few days each year

Opening Hours

Partially open Monday to Friday between 09:00 and 12:00. Last entry 11:30
(I'm not exactly sure what partially open means)

Price

Free

Traveller Tips

You will need to bring your passport to gain entry and your bags will be searched upon entry.

The Taipei Guest House is also open on the same weekend dates, located within walking distance.

Presidential Palace Location

📍 Closest MRT: NTU Hospital (red line - exit 1)

title: Taipei Guest House - Beautifully Baroque
excerpt: A Baroque former residence for Japanese diplomats, open to the public only a handful of days each year. When those dates fall and what to see.
content:
Note that the Taipei Guest House is only open a few days each year (see Opening Hours below for dates)

The Taipei Guest House is a Western style building constructed at the turn of last century that was used to house Japanese diplomats and officials. It has since been declared a national historic building and was opened to the public in 2006.

You can gain special permission to visit the Guest House if you need to do research. However, for most people you only have a few days each year to see it. It's open on the same dates as the Presidential Building located just 10 minutes walk away, so it's definitely worth visiting both.

The furnishings within the Guest House have been restored with great care, with the Victorian fireplaces originally imported from the United Kingdom. Some rooms are restricted to viewing from the doorway to avoid wearing down the beautiful rugs.

The Japanese style garden and pond at the rear of the building are beautifully well kept, featuring a pavilion, stone tables, and masonry bridges, although access is restricted to only a few places here.

The front garden is of French baroque style, with a fountain as it's centrepiece.

The Guest House building features many balconies, double columns, and arches.

With it's very limited opening days, if one of these does fall into your holiday period, then the Taipei Guest House should not be missed.

Pros

  • Interior and exterior in immaculate condition

Cons

  • Only open a few days each year

Opening Hours

Price

Free

Traveller Tips

Photos are allowed but no flash or tripods.

The Presidential Office Building is also open on the same dates, located within walking distance

Location

📍 Closest MRT: NTU Hospital (red line - exit 2)

title: Take a Stroll at Chiang Kai-Shek Shilin Residence
excerpt: Chiang Kai-Shek's former home in Shilin, with rose gardens, a chapel and acres of grounds. Opening hours, tickets and what to see.
content:
The Chiang Kai-Shek Shilin Residence was the home to former military leader of Taiwan until his death in 1975.

Located in the Shilin district of Taipei, the residence is surrounded by many acres of pristine gardens and out-buildings, all of which are free to walk around.

The main house is the only building requiring entry cost. This is a strictly no camera zone, but I can assure you that it's worth the cost of entry. The air-conditioned rooms, of which there are a dozen or so, are all in immaculate condition.

The rooms are laid out as they were, and owe much more to western design than the elaborate Chinese homes of the time. The furniture, books, clothes and other items on display have been restored to almost 'as new'. The study upstairs was used to accommodate Richard Nixon during his stay in Taiwan in the 1950s.

The gardens are equally as well-kept, with some eccentric sculptures nestled within the large open spaces.

The out-buildings consist of a chapel, where Chiang Kai-shek and his wife would attend their religious services, a pavilion and a garage complete with his original Cadillac.

The main building is closed for 1.5 hours over lunch but you can still enjoy walking around the extensive gardens and out-buildings while you wait for it to open. There's also a cafe near the entrance and one near the chapel, selling drinks, snacks and ice cream.

Chiang Kai-Shek Shilin Residence is located within a 15 minute walk of the Shilin Night Market, and it's a great place to enjoy some tranquillity before entering the hustle and bustle of the night market.

Virtual Tour of Gardens

Pros

  • The residence is in exquisite condition
  • Large and beautiful gardens

Cons

  • 15 minute walk from the closest MRT station

Opening Hours

09:30 - 12:00 and 13:30 - 17:00 every day
Closed on Mondays

Price

NT$100
NT$50 for senior citizens
Gardens and out-buildings are free

You could also purchase a ticket for Klook to avoid queuing, plus there is an option to buy a combo ticket which includes entry to the National Palace Museum (also located in Shilin) for NT$450

Klook.com

Traveller Tips

The residence is closed for 1.5 hours during lunch. However, the gardens remain open.

If you're here in Autumn, don't miss the Shilin Residence Chrysanthemum Show. The gardens will be in full bloom, with many flower arrangements, street artists performances, music performances, and arts and cultural activities for you to enjoy.

Chiang Kai-Shek Shilin Residence Location

📍 Closest MRT: Shilin Station (red line - exit 2)
15 minute walk

This is also one of the stops on the Sightseeing Bus tour.

title: The Best Places to Enjoy a Fine Craft Beer
excerpt: Taiwan's taste for craft beer has become increasingly popular over the last few years, with some local breweries cropping up.
content:
Taiwan now has many local breweries producing some fine craft ales. Some have established their own tap rooms, while there are many bars and restaurants serving them. These are the best places to try some international or local craft ales.

Click here to see all my 'best of' lists

Taihu Craft Beer Tasting Room

Founded in 2013, Taihu is one of the most prolific craft ale creators in Taipei, experimenting with smoked, soured, barrel-aged and steeped brews alongside the classics. They have three taprooms in the city to promote their fine drinks, the best of which is the Taihu Craft Beer Tasting Room, found close to the Zhongxiao Fuxing MRT. They have over 20 different ales, and some great burger and bar food to go with them.

Click here to read more about Taihu Craft Beer Tasting Room

Revolver

Located just across the road from the Chiang Kai-Shek Memorial Hall and run by a British expat with a taste for obscure music, Revolver is primarily a music venue but also boasts a good selection of craft ales, including Scotland's Brewdog and Taiwan's own Taihu and 23. It doesn't look like much by day, but comes alive at night, with drinkers often spilling out onto the street. Revolver also have the best happy hour deals in Taipei, including draft craft ale for only NT$150.

Click here to read more about Revolver

23 Public

23 is a Taiwanese brewery slowly gaining prominence in the city, with a couple of nice tap rooms in Taipei, the best of which is close to the Shida Night Market. Serving mainly ales from their own brewery, there are many exotically named and tasting beers to try here.

Click here to read more about 23 Public

Locations

title: Where to Find Christmas Dinners in Taipei 2026
excerpt: Everything you need to know about Christmas dinner in Taipei this year.
content:
With many expats staying put this Christmas, and the growing popularity of celebrating the holiday in Taiwan, many restaurants, bars, hotels, and bistros are rolling out their Christmas dinners. From turkey to ham, crème brulee to cranberry, here’s everything you need to know about Christmas dinner in Taipei this year.

Watch this space for continual updates as more information becomes available.

Click here to see all my 'best of' lists

  Jump To:
  • IKEA
  • Far Eastern Plaza Hotel
  • Amba Hotel Songshan
  • The Brass Monkey
  • On Tap

IKEA

The Swedish furniture giant has been slowly adding to their variety of imported foods in their Hej! Bistro, and this year they’re offering a complete dinner set for Christmas.

The IKEA takeaway party set is for four to five people and includes honey roasted chicken, Swedish meatballs, avocado and shrimp Caesar salad, and baked chicken alfredo as mains. Sides include cheesy herb turkey sausage and French Fries, along with the chain’s famous vegetable medallions. Top it off with crème brulee and sparking apple and lingon or pear drinks.

The components of the set can be ordered separately, with other add-ons including roasted pork ribs, pork knuckle, and chicken wings. The add-ons range from NT$100 to NT$450 each.

How to order

Early bird ordering, from November 1 to November 30, costs NT$1,580. From December 1st through 28th, the set is NT$1,880.

Orders must be placed in-person at any IKEA location and paid for on the same day. Orders should be at least five days in advance from the date of pickup.

Far Eastern Plaza Hotel

This luxury hotel, located on Dunhua S. Road, is offering three takeaway box dinners through their first floor Cake Room.

The NT$4,800 roasted beef ribeye with mashed potatoes, mushrooms, and carrots in a red wine gravy is suitable for 6-8 people.

An 8-10 person feast of turkey with honey chestnut stuffing, mashed potatoes, brussels sprouts, cabbage, and a side of cranberry and gravy can be had for NT$3,480.

A glazed ham with home-style roasted potatoes, sautéed winter vegetables, pineapple gravy, and mustard makes up the 6-8 serving, NT$2,800 final box.

How to order

Orders must be placed by phone at 02 7700 3155

Amba Hotel Songshan

The Amba Hotel Songshan is offering an extensive Christmas menus as well as a buffet for diners this holiday season in the Que woodfired grill on its 17th floor.

Starting Christmas Eve, Que will offer a Christmas semi-buffet menu from 17:30 to 21:30. On the menu are unlimited starters, a seafood bar, soups and sides, dessert, soft drinks, coffee, and tea. For main dishes, enjoy lobster, prime steak, lamb chops, or Norwegian salmon.

Dinner is NT$2,200 per person for those aged 13 and up, NT$1,200 for children aged 6 to 12, and free for children under 6.

From December 19th to 23rd and 25th to 27th, Amba offers a sharing set for two. The set includes honey cranberry walnut bread, soup, salad, and a choice of roasted turkey or beef wellington. For sides, diners can choose truffle fries, roasted vegetables, or mashed potatoes. A festive Christmas tree cake tops off the meal. The set is NT$4,200 for two and available from 17:30 to 21:30.

Bringing kids? Santa will pay a visit to Amba on Christmas Eve from 20:00 to 21:00 to hand out treats for the little ones.

How to order

Reservations can be made from December 19th to 27th by calling 02 2653 2899

The Brass Monkey

The Brass Monkey will be serving Christmas Meals for just three days over the Christmas period.

You'll get everything you would expect from a yuletide meal, including turkey, sausages, mash, stuffing, a medley of vegetables (including of course brussels sprouts), along with gravy, cranberry and bread sauces.

The NT$850 price will also include a starter, dessert, and tea/coffee. For an extra NT$200 you can add two glasses of wine or two bottles of beer.

How to order

23rd to 25th December inclusive from 17:00

You will need to book at least 2 days in advance. Call 02 2547-5050

On Tap

On Tap have just released their Christmas Menu details for 2026. For only 4 days, they will be serving authentic Christmas meals.

For NT$850 you'll get the following:

  • Soup of the Day
  • Roast Turkey Dinner (including Roast Potatoes, Pigs-in-Blankets, Stuffing, Carrots, Brussels, Broccoli, Mashed Potato, Cranberry Sauce, Gravy)
  • Home-made Fruit Cake with Rum Sauce or Chocolate Brownies with Ice Cream
  • Glass of Wine or English Ale

How to order

From Thursday December 24th to Sunday December 27th inclusive.

Either email them at ontaptaipei@gmail.com, or call 02 2741-5365 after 17:00

title: Taiwan EasyCard: How to Buy, Top Up & Use It (2026)
excerpt: NT$100 from any MRT station or 7-Eleven. Still required for YouBike and simplest on buses and trains — even now that phones and bank cards work on the MRT.
content:
Whether you're visiting Taiwan for a short trip or choosing to move here, the versatile EasyCard (commonly referred to by locals as the yoyo ka 悠遊卡) is your single most important travel purchase.

💡 The Quick Verdict: EasyCard

  • Get a Standard EasyCard (NT$100): it's 100% standalone, needs no app or account, and works on the MRT, buses, YouBike, trains, and at convenience stores nationwide.
  • Your phone or bank card works at MRT gates too, but a physical EasyCard is still required for YouBike, buses, and the TPASS monthly pass - so get one regardless.
  • Buy it: at any MRT station, the airport on arrival, any convenience store (7-Eleven, FamilyMart, Hi-Life, OK Mart), or pre-order online for instant pickup.

What is an EasyCard?

An EasyCard is a contactless smartcard that you load with credit. It provides seamless tap-and-go access to Taiwan’s transit network (MRT, buses, trains, YouBike) and can be used to pay for items at convenience stores, supermarkets, taxis, and attractions across the country.

EasyCard vs TPASS 1200 vs Taipei Fun Pass (Which Pass Should You Buy?)

If you're wondering which ticket option is best for your specific itinerary, here is a quick side-by-side comparison of the most popular transport passes:

Pass Option Price Best For Included Transit
Standard EasyCard / iPASS NT$100 (card fee) + top-up Flexible, pay-as-you-go travelers or short stays (1–7 days) All Taipei MRT, Airport MRT, buses, YouBike, TRA trains, and convenience stores
TPASS 1200 Pass NT$1,200 (valid for 30 days) Longer stays of 3+ weeks with daily transit use (NT$1,200 = ~NT$40/day) Unlimited Taipei MRT, Airport MRT, local buses, TRA trains, and YouBike (first 30 mins free)
Taipei Fun Pass (Unlimited) From NT$1,300 (1-Day) to NT$2,000 (3-Day) Tourists packing high-density sightseeing and transit together Unlimited Taipei MRT, city buses, Taiwan Tourist Shuttles, and free entry to 25+ top attractions
Contactless Credit Card / Mobile Pay Standard single fare Convenient single rides without buying a physical card Taipei MRT and Taoyuan Airport MRT turnstiles (does not support buses or YouBike)

Where to Buy an EasyCard

A standard physical EasyCard costs NT$100 (card purchase fee, non-refundable). You will need to top it up with cash credit before riding.

  • Convenience stores: 7-Eleven, FamilyMart, Hi-Life and OK Mart - on practically every corner, with a rack of character-themed designs by the till. Usually the easiest option.
  • MRT stations: the information counter at any station in Taipei, Kaohsiung or Taichung, or a machine marked EasyCard Sales and Top-Up – both pictured below. The standard blue top-up machines only add credit to a card you already have.
  • At the airport on arrival: service desks and kiosks at Taoyuan Airport (Terminal 1 & Terminal 2) and Songshan Airport.
  • Pre-order online: collect at Taoyuan (TPE) or Kaohsiung (KHH) airport, so it's in your hand the moment you land.
Pre-Order EasyCard with TPE/KHH Airport Pickup on Klook

Pre-ordering also lets you pick your collection airport (Taoyuan or Kaohsiung), start with NT$200 or NT$400 already loaded, and optionally add a tourist SIM card (3 to 15 days) collected from the same counter.

One thing worth knowing: you no longer need to grab a card at the airport just to get into the city. The Airport MRT - and, since July 2026, the whole Taipei MRT network - accepts contactless bank cards and phone wallets straight at the gate. You'll still want an EasyCard before long though, as buses and YouBike don't accept contactless bank cards.

How to Top Up

You can top up your EasyCard with cash at:

  • MRT Top-Up Machines & Information Counters: Insert notes or coins at any station. The machine will display your current balance and ask how much you want to add. It accepts notes and coins.
  • Convenience Stores: Hand your card and cash to the cashier at any 7-Eleven, FamilyMart, Hi-Life, or OK Mart. Tell them how much you want to add and they'll load it instantly.

Note: EasyCard top-ups must be made with cash (NTD notes/coins). Credit cards are not accepted for reloading standard tourist EasyCard balances.

How Much Should You Load?

NT$500 is a sensible starting amount for most visitors. That covers the Airport MRT into the city (NT$160) with plenty left for several days of MRT rides, buses, and drinks or snacks at convenience stores.

There is no need to load more up front. Top-ups take seconds at any MRT machine or convenience store counter, and 7-Eleven, FamilyMart, Hi-Life and OK Mart are on almost every corner - so it is easy to add credit as you go. Over-loading is the one thing to avoid: refunding an unused balance carries an NT$20 fee, and the NT$100 card fee is non-refundable either way.

Where Can an EasyCard be Used?

In Taipei

Transport TypeNotes & Discount Info
Taipei MRTTap at turnstiles. Longer stays: 11+ rides in a calendar month earns a 5%–15% rebate, but it is credited the following month - so it only pays off if you are here beyond a single trip.
Taoyuan Airport MRTAccepted on both services - the faster Express (widely called the Airport Express) and the all-stops Commuter train.
City & Regional BusesTap upon boarding and exiting. Interchanging between MRT & bus within 1 hour earns an NT$8 transfer discount.
YouBike Public BicyclesEssential for unlocking bikes (requires linking with a valid phone number at kiosk or app).
Maokong GondolaWeekday fare discount when tapping with EasyCard.

Across Taiwan

Transit / LocationNotes
Taiwan Railways (TRA)Accepted on local and fast trains across Taiwan (10% discount for journeys under 70km). Not valid on reserved seats (Taroko/Puyuma/EMU3000).
Taiwan High Speed Rail (THSR)Not accepted with a standard EasyCard - THSR tickets must be bought separately. (Co-branded bank EasyCards work for non-reserved seats, but these are a residents-only product.)
Kaohsiung MRT & Light Rail15% discount on Kaohsiung MRT.
Taichung Metro (Green Line)Full tap-and-go access on Taichung MRT gates.
Convenience Stores & Retail7-Eleven, FamilyMart, Hi-Life, OK Mart, Carrefour, PX Mart, Starbucks, and 10,000+ shops.
Sightseeing & AmenitiesMuseums, Taipei Zoo, MRT station lockers, vending machines, and car parks.

Can I Just Use My Phone or Bank Card?

New Feature: Both Taipei Metro and Taoyuan Airport MRT gates now take payment straight from a card or phone - Visa, Mastercard and JCB on both systems, plus Discover and Diners Club on the Taipei Metro and UnionPay on the Airport MRT, along with Apple Pay, Google Pay and Samsung Pay. QR-code wallets such as Line Pay, TWQR and iPass Money are also accepted on the Metro and on city buses.

While you can now tap straight through those gates with your phone or a contactless bank card, we still strongly recommend getting a physical EasyCard for your trip. Here is why:

  • YouBike Rentals: YouBike 2.0 stations require a physical EasyCard/iPASS linked to your account. Credit cards are not supported at standard YouBike docks.
  • Buses & Convenience Stores: Physical EasyCards work universally on all city buses, intercity coaches, and small shops.
  • TPASS Monthly Pass: If you buy a TPASS commuter pass, it must be loaded onto a physical EasyCard.

Refunds, Card Validity & Reactivation

Any remaining cash balance on your EasyCard can be refunded at MRT Information Desks (a small NT$20 processing fee applies). However, the initial NT$100 card purchase fee is non-refundable.

Pro Tip: Instead of paying a refund fee, simply spend down any remaining balance at a 7-Eleven or airport shop before flying home!

Card Validity & Free Reactivation

EasyCards do not expire for 20 years. If your card has been unused for several years and appears locked, you do not need to buy a new one—simply tapping it at any MRT station ticket machine or 7-Eleven cashier will reactivate it instantly for free.

Emergency Overdraft (-NT$60 Grace Limit)

What happens if your card balance is only NT$5, but your MRT or bus fare is NT$25?

The EasyCard system has a built-in emergency grace overdraft of up to -NT$60. The turnstile gate will still let you exit smoothly, and your card balance will display -NT$20. This prevents travelers from getting stranded behind gates if they run a few NTD short! The negative balance will simply be deducted automatically the next time you top up with cash.

TPASS 1200 Regional Monthly Pass

If you are staying in Northern Taiwan for 3 weeks or longer, the TPASS 1200 regional monthly pass (also called the "Megacity Pass") is a great deal. For NT$1,200, you get 30 consecutive days of unlimited rides on the Taipei MRT, Taoyuan Airport MRT, TRA local trains, city buses across Taipei/New Taipei/Keelung/Taoyuan, plus 30 minutes free on YouBikes in the same region.

Who Can Buy It?

You can purchase TPASS using a standard or student EasyCard (regular full-fare cards only — not concession cards like senior or charity cards). Tourist travelers can buy TPASS on a standard EasyCard just like anyone else.

Important: Most regions (including the Northern/Taipei version) require your EasyCard to be registered (記名) to your name before you load the pass. If your EasyCard is anonymous/unregistered, you'll need to register it first — this takes 5 minutes at an MRT station service desk or online on the EasyCard website.

How to Buy and Load It

You have three main options, though only the first two are open to short-term visitors:

  • FamilyMart FamiPort Kiosk (easiest for visitors) — Go to any FamilyMart convenience store (there are thousands across Taiwan) and use the red FamiPort machine. Select "交通票證" (Transportation Tickets), then "TPASS通勤月票", then follow the on-screen prompts to select the Northern Taiwan region and pay.
  • MRT Station Service Desk — Visit a Taipei Metro or Taoyuan Metro service window during opening hours, show them your EasyCard, and ask them to load TPASS 1200. Staff will charge your card and activate it on the spot. Useful if you would rather have staff confirm it worked.
  • EasyWallet App — residents only — If you have a phone that supports mobile NFC (most smartphones do), download the "EasyWallet" app, link your EasyCard, and purchase TPASS directly in the app anytime, anywhere. The app will deduct NT$1,200 from your card's balance and activate the pass instantly. However, registering the app requires a Taiwanese ID or ARC, so short-term visitors cannot use it - use one of the two options above instead.

Activation

Once you've purchased it, you must activate the pass within 30 days by tapping your EasyCard on any MRT gate, bus validator, or station payment terminal. After that, it's live for the next 30 consecutive days.

Is TPASS Worth It?

TPASS makes sense if you're staying 3+ weeks and using public transit daily. For shorter trips or lighter transit use, an EasyCard with top-up credit is more flexible — you only pay for what you use and don't have to commit to 30 days upfront.

iPASS & icash 2.0 Interoperability

In addition to the EasyCard, you may see iPASS (popular in Kaohsiung/Southern Taiwan) or icash 2.0 (by 7-Eleven) for sale. Today, all three major cards are 99% interchangeable across Taipei Metro, TRA trains, buses, and YouBikes. If you accidentally purchase an iPASS at the airport, it will work seamlessly in Taipei as well!

Standard EasyCard vs EasyCard SuperCard

You may also see the EasyCard SuperCard (悠遊超級卡, NT$150) on sale. It adds mobile NFC top-ups, but only once linked to an EasyWallet account with a Taiwanese ID or ARC - so it's really only useful for residents, not visiting tourists.

Tourist Recommendation: Buy the Standard EasyCard (NT$100). No apps or registration needed - just buy it, top up with cash, and go.

3D Novelty & Souvenir EasyCards

EasyCards aren't just flat plastic cards! In Taiwan, 7-Eleven, FamilyMart, and airport convenience stores sell iconic 3D novelty EasyCards.

These come in fun shapes—including boba tea cups, Taiwan Beer cans, Pokébólls, anime wands, Sailor Moon keychains, and local food items (costing around NT$300–NT$500). They function identically to standard EasyCards on public transit and make fantastic, practical souvenirs to take home!

title: Discover Taipei in 2026: Your Ultimate Travel Guide
excerpt: Plan your dream trip to Taipei with this in-depth guide.
content:
The capital city of Taiwan, Taipei is a city that's often overlooked by travellers touring the Asian region, but it's one that definitely deserves a visit.

A haven for food, with many Night Markets packed with delicious food stalls, it also has unmissable attractions such as the iconic Taipei 101, the staggering Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall, and the National Palace Museum, which contains the largest collection of ancient Chinese artefacts in the world.

The city of Taipei, where the main bulk of the attractions are, is just a few kilometres across, so you don't need to travel far to experience most things. The fast and reliable MRT system also extends further to New Taipei City, so you can easily escape the confounds of the city centre to experience more rural parts.

Before You Arrive: Quick Checklist

  • Check your visa status - most nationalities can enter visa-free for up to 90 days, but confirm yours and what's needed. Visa & Entry Requirements
  • Fill in your Online Arrival Card - now required before flying instead of a paper form on the plane. How to fill it in
  • Pre-order a SIM card or eSIM - usually cheaper than buying on arrival, and you land already connected. SIM Card guide
  • Consider pre-ordering an EasyCard - skip the queue at the airport, and it can be bundled with your SIM for extra savings. EasyCard guide
  • Decide where to stay - the best area depends on whether you're shopping, travelling with family, or after nightlife. Where to Stay
  • Sketch out an itinerary - even a rough plan saves you criss-crossing the city. 1 Day Itineraries / 3-5 Day Itineraries
  • Book ahead for the busiest restaurants - places like RAW get booked out weeks in advance, so reserve before you land if there's somewhere specific you want to eat.

What are Taiwanese People Like?

Taipei is the safest capital city I have ever visited. In the four years I've lived here, I've never encountered any trouble. The people here are generally warm, friendly and helpful.

Even though Taiwan's population are mainly of Chinese ethnicity, they actually bear a closer resemblance to their neighbour Japan. Much like the Japanese, many Taiwanese people are reserved and courteous, and will go out of their way to help you.

Is English Spoken in Taiwan?

Chinese is the most widely spoken language in Taiwan, although the further south you go, they'll tend to speak more Taiwanese.

English is taught in most schools, and there are many cram schools dedicated to teaching English. The younger population have a better grasp of English than the older generation.

Local restaurants and shops will often not speak much English but larger shops and restaurant chains will usually be able to understand English.

Almost all signs are translated to English however, and their underground system (MRT) is all translated, as are the announcements on the MRT and buses.

If you do not speak Mandarin Chinese, it may be helpful to bring a phrasebook or download a translation app to help you communicate during your visit to Taiwan. You could also try some guided tours to some of Taipei's top attractions and night markets.

How Crowded is Taipei?

Taipei has a population of around 2.7 million people.

It's a busy city, especially during commuting times and on weekends but it doesn't get nearly as crowded as places such as Hong Kong.

Taipei Main Station gets especially busy during peak times, so expect to queue for trains here, and expect to be crammed into carriages.

There are many parks and other more peaceful areas you can use to escape from the busy streets.

Weather in Taipei

December to March

The coldest time of year, this period is also the driest. When the sun is out, the temperature is actually very pleasant (mid 20s Celsius) but when it rains the temperature can drop to single figures. This is the best time to visit if you want to avoid rain but don't mind being chilly some days.

April to May / October to November

Spring and Autumn periods can vary from very hot to quite chilly. One day you'll find it quite humid, while other days you'll need a jumper or coat. If you can't bear the intense heat of the summer, these months are probably your best bet as they can be very nice. You can also expect extended periods of rain.

June to September

Being in a subtropical climate, Taipei can get very hot and humid in the summer, with temperatures in the low 40s not out of the question. There can also be spells of rain lasting days.

There's also a risk of typhoons, with generally 3 to 5 affecting Taiwan each year (though usually only 1 or 2 make direct landfall). The eye of the storm will pass in a few hours, but during this time you'll be stranded in your hotel, and most places will close down for a day or sometimes two days.

If it is raining, I have a post on places you can visit.

Air Pollution in Taipei

For a capital city, the pollution in Taipei isn't too bad.

My girlfriend is generally very sensitive to high levels of pollution, and suffers in Hong Kong. In Taipei however, she is fine, and the air never looks or smells bad.

Plugs In Taiwan

Taiwan uses the same plug sockets as the US and Canada: 110V, 60Hz AC.

If you are travelling from Europe, Australia or Southeast Asia, you'll need to bring or buy an adaptor.

The following plugs are used:

You'll only need an adaptor for Type A, as these will also fit into Type B (but not the other way round).

Visa Requirements & Entry

Most visitors don't need a visa at all – passport holders from a large number of countries, including the US, UK, most of the EU, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Japan and South Korea, can currently enter visa-free for up to 90 days. A smaller number of nationalities get shorter visa-free stays (commonly 14 or 30 days), and everyone now completes an online arrival card before flying rather than a paper form on the plane.

Since 1 October 2025, Taiwan no longer hands out paper arrival cards on the plane. Every visitor now submits a Taiwan Arrival Card (TWAC) online instead – ideally in the 7 days before you fly, though you can also do it at an airport kiosk or on your phone in the immigration queue if you forget. Filling it in beforehand means walking straight up to the desk instead of filling in a form on your phone in the arrivals hall.

See my full guide below for more details.

Click here to read my full Taiwan Visa & Entry Requirements guide

SIM Cards and Network coverage

Taipei has very good network coverage and has very fast connection speeds.

Your best option is getting an eSIM before you fly – it's usually the cheapest choice and you're connected the moment you land. Otherwise, you can pick up a pre-paid SIM card directly from either airport. There are deals in the city but they're generally not as good and harder to find.

Taiwan has three network operators – Chunghwa Telecom, Taiwan Mobile and FarEasTone (T Star has since merged into Taiwan Mobile) – with Chunghwa Telecom having the best coverage in more rural areas, although all networks are fine for Taipei.

See my Pre-paid SIM Card page for a full comparison of all SIM Cards in Taipei.

Money, Cards and Budget

The local currency is the New Taiwan Dollar (NT$100 is roughly USD$3.23). Taipei is cheap for a capital city - noticeably cheaper than Hong Kong, Singapore or Tokyo. Expect NT$3,000–5,000 per person per day including a mid-range hotel, or around NT$1,200–1,800 in a hostel eating at night markets. Accommodation is what moves that number: a hostel bed is about NT$600 a night against roughly NT$6,000 for a boutique hotel.

Credit cards work at malls and larger restaurants, but local places and night markets want cash. Cash machines are everywhere, including in most convenience stores.

You can change money at either airport, though as usual you pay slightly more for the convenience. Bank of Taiwan branches give a better rate - just note that banks in Taipei generally close at 15:30.

Click here for a full breakdown of what a trip to Taipei costs

How Long to Stay

If you just intend a quick visit to see the main attractions, then 3 or 4 days would be ample.

If you can afford more time, and maybe incorporate a day trip or two, then 1 week would be enough but there's plenty to see here for a much longer stay.

Transport Options

Get an EasyCard before you travel anywhere in Taipei - it works on the MRT, buses, YouBike and the Airport Express. An excellent alternative is the Taipei Fun Pass, which comes in three variants, two of which include free public transport plus entry to top attractions.

Taipei is served by two airports - Taoyuan, the main international gateway, connected to the city by the Airport Express, and the smaller, more central Songshan, just a few MRT stops from the centre. Once in the city, the MRT is the best way to get around, backed up by city buses, taxis, YouBikes and sightseeing buses. Heading further afield, the Taiwan High Speed Rail reaches every major city on the west coast in under 100 minutes, and Tourist Shuttle Buses cover the scenic spots the train doesn't reach.

Click here for my full guide to getting around Taipei, including both airports, the MRT, buses, YouBikes, boats, and travelling outside the city.

Where to Stay

There are several areas in Taipei that are popular with tourists and expats, each with its own distinct character and amenities.

Some of the best areas to stay in Taipei include:

  • Xinyi District: This is the modern business and financial hub of Taipei, home to the iconic Taipei 101 skyscraper. The area is known for its shopping, dining, and nightlife, as well as its convenient location near many of the city's major landmarks. Many of the best hotels in Taipei are found within this district.
  • Zhongzheng District: This is the historical and cultural centre of Taipei, home to many of the city's temples and museums. The area is more laid back and residential than Xinyi, but still has plenty of restaurants and shops, while there is some nice cheap accommodation here, including many hostels found close to Taipei Main Station. It's the best place to stay for connectivity to other areas.
  • Daan District: This is a trendy and upscale area known for its fashionable boutiques and cafes. It is also home to several universities, so the area has a youthful and energetic vibe. There are some excellent boutique hotels in this district, and great connection to other areas in Taipei.
  • Songshan District: This is a more traditional and residential area, known for its relaxed atmosphere and local markets. It is home to the Raohe Street Night Market, one of the oldest and most popular night markets in Taipei. Transportations options are more limited in this district however.
  • Wanhua District: Home to the Ximending shopping area, which is known for its street food, shopping, and nightlife. Wanhua District is a lively and vibrant part of Taipei with a rich history and culture. Ximending is also a very popular destination for the younger generation and the LGBT community.
  • Beitou District: If you would prefer to stay in a more rural setting, I would recommend staying in Beitou for a night, as the region has many hotels with natural hot springs to relax in.

For a deep-dive into the best areas and hotels to stay in during your trip, I have a post to help you out.

Ultimately, the best area to stay in Taipei will depend on your personal preferences and the purpose of your trip. If you want to be in the heart of the action, Xinyi, Wanhua or Daan might be the best choice. If you prefer a more laid-back atmosphere, Songshan or Beitou might be better options.

Which Places to Visit in Taipei

Attractions

Taipei is a city with many attractions, both cultural and modern. Here are a few places you might want to visit during your trip:

  • National Palace Museum: This museum is home to a vast collection of Chinese art and artefacts, including ceramics, jade, and bronze. It is one of the most visited museums in Taiwan and a must-see for anyone interested in Chinese history and culture.
  • Taipei 101: This beautiful skyscraper was once the tallest building in the world and remains an iconic symbol of the city. You can go to the observation deck for panoramic views of Taipei, or visit the mall at the base of the building for shopping and dining.
  • Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall: This is a national monument and popular tourist destination in Taipei, dedicated to the former President of the Republic of China. The hall features a large bronze statue of Chiang Kai-shek, as well as an exhibition on the history of the Republic of China.
  • Shilin Night Market: This is the largest and most popular night market in Taipei, known for its food stalls and shopping. You can find all kinds of street food and snacks here, as well as clothes, electronics, and other goods.
  • Temples: Taipei has dozens of temples located all over the city. Longshan Temple is one of the oldest and most beautiful, while Hsing Tian Kong Temple is one of the most sacred temples in Taiwan.
  • Creative Parks: There are 2 really cool creative parks in Taipei, with gift shops, cafes, independent cinemas and usually a few exhibitions showcasing art or design. Both Huashan 1914 Creative Park and the Songshan Cultural and Creative Park are worthy of a visit.
  • Taipei Zoo & Maokong Gondola: Taipei Zoo is one of the best zoos in Asia, while the Maokong Gondola is a fantastic cable car ride into the mountains. One of the stations for the gondola is inside the zoo.
  • Hiking: Taipei is surrounded by mountains to north and east, including Elephant Mountain and Tiger Mountain, both of which offer fantastic views of the city including Taipei 101

You will find many attractions are closed on Mondays, including some enclosures at Taipei Zoo, while many restaurants will also be closed during Monday.

Please read my Essentials Guide, for a list of all the must-see attractions. If your stay is longer, you can also see my Top Picks to go alongside the essential attractions.

If you intend on visiting many of Taipei's attractions, I would recommend purchasing a Taipei Fun Pass. This will get you free entry to many top attractions including Taipei 101 and the National Palace Museum, plus many more museums, art galleries and other attractions such as Taipei Zoo.

Click here to read my comprehensive guide on the Taipei Fun Pass

Areas

I would recommend visiting these areas, found within central Taipei and to the north:

For a full breakdown of every district in Taipei, not just these highlights, I have a dedicated guide to every area and what it's known for.

  • Ximending Youth Shopping District: One of the most vibrant areas in Taipei, this largely pedestrianised area is packed with food stalls, restaurants, bars, street art and performers.
  • Xinyi Shopping District: With 13 shopping malls, this pedestrianised, modern urban area is awash with fine restaurants and has some great nightclubs. Taipei 101 is also found here.
  • Yongkang Street: Recently voted the 4th coolest street in the world, this is a great place to try some bubble tea or shaved ice dishes, and perfect for gift shopping. The original Din Tai Fung is also located here.
  • Taipei East District: Has an abundance is cool shops, bars, cafes and restaurants found nowhere else in Taipei
  • Beitou Hot Springs: Taipei is home to several hot springs, and Beitou is the most famous and easily accessible by the MRT. You can visit one of the public baths or enjoy a relaxing soak at a private bathhouse.
  • Danshui Riverside: Another area in the northern part of New Taipei City, Danshui has a nice riverside walk with many cafes, restaurants and attractions including Fort San Domingo. You can also witness a stunning sunset here.

Alternatively, try one of my routes, taking you around places of interest in and around the Taipei area.

If you want to travel outside of the city for a few hours, there are some great day trips I would recommend,

Where to Eat & Drink in Taipei

Night Markets are your best bet to experience some traditional food and snacks.

While Shilin Night Market is the largest and has the most variety of food stalls, Raohe Night Market is arguably the best for food. If you prefer to visit a less touristic night market, then Linjiang Street Night Market has a lot to offer in terms of food.

If you want to experience some Michelin recognised food at night markets, I have a post which will help you find the locations of all of these at every night market.

To experience slightly more refined Taiwanese food, then the very popular Din Tai Fung should definitely be on your list. This world-renowned chain of restaurants originated in Taipei and is best known for its xiaolongbao (soup dumplings). You can find branches all over the city, although finding a table is sometimes difficult since Din Tai Fung do not have a table reservation service.

Read my post to find out the best way to skip the queues here

For a traditional Taiwanese breakfast, I would recommend Fu Hang Soy Milk. This local breakfast spot is known for its fresh soy milk and savoury fried dough sticks. The restaurant is always busy, but it's worth the wait for a taste of these Taiwanese favourites. If you can't face queuing an hour for breakfast, then Yong He Soy Milk King is a great alternative.

If you prefer a slightly fancier brunch, there are some nice brunch spots found around the city, including the very delicious (but very popular) Antipodean Specialty Coffee.

I would also recommend trying some beef noodle and braised pork rice dishes, both of which are very popular in Taiwan. Yong Kang Beef Noodles and Jin Feng Braised Pork Rice are the most famous and best in the city.

If you're a lover of seafood, then you should check out Addiction Aquatic Development. Taipei's largest fish market also doubles as a fantastic dining experience, with many seafood restaurants and a large grill area where you can pick your own seafood, meat and vegetables.

Vegetarians are well catered for in Taipei. Aside from the night markets, there are some excellent vegetarian and vegan restaurants.

I sometimes find that I need some respite from all the fried foods on offer, but luckily there are some nice healthier options.

Please visit the Eat pages for a full list of my favourite places to eat in Taipei.

Drink

There are hundreds of tea shops selling a large variety or hot and chilled teas, including bubble tea, the city's most famous drink, which is made with sweetened tea, milk, and chewy tapioca pearls.

Taipei is home to a thriving cafe culture, offering a wide range of options for coffee lovers and casual drinkers alike. From traditional tea houses to modern, hipster-style cafes, there's something for everyone in Taipei's cafe scene.

Visitors can enjoy a traditional Taiwanese tea ceremony in a cosy tea house, complete with beautiful teapots, intricate tea sets, and an array of teas to choose from. For coffee aficionados, Taipei has plenty of options, from independent cafes to international chains, all serving up high-quality coffee and espresso drinks. If you're on a tight budget, there are some nice cheap cafes selling espresso-based coffees for under NT$50.

If you're looking for something a bit stronger, Taipei's night markets offer an array of traditional Taiwanese liquor, such as rice wine and herbal liqueurs, made from ingredients like ginseng and goji berries.

There are also some great bars in Taipei, including expat bars with some nice happy hour deals, or you could try some of Taipei's homegrown craft ales, or cocktail bars such as the speakeasy Hanko 60.

1 Day Itineraries

Here are some ideas to help you get the most out of the day:

Click here to read more about these itineraries

  • SHOPPERS: Walk around the Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall, see some exhibitions at the Songshan Creative Park, walk through the huge Xinyi Shopping District and end with Taipei 101
  • FAMILY: Spend the day at Taipei Zoo and take the Maokong Gondola to Maokong
  • KNOWLEDGE: Go on a city guided tour, visiting historical areas, cultural landmarks or try some local cuisine
  • WEEKENDS: Visit the Flower & Jade Markets, walk through Daan Park, visit the cool Yongkang Street, see the magnificent Chiang-Kai Shek Memorial Hall
  • HASSLE-FREE: Take the Sightseeing Bus around central Taipei and on the following day visit the National Palace Museum and Shilin Night Market
  • HOT SPRINGS and SUNSET: Visit the beautiful districts of Xinbeitou and Danshui, taking in the hot springs and sunset
  • ADVENTURE: Take a day trip to one of the many beautiful scenic areas and townships within 90 minutes of Taipei
  • KIDS: Visit the Astronomical Museum, Science Education Center, Amusement Park and Shilin Night Market, all located in the same vicinity

3-5 Day Itineraries

If you're staying longer, it's worth planning day-by-day rather than winging it - Taipei's attractions cluster naturally by district, so a bit of grouping saves you from criss-crossing the city.

Click here for my full 3-5 day Taipei itinerary

Shopping & Tax Rebate

Taipei has more shopping malls than any other city I've ever been to. There are dozens scattered throughout the city, especially in the Xinyi district, where you'll find no less than 13 malls. I've compiled a list of all the best shopping malls in Taipei to help you decide.

Aside from malls, there are some other great areas for shopping, whether it's clothes, bargains, tech or gifts you're after, these are all the places I recommend visiting.

If you spend over NT$2,000 on shopping from designated places including most shopping malls, you are eligible for a 5% VAT tax rebate.

Click here for my full guide on VAT tax refunds

General Tips for Taipei

There are three items you should probably never be without.

  • Umbrella
  • Mosquito Spray
  • EasyCard

Even when it isn't raining, the Sun's rays can often be too much to bear and you can easily be caught out by a sudden rain shower out of nowhere.

Taipei isn't short on Mosquitoes, even during the winter months, so Mosquito Spray is essential!

An EasyCard is incredibly useful to get around, and can even be used to purchase goods from many shops.

If you are going to spend the day shopping, I would also recommend you take your passport with you, as you'll need this if you want to take advantage of the VAT refund scheme.

During the summer months, you'll also need sunscreen (and sunglasses)!

title: Taipei Money Guide: Costs, Cash, Cards & ATMs (2026)
excerpt: What Taipei costs per day, plus how to pay for it - cash vs card vs EasyCard, ATM fees, changing money and the tax refund. Budget from NT$1,200 a day.
content:
Taipei is one of the cheaper big cities in Asia to visit - noticeably cheaper than Hong Kong, Singapore or Tokyo. Getting around costs very little and eating well costs even less. What actually moves your budget is where you sleep.

💡 The Quick Verdict: Money in Taipei

  • Budget NT$3,000–5,000 per person per day mid-range, or NT$1,200–1,800 doing it cheaply. Accommodation is the swing factor - a hostel bed is about NT$600 against roughly NT$6,000 for a boutique hotel, while everything else varies far less.
  • Carry cash. Night market stalls, most taxis and EasyCard top-ups all want notes. Cards are fine in hotels, malls and larger restaurants, and not much below that.
  • Get an EasyCard first: NT$600 covers it - NT$100 for the card plus NT$500 of credit, enough for your first few days of transport.
  • At the ATM, decline the machine’s own currency conversion and pay in New Taiwan Dollars. Expect roughly NT$100–200 per withdrawal from the local bank, so take out larger amounts less often.

What You Will Spend Per Day

Per person, per day. Accommodation figures are for a room or bed, so a couple sharing a mid-range hotel effectively halves that line.

ItemCheapMid-rangeComfortable
Bed600 (hostel)1,500–3,000 (hotel)6,000+ (boutique)
Food300–600800–1,5002,000+
Transport120150–200200 + taxis
Attractions0–300300–600600–1,000
Drinks and snacks100400800+
Rough daily total1,200–1,8003,000–5,0009,000+

What a Real Day Looks Like

A fairly typical mid-range day, sightseeing and eating well without trying to economise:

MRT, four or five journeysNT$100–150
Breakfast and coffeeNT$120
Lunch at a local placeNT$150
Taipei 101 ObservatoryNT$600
Night market dinner with snacksNT$250
A beer, or a cocktail if you are out properlyNT$150–400
Day total, excluding your roomNT$1,400–1,700

Add accommodation on top and you can see how the daily figure lands where it does. Skip the paid attraction and eat entirely at night markets and the same day comes in under NT$700.

Rough Totals by Trip Length

Per person, including accommodation, excluding flights.

TripCheapMid-range
3 daysNT$4,000–5,500NT$9,000–15,000
5 daysNT$6,000–9,000NT$15,000–25,000
1 weekNT$8,500–12,500NT$21,000–35,000

Food and Drink

This is where Taipei is genuinely cheap, and where most visitors overestimate.

Night markets are the best value in the city. You can eat a full meal and try several snacks for about NT$150–300 per person (roughly US$5–10 / £4–8). Individual snacks and drinks run NT$30–100 each, so a night market dinner for two rarely passes NT$600 even if you graze widely.

WherePer person, per meal
Night market (full meal plus snacks)NT$150–300
Single night market snack or drinkNT$30–100
Local restaurant or mall food courtNT$100–200
Mid-range or Western restaurantNT$600–1,400
Coffee at a cheap chain or 7-ElevenNT$35–65
Coffee at a caféNT$60–85
Beer in a bar (happy hour)NT$100–150
Cocktail at a good barNT$350–500

Two people can eat properly at local places for under NT$250 together. A mid-range restaurant will be three or four times that each, so the gap between eating like a local and eating like a tourist is the single biggest lever on your food budget.

Getting In From the Airport

OptionCostTime
Airport MRTNT$160~35 min
Airport Bus (runs 24 hours)NT$125~55 min
Taxi or UberNT$1,000–1,200~45 min

The MRT is both the fastest and the cheapest, so the taxi is only worth it if you land after the MRT has stopped or you have a lot of luggage.

Getting Around

  • MRT: NT$20–65 depending on distance. Most trips within the city are NT$20–30.
  • City buses: NT$15. Exact coins only - the farebox gives no change.
  • YouBike: free for the first 30 minutes, then NT$10 per 30 minutes.
  • Taxi: NT$85 for the first 1.25km, then NT$5 per 200m.
  • Maokong Gondola: NT$180 single, NT$300 for a day pass.

Realistically that comes to NT$120–200 a day for normal sightseeing. A TPASS at NT$1,200 for 30 days only makes sense if you are staying three weeks or more - see the EasyCard guide for the comparison.

Attractions

  • Taipei 101 Observatory: NT$600, or NT$980 including floor 101.
  • Sightseeing Bus: NT$330 for 4 hours up to NT$1,100 for 48 hours.
  • Taipei Fun Pass: NT$1,300 for one day to NT$2,000 for three. Only worth it if you are visiting several paid attractions a day.

Plenty costs nothing — the memorial halls, temples, parks, night markets, hiking trails and the NTU campus are all free. See Taipei on a Budget for a fuller list.

Staying Connected

An eSIM starts at about NT$240 for 5 days; a physical SIM from an airport counter is NT$450–500 for 7 days. The SIM card guide compares every option.

Cash, Cards and Getting Tax Back

Taipei is more cash-dependent than most visitors expect. Night market stalls are almost all cash, and topping up an EasyCard means cash — card isn't accepted for tourist cards. Buses and the MRT are the easy part: just tap your EasyCard. If you do pay a bus fare in cash you need exact coins, since the farebox gives no change.

Is It Safe to Carry Cash?

Yes. Taiwan is one of the safest places you can travel, and locals routinely carry substantial amounts of cash without a second thought. Pickpocketing is rare even in packed night markets, and walking back to your hotel late at night is normal rather than a risk.

That is not an argument for carelessness. Keep your cash somewhere sensible rather than a back pocket, do not leave a bag hanging on a chair, and be a little more aware in the busiest market crowds - the same habits you would use anywhere. But you should not feel you need to ration withdrawals out of nervousness.

What Takes Cash, Card or EasyCard

Roughly what to expect. Card here means a contactless bank card or a phone wallet.

WhereCashCardEasyCard
Taipei MRTYes, tokenYesYes
Airport MRTYes, tokenYesYes
City busesYes, exact coinsQR wallets onlyYes
YouBikeNoVia the appYes
Street taxiYes, usually neededNoSometimes
UberNoYes, in the appNo
Night market stallsCash onlyRarelyRarely
Convenience storesYesYesYes
Small local eateriesYesOften notSometimes
Mid-range restaurantsYesYesUsually not
Department stores and mallsYesYesYes
HotelsYesYesNo
Topping up an EasyCardCash onlyNo–

The short version: carry cash for night markets, use your EasyCard for anything that moves, and keep a card for hotels and shopping. Some taxis take an EasyCard, but do not count on it - have notes ready.

Getting Cash Out

ATMs are everywhere, including inside every convenience store, and most accept foreign Visa and Mastercard. Bank of Taiwan, Taipei Fubon and Cathay United machines are all reliable for overseas cards.

Expect the local bank to charge somewhere around NT$100–200 per withdrawal, on top of whatever your own bank adds. The exact amount varies by bank and changes from time to time, so take out a larger sum less often rather than small amounts repeatedly.

One tip that genuinely saves money: if the machine offers to bill you in your home currency, decline and choose to be charged in New Taiwan Dollars. Letting the ATM do the conversion is almost always the worse rate.

Changing Money

Taiwan is unusual in that changing money at the airport is perfectly reasonable. Bank of Taiwan counters in both Taoyuan terminals are open 24 hours, with Mega International also open round the clock in Terminal 2, and a bank charges the same rate at its airport desk as at its city branches. There is a flat NT$30 admin fee per transaction at the airport, which city branches do not charge - so change what you need on arrival and do any larger amount in town if you would rather save the NT$30.

Getting Tax Back

If you spend NT$2,000 or more at one participating store on the same day, you can claim the 5% VAT back - worth knowing before a shopping trip. Details in the tax refund guide.

title: Over 1,500 Plant Species at Taipei Botanical Garden
excerpt: Over 1,500 plant species across 8 hectares, with a lotus pond and two museums — a quieter alternative to Daan Forest Park.
content:
If you're a lover of all things flora, the Taipei Botanical Garden is a great place to stroll around and enjoy the many species of plants here.

At over 8 hectares, the garden also features a large Lotus Pond and two museums, one of which is also a heritage building. The National Museum of History is also right next to the garden .

The Taipei Botanical Garden is divided into over 20 different sections, most of which will group plants of the same type or habitat. These include:

  • Ferns
  • Succulents
  • Bamboos
  • Australian Flora
  • Palms

Pathways have been well designed, with many taking you right into the heart of the trees or plants.

The large Lotus Pond in the south-west corner of the garden is arguably the most beautiful area. Although the lotuses weren't in flower during my visit, it still looked quite exquisite. If you come during June or July when they are in full bloom, I'm sure it would spectacular.

The Succulents area is another great section, with many different species surrounded by small streams. The small greenhouse next to this was unfortunately closed during my visit however.

The Ferns section adjacent to the succulents will allow you the get up-close-and-personal with the plants, with the paths weaving directly between them.

The Taipei climate is perfect for bamboos and palms, and there are many species of each to be found at the Taipei Botanical Garden.

Almost all of the plants are labelled with descriptions. A very neat feature is they'll label the plants which are currently 'at their best'. If you want to find out which flowers are currently in bloom at the garden, you can visit this website.

The main greenhouse is located next to the crops and forest foods was also closed during my visit. In fact, all the greenhouses here were.

There are two museums found in the Taipei Botanical Garden. The Herbarium and the Guest House of Imperial Envoys.

The former is a small museum that details the "Taiwan Plant Investigation Project", which aimed to collect, identify and preserve many different species of Taiwanese flora. It was the first project of its kind in Taiwan.

The Guest House of Imperial Envoys is a Qing Dynasty heritage building. Built in 1894 and originally located about half a kilometre north of here, it was the Governor's Office until the current Presidential Office was built in 1919.

The Taipei Botanical Garden has many other sections not detailed here. If you enjoy walking and plants, this is the perfect place to spend a couple of hours.

Just don't forget to take some mosquito spray with you!

Virtual Tour

Pros

  • Beautiful gardens
  • Usually quiet

Cons

  • Mosquitoes galore
  • Greenhouse were all closed during my visit

title: Craft Ales and Meals at Redpoint Brewing Co. Taproom (Permanently Closed)
content:
Permanent Closure Notice

Please note: Redpoint Brewing Co. Taproom has permanently closed.

Notice: Redpoint Brewing Co. Taproom has permanently closed.

Looking for great craft beer and expat pubs in Taipei? Check out our updated guides to the Best Bars in Taipei and Best Craft Beer Spots in Taipei.

Redpoint was the first American style craft beer brewery in Taiwan, and they've since opened their first Redpoint Taproom to help sell and promote their real ale range.

This bar/restaurant has only been open a few months, but it's already established itself as one of the best places for real ales and western food in Taipei.

It's usually busy here, but there are enough tables to get seated straight away. It's roomy and comfortable with a vibrant atmosphere, and a good sound system playing sophisticated music.

There are 12 taps of real ale, most with outlandish names such as the Disco Macaw or the Hazy Platypus all varying in degrees of strength and colour.

They can be purchased as half pints, pints or pitchers. If you're there before 20:00 they have a happy hour with decent discounts on most beers, around NT$20 - NT$40 depending on what you buy.

They even serve some mixed with fruit and herbs, such as pineapple and mint!

While drinks are their speciality, the Redpoint Taproom also serves some of the best western food available in Taiwan.

Their Cider Sea Bass, with two beautifully cooked fillets sitting atop of potatoes, apples and spinach, with a bed of apple cider butter is very fine.

They have a wide selection of delicious small plates, with the likes of lemon shrimp drowned in a bowl of long dong lager, garlic and pepper, with a french baguette to soak it all up .

The seared tuna tataki salad, with avocado, radish, greens and crispy onion strings, with a ginger vinaigrette was completely different to any other salad we've has in Taipei, and all the better for it.

Probably the only slight letdown were the mozzarella sticks - while they weren't bad, we've had much better.

They also serve burgers and large meat sharing plates. Their Whole Roasted Beer Can Chicken looks spectacular, and we would have gone for this instead had it not only been available during the weekend!

Their dessert menu, while only consisting of 3 items, just looked far to good to resist! We opted for the Triple Chocolate Stout Cake, which was homely and delicious, and easily big enough for 2 to share.

Redpoint Taproom is fast becoming one of our main go-to places for western food and real-ales in Taipei!

Pros

  • Some of the best western food in Taipei
  • Great selection of real ales

Cons

Price: $$$

Level of English: Excellent (English on menu)
