title: The Best Places to Appreciate Art in Taipei
excerpt: Whether you prefer contemporary or more traditional Chinese artwork, or your preference is street art, Taipei has a good variety.
content:
Whether you prefer traditional Chinese artwork, or your preference is more contemporary, Taipei has a great variety of art which can be found in galleries, parks, and around the walls and streets of the city.

Click here to see all my 'best of' lists

Fine Arts Museum

The Taipei Fine Arts Museum building is itself a work of art. Inside, there are three floors filled with both Chinese and international contemporary and modern art, and it's a bargain to enter.

Click here to read more about Fine Arts Museum

MOCA

The Museum of Contemporary Arts, located close to the Taipei Main Station, showcases modern and contemporary art-forms with a heavy emphasis on multimedia exhibitions, sometimes with a strong political or cultural message.

Click here to read more about MOCA

Ximending Street Art

Ximending district is filled with shops and food stands, but tucked away down some alleys you'll find the best street art in Taipei. I've added a map of their locations in the Ximending post to help you out.

Click here to read more about Ximending

National Palace Museum

If your preference is more traditional Chinese artwork and sculptures, then the National Palace Museum has many pieces of interest. The exquisite Jadeite Cabbage is the star of the show, but there are hundreds of pieces on show at any given time, and many thousands more held in storage until the time comes.

Click here to read more about National Palace Museum

Treasure Hill

Home to many local and international artists, Treasure Hill is a converted hillside village that has studios where you can watch the artists at work, and exhibitions showcasing their work. The many winding paths are also filled with eye-opening artwork.

Click here to read more about Treasure Hill

Sun Yat-Sen Memorial Hall

The huge shrine to The Father of the Nation also has eight galleries inside, most of them featuring temporary art and photography exhibitions. The Chungshan National Gallery is the best of these, with exhibitions from internationally renowned artists.

Click here to read more about Sun Yat-Sen Memorial Hall

Annual Art Exhibitions

If you're in Taipei during January or October, there are two huge art exhibitions featuring hundreds of artists from all over the world. Taipei Dangdai and Art Taipei should not be missed.

Click here to read more about these Art Exhibitions

Honorable Mention - Jimmy Liao

If you happen to find yourself at Nangang MRT station (not Nangang Exhibition Centre MRT), then you must check out the artwork of Jimmy Liao. Taiwan's most famous book illustrator and writer, the walls around the station are filled with his artwork.

title: Healthy Restaurants That Don't Compromise on Taste
excerpt: Looking for a healthy restaurant that doesn't compromise on taste? Here are some of the very best to be found in Taipei.
content:
Looking for a place which serves delicious food without the guilt-factor attached? Taipei has some great restaurants which serve that exact purpose, from bowl food to Mediterranean, Italian and brunch spots.

Click here to see all my 'best of' lists

Sugar Pea Cafe

Its tagline is "Wholesome, Seasonal, Simple Cuisine" – serving seasonal salads and bowls of goodness with rice, quinoa, grains or legumes as their base, Sugar Pea Cafe's dishes are healthy and fresh without compromising on the taste.

Click here to read more about the Sugar Pea Cafe

Gonna

A great Mediterranean restaurant serving a large number of healthy dishes and drinks, in a playful setting with amusing one-liners on the walls ("One Day I Am Gonna Make Onion Cry"). It started out as a single Da'an restaurant and has since expanded to three branches across the city. Their salads are some of the best in Taipei, while their smoothies go down a treat – they do also serve less healthy food such as burgers if you're feeling more indulgent.

Click here to read more about Gonna

Miacucina

Miacucina means "My Kitchen" in Italian, and with a menu that seems to go on forever, it's a great vegetarian restaurant with a few branches in Taipei – the Neihu branch especially is one of the nicest places we've dined in Taipei. While their menu does contain many not-so-healthy dishes, their healthy range, especially their fantastic Buddha Bowls, are bound to get your taste buds tingling.

Click here to read more about Miacucina

Tamed Fox

One of the best brunch spots in Taipei, Tamed Fox has some excellent yogurt bowls and other plates with a heavy emphasis on salad and vegetables. The dining area is spacious but has only a few tables, including a large sharing table, so be prepared to wait to be seated. They serve delicious vegetarian and non-vegetarian food.

Click here to read more about Tamed Fox

title: Famous Taipei Restaurants Worth Queuing For
excerpt: The most established and well known local restaurants in Taipei, all these places are definitely worth queuing for.
content:
These hugely popular local restaurants and food stands have finely-tuned their recipes over many years and established themselves as some of the best places to eat in Taipei. Having been featured in many magazines and even on TV, they are well-known throughout Taiwan.

Around the holidays, see also our guide to Christmas dinners in Taipei. However, they're very popular and thus you'll usually need to wait a while to served - I've added the best time to visit each place below.

Click here to see all my 'best of' lists

Jin Feng Braised Pork Rice

Probably the most famous local restaurant in Taipei, their braised pork rice dish is immensely popular with both the locals and tourists, although you'll need to be prepared for a long wait to get a table. If you're visiting the Chiang-Kai Shek Memorial Hall, Jin Feng is very close by so I would urge you to visit here and sample their delicious (and very cheap) dishes.

Best Time to Visit:

Weekday evenings 19:00 - 00:00

Click here to read more about Jin Feng Braised Pork Rice

Yong Kang Beef Noodles

Another extremely popular local restaurant, Yong Kang Beef Noodles have been serving their famous beef noodle dishes since 1963. The dish is deep and rich in flavour, and their side dishes are pretty great too. The best time to eat here is during a weekday evening - if you're lucky, you may even avoid queuing.

Best Time to Visit:

Weekday evenings 19:00 - 20:00

Click here to read more about Yong Kang Beef Noodles

Ay Chung Flour Rice Noodles

Another extremely popular local place, Ay Chung have been serving flour rice noodles since 1975. If you can stomach the pieces of pig intestines found within, it's definitely worth queuing for. The good news is the staff are extremely efficient at serving people, so don't be daunted by the long queues.

Best Time to Visit:

Weekday afternoons 14:00 - 17:00

Click here to read more about Ay Chung Flour Rice Noodles

Fuhang Soy Milk

Arguably the most popular breakfast place in Taiwan, Fuhang Soy Milk consequently attracts huge numbers of hungry folk who flock here to sample their delicious soy milk, deep-fried dough sticks and freshly roasted buns. Queue times here will often exceed an hour so you'll need to wake very early to see what all the fuss is about.

Best Time to Visit:

Tuesday - Friday, 05:30 - 07:30

Click here to read more about Fuhang Soy Milk

Yong He Soy Milk King

If you don't won't to queue for an age at Fuhang Soy Milk, Yong He Soy Milk King is a very good alternative. Their savoury churros are some of the best in Taipei, while their soy milk and deep-fried radish cakes are delicious. Open 24/7 except for Sunday afternoon when they give the place a thorough clean, you've no excuse not to give them a try.

Best Time to Visit:

Tuesday - Friday, 05:30 - 09:00

Click here to read more about Yong He Soy Milk King

Eastern Ice Store

Situated in the heart of the Daan district, Eastern Ice Store is one of the most popular dessert places in Taipei. You can choose your ice mix from many softened and sweetened ingredients such as taro, sweet potato, tapioca, peanuts, beans and jellies. Having first opened over 20 years ago, they have gained a huge reputation for they deliciously refreshing desserts.

Best Time to Visit:

Weekday afternoons

Click here to read more about the Eastern Ice Store

Tian Jin Onion Pancake

Found on the famous Yongkang Street, this very popular stand has been serving these delicious breakfast pancakes for many a year. The pancake dough is mixed with scallion, and then fried and beaten until soft and flaky. With the addition of some tasty fillings such as egg, cheese and sweetcorn, these moreish snacks will have you coming back again and again. Expect long queues, especially at weekends.

Best Time to Visit:

Early weekdays (open from 08:00)

Click here to read more about Tian Jin Onion Pancake

Lan Jia Traditional Taiwanese Snack

Found within Gongguan Night Market, the best way to describe Lan Jia Traditional Taiwanese Snack is like a Taiwanese Hamburger. The steamed soft white bao buns are filled with marinated fatty pork meat that's been mixed with pickles, peanut powder and coriander. So good are these, they have even been recommended in the official Michelin Guide. Be aware that there are two queues here - one for eat-in and one for takeaway.

Best Time to Visit:

Weekdays mid-afternoon or late night (closes at 23:00)

Click here to read more about Lan Jia Traditional Taiwanese Snack

Locations

title: Vegetarian & Vegan Restaurants You'll Love
excerpt: Taipei has an abundance of vegetarian and vegan restaurants, from Miss Green's gluten-free cakes to BaganHood's Omnipork burgers, serving both western and eastern variations.
content:
Taipei isn't short on restaurants which cater to those who prefer a meat or animal-product free experience. There are some great choices for both western and eastern cuisine, and the city's vegan scene in particular has grown fast over the last few years, with more places catering to gluten-free and other dietary needs too.

Below are some of my favourite vegetarian and vegan restaurants in Taipei.

Click here to see all my 'best of' lists

Miss Green

Serving salads, wraps, paninis and handcraft vegan burgers, Miss Green also have a few pasta and risotto dishes which go down a treat, and their gluten-free vegan cakes and smoothies are some of the best we've tried in Taipei. It's a small, relaxed place near Xinyi Anhe Station, with extra seating in the basement, and if you add them on the Line app they'll even throw in a free cake.

Click here to read more about Miss Green

Plants

Another vegan restaurant in the Daan district, Plants is a popular place to brunch, with all their food also gluten-free and with no unrefined sugars or additives. They also serve a few 'raw' dishes, cooked at under 45°C to retain as many nutrients as possible. Their dishes are made with care and precision and they have a great selection of vegan cakes too, though it's not cheap, with two dishes and drinks coming to around NT$1,000.

Click here to read more about Plants

Miacucina

Meaning 'My Kitchen' in Italian, Miacucina have five branches around Taipei (Fuxing, Xinyi, Nanxi, Shilin and Neihu), and have arguably the largest vegetarian menu throughout the city, with many types of delicious vegetarian food for any time of the day. Their Budda Bowls especially, are a knockout, and the Neihu branch is one of the nicest places we've dined in Taipei.

Click here to read more about Miacucina

BaganHood

Opened in mid 2019 right next door to the Songshan Cultural and Creative Park, BaganHood has quickly gained a devout vegan following. Serving pizzas, burgers and some delicious vegan bowls made with Omnipork and Beyond Meat, their deep and complex flavours make for one of the best vegan restaurants in Taipei – there's even a small mini-supermarket at the back selling the vegan meat and dairy substitutes they use.

Click here to read more about BaganHood

title: The Best Museums in Taipei - And Which Are Worth Your Time
excerpt: A guide to the best museums in Taipei, from the National Palace Museum and the new National Railway Museum to hands-on papermaking and free hot spring bathhouses.
content:
For a city this compact, Taipei has an unreasonable number of museums – and they are far stranger and more varied than the usual "world-class collection of Chinese antiquities" line suggests. You can spend a morning with thousand-year-old jade carvings and an afternoon inside a dismantled diesel locomotive, or making your own sheet of paper by hand. Several are free. Most cost less than a coffee and a pastry.

What follows isn't a ranked list so much as a guide to which ones are actually worth your limited holiday time, depending on what you're into and who you're dragging along.

Two things to know before you go. Almost every museum here closes on Mondays – the National Palace Museum is the notable exception, opening daily. And a Taipei Fun Pass covers free entry to a lot of them, which is worth doing the sums on if museums are your main reason for visiting.

If it's paintings and contemporary galleries you're after rather than museums proper, I've kept those in a separate guide to the best places to see art in Taipei.

The Two You've Probably Already Heard Of

The National Palace Museum (NT$350) holds the largest collection of ancient Chinese artefacts anywhere in the world, most of it shipped across the strait in 1949. Four floors of bronzes, ceramics, calligraphy and jade spanning several thousand years, with the famously fiddly Jadeite Cabbage as the thing everyone queues for. It is genuinely enormous, and the honest advice is not to try to see it all – pick two or three floors, and leave time for the gardens outside, which most visitors walk straight past.

It's also the one museum here where timing really matters. Go early or go late; the tour groups arrive mid-morning and it becomes a very different experience. Before you commit a morning to it, it's worth seeing which temporary exhibitions are running, because they rotate often and are frequently the best thing in the building – and my full guide to the Palace Museum covers what to prioritise and how long to allow.

The National Taiwan Museum is the older institution and, for understanding the island rather than the mainland, the more useful one. It covers Taiwan's natural history, its indigenous peoples and its colonial past, and the dinosaur hall makes it an easy sell to children who have already decided museums are boring.

What catches people out is that it isn't one building. It's four, scattered around Zhongzheng and Datong: the grand main hall by 228 Peace Park, the Land Bank building opposite with the fossils, the Nanmen Park site in an old camphor factory, and the Railway Department Park near Beimen, which is a beautifully restored Japanese-era headquarters and arguably the best of the lot. One modest ticket covers more than you'd expect, so check what's included before paying twice – I've broken down each of the four sites in my guide to the National Taiwan Museum, and you can see what's on temporarily on their own site.

Making Sense of Taiwan's Own History

If you visit one museum for context rather than objects, make it the Taipei 228 Memorial Hall (NT$20). It sits inside 228 Peace Park, on the site where the February 28 Incident of 1947 began – the killings that opened the White Terror and nearly four decades of martial law. It's a small museum and a sobering hour, but almost everything about modern Taiwanese politics makes more sense afterwards. Go here before you form opinions about anything else on the island.

A short walk south, the National Museum of History (NT$80) reopened in February 2024 after five years shut for renovation, and remains oddly overlooked. Its strength is ceramics – particularly a Tang dynasty sancai collection brought over from the Henan Museum – and because nobody has caught on yet, you'll often have the galleries largely to yourself. It backs onto the Botanical Garden, which makes for a pleasant pairing.

For indigenous Taiwan, the place to go is the Shung Ye Museum of Formosan Aborigines (NT$150), which sits diagonally opposite the National Palace Museum and is very easy to combine with it – there's a joint ticket if you ask. Four floors of textiles, carvings, weapons and ritual objects from Taiwan's recognised indigenous peoples, and a free English guided tour on Saturday afternoons. Given that the Palace Museum tells a story about China, spending an hour across the road on the people who were here first feels like the right correction.

Also worth knowing about: Ching-Kuo Chi-Hai Cultural Park near Yuanshan (from NT$100), the former residence of Chiang Ching-kuo, opened to the public relatively recently. It's a quieter, more domestic counterpart to the grand memorial halls, and pairs neatly with the Shilin Residence if you're interested in that family's long shadow.

Trains, Water and Industrial Taipei

Taipei has quietly become good for industrial heritage, and the headline act is the National Railway Museum on Civic Boulevard in Xinyi (NT$100, closed Mondays). This is the old Taipei Railway Workshop, the largest industrial heritage restoration project in the country, and it's genuinely impressive – enormous workshop halls with the machinery still in place, and locomotives being conserved where they were once repaired.

Be aware that it is still opening in stages. At the moment the ticketed area is essentially the Diesel-Electric Locomotive Workshop, so treat it as a compelling hour rather than a full afternoon, and expect it to grow considerably over the next few years. The nearest MRT is Nanjing Sanmin, about ten minutes' walk.

Two railway museums, easily confused. The National Railway Museum in Xinyi is the workshop site described above. The Railway Department Park near Beimen is a branch of the National Taiwan Museum, in the restored Japanese-era administrative headquarters. They're different places, in different districts, on different tickets. If you only do one, the Beimen site is the prettier building and the Xinyi site is the more remarkable industrial space.

In the same spirit, the Drinking Water Museum at Taipei Water Park in Gongguan is a gorgeous 1908 baroque pumping station, all columns and arched windows, which is why it turns up in wedding photographs far more often than in guidebooks. It's included with entry to the water park, so on a hot day you can combine it with the water play area and let everyone get soaked afterwards.

If You're Travelling with Children

The Taipei Astronomical Museum (NT$40) is the strongest option here and absurd value. Three floors of hands-on exhibits on space, gravity and the solar system, plus an IMAX and 3D theatre, a motion-simulator ride and a public telescope for clear-night viewing sessions.

Crucially, it's a two-minute walk from the National Taiwan Science Education Center (NT$100), which has six floors of the same kind of thing plus the Sky Bike – a pedal-powered rail suspended several storeys up in the atrium. Between them you can fill an entire day in one spot at Shilin, which is a rare gift when you're travelling with children and running out of ideas.

The Miniatures Museum of Taiwan (NT$200) is the one that surprises adults. Over a hundred scenes built mostly at 1:12 scale, with craftsmanship so fine that magnifying glasses are provided for the details you'd otherwise miss. It's widely rated among the best miniature collections in the world, and it's tucked in a basement near Songjiang Nanjing that you would never find by accident.

Small, Odd and Quietly Brilliant

The Suho Memorial Paper Museum in Zhongshan (around NT$100–150) is Taiwan's only museum devoted to paper, spread over four small floors of a converted townhouse. The reason to go isn't the displays, it's the hands-on papermaking sessions run several times a day, where you make and press your own sheet. It's the best souvenir you'll bring home from Taipei, and it takes under an hour.

The Taipei Story House is a tiny half-timbered Tudor-style villa from 1914 sitting incongruously beside the Fine Arts Museum, built by a tea merchant and now hosting small exhibitions. It's more curiosity than museum, but it takes fifteen minutes and there's a tearoom.

Up in Beitou, the Beitou Hot Spring Museum is free and occupies the old Japanese public bathhouse from 1913, complete with the original Roman-style bathing pool and tatami lounge. Since you're going to Beitou for the hot springs anyway, there's no reason not to.

And for the genuinely curious, National Taiwan University has more than half a dozen tiny specialist museums scattered across its campus – anthropology, physics, geology, and an entire museum devoted to insects. Most are free, most are empty, and wandering between them through the palm-lined campus is a lovely way to spend a slow afternoon in Gongguan.

Worth Leaving the City For

The best day out of the lot is Fort San Domingo (NT$80) at the end of the red line in Tamsui. Built by the Spanish in 1628, rebuilt by the Dutch, then leased to the British as a consulate for the best part of a century – there is nowhere else in Taiwan with quite that layering. The ticket also covers the Little White House and Hobe Fort nearby, and the whole thing sits above the river, so you can finish with the sunset.

Two more in New Taipei are worth the train ride. The Chi Po-Lin Museum in Tamsui (NT$150) is devoted to the aerial photographer whose documentary Beyond Beauty changed how Taiwan saw its own landscape, and who died filming the sequel – a small, moving space. Out at Yingge, the Yingge Ceramics Museum (NT$80) is excellent and sits in a whole town of pottery shops, now joined by the brand new New Taipei City Art Museum a few minutes away.

The Lin Family Mansion and Garden in Banqiao (NT$80) is the finest surviving Qing-era garden complex in northern Taiwan, and reachable on the blue line without leaving the MRT network at all.

Finally, an unexpected one: the Museum of World Religions in Yonghe (NT$150) does something no other museum here attempts, walking through the world's major faiths with real artefacts and a hall of extraordinarily detailed architectural models of religious buildings. Free if you're over 65. It's an odd thing to find above a shopping centre in a New Taipei suburb, and better than it has any right to be.

Klook.com

Planning a Museum Day

A few things that will save you time. Mondays are the problem – nearly everything above closes, so build a Monday around the Palace Museum, a park or a night market instead. Most of the state museums close at 17:00 and stop selling tickets half an hour before, which is earlier than visitors expect in a city that stays up so late.

Geographically, they cluster helpfully. Shilin gives you the Palace Museum, Shung Ye, the Astronomical Museum and the Science Education Center. Zhongzheng gives you the National Taiwan Museum, the Land Bank hall, 228 and the Museum of History within a few minutes' walk. Almost all of it is reachable on the MRT, and the few that aren't are a short bus or taxi from a station.

That's the pick of them, but there are more – you can browse every museum I've written about if you'd rather work through the lot.

title: The Best Film Festivals in Taipei
excerpt: Film festivals showing acclaimed international and local films
content:
For film geeks, Taipei has a number of prominent film festivals playing a wide variety of Eastern and Western films, documentaries, and other films not normally shown on the big screens.

Click here to see all my 'best of' lists

Golden Horse Film Festival

Often dubbed the Chinese Oscars, the Golden Horse Film Festival is the premier cinema event in Taiwan (and possibly Asia). With films playing mainly in cinemas near Ximending, along with the Vieshow in Xinyi, it shows a number of high profile films from all over the globe. Many films are shown with English subtitles, and the director will be invited to some for a Q&A after the film. Booking ahead is advised for popular films.

2020 Dates: TBC (Usually Nov - Dec)

Golden Horse Film Festival

Taipei Film Festival

Playing second fiddle to the Golden Horse, the 2-week Taipei Film Festival does still show a wide variety of international films, including some in Virtual Reality. With two cinemas participating near Ximending, and the Spot Huashan cinema also taking part, cheaper early bird and matinee tickets are also available.

2020 Dates: 25th June - 11th July

Taipei Film Festival

Urban Nomad Film Festival

Taiwan's answer to the SXSW festival in Texas, Urban Nomad serves as a platform for independent film, music, and art. Held over 10 days in Spring, it also features a 2-day music festival held at Tiger Mountain (curated by the same people as the Tiger Mountain Festival) and other live performances in the city. The film festival runs in just one cinema (Wonderful Theater in Ximending), and some films are followed by Q&A sessions by the film's director.

2020 Dates: TBC (April - May)

Urban Nomad Film Festival

Taiwan International Documentary Festival

Founded in 1998, the Taiwan International Documentary Festival is one of the largest festivals in Asia with a focus on documentaries. Held every other year, the festival will run in 2020 for 9 days and features many documentaries with a social or human interest. Films are mainly shown in Ximending and Huashan, with the Museum of Contemporary Arts showing video art and hosting discussion panels.

2020 Dates: 1st - 10th May

Taiwan International Documentary Festival

Taiwan European Film Festival

With films shown all over Taiwan including many in Taipei, the TEFF shows films chosen by 17 European countries at cinemas, art spaces and colleges. The 7-week long festival does include both English and Chinese subtitles for all films.

2020 Dates: TBC (Nov - Jan)

Taiwan European Film Festival

title: The Best Places to Drink Outdoors in Taipei
excerpt: From Xinyi rooftops staring straight at Taipei 101 to proper beer gardens and a whole street of open-air bars - where to drink outside in Taipei.
content:
Taipei is a famously compact, high-rise city, and most bars here make do with four walls and air conditioning rather than a terrace. Look in the right places, though, and there's a genuine outdoor drinking scene to be found – skyline-view rooftops staring straight at Taipei 101, proper beer gardens, and even a whole street given over to outdoor tables. Here's where to find it, depending on what you're after.

Click here to see all my 'best of' lists

For the View

If a Taipei 101 backdrop matters as much as what's in your glass, head for Xinyi. A small cluster of high-rise terraces here all look straight at the tower, each with a slightly different personality.

Hooters Xinyi, on the 14th floor of the Far Eastern Department Store's A13 building, has the most dramatic terrace of the bunch – tables spill out right alongside the tower itself, and it's especially good around sunset. It's a proper sports-bar atmosphere with big screens inside, and the daily happy hour (3pm–6:30pm) runs buy-one-get-one-free on beer.

A few floors up in the Neo19 building, Barcode's Sky Garden terrace trades the sports-bar energy for a late-night lounge feel – it doesn't get going until 9pm, and stays open past 2am most nights, 3am at the weekend.

For something calmer, The Terrace Bar on the 6th floor of the Humble House hotel keeps the same Taipei 101 backdrop but in a more polished, hotel-bar setting – a good option if Hooters and Barcode sound like too much.

For a Proper Pint

If it's the beer itself you're after rather than the view, these are about the drink more than the backdrop.

Found in the popular Xinyi Shopping District, Landmark Taihu has a large selection of very fine craft ales brewed from Taihu's own brewery. Tables here don't come with stools, so if your legs are tired from a day of sightseeing or shopping, you should probably look elsewhere.

Plan B (歐陸街頭市集小酒館), just off Zhongxiao Dunhua, is a European-style bistro partnered with Erdinger Weissbier, tucked down a covered alleyway that opens onto a proper little courtyard beer garden – wooden tables and chairs on brick paving, string lighting, patio heaters for cooler evenings. It's a genuinely nice spot to sit outside with a stein rather than just a beer.

Widely considered the best expat bar in Taipei, On Tap has a decent-sized outdoor area at the front of the pub. The outdoor tables have to close at 11pm given the central location, but that still leaves plenty of time to work through their huge range of drinks and food.

Found within Maji Square at the Taipei Expo Park, The Three Lions Inn is a British-style pub with a large outdoor seating area that's protected from the elements by a roof covering the entire square – a good shout on a rainy day. There are some good happy hour deals during the day, plus a large range of food, although there are many other restaurants in the square too.

Worth the trip out to Beitou is Kahu Craft Beer Garden – a proper waterside beer garden with a hot springs stream running along the back of it, close enough to Beitou Thermal Valley that you can follow the steam there with a cold one in hand. It's a green, plant-filled space with picnic tables and umbrellas, pouring mostly Island Life beers from Tamsui alongside pub food like pizza and Mexican, plus regular live music and a weekend brunch menu.

For Something Different

And then there are two places that don't really fit either category.

Without question, the Ximen Outdoor Drinking Area is the largest and best place in Taipei for drinking outside, full stop – a whole street given over to it. There are several bars to choose from, each with their own deals (some with buy-2-get-1-free on all drinks), decent food, and hookah pipes. The area is also a popular hangout for the LGBT community and gets lively over weekend evenings.

Out in Neihu, near Gangqian MRT, Knock Knock Heaven (formerly Lazy Point Restaurant & Bar, still the name on some older reviews) is a three-storey restaurant with a lush, plant-filled terrace on the third floor – more intimate and secluded than a skyline view, and a good escape if you want greenery over glass towers. There's an open-air bar up there too, with its own view over the Taipei skyline if you do want one after all. The rebrand brought a new fusion menu with it, mixing Sichuan, Southeast Asian, Japanese and American influences – think numbing-spice chicken spring rolls, Sichuan beef noodles and Japanese-style fried chicken, all against a street-art, industrial-style interior.

Locations

The map below covers the original four spots – Hooters, Barcode, The Terrace Bar and Knock Knock Heaven are all easy enough to find via the map links above.

title: Middle-Eastern Delights at Flux by Fancia
excerpt: Arguably Taipei's best Middle Eastern food, near Ximending — though the restaurant itself is tiny, with no proper tables.
content:
In recent years, Taipei has seen a healthy influx (no pun intended) of restaurants serving some great middle-eastern food. Flux by Fancia, a delightful restaurant near Ximending, serves arguably the very best in Taipei.

Flux by Fancia is very small however, with no proper tables to sit at, there is a bench with some side-tables, plus some stools at the bar area and a small bench outside.

Food at Flux by Fancia is divided into two categories - Pita Sandwiches and Salad Platters, both offering classic middle-eastern food such as falafel, hummus, roasted eggplant and lamb meatballs.

They also have a specials board that has other dishes such as risotto, pasta, and even chicken tikka masala.

However, we came to try their middle-eastern food, in particular, their hummus and falafel. The Hummus Platter, served with salad and pita was the obviously choice.

A nicely presented and very inviting looking dish came out, with all the salad items crisply fresh. The homemade hummus and falafel were both outstanding, and the warm pita bread was soft and delicious. I've had many falafel dishes in Taipei, but I don't think I've had a better one than this.

We had to try one of their pita sandwich dishes too. Seeing as we'd already tried the falafel, we opted for the Chicken Paprikash pita, pan-fried chicken with paprika, hummus, salad and pickles.

Again, it was very well executed - the paprika heat combined with the sharpness from the pickles. The chicken was still moist and the hummus and tahini brought everything together. Top marks!

Flux by Fancia have a very eclectic mix for drinks too. Espresso based coffees, teas, lassis and even mojitos (which I believe are non-alcoholic). We decided to try their Pink Lemonade, which was lovely, sweet drink with a fizzy-velvety texture.

All the dishes we saw served to other customers looked quite amazing too, especially the pasta dish. Flux by Fancia's desserts and cakes also looked quite special. We'll definitely be back to try some other dishes from their menu, as everything we tried was faultless.

Menu

Pros

  • Great food and drinks
  • Nice interior

Cons

  • Limited seating
  • A little out the way

Price: $$

Level of English: Good (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

Check their specials board for more options

title: Five Cool Convenience Stores You Should Visit
excerpt: Convenience stores that offer something a little bit different from the others
content:
Taipei has hundreds of convenience stores all over the city (see our rundown of the main chains), but there are a handful which offer something slightly different from all of the others. These are some of the coolest convenience stores in Taipei.

Click here to see all my 'best of' lists

7-Eleven Dominoes (Xinyi)

This 7-Eleven, found just north of the City Hall MRT station, is one of the largest convenience stores in the city at 85 ping. As a bonus, it's also home to a 5 ping Domino's Pizza kitchen tucked inside – Taiwan's first convenience-store-and-pizza-chain crossover – serving 6-inch and 9-inch pizzas from NT$89 to NT$208, ready in around 3 minutes.

Family Mart (Daan)

This Family Mart, found in the heart of the Daan district, also doubles as a cafe. With loads of comfortable seating, it also serves food and beverages you wouldn't normally find in a convenience store.

7-Eleven X

There are a couple of 7-Eleven X stores found in Taipei, part of a fully self-service, unmanned concept that's proven successful enough to expand to nine stores across Taiwan. They use facial recognition to enter the store, although registration is required to make use of one.

Family Mart (Songshan)

Not far from Taipei Arena, this Family Mart is easy to miss, but has many seats, including some sofas at the back.

7-Eleven (Ximen)

From the outside, this 7-Eleven in Ximen looks like any other convenience store. However, found on the second floor is a cool seating area where the walls are adorned with pop-art.

Locations

title: Apple Museum Cafe, Taipei (Permanently Closed)
content:
Permanent Closure Notice

Please note: Apple Museum Cafe has permanently closed.

For lovers of Apple products, or those simply interested in the history of technology, the Apple Museum Cafe is Taipei's Garden of Eden.

The cafe has a wealth of Apple products from their early days, right up to the present.

Old PCs and laptops, including many Macs/MacBooks and the multi-coloured iMac G3s, Apple Newtons (one of the first pocket touch-screen devices), iPods, watches, even some Apple QuickTakes (their failed foray into the photography market).

Their rarest and probably most valuable antique is an original Apple Lisa 2 (re-branded later as the Macintosh XL), one of the first computers to have a graphical user interface.

The Apple Museum Cafe's website is rather nicely designed to pay homage to the old Operating System of this very machine, although if you want some information about the cafe, it's best to visit their Facebook page.

You can also reserve seats on Facebook, which is recommended as the cafe is often packed out, sometimes with a queue of people waiting outside.

There is enough seating for around 30 people here, some of which is great for taking your macBook (or non-Apple laptop), plus some more comfortable seating in an area at the back.

Of course, ordering food or drink at the Apple Museum Cafe is done via an iPad.

There's a good selection of food, of which I have yet to try - most are well priced below NT$200. The chocolate milk I had was very reasonably priced at NT$99.

Another great feature about the Apple Museum Cafe is they actually repair Apple products on-site. Their engineers have many years experience, and although I didn't have anything that required repairing, I was avidly watching one as he took apart a MacBook. He sure looked like he knew what he was doing!

For Apple fanboys, technology enthusiasts, or if you're just looking for a place to relax or work, the Apple Museum Cafe is a great place to visit.

  • Ideal for Apple fan-boys

title: Coffee Lover's Planet - For Coffee (& Sandwich) Lovers
excerpt: Serious single-origin coffee and a small selection of gourmet sandwiches, in the basement of a SOGO shopping mall.
content:
If you're looking for a serious coffee in Taipei, Coffee Lover's Planet serves some fantastic coffees, including some of single origin, and have a small but fantastic selection of gourmet sandwiches and cakes to accompany them.

Set in the basement of one of the SOGO shopping malls in Taipei's East District, it's also one of the nicest looking places to enjoy a brew, with an elegant centrepiece and nice seating area.

Coffees come from all the major coffee producing countries in Africa, South America and Asia, and include a home-grown coffee grown from the Alishan Township, found in central Taiwan.

Coffees are colour-coded into different categories - Nutty Cocoa, Sweet, Floral and Fruity.

All are available to sniff prior to buying, and they have samples of the coffee beans (both before and after roasting). After selecting your desired beans, you then have a few options for brewing.

Prices for the coffees at Coffee Lover's Planet range from NT$200 to NT$550, with the majority costing around NT$270, which is by no means cheap. The coffees are beautifully presented however, and come in a jug that is enough for two or three cups.

The tray also comes with a sample of the roasted and grinded beans, along with a shot of espresso cold brew of your chosen coffee.

Coffee Lover's Planet also cater to lovers of sandwiches. Although they only have six sandwiches to choose from, including some open-sandwiches, all are high-end gourmet style. These cost between NT$250 and NT$300.

The Roast Beef with Mayonnaise open-sandwich comes with salad and sits on a lightly toasted piece of brown bread. It's a beautifully made sandwich, with succulent slices of beef and a generous dollop of mayonnaise.

Both the Roast Chicken and Avocado Vegetarian Sandwiches come generously filled with fresh ingredients, within two thick pieces of brown bread. You'll need an quite a bite to eat them, otherwise a knife and fork are available to help.

Aside from the delicious coffees and sandwiches, This Coffee Lover's Planet also have a fine looking selection of cakes, of which we've yet to try.

For connoisseurs of coffee, sandwiches and cakes, Coffee Lover's Planet is an out-of-this-world experience. One of the best in Taipei.

Menu

  • Nice dining environment

Cons

title: Yong Kang Beef Noodles - Still the Best in Taipei?
excerpt: Taipei's most famous beef noodle shop, near Yongkang Street. What to order, what it costs, and whether it lives up to the queue.
content:
If you're looking to try one of Taiwan's popular beef noodles dishes, then Yong Kang Beef Noodles, found close to the touristic Yong Kang Street, is one of the most popular and famous restaurants in Taiwan.

Having served this Taiwanese delicacy for well over 50 years, the two storey establishment knows a thing or two about making these delicious broths.

The only issue is getting a table here. Taiwanese people don't mind queuing for 30 minutes, sometimes much longer, for a dish they know will satisfy them. At Yong Kong Beef Noodles, lunch hours, especially over the weekend, are when you'll see the longest queues.

Dinner hours during the week however, are much more manageable. The most recent time we visited, which was during peak dinner hours around 6pm on a weekday, there was no queue, and there were even some empty tables.

The first time we've never had to queue here.

A likely explanation of why there was no queue, is the gradual price hike Yong Kang Beef Noodles have been applying to their dishes.

I know when we have previously eaten here (back in 2018), the prices for their signature dish, the Braised Beef Noodle Soup, were NT$200 & NT$230 for a small/large dish. The prices are now NT$240 & NT$270, which is certainly not cheap.

The dish however, is still on a par with how it tasted previously. A deep, intense broth, slightly spicy, with the Australian beef they use being tender and packed with flavour.

If you prefer something slightly less intense, they also serve a Stewed Beef with Noodle Soup, which comes with a clear broth that's less herby. Both are the same price.

If you're not a huge fan of noodle soups, Yong Kang Beef Noodle have a total of 9 main dishes, 5 of them being non-soupy.

If you're looking for something extra spicy, I would recommend the Spicy Dumplings. They come in a sesame sauce with plenty of chilli heat. I have a strange affliction which causes me to hiccup uncontrollably when I eat something very spicy. These cause me to hiccup like crazy, but the dish is very satisfying and the dumplings are well made.

To accompany the main dishes, Yong Kang Beef Noodles have a selection of vegetables and other dishes you can choose as you walk in.

I would recommend getting at least a couple of these, to eat either while waiting for you main to arrive, or as we prefer, to eat with them.

The bean sprouts and green beans side dishes are two of our favourites, but there are many others including tofu and even kimchi.

The question is, whether it's still worth paying for the slightly-on-the-expensive-side noodles at Yong Kang Beef Noodles.

There are many other beef noodles places in Taipei, and even quite a few near Yong Kang Street. The ones here are still the best we've tried, and their tasty side dishes are an added bonus.

If this is your first visit to Taipei, then I wouldn't look any further. Just try to avoid weekends.

Menu

  • Nice side dishes

Cons

title: Hearty Cuban Sandwiches at Chinita's Cubano
excerpt: The only place in Taipei doing an authentic Cubano — Cuban bread, meat, cheese, pickles and mustard sauce.
content:
As far as I'm aware, Chinita's Cubano is the only place in Taipei where you can try an authentic Cubano.

For the uninitiated, a Cubano is a Cuban toasted sandwich made with Cuban bread, meat, cheese, pickles and a sauce, usually mustard. The large influx of Cubans to Florida in the early 20th century made them popular there too, albeit with some minor changes to the ingredients (mayonnaise instead of mustard, for example).

The Taiwanese owner of Chinita's Cubano studied in Florida and immediately fell in love with these toasted treats. Her passion drove her to set up a Cubano place in Taipei to spread the love to others.

Chinita's Cubano mainly caters to takeaways, although there are a few stools available should you wish to eat there. The menu only consists of three sandwiches, with some drinks and homemade cookies.

The Cubano is made with pulled pork & ham, the Jamaican contains jerk chicken, plus there's a vegetarian option with bell peppers and eggplant.

These all come in two sizes, the difference being the amount of filling inside:

  • Lite, for NT$120
  • Regular, for NT$200

She also has a monthly special, which during my visit was the aptly named Barbie Chick, with BBQ chicken, cheese, bacon and fried shallots.

After the sandwich is prepped, it's pressed onto the grill for a few minutes and cut in two.

The Cuban bread, which she makes before opening shop each day, is soft inside with a toasted crispiness. The generous filling of a regular size Cubano is a delicious mix of succulent meat, sharp pickles and comforting melted cheese, and is plenty to satisfy any lunchtime cravings you have.

A hearty sandwich in every sense of the word!

A revisit is definitely on the cards to try the Jamaican version.

Chinita's Cubano offers a unique chance to try some authentic Cuban sandwiches - made with love.

Menu

Pros

  • Authentic Cubanos
  • Friendly service

Cons

title: Supermarkets & Delis with Great Western Produce
excerpt: The best supermarkets and delis to buy great western (and local) produce, from Addiction Aquatic Development's fish market to Mia C'bon (formerly Jason's Market Place).
content:
Supermarkets such as PX Mart and Wellcome have a few western products on their shelves, but there are some supermarkets and delis which are great for buying not only produce from the west, but high quality local produce too.

Click here to see all my 'best of' lists

Addiction Aquatic Development Deli

Addiction Aquatic Development is not only one of the best places to dine in Taipei - it's the largest fish market in the city, with six seafood restaurants and its own aquarium - but it also has it own super little deli with a great selection of produce. Aside from seafood, it sells dairy produce and very fresh vegetables at a competitive rate.

City Super

City Super is usually the first place I visit when I'm looking for some less popular western ingredients and food. The Hong Kong retail chain, founded in 1996 as an upmarket specialty grocer, now has around ten stores across Taiwan, with the Fuxing Sogo store most conveniently located while stocking a large range of products.

IKEA Supermarket

IKEA's Taipei Arena store, the only full IKEA within Taipei City itself, has a small but great supermarket attached that's stocked with western drinks, snacks, tinned, and frozen food (with further IKEA supermarkets a little further out in New Taipei if you don't mind the trip). Much of it is imported from Sweden, and their range of drinks and frozen fish are alone worth going for.

Mia C'bon (formerly Jason's Market Place)

Jason's Market Place, the upscale supermarket chain that first opened in Taipei at Taipei 101 back in 2003, was rebranded to Mia C'bon in 2022 after Carrefour Taiwan took over its parent company. It still has a number of well-located stores in the centre of Taipei under the new name, and much like City Super, sells a wide range of western produce imported from many countries.

Maji Deli

Maji Square, a covered outdoor dining and drinking area within the Taipei Expo Park that's also home to a dozen or so restaurants, bars and craft shops, has it's own deli which is crammed full of high quality produce. While the deli does perhaps have more local than western products on it's shelves, it's all top-grade stuff.

title: Cafes Ideal for Taking Your Laptop
excerpt: Some of the best cafes to work from, including WiFi, Plugs and Seating.
content:
Even though Taipei has an almost infinite number of cafes, it can be difficult finding ones with enough seats, decent WIFI, and good plug socket availability. A local SIM or eSIM saves relying on cafe wifi altogether. There are plenty of large Starbucks in the city, but these aren't great for WIFI or plugs.

These are some of the best cafes to work from.

Click here to see all my 'best of' lists

Youmoutoohana Coffee

If you're after a treat rather than a laptop spot, Coffee Alley's waffles and smoothies are worth the detour. Although their name is virtually impossible to pronounce, Youmoutoohana Coffee is ideal for working. Located just off Yongkang Street, it has many plugs, great WIFI and plenty of seating, plus it's never too noisy and the music is largely unobtrusive.

Click here to read more about Youmoutoohana Coffee

Café Costumice

One of the coolest cafes in Taipei is also one of the best for working. Café Costumice even have four-way extension plugs on some tables, and their WIFI is fast. They have a great area outside for working too, although expect noise levels slightly higher than other cafes on this list.

Click here to read more about the Café Costumice

Yaboo Café

If you prefer working in almost total silence, Yaboo Café is one of the quietest cafes to take your laptop to. Almost everyone here comes to work, but consequently you may have difficultly finding a seat. Plug extension leads can be provided, and the food and drink are both excellent.

Click here to read more about Yaboo Café

Campus Café

Another place that's more of an eatery than a café, Campus Café have a few locations in Taipei, although the only ones I would recommend taking your laptop to are the Zhongxiao, Zhongzheng and Neihu branches (added to map below). They're spacious, have decent WIFI and have a large food and beverage menu should you become peckish. If you're a fan of US Sport, they all have screens showing the latest games.

Click here to read more about Campus Café

Louisa

Louisa have dozens and dozens of cafes all around Taipei, although most of too small for working in. I've added many of the largest ones in my post to help you. Louisa is great if you're on a budget, as their food and beverage range are excellent value.

Click here to read more about Louisa

Other Cafes I Recommend...

Cho Café

Located in Ximending, Cho Café serves nice drinks and has ample seating including many two-seaters and shared tables. Plug sockets can only be found near walls however but the WIFI here is also good.

Locations

Louisa Cafes in orange, Campus Cafes in yellow

title: Avenue Fast Casual Eatery - Urban & Hip Cafe/Restaurant (Permanently Closed)
content:
Permanent Closure Notice

Please note: Avenue Fast Casual Eatery has permanently closed.

I like places that describe exactly what they're about. Avenue Fast Casual Eatery is such a place. A casual, urban looking cafe/restaurant with quick service.

That's all you need to know.

I guess I should divulge somewhat.

Located in B1 next to a large coworking space, Avenue Fast Casual Eatery is one of the hippest, slickest, urbanest cafes (or restaurants) I have been to in Taipei.

With two large rooms and a seating area outside, there's plenty of space here, whether you prefer a simple drink, a meal, to socialise or to work, Avenue (I'm getting tired of writing out it's full name) is great for all of these.

The back room especially has ample space, with tables suitable for sharing or sitting on your own if you're feeling anti-social.

Avenue's all-western menu is varied enough to appeal to most. Pizza, pasta, sandwiches and burgers, and some salads if you're feeling more healthy. Small bites and desserts are also available.

They also have a nice looking brunch menu, but this is only available during weekends.

In honesty, we've yet to try any of their main dishes, simply opting for their Blueberry Tart, but it was exceedingly tasty.

We will be back to try more, to see if the 'Fast' part of their name is true.

Avenue have lots of cafe-type drinks, including of course plenty of espresso-based coffees. They're not large, but they're tasty.

The restaurant side of them serves wines and draft craft ales, and they have a nice happy hour for these - only NT$150 for a Redpoint or Taihu ale. Avenue also serve some amusingly named cocktails such as Death in the Afternoon and Call Me a Cab, all for NT$300.

Even though Avenue is located a fair way from any MRT station, it's modern and urban setting make for one of the nicest eateries in Taipei, and is also a great place to take your laptop.

Pros

  • Stylish and modern
  • Good for working

Cons

  • Quite a walk to the closest MRT

Level of English: Good (English on menu)

Closed on Sundays and Mondays

title: The Best Places for a Cheap but Tasty Coffee
excerpt: Where to get your coffee fix without putting too much of a dent in your wallet.
content:
Getting a nice tasting but cheap coffee in Taipei can be difficult. With real estate prices high, many cafes need to raise their retail prices in order to survive. There are still a few places you can grab a cheap but great tasting espresso-based coffee.

Click here to see all my 'best of' lists

Louisa

With well over a hundred cafes located all around Taipei, Louisa serves very decent coffees and teas as well as some tasty breakfast sandwiches. While the branches vary wildly in size, the high standard of the coffees is much the same. Click my post for locations of the nicest branches to visit.

Latte Prices: Medium - NT$65 / Large - NT$85

Click here to read more about Louisa

Unicofa Coffee

Much like Louisa, Unicofa sell well-priced and good quality espresso-based coffees, although they only have a handful of branches located around Taipei.

Latte Prices: Medium only - NT$65

Click here to read more about Unicofa Coffee

Yolo's Cafe

Yolo's have several cafes located around Taipei, and serve good value beverages and some nice snacks including hot dogs and toasties.

Latte Prices: Medium - NT$65 / Large - NT$85

Click here to read more about the Yolo's Cafe

Ray Cafe

With just one cafe found in the heart of Taipei's East District, Ray Cafe serves a large range of very good espresso-based coffees, drip coffees and flavoured milk drinks. Their waffles are also worth a try.

Latte Prices: Small - NT$60 / Large - NT$80

Click here to read more about Ray Cafe

Honourable Mention - 7-Eleven

If you're looking for a cheap coffee to go, 7-Eleven sell probably the cheapest in Taipei. While other convenience stores also sell coffees for the same price, 7-Eleven use the same coffee beans as Starbucks, and they taste very good for the price.

As a bonus, 7-Eleven will often have buy-one-get-second-half-price deals, which you can even buy in bulk and use any time (although it must be from the same store you purchased your original coffee from).

title: Cheap Coffees & Teas at Unicofa Coffee
excerpt: A Taiwanese cafe chain offering some of the cheapest coffee in the city, in the same vein as Louisa - and a Golden Cup Award winner too.
content:
A Taiwanese cafe chain with a few locations around Taipei, Unicofa Coffee (歐克法咖啡) serves some of the cheapest beverages in the city. It's not just about the price either – founded in 2013, they've picked up a Golden Cup Award from the Taipei Specialty Coffee Association in the espresso category, for a blend built from Brazilian, Ethiopian, El Salvadoran and Guatemalan beans, all scoring above 80 points by SCA standards.

With a similar pricing to the very popular Louisa Cafes, the success of that chain has inspired Unicofa to offer a similar experience, serving a selection of decent and competitively priced drinks.

Much like Louisa, some of the Unicofa cafes are quite small, although there are others with more space and seating available. The cafes are quite basic but for the price you need to pay for drinks here, how can anyone complain?

Unicofa serve a large selection of espresso based coffees, hot or iced, in just one size for between NT$60 and NT$65, which compared to most cafes in Taipei is one-half or even one-third the cost of these.

They also serve fruit teas, English teas, smoothies, single origin coffees and a few other drinks.

Great value, good taste.

Menu

Traveller Tips

Ideal for takeaways. The English level is okay (there's English on the menu), and while it's not quite Louisa, for the price it's hard to complain.

title: Where to Get Your Quick & Healthy Fix in Taipei
excerpt: Where to find a quick and healthy meal in Taipei that's light but filling enough to keep you going - from customisable poke bowls to nourishing bento boxes.
content:
If you're looking for a quick and healthy meal that's light yet filling enough to keep your energy levels up, Taipei now has some great little establishments that offer exactly that.

Click here to see all my 'best of' lists

Haloa Poke

In my opinion the best of the many Poke places now in Taipei, Haloa Poke serves some fine Hawaiian style bowls, tucked away in the Zhongzheng district close to the 228 Peace Memorial Park. If you don't like the sound of any of their four set bowls, you can make your own from the extensive list of fine ingredients for NT$135.

Click here to read more about Haloa Poke

Miss Energy

Miss Energy has quickly grown from just a single small branch into at least six now found within central Taipei. Mainly catering to business lunch hours and closed over the weekend, their bento-style boxes are healthy and filling, cost only around NT$100, and are ideal for taking away - calories are even shown on the menu for each one, ranging from about 430 to 540.

Click here to read more about the Miss Energy

Yu Poke

Another Hawaiian Poke place that comes highly recommended, Yu Poke can be found in the heart of the Gongguan Night Market. The location means that queuing for your poke is highly likely, but it's worth the wait as their fully customisable bowls - fish or meat, base, four mixes, sauce and topping - cost just NT$160 and are fresh, tasty and healthy.

Click here to see all the places to visit for a quick meal

title: Haloa Poke - Healthy & Tasty Hawaiian Bowls
excerpt: Fresh Hawaiian poke bowls in Zhongzheng, one of only a handful of places in Taipei doing them properly.
content:
Before coming to Taiwan, I was completely unaware what exactly a poke dish was. Now I'm here, I can't get enough of them. Haloa Poke is one of a few poke places in Taipei, selling delicious and fresh Hawaiian bowls.

Located in the Zhongzheng district, very close to the 228 Peace Memorial Park, it's a small place which gets much of its business from takeaways. There are a few seats inside however, which is one of the more modern and clean places I've eaten in.

Haloa Poke have a choice of four bowls. If none of these appeal, you can also make-your-own bowl.

The four bowls available contain either Salmon & Tuna, Chicken & Shrimp, Tuna & Chicken or Non-GM Tofu. All these come with a selection of vegetables, avocado sauce, and a choice of white/brown/half-and-half rice or mixed greens.

For the custom bowl, you get the same choice of bases, one choice of protein, 5 toppings, a sauce and a sprinkle.

Being my first visit, I went for one of the set bowls - the Chicken & Shrimp, with half-and-half rice.

Very neatly presented in a wooden bowl, with cute wooden cutlery and tray.

The vegetables they choose for your bowl will change according to the time of year, but I was happy with all the ingredients here. Everything was fresh and crunchy when it needed to be, and the chicken and shrimp were both succulent.

The sauce brought everything together along with the sprinkling of sesame. Maybe the only complaint was with the rather stingy amount of rice. I'm not a big eater, so it was fine for me but I'm sure others would disagree.

I suppose you could always customise your bowl instead, and add extra elements. The custom bowls cost NT$135, but you can top up with more rice or other items for a bit extra.

Think I'll be doing that next time. The fresh ingredients, nice presentation and clean eating environment all add up to the best poke place I've been to in Taipei.

Delicious, fresh and healthy!

Menu

Pros

  • Fresh and tasty
  • Very clean environment

Cons

  • Not much seating
  • Probably won't satisfy everyone's hunger

title: Cafe Costumice - Great for Working or Socialising
excerpt: A relaxed East District cafe good for working, socialising or an outdoor drink, with comfortable indoor seating too.
content:
Found in the East District of Taipei, Cafe Costumice is a very cool and relaxed place that's great for working, socialising or enjoying an outdoor drink.

With a great indoor seating area, Cafe Costumice has some very comfortable seating that's perfect for a relaxed drink.

The other side of the room is designed more for working, with a large table that even has a four-way plug extension in the middle. I struggle to find plugs in so many cafes I've been to in Taipei, so this was more than welcome.

I believe one of the owners of Cafe Costumice is a clothes designer, who obviously has a knack for interior design too.

It really is one of the most nicely decked out cafes I've been to in Taipei, which looks especially nice once it gets dark. They'll dim the lights and bring out gaslights for each table.

Cafe Costumice has some of the nicest outdoor seating found anywhere in central Taipei. The cafe's location, towards the end of a no-through-road, also means that there is little traffic noise. The main outside seating area is covered, with enough room for around 25 people.

There's also a smaller seating area for people to relax or smoke, and many well-placed plants throughout the area.

Serving teas and coffees, Cafe Costumice also have a range of draft beers, including Taihu and 23, and sell a selection of cakes and other small bites.

The Caramel Milk Tea and Cheesecake I tried were actually rather delicious.

If you're coming here to work, the music is never too intrusive, although sometimes the chatter does get a bit too much. But the WiFi is good, and the mere fact that there are plugs here is a massive bonus.

Cafe Costumice will definitely become one of my go-to places to work. If you see me in there, say hi!

Pros

  • Great indoor and outdoor seating areas
  • Plugs!

Cons

  • Slightly noisy

Price: $$$

Level of English: Good (English on menu)

Go earlier to avoid the busiest and noisiest times

title: Monstrous Breakfasts at Golden Flower Grilled Toast
excerpt: A messy, indulgent toasted-sandwich spot tucked behind the Ximending Outdoor Drinking Area. Not for the health-conscious.
content:
If you're looking for a really sticky, messy and unhealthy breakfast bite, Golden Flower Grilled Toast is the place to visit.

Located directly behind the Outdoor Drinking Area in Ximending, this small breakfast spot specialises in toasted sandwiches, some of which come smothered in melted cheese that will certainly do no favours to your waistline.

The menu above their counter reminds me of an old B-Movie poster - maybe it was Attack of the Giant Cheese Monsters, featuring Gorgonzilla.

Anyway.

Golden Flower Grilled Toast's menu is a bit confusing. The one they will hand you doesn't seem to have everything, as there were others I noticed above their counter. Being a huge fan of tuna melts, I cast my eyes on the Tuna Fish & Lemon Curd. It didn't look as monstrous as some of the others, and I'm not a huge eater in the morning.

More like a mini-monster. It did look very appetising though, although I didn't have a clue how I was going to eat it. Thankfully, Golden Flower Grilled Toast provide disposable gloves to eat them with, along with plenty of tissues.

Some of the menu items above the counter aren't translated unfortunately, but the staff are versed enough in English to translate them for you. We pointed to one of the monsters, which I believe was the Pork Floss with Cheese, Egg & Condensed Milk, which came with a sprinkling of seaweed.

Once we figured out how to eat them, they were both quite delicious. The toast was still crispy and not soggy thankfully, and the filling tasted as good as they looked. The lemon curd in the tuna worked well, and not too overpowering. The pork one was slightly sweet but not too much so.

Golden Flower Grilled Toast also have many not cheesy sandwiches, some of which come with 6 slices of toast and many different fillings. These looked too large for us, but we did try one of their Taiwanese Egg Rolls (known as Dan Bing), which are like savoury crepes. The Tuna Fish Salad Egg Roll was a very decent effort. Not sure why they said there was salad in it though.

One final confusing thing about Golden Flower Grilled Toast is they also have a tea shop next door but one. If you buy one of the few drinks they have at the grilled toast place, they'll give you a receipt to take to the tea shop to get it.

However, the tea shop has a much wider range of drinks, including bubble teas and milkshakes, so it's best just to buy from directly from there.

There is limited covered outdoor seating here, which does often get filled up. However, the Ximending Outdoor Drinking Area is literally 10 seconds away, and is virtually empty during the day, so you can use these instead.

Although it's a bit difficult to get your head around ordering here, Golden Flower Grilled Toast do serve some delicious toasted treats that will definitely give you the energy needed for a morning of sightseeing.

title: Fuhang Soy Milk - Taipei's Most Popular Breakfast
excerpt: Taipei's most famous breakfast, Michelin-listed and serving since 1958. What to order, how long the queue really is, and when to arrive.
content:
Unquestionably the most popular breakfast spot in Taipei, Fuhang Soy Milk is also one of the oldest and most respected.

They have been serving up breakfasts to the locals since 1958, and over time have become a number one choice for a local breakfast. They have also been represented in the Michelin Guide for the last few years, including this one.

Due to this, if you want to give Fuhang Soy Milk a try, I suggest you come early.

This is what the queue looks like at 08:15 on a weekday. It took us about 20 minutes to get served.

At 09:15, the queue had extended around the corner, with waiting times of about an hour.

Queue times over the weekend are much longer, so I would strongly recommend going Tuesday to Friday (it is closed on Mondays).

As Fuhang Soy Milk's name suggests, one of the main reasons local folk (and now tourists) flock here is their Soy Milk.

The sweet ones are served hot or cold, and come served in either a bowl, much like soup, or a cup.

The salty ones must be served in a bowl, since they come with green onion, pickles and bits of shrimp - not great for drinking I imagine!

Ordering food at Fuhang Soy Milk is quite straight forward. You choose which soy milk you want first. They'll then hand you a menu with English and pictures (see menu section), and you can simply point. Over the years of working here, some of the staff can speak decent English too.

It probably is worthwhile spending some time thinking about what you are going to order before you get here though, as you will be rushed if you take too long.

Another dish Fuhang Soy Milk are famous for are their Deep Fried Chinese Donuts (or savoury churros as we prefer to call them). These are served in a choice of two types of bread or on their own. Their signature dish for these, is the Thick Bread with Eggs and Donut Stick.

The fried eggs are mixed with scallion, but apart from that, it's exactly what it says on the tin. The churros are light and crispy (and not too greasy as they are in other places). A delicious meal that will fill most mortals up!

The eggs can also be purchased separately if desired.

You can also purchase a Chinese Donut inside flat bread. You'll see them making both types of bread, baked in a special barrel-like oven as you're queuing to be served. The breads can also be purchased on their own, or just with the egg if you think that the addition of the churro will be just too much.

Fuhang Soy Milk also bake 3 types of buns, with either caramel, scallion or dried radish, and all topped with sesame seeds. If you found yourself ordering too much (as most people do), these are great for eating later.

Another thing I would recommend (although in truth I've not tried them here) are the Egg Pancakes. Locally known as Dan Bing, these are some of my favourite breakfast items in Taipei. They're basically like savoury crepes, and done well they're delicious.

You won't have trouble finding tables here, as Fuhang Soy Milk is part of a large shared dining hall with loads of small tables, and a couple of larger ones for sharing.

A typical breakfast for 2 (including soy milk of course) will set you back just over NT$200, which is great value, especially since you're likely to not get hungry again until at least a few hours.

Is Fuhang Soy Milk worth the wait? I probably wouldn't queue up for over 40 minutes to dine here, as there are good alternatives in Taipei such as Yong He Soy Milk King. However, if you do manage to beat most of the queues then it's certainly worth visiting to sample their delicious soy milk and Chinese donuts!

Menu

Pros

  • Top class Taiwanese breakfast
  • Large seating area

Cons

  • Huge queues to be expected

Price: $

Level of English: Some (English menu available)

Traveller Tips

Get here before 08:30 on a weekday to avoid long queues

Closed on Mondays

Fuhang Soy Milk Location

title: Taihu Ales with a Beach Vibe at Driftwood
excerpt: The original Taihu craft beer bar in Ximending, attached to the Papa Whale hotel. What the vibe is like and what's on tap.
content:
Driftwood was the first Taihu bar I experienced in Taipei. Located in the Ximending area, it's adjoined onto the very cool Papa Whale hotel, and it seems that a lot of that coolness has drifted into this hip bar.

Maybe cool is the wrong word. Driftwood have gone for the opposite. More of a summery hot vibe would be more apt, as their bar is styled into a beach hut of sorts.

With the walls, floors and beams largely made of wood (driftwood perhaps), some of the tables have little angular straw roofs, while drapes of cloth hang over other areas. Supping one of their fine ales here really does give you a tropical beach holiday vibe.

The windows at the front of the bar are usually fully open, letting in a nice breeze that only adds to the sense of being in the open.

For those not in the know, Taihu is arguably the largest producer of craft beer in Taiwan, and also one of the best. Their range of ales is quite vast, and cater to everyone's tastes - be it light or dark, fruity or sour.

I'm not going to go into detail here, as the ales here are much the same as their other two bars. If you're interested, you could read one of these posts:

Click to read about Taihu Craft Beer Tasting Room
Click to read about Landmark Taihu

Drinks are served in small 330ml glasses or larger 500ml ones. Pricing at Driftwood is much the same as their other bars too, with the smaller drinks costing anything over NT$200, while the larger ones priced about NT$100 extra.

The clientele at Driftwood is a good mixture of both locals and foreign-folk. There was a nice buzz to the vibe without it being too noisy, even though it became rather full later on.

Out of the three Taihu bars, this one is probably the best for a relaxed drink. There is bar food available here, but if you're looking for a meal with your drink, head on over to their craft beer tasting room. They have a larger selection of ales and have great food too.

Pros

  • Great range of Taihu ales
  • Exotic setting

Cons

  • Ales are quite expensive

Traveller Tips

You can also try a flight of smaller ales, which come with four 200ml glasses

Driftwood Location

title: Movie Themed Cocktails at Hanko 60
excerpt: A speakeasy cocktail bar in Ximending disguised as a retro cinema showing only Bruce Lee films. How to find the entrance.
content:
Ximending is cinema capital of Taipei. One of the coolest cinemas in the area is Hanko 60.

Showing only Bruce Lee movies, Hanko 60 is...

Ok. You got me. It's not really a cinema. Hanko 60 is in fact a speakeasy cocktail bar disguised as a retro cinema, which has arguably the coolest front entrance in Taipei.

Mixing movie/television themed cocktails, they have a large selection of fun and frivolous cocktails designed to have that wow factor.

Now I'm going to get one thing straight here. If you're looking for the best cocktails in Taipei, I would suggest you go elsewhere. Hanko 60's cocktails do look the part...but that's where it ends. Taste-wise, they're not bad - just not great.

Having said that, for novelty value, Hanko 60 would get an 88% rating on Rotten Tomatoes.

For taste however, they would get a Hanko 60%. Certainly not deserving of the 4.9 rating on Google maps (YVVM).

The True Blood cocktail comes in a blood bag of course, with dry-ice added to give it a spooky cinematic effect. Combining vodka, blueberry and a heering cherry brandy, it was distinctly average in taste.

The Movie Street on the other hand, is cleverly disguised as a bag of popcorn. It's a great way to smuggle drinks into a cinema. Mixing rum, yogurt liqueur, milk and sea salt, it's quite sickly sweet and difficult to finish.

Hanko 60 do mix a range of classic cocktails too, and have an interesting selection of bar food available, including fish cigars, which are spring rolls made to look like cigars. Their Fried Tempura, which we thought was going to be tempura vegetables, was actually more like prawn crackers. They were surprisingly good.

Another disappointing aspect of Hanko 60 is the interior of the bar. It really is nothing special, and I've been to much nicer bars in Taipei.

I would never have recommended Hanko 60 if it wasn't for the novelty factor. Geeks like movie related gimmicks, and Hanko 60 ticks all those boxes in that regard.

Pros

  • Very cool entrance
  • Fun cocktails

Cons

  • Don't expect the cocktails to taste great
  • Interior nothing special

Traveller Tips

Booking ahead is advised, especially on weekends

Hanko 60 Location

📍 Closest MRT: Ximen Station (green/blue lines - exit 1)

title: Swing in a Hammock Chair at Wengu Cafe (Permanently Closed)
content:
Permanent Closure Notice

Please note: Wengu Cafe has permanently closed.

As cool cafes go, they don't come much cooler than Wengu Cafe. Found in the east district of Taipei, this small but delightful cafe is a relaxed environment and a great escape of the busy streets outside.

Even from the outside, Wengu Cafe screams cool. Plants are a central feature before you walk in, and even more so inside.

The serving area is virtually camouflaged by plants, with many others around the walls and neatly placed on shelves.

But the coolest part about Wengu Cafe are the swinging hammock chairs suspended from the ceiling as you walk in.

With six in total, they were all unfortunately taken when we were there. We found out later that reservations are accepted here, so I imagine you can specifically reserve a hammock chair. Message them from their Facebook page.

Wengu Cafe is a small place, with about 6 other tables. We have tried to come here before at the weekend and were turned away as it was full to the brim. Since we didn't realise we could reserve a spot, this time we arrived early afternoon during the week when it wasn't too busy.

The rest of the seating is nice enough, and I really like the music they play here. Interesting folk music that was certainly very different to any other cafe we've visited in Taipei.

They do have some food at Wengu Cafe, although I've heard it's nothing special. The drinks however are very nice.

I know what you're thinking. Yes, it is actually a drink. Their 'signature plant beverages' are ingenious plant-pot-like drinks with a layer of cocoa on top and a sprig of mint. The Plant Cocoa and Iced Yuzu Citron Tea were both very well made drinks.

Service here is also on point. The guy serving us (I'm not sure if he was the owner) was friendly and attentive.

We'll no doubt be returning to Wengu Cafe - next time we'll book ahead though!

Pros

  • Hammock chairs can be reserved
  • Very nice drinks
  • Cool environment

Cons

  • Small place
  • Average food (so I've heard)

Price: $$$

Level of English: Good (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

Reserve your hammock today!

title: Rooftop View of Taipei 101 at Tap Bistro Zhangmen (Permanently Closed)
content:
Permanent Closure Notice

Please note: Tap Bistro Zhangmen has permanently closed.

Permanent Closure Notice

Please note: Tap Bistro Zhangmen has permanently closed.

If you're looking for a place to drink on a rooftop with views of Taipei 101, probably the most popular place to visit would be Frank. This does have a couple of drawbacks however. You'll normally need to queue there, and Frank's late opening times of 9 pm is far from ideal.

Tap Bistro Zhangmen, on the other hand, is a great little bar/bistro you can usually walk straight in to, and opens much earlier.

The only problem is finding it!

Located on the 4th floor of the Breeze Songgao mall, you'll need to locate the elevator near one of doors outside the mall, which is on the ground floor (1F) between the malls.

Just look out for the Zhangmen sign, walk inside and take the elevator directly inside to the 4th floor, which will take you straight to the bar.

Tap Bistro Zhangmen's inside space is small, with only a few tables.

Although there are a few other Zhangmen bars in Taipei, I had yet to try any of them. Zhangmen is a Taiwanese brewery established in 2014 who have since expanded overseas. Tap Bistro Zhangmen serves a selection of their ales, plus some bistro-type bar food.

Ales cost between NT$200 and NT$240 for a small 330ml glass, which is definitely not on the cheap side, but it's worth it for you view when you walk outside.

It's a very large seating area, although most of the seats were folded away as it had been raining. They describe the area as 200 ping in size, which in English equates to around 650 sq m.

With fantastic views of Taipei 101, I'm sure that when the weather is nicer, Tap Bistro Zhangmen will draw quite a crowd.

I've yet to try any of the food here, which consists of fried items such as french fries, onion rings and mozzarella sticks. They also have pizza, pasta, chicken wings and a few others on their rather compact menu.

I will need to pay Tap Bistro Zhangmen another visit when the weather is nicer, but for a outdoor ale with great views, it's surely one of the best places to visit in Taipei.

Pros

  • Great outdoor seating with views of Taipei 101
  • Nice tap ales
  • Early opening hours

Cons

  • Difficult to find
