title: Admire the Beautiful Hsing Tian Kong Temple
excerpt: A working temple dedicated to Kuan Yu, and the first in Taiwan to ban incense entirely in 2014. What happens inside and how to take part respectfully.
content:
Kuan Yu is the primary deity worshipped at Hsing Tian Kong Temple, who possessed great loyalty and justice among men. The God has thus become as famous as Confucius, and has also been honoured by the name Kuan En Zu - meaning saviour of the world.

Hsing Tian Kong Temple was one of three built under the guidance of Master Hsuan Kung (黃欉), a coal mine businessman turned devotee who personally funded all three and served as their first chief abbot. The Beitou branch came first in 1960, followed by the Sanxia Xingxiu Temple in 1965, with this main Zhongshan District temple completed last, on 25th January 1968.

People will come in their droves to pay their respect and ask for answers to important questions.

By throwing divination blocks (two wooden objects with one flat side) onto the ground, they will pose a question that only requires a yes/no answer.

How the blocks land will determine the answer:

  • One lands flat side up, the other rounded side up - 'Yes' answer
  • Both land rounded side up - 'No' answer
  • Both land flat side up - Uncertain

If the answer is uncertain, they will essentially throw again until a definitive answer is returned.

Look out too for the temple's shou jing (soul-calming) ritual, performed for free by volunteers in blue robes – mostly elderly women – usually between 11:20am and 6:30pm. It's meant to settle a person's spirit after a fright or a run of bad luck, gently coaxing it back into the body.

Since August 2014, Hsing Tian Kong has also been the first major temple in Taiwan to ban burning incense altogether, removing its censers and offering tables in favour of worshipping with clasped hands alone. It followed Master Hsuan Kung's own teaching: that arriving without incense or flowers doesn't matter, since a good heart naturally gives off its own moral fragrance – the offering the deity likes best. Only fresh flowers and clear tea are left on the altar today.

One of the most sacred temples in Taiwan, the Hsing Tian Kong Temple is a beautiful and tranquil place – just be aware it's only served by the orange line, so it takes a little more effort to reach than some of the more central temples.

Traveller Tips

Ensure you are dressed appropriately

title: See the Drinking Water Museum at Taipei Water Park
excerpt: A baroque pumping station turned museum, set in a park that is far nicer than Google Maps suggests. Tickets, hours and what to see.
content:
Until recently, I had little intention of going to the Taipei Water Park, as it's described on Google Maps as an amusement arcade. While this is true in part, it's largely a great area to walk around, with a nice little museum and many trails that lead you to great vantage points for viewing Taipei.

One of the trails leads to the Treasure Hill Artists' Village, which in it's own right is a great place to explore.

The amusement arcade reference comes from Road Castle, which is a children's water park and costs extra to enter. The cost to enter the rest of the site is only NT$50 or NT$80, depending on the time of year you go.

The Museum of Drinking Water is a relic to the bygone days of water filtration and purification.

Built in 1908, this Grade-3 listed building was used as a pumping station to send the filtered water to a large reservoir high on the hill, which could take advantage of the high location and let gravity do the rest, sending the water to the residents and businesses below.

All the original piping and equipment within the old pumping station can be perused up close and personal. In it's day, the plant was able to produce 480,000 tonnes of clean water per day.

Outside the museum, the many paths within the water park will take you to other parts of the plant, including the reservoir where the water was sent to.

Other paths lead to areas offering great views of Taipei.

As previously mentioned, one of these paths will take you to Treasure Hill, an artists village set on the hillside. I would definitely recommend paying this a visit too, but be aware that once you leave the water park area, you're unable to get back in. The one-way gate will prevent you from doing so!

The Taipei Water Park is a lovely place to visit, to escape the hectic Gongguan area for a while, and with the added bonus of getting easy access to Treasure Hill, it will provide a nice scenic afternoon.

  • Small but nice museum
  • Many walking trails
  • Easy access to Treasure Hill

title: Ho's Sweet Potato Balls - Light and Crispy
excerpt: A Gongguan Night Market stall with a near-permanent queue, selling light, crispy sweet potato balls.
content:
We've walked past this small stand in the Gongguan Night Market many times, and each time there's a enormous queue of people that winds around the corner.

Fortunately, we walked past one day and the queue was only about 20 people deep. We quickly joined it and waited while they made their sweet potato balls.

The team of four each have their own role. The old lady will roll and cut the dough, then pass them onto a guy a the back who will carefully tend to the frying, tossing and squeezing the balls until the are light and golden.

They are then drained and ready to serve. You can purchase the balls in three sizes, with the small portion containing around 6, the medium around 10, and the large portion of over 20. These cost NT$20, NT$30 and NT$50 respectively, and we opted for the medium size.

We've tried sweet potato balls from many other stands in Taipei, and it was immediately clear why this one was proving just so popular. By far the lightest and crispiest we've tried, completely devoid of any grease. The size of the balls is much larger too, no doubt due to just how airy they become.

The balls have a lovely crispy texture, but once you start to eat them they turn more chewy. Absolutely delicious!

Ho's Sweet Potato Balls is certainly one of the must-try food stands in Gongguan!

Pros

  • Very cheap
  • Best sweet potato balls in Taipei

Cons

  • Huge queue likely

Price: $

Level of English: Low (No English on menu)

Traveller Tips

Try to avoid coming here at the weekend

title: FuMu - Amazing Authentic English Breakfasts
excerpt: Authentic English breakfasts in Taipei, served by the Mama side of a restaurant that turns into a bar at night. What we ate and what it cost.
content:
FuMu has a split personality. By day, the 'Mama' side serves breakfasts which cater to both western and eastern tastes. By night, the 'Dada' side takes over as it becomes more of a bar.

As we really fancied a breakfast, we went in the morning to see what Mama could serve up.

We really liked the layout of the restaurant. It has a nice summery vibe, with the walls covered in retro posters, and wooden panelling on the walls, floor and ceiling. I usually tend to avoid the subject of Toilets. Many of Taipei's restaurants can sometimes leave a lot to be desired, but the ones here are spotless and smell fresh.

They have an excellent sound system here too, and the 80's tunes they've picked adds to the vibe. With the likes of Tears for Fears, Madness, Duran Duran, OMD and Fleetwood Mac, FuMu plays some of the best music I've heard in any Taipei restaurant!

FuMu's menu has a lot of very tempting breakfast dishes. However, I came for the full English breakfast, of which they have two choices. The standard or the jumbo. Both come with toast, fried egg, grilled tomato, baked beans, sausage, mushroom and bacon. The jumbo comes with an extra sausage and egg, hash browns and black tea/coffee.

I chose the standard English Breakfast and was extremely pleased with what came out.

It looked exactly like many I've had in the UK, and came with a good helping of baked beans. But looks aren't everything...it's the taste that really matters.

It didn't disappoint.

I'm sure the chef/owner must have lived in the UK for some time (they are Taiwanese), as I couldn't fault this in any way. In fact, it was better than most I've tried in the UK too. At only NT$200, we thought it was very, very well priced.

I will have to come back to try the jumbo version too!

The Mama's Breakfast Board is another dish we had to try, as it comes with egg 'n' soldiers, which is something I've not eaten since moving to Taipei. It also comes with asparagus, grilled tomato, a mixed berry smoothie, hash browns and a green juice shot (which was kale).

The egg was cooked to perfection, and coupled with the toast fingers, butter and some salt, it really was a blast from the past. The hash browns and smoothie, which turned out to be more of a yogurt than drink, were also excellent. The cost of all this? Only NT$150, which if you ask me, is an absolute bargain!

Another breakfast item we rarely see in Taipei are breakfast butties. Fumu has bacon and Sausage Butties (with a choice of either breakfast or chorizo sausages). Seeing as it was breakfast, we chose the former.

The butties also contain fried onion and peppers, and mustard. The butty tasted great - just like the sausages back home - and the chips were crispy and delicious too.

Fumu even has sausage rolls, which is another thing I have rarely (if ever) seen in Taipei. These come on their own (NT$100 each), or as a set with baken beans and two eggs. Another thing to add to my 'to eat' list.

If you prefer to try a more traditional breakfast, Fumu make an excellent with Dan Bing (Taiwanese breakfast pancakes) along with turnip cake and a hash brown.

The Dan Bing comes with a choice of fillings, including tuna, bacon, and cheese. This also comes with a pot of tea, all for only NT$150.

Drinks-wise, there's the usual mix of espresso coffees and teas, while their fab orange juice is freshly squeezed and comes in an extra large glass. Or if you prefer some hair-of-the-dog, there are bloody Marys and espresso martinis available.

Another great thing about FuMu is that they have no 10% service charge, so what-you-see-is-what-you-pay-for!

I have a feeling that FuMu is going to become a regular breakfast place of ours, as it's fairly centrally located, great value, and above all, serves the most authentic English style breakfasts in Taipei!

Pros

  • Good value
  • Nice toilets

title: Take a Walk Through the Bopiliao Historical Block
excerpt: A well-preserved Qing Dynasty street that was once one of Taipei's busiest passages. What survives today and how to see it.
content:
Known today as Kangding Road, the Bopiliao Historical Block is a well-preserved Qing Dynasty street which formed over 200 years ago as a key route between Monga (modern-day Wanhua) and Guting.

The name itself is a bit of a mystery. The popular story is that it comes from stripping bark off timber shipped in from Fuzhou, or from an old hide-tanning pool – but neither has solid evidence behind it. The best-documented explanation is more mundane: old land deeds recorded the area as "Bak-phoe-liau", and since that sounds almost identical to "Bopiliao" in Hokkien, the name likely just drifted into its current form over time.

This made it one of the busiest and wealthiest areas in Taipei, until Japanese rule in the early 20th century displaced the street with newer roads. In 1941, the block was zoned as the future site of Laosong Elementary School, which froze it against redevelopment even as it fell into disuse – the very restriction that ended up preserving its mix of Hokkien and Western-style architecture.

The Taipei City Government began renovating the area in earnest from 2003 until 2009, and it's become considerably more famous since – the 2010 gangster film Monga, set in 1980s Taipei, was shot on location here, and tourism has followed. Current work is still going on, and they are extending the street with new buildings in the same style.

Many of the buildings are open to the public, and a museum can be found towards the end of the street, with exhibitions on education and health.

The street is located very close to Longshan Temple and the Huaxi Street Night Market, so come in the early evening before it gets dark. Then you can see the beautiful temple at night and visit the night market, making it an evening well spent.

  • Free

title: How to use the Gym at a Public Sports Centre
excerpt: Every Taipei district has a public sports centre with a pay-as-you-go gym — no membership needed for a short stay.
content:
Taipei has a public sports centre located in every district in Taipei. Each one is equipped with a number of different sporting facilities, including a public gym which anyone can visit on a pay-as-you-go basis.

If you're only in Taipei for a short while, or don't want to commit yourself to a membership, sports centre gyms are a cheap and convenient way to keep fit.

The gyms will be busiest at evenings and over the weekend but there's always equipment available to use. If you click on a specific sports centre on the map below and click the link in the description, most will tell you how many people are currently using the gym, along with its capacity.

The locations of the sports centres are:

Depending on the one you visit, the variety and quality of the gym equipment will vary, but all will come with the basic equipment.

Cardio-vascular
Treadmills, Cycle Training Machines, Ladder Machines, Rowing Machines, Cross-training Machines

Weight Training
Back stretcher, Abdominal Training Chair, Flat Pusher, Tilting Bench, Weight Lifting, Bicep Curling, Lifting Frame, Abdominal Flexion Rack, Lower Extremity Pusher, Shoulder Pusher, Chest Pusher, Sitting Butterfly/Rear Deltoid Trainer, Back Stretcher, Waist Rotation Trainer, Hip Contraction, Smith Training Stand, Single Parallel Weight Auxiliary Training Machine, Stretching Training Machine, Functional Training Station

Probably the newest and best of the gyms is the Danshui Sports Centre, although this is also the furthest from the city. Older gyms such as the Xinyi one are still fine for most people.

How to Use the Gym at a Sports Centre

When you arrive at the sports centre, you'll first need to purchase a card from the service counter, usually found on the first floor.

These will cost NT$50 per hour, and will give you access to all the gym equipment. If you are planning on going multiple times, there are some good deals available (see Prices section).

Before you enter the gym, you can lock any belongings in one of the lockers for NT$10 (make sure you have a coin handy).

They only allow small bags into the gym and you'll need to take a towel, otherwise you won't be let in.

Hold the card against the turnstile, and keep it safe as you'll need to when you're leaving.

Most of the gym equipment is easy to use, and they do have English instructions.

With so many locations spread across the city, there's no excuse not to get fit!

title: First Class Brunch at ACME Breakfast Club
excerpt: Now relocated to the Taipei Performing Arts Center in Shilin as ACME Cafe Bar & Restaurant. What the brunch is like and whether it is worth the trip.
content:
ACME Breakfast Club has now relocated to within the Taipei Performing Arts Center in Shilin, under the new name ACME｜Cafe Bar & Restaurant. They are still serving their delicious brunches!

We've been meaning to try the ACME Breakfast Club for some time now, ever since it came under our radar when we saw the delightful looking pictures of their food on Google.

All I can say is, we wish it hadn't taken us so long. The food here tastes every bit as good as it looks!

Located in Ximending, on the third floor of a building tucked away down a side street, we were hoping to book a table here as it's unclear from their website if this is possible.

Unfortunately, no reservations are allowed, and we were told that there's normally a wait.

When we arrived (about 13:30), there were two groups in front of us and we were told it would be about a 30 minute wait. We had plenty of time so this wasn't a problem, and it gave us enough time to decide what to have.

Their menu isn't huge, but there are so many inviting dishes it took us the full 30 minutes to choose.

We were going to try their set meal for 2, which includes two meals, fries, desserts and drinks, but this seemed a little too much.

I opted for the Tuna Patties with Eggs Benedict and Smoked Salmon. Boy was I happy with my choice!

The tuna patties reminded me of fish cakes, crispy on the outside and a soft centre. Combined with the perfectly poached eggs, salmon and Hollandaise sauce, it was by far the best eggs Benedict dish I've had in Taipei. Up there with the best breakfast dishes I've had here.

My girlfriend chose the Seared Chicken Breast Salad Bowl – one of the better salads in Taipei. Coming with grilled pumpkin, lettuce, tomatoes, a boiled egg and a pesto sauce, it was another cracker.

The sauce was so good we were going to ask them how it was made. The only ingredient we thought was astray were the raspberries - they really didn't belong here, but just a minor quibble.

These were the two most expensive items on their menu, at NT$340 each but were totally worth the money!

We have since revisited ACME Breakfast Club to try a couple more of their dishes to see if they could reach the dizzy heights of these.

The Mashed Avocado Toast with Poached Eggs was the one that took my fancy. Another very handsome plate of food, again perfectly executed, with the rich egg yolk coupled with the soft avocado mash and toast a winning combination.

Although their menu is mainly savoury, there are 3 sweet brunch options available. The Acai Smoothie bowl was a tempter, but French Toast with Fresh Figs and Strawberries was the one we chose.

The presentation, like with all the dishes was immaculate. We were really hoping it would taste as good as it looked, and you know what? It did! The best French toast we've tried in Taipei, soft in the middle, slightly crispy on the outside and deliciously sweet. Combined with the syrup and the sweet fruit and a sprinkling of pistachios, it's definitely only for those with a very sweet tooth. But it was a crackerjack!

Since the ACME Breakfast Club is an all day breakfast place, their drinks include alcoholic ones such as beers, ciders, cocktails and wines. These all look very tempting but it was too early.

We went for the Hot Ginger Sugar Latte and Mixed Berries Yogurt Smoothie. Juices, teas, milk shakes and others are available. My smoothie was smooth and fruity, and the latte had a hint of ginger (maybe we were looking for more of a kick?).

All the ingredients at the ACME Breakfast Club are internationally sourced. We saw that they used some of the best Greek yogurt for the smoothie, and it was clear from our meals that the produce was all top grade.

Like I said, we've already been back here since and will no doubt be coming a few more times to give most things on their menu a try, and maybe even try a couple of their alcoholic drinks.

ACME Breakfast Club is up there with the very best brunches we've had in Taipei, and is a club you should definitely join!

Pros

  • Food tastes as good as it looks
  • Airy and inviting room

Cons

  • No reservations

Price: $$$

Try their set menus for 2 or 4 people (see menu section).

title: Addiction Aquatic Development - For Seafood Addicts
excerpt: Taipei's largest fish market rebuilt as a seafood experience: standing sushi bars, a grill, a supermarket and what to order at each.
content:
If you love seafood, then Addiction Aquatic Development is the place in Taipei to visit.

The largest fish market in the city also doubles as the ultimate seafood experience. With several restaurants, an aquamarine and a small but fantastic supermarket, walking around the well designed contemporary areas will certainly give you a sense of anticipation of what's to come.

There are six seafood restaurants found in Addiction Aquatic Development:

  • The Charcoal Grill
  • Tresors de la Mer
  • The Hot Pot
  • The Sushi Bar
  • The Seafood Bar
  • The Seafood Snacks

Only the Hot Pot and Tresors de la Mer restaurants can be reserved beforehand.

The main restaurant is the Charcoal Grill, which is set within a large covered outdoor area.

The space has been very well thought out, and has a large screen showing old movies such as Charlie Chaplain.

The waiters here will show you around the huge selection of seafood. If you find something that takes your fancy, they tell you how it will be cooked before you order it. With so much variety on offer, it's easy to get carried away.

As the restaurant name suggests, most of the seafood is char-grilled, but some crustaceans will need to be boiled.

To accompany the seafood, they have a wide selection of vegetables and meats. As much as I enjoy a surf and turf, it felt slightly wrong to get meat in a fish market so we just opted for vegetables.

The food will be cooked and the waiters will periodically take it to one of the pre-heated bowls on your table. Our vegetables arrived first, with the sweetcorn, ocra, mushrooms and peppers all juicy and delicious.

The seafood dishes we chose were the crab, which was boiled in garlic, onion and sake.

Will also tried the Argentinean Shrimp, scallops and red snapper, which I've never tried before but was succulent and perfectly well cooked, just like everything else.

The only criticism is perhaps we would have liked the vegetables to arrive with the fish, but all in all it was delicious.

There's also a bar on the site, selling cocktails and some very nice beers. The Maisels Weisse, a German beer which tasted more like a Belgian ale was so nice we even purchased a couple of bottles from the supermarket.

The cost of everything was in excess of NT$2,000, so it's probably only a place you should visit for special occasions, but well worth the money. Everything at Addiction Aquatic Development is cash only, although there is a cash machine should you forget to bring some.

We've yet to try the other restaurants here, but we had a walk around and they all look highly promising. Tresors de la Mer is slightly more upmarket and can select your seafood to be cooked or have it sashimi style.

The hot pot restaurant is on the second floor, while the rest of the restaurants are standing only. The sushi and seafood bars were all packed, and waiting is likely here but the prices are very competitive, especially considering how fresh the seafood is.

Another option for food here is the aquamarine. You can walk around the large area packed to the brim with crustaceans and fish, choose what you like and they'll have it cooked for you.

It's cheaper than the char-grill restaurant and is a great option if you don't mind standing next to one of the tables outside.

It's also worth a look around the supermarket. Of course there's plenty of seafood you can buy, but there's also a great selection of cheap vegetables, drinks, flowers and many more produce.

Addiction Aquatic Development is a unique eating experience in Taipei and offers something for all lovers of seafood. It's a bit of a walk from the closest MRT station but it's a walk you can use to your advantage, to walk off some of the food in your belly!

Pros

  • Best seafood in Taipei
  • Huge choice
  • Great area to dine

Cons

  • Cost can quickly add up
  • Not close to any MRT station

Traveller Tips

Everything here is cash only

title: Taoyuan Airport MRT: Times, Prices and Tips
excerpt: Using the Taoyuan Airport MRT (also known as the Airport Express) to travel to and from Taoyuan airport
content:
The Taoyuan Airport MRT - sometimes known as the Airport Express - is the quickest way to travel between Taoyuan Airport and Taipei Main Station.

💡 The Quick Verdict: Airport MRT vs Bus vs Taxi

  • Airport MRT (NT$160, 35-39 min express): the fastest and cheapest option to/from Taipei Main Station - and you can now just tap a contactless credit card or your phone at the gate. There's also a slower, all-stops commuter train on the same line - about an hour instead of 35-39 minutes, but it keeps running later into the night after the last express has gone.
  • Kuo-Kuang 1819 bus (about NT$135, 55-75 min): slightly cheaper, runs 24 hours, and the only option if you land in the middle of the night.
  • Taxi/Uber (NT$1,000-1,200, ~45 min): worth it outside MRT hours, or with a group and lots of luggage.

The express trains run from both terminals every 15 minutes, and take 35 minutes from Terminal 1 or 39 minutes from Terminal 2.

The trains are comfortable, with free WiFi, luggage racks and USB charging points in the arm rests.

Cost

You no longer need a ticket at all. Just tap a contactless credit or debit card - Visa, Mastercard or JCB - or your phone with Apple Pay, Google Pay or Samsung Pay, straight onto the reader at the gate. Tap the same card again on the way out, and the fare is charged to it. No queue, no machine, no working out which ticket you need.

This is the easiest way to ride, and it's what I'd do on arrival. Use the same card or phone at both ends of the journey, or the gate won't let you out.

A single fare to or from Taipei Main Station costs NT$160. There are no return tickets.

If you'd rather have a physical ticket, tokens are sold from the machines and information booths directly before the turnstiles, and they take cash, credit cards and mobile payments. An EasyCard works on the Airport MRT too, at the same price as a token.

You can also pre-book on Klook, which gives you a QR code to scan at the gate and offers a return ticket valid for 60 days. Be aware that the discount here has narrowed a lot – it's worth comparing against the NT$160 walk-up fare before booking, because tapping your own card may well be simpler for the sake of a few dollars.

Check the current Taoyuan Airport MRT ticket price on Klook

Klook.com

Taoyuan Airport to Taipei Main

The Taoyuan Airport MRT station is easy to find from both terminals as it's well signed and is just a 10 minute walk from either Arrival hall.

Just follow the purple signs for the 'Taoyuan Airport MRT', which is located 2 levels down from the arrival halls.

Express Train Times

Express departures are at the same minutes past every hour, so you only need to remember four numbers:

After the last express, slower commuter trains keep running for another 40 minutes or so – roughly every 15 minutes until about 23:35.

Check the live timetable before you travel – these times do get adjusted.

Note that the commuter train runs on the same line and stops everywhere, taking around an hour. It's noticeably less comfortable, so take the express if you can.

The Express trains will have a purple stripe along the side (and purple seating), whereas the commuter trains will be blue.

You may also see an Extended Express on the boards. It's the same fast service to Taipei, but in the other direction it carries on past the airport to Taoyuan HSR station and Huanbei – handy if you're connecting to the high speed rail rather than going into Taipei.

What to Buy Before You Leave the Airport

Two things are worth picking up in the arrivals hall rather than in the city:

EasyCard

An EasyCard remains highly useful for quick cashless purchases at convenience stores, vending machines, and local shops across Taiwan.

Click here to find out more about the EasyCard

In both terminals, the Taoyuan Airport MRT service booth will sell EasyCards, and can be found immediately after the final customs check, in the arrival halls.

You can also return your EasyCard here at the end of your trip for a refund.

Where the Booths Are

Terminal 1

Terminal 2

These are open from 08:00 - 21:30. If you arrive outside of these times, buy a token just before the station entrance, or simply tap your contactless card and sort out an EasyCard later from any of the locations on the EasyCard page.

Taiwan SIM Card or eSIM

You have two options here, and which one is cheaper depends entirely on how long you're staying.

For a short trip, the easiest thing by far is a data-only eSIM bought online before you fly. There's no passport check, no queue and nothing to collect – you land already connected, which is worth a lot when you're stood in arrivals trying to work out which way the MRT is. For trips of up to a couple of weeks it usually works out cheapest as well.

Buy from an airport counter instead if you need a Taiwanese phone number, or if you're here for a month or more – the volume discounts at the desks overtake an eSIM at around the 30 day mark, and past 60 days they're the only option. Bring your passport plus a second form of ID.

The carrier booths open at 06:00 or 07:00 and close somewhere between 22:00 and 00:00 depending on the terminal. If you land after they've shut, don't rush into a bad deal – the city branches can sort you out the next day.

Read my full Taiwan SIM card & eSIM guide for a price comparison across all three carriers – or skip straight to the eSIM options or the airport price comparison.

Klook.com

Taipei Main to Taoyuan Airport

When heading back to the airport after your holiday, you'll need to get to the Taoyuan Airport MRT near Taipei Main Station.

Taipei Main is a huge place, so it could take you 15-20 minutes to walk there. If you're in a hurry, I would recommend getting a taxi instead, as it will take you directly to the Airport MRT station.

Be aware that the train service to Taoyuan will either be signed:

  • Taoyuan Airport MRT
  • Airport Express

Both the signs will have a purple train symbol:

Train Times

If you miss the 23:00, there's a commuter train at 23:08 and two more airport-bound services at 23:23 and 23:38 – all slower, stopping everywhere, but they'll still get you there.

All trains stop at both terminals, Terminal 1 first. Make sure you know which one you're flying from.

In-Town Check-In

The Taoyuan Airport MRT station at Taipei Main has an In-Town Check-In facility for certain airlines. This very handy facility allows you to check in early for your flight and drop your hold luggage in the city, so you can spend your last day in Taipei without dragging a suitcase around.

It's on B1, directly above the Taoyuan Airport MRT station, signed In-Town Check-In Area. You need to be there at least 3 hours before departure, and it only covers flights leaving Taoyuan the same day.

There are actually two stations offering it, and they don't cover the same airlines:

So if you're flying Tigerair, Taipei Main can't check you in – only A3 can. And STARLUX and Cathay Pacific are the other way round.

If you have any purchased goods requiring a Tax Refund, there is a refund desk very close by

Before You Fly Home

When you arrive at Taoyuan Airport, you can refund any remaining cash balance on your EasyCard at the MRT Information Desk (minus a NT$20 fee). Note that the physical card purchase fee of NT$100 is non-refundable, so many travellers prefer to keep the card as a souvenir or spend the remaining balance at airport stores before flying.

You can also use the tax refund desk to claim any rebates on large purchases you've made during your stay. There is a tax refund booth at both terminals, and there's also one near the Taoyuan Airport MRT station at Taipei Main. See this post for locations and more details.

Check to see if your flight is on time from their flight departure web page

Other Ways to Travel Between Taoyuan Airport and Taipei

If your flight arrives or departs outside the Airport MRT's hours, or you simply don't fancy the walk through Taipei Main, you have two alternatives:

The Airport Express Bus runs 24/7 and connects both Taoyuan Airport terminals to Taipei Main Station.

  • Terminal 1: B1 Arrivals Zone
  • Terminal 2: At the northeast arcade of the 1st floor Arrivals lobby.

Bus stations at both terminals are within 5 minutes walk of the arrivals halls. There are a few buses that take you to different destinations, but the 24 hour bus is the 1819 to Taipei Main Station.

It leaves every 15 or 20 minutes and takes 55 minutes in light traffic, though rush hour (07:00-09:00 and 17:00-19:30) can add another 20-30 minutes. Buy a ticket from the correct ticketing booth – look out for the 1819 on the signs above the booths – or book a round trip online in advance.

Pre-book Taoyuan Airport Kuo-Kuang Bus Tickets on Klook

Klook.com

A taxi will normally set you back between NT$1,000–1,200 and will take about 45 minutes to travel between Taipei Main Station and Taoyuan Airport (depending on the traffic).

You can easily arrange a taxi at either terminal in Taoyuan Airport. Alternatively, there will be loads of Uber drivers waiting near the airport, and their prices are usually a little below the metered taxi fare.

Useful Information

  • Free WiFi is available at the Airport MRT stations and on the trains. You get 30 minutes at a time, but you can simply connect again when it runs out. The networks are TyMetro and TyMetro-train
  • The express only stops at Taipei Main (A1), New Taipei Industrial Park (A3), Chang Gung Memorial Hospital (A8) and the two airport terminals. The commuter train stops at all 21 stations, which is why it takes an hour
  • The line continues past the airport to Taoyuan HSR station and on to Laojie River (A22), so don't panic if the train you're on is signed beyond the airport
  • There are luggage racks in all carriages, and USB charging points in the arm rests of the express trains

Go back to my Taipei Public Transport guide

title: Taipei MRT Guide: Fares, Lines & How to Ride
excerpt: How to ride the Taipei MRT - what a journey costs, how to pay with a card or your phone, all six lines and the attractions on each, and the rules worth knowing.
content:
Taipei's underground public transportation system, the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) is one of the most reliable and clean public underground services in the world.

💡 The Quick Verdict: Cost & How to Ride

  • Cost: NT$20-65 per journey depending on distance - most cross-city trips land somewhere in the middle.
  • Simplest way to ride: tap an EasyCard, or tap a contactless Visa/Mastercard or Apple/Google/Samsung Pay directly at the gate - no ticket machine, no queue, just tap in and tap out.
  • Only doing the MRT? Your own contactless card is genuinely enough. Riding buses, YouBike, or getting a TPASS too? Get a physical EasyCard as well.

Sometimes known as Metro Taipei, it is an efficient and convenient way to get around the city, with trains running frequently and serving a wide area.

The hub of the MRT is Taipei Main Station, a vast complex that connects the MRT to the Airport Express, the Taiwan High Speed Rail (THSR) and the Bus Station.

Map of Taipei MRT

I would recommend downloading this free app (Android / iPhone) for a useful map of the underground network on your phone.

Tapping on any MRT station will give you the approximate journey time to each station, and you can change it to show the cost instead.

MRT Cost & Frequent Rider Discount

The Taipei Metro uses a distance-based fare system starting at NT$20 for single journeys up to 5km, rising to NT$65 for longer journeys across the network.

Ticket TypeMin FareMax FareDiscount Info
Single Journey TokenNT$20NT$65Standard cash fare token purchased at station vending machines
EasyCard / iPASSNT$20NT$65Qualifies for 5%–15% monthly cash rebate (based on total monthly rides)

Frequent Rider Rebate Program: Taipei Metro replaced the old flat 20% discount with a monthly rebate program. If you take 11 or more MRT rides in a calendar month, a cash rebate (between 5% and 15%) is automatically credited back to your EasyCard balance upon your first tap in the following month!

Monthly MRT RidesRebate Percentage
11 to 20 rides5% Cash Rebate
21 to 40 rides10% Cash Rebate
41+ rides15% Cash Rebate

Visiting for a few days? This probably won't affect you at all. The rebate isn't taken off at the gate – it's worked out from last month's travel and only lands when you next tap through in the following calendar month. So even if you manage 11 rides in a week, you'll have flown home before it pays out. It's a perk for residents and commuters, and you can safely ignore it when budgeting.

Two things make it even less likely to help: the count resets on the 1st, so a trip straddling the end of a month splits your rides across two totals – and it only ever pays onto the same card. That said, the cashback sits there for a year, so if you keep your EasyCard and come back within twelve months, you will get it eventually.

Coming off a bus? Tap onto the Metro with the same card shortly afterwards and you get NT$8 knocked off the fare – and it works in the other direction too. It happens automatically, so there's nothing to claim.

Children & Senior Discounts

Children under the age of 6 or below 115cm travel for free when accompanied by a paying adult. One adult can bring up to four children free on the Metro.

For older passengers the answer is less generous, and worth being blunt about. There is a half-price concession fare for over-65s, but claiming it requires Taiwanese ID or an APRC (permanent residency). A visiting pensioner on a tourist stamp pays exactly the same fare as everyone else, whatever their passport says. There's no senior rate on the Fun Pass either – that only comes in adult and child versions.

Taipei residents aged 65 and over do rather well out of it, mind. They can get a Senior EasyCard loaded with a monthly travel credit that covers the MRT, city buses and the Maokong Gondola. Welfare cards like this are excluded from the frequent rider rebate above, on the basis that they're already discounted.

One consolation if you're travelling with older relatives: the Double-Decker Sightseeing Bus does give over-65s half price on production of a passport. It's one of the few Taipei fares where age helps regardless of where you're from.

Unlimited Travel Passes

If you're planning to ride constantly, the Metro sells its own unlimited passes covering the Taipei Metro and the New Taipei Circular Line. Buy them from the information counter at any station.

The difference between the first two matters. The NT$150 One-Day Pass expires at the end of service that day, while the NT$180 pass runs a full 24 hours from your first tap – so if you're starting after lunch, the dearer one is usually better value.

Honestly though, at NT$20–65 a journey you'd need to make five or more trips in a day before a pass pays for itself, and most sightseeing days don't involve that much riding. Tapping a card as you go is usually cheaper.

Contactless Credit Cards & Mobile Pay at Gates

Taipei Metro turnstile gates support direct tap-and-go payment using Visa, Mastercard, Apple Pay, Google Pay and Samsung Pay. There's also a Transit QR Code option through several Taiwanese e-payment apps, which earns the same frequent rider cashback – paid into your e-payment account on the 5th of the month rather than onto a card.

While tapping into MRT gates with Apple Pay or a contactless credit card is very convenient, we still strongly recommend getting a physical EasyCard for your trip. Here is why:

  • YouBike 2.0 Rentals: YouBike docks require a physical EasyCard or iPASS linked to your mobile phone number. Credit cards are not supported at standard YouBike docking stations.
  • City & Intercity Buses: Physical EasyCards work universally across all city buses, intercity coaches, and small local shops.
  • TPASS Monthly Pass: If you purchase a TPASS regional monthly pass, it must be loaded onto a physical EasyCard.

MRT Operating Times & Frequency

The Taipei MRT operates from 06:00 to midnight every day, although at some stations trains can depart up to 1 hour after midnight.

Click here to find the first and last train departures from each station

Select the station name from the drop-down menu

Train Frequency

Peak hours are between 07:00 - 09:00 and 17:00 - 19:30 during weekdays only.

Trains will allow between 25 & 50 seconds for people to board.

How to Use the MRT

There are four ways to pay and they all work at the same gates:

  • EasyCard or iPASS – tap in, tap out. Still the most useful option if you're also riding buses or YouBike
  • A contactless Visa or Mastercard – tap it straight on the gate, nothing to buy first
  • Your phone – Apple Pay, Google Pay or Samsung Pay, exactly the same way
  • A single-journey ticket from the machines in the station, if you'd rather not use a card at all

Whichever you choose, use the same one at both ends of the journey. Tap in with your phone and try to tap out with a bank card and the gate won't open.

  • Use the MRT app to see which MRT line(s) you need to travel on, and if you will need to transfer at another station
  • Have your card, phone or ticket ready before you reach the gates – and if you're using an EasyCard, check it has enough credit for the journey

Click here to see how to purchase and top-up an EasyCard

  • If the MRT station has multiple lines, ensure you are entering through the correct turnstile first
  • Tap your card or phone on the sensor on the right-hand side of the turnstile to enter. Single-journey tickets from the machines are now issued as QR codes, so hold the code about 4–5cm from the scanner instead
  • Ensure you know which direction you want to travel

When choosing your direction to travel, you will need to know the name of the terminal station. For instance, if travelling on the red line, the terminal stations are Tamsui and Xiangshan, so ensure you pick the appropriate direction to travel.

Be aware that trains will sometimes terminate before they reach the end of the line, so watch the displays to see the name of the terminal station. If you do accidentally get on a train that terminates early, you simply need to get off and catch the next train.

I have added the terminal stations and where trains can terminate early to the MRT Lines section below

  • Wait within one of the designated areas until the train arrives
  • Do not sit on the dark blue seating inside the train unless you fit the criteria (see Restrictions section below)

The trains get very busy during peak commuting hours so expect to be crammed in at times.

  • There are electronic displays on every train that will display the next station and destination station, and an English announcement will tell you the next station before it arrives there
  • Alight the train and locate the appropriate exit. There will be 3 information maps to help you (see MRT Stations section below for a picture of these)
  • Tap or scan again at the turnstile to exit, with the same card, phone or ticket you came in with

The turnstile plays a little piano note as you tap through. If you're using an EasyCard, it plays a different one to warn you the balance is getting low.

Transferring between MRT Lines

You will sometimes need to use multiple MRT lines for your journey.

You simply need to alight at the station you are changing and then locate the next line. This can be done without needing to exit the MRT system, so you will not be charged extra.

There are two exceptions, both where the Circular (yellow) line meets the Bannan (blue) line. At Banqiao, and between Xinpu Minsheng and Xinpu, the two lines aren't connected inside the paid area, so you have to tap out and tap back in. You won't be charged twice – you get a 20 minute window and it still counts as one journey – but it's alarming the first time it happens.

There are some stations where the other line is situated directly opposite your line, so you can sometimes transfer in a matter of seconds.

For instance, the Chiang-Kai Shek Memorial Hall station has RED (south) and GREEN (south) lines, RED (north) and GREEN (north) lines opposite each other.

MRT Stations

All maps and notices have English wording, and there are English announcements on all trains.

Look out for the following sign when trying to locate an MRT station entrance.

All MRT stations have machines for topping up your EasyCard and MRT information desks which can also be used to top-up your card.

Click here to read more about topping up your EasyCard

Most stations will have public toilets, and will often have other facilities such as baby-changing rooms. Toilets are sometimes situated within the paid areas but you can enter and exit the area free of charge if you're only using the toilet.

Additionally, each MRT station is equipped with facilities for disabled passengers, and access from the train to the street in a wheelchair is possible from every station.

Click here to see all available services and facilities at each station

Select the station name from the drop-down menu

All MRT stations have three information maps showing you the best exit to take when leaving. The maps don't always point north however, which can be confusing.

All of my posts will tell you the appropriate exit to take for every attraction

Throughout the MRT stations are lockers should you wish to secure any belongings for a few hours. They cost either NT$10 or NT$20 per hour depending on the size of the locker you need. Anything under an hour is charged as a full hour, and the maximum rental is 24 hours – after that the locker company empties it and holds your things elsewhere for 30 days.

Click here to see the available lockers at each station

You can pay with cash, an EasyCard, or a mobile wallet such as LINE Pay, TaiwanPay or Alipay. The locker prints a single-use PIN rather than giving you a key, so don't lose it.

Most MRT stations also have free WiFi available. Simply connect to TPE-Free on you phone. 

MRT Lines

There are six MRT lines, all colour-coded for clarity.

Selected stations listed below are where you'll find many of Taipei's popular attractions.
Tap on a link to find out more about each attraction

Tamsui-Xinyi Line (Red)

Early terminal stations in brackets

The Tamsui-Xinyi (RED) Line is one of the busiest lines on the MRT. It passes through Taipei Main Station and is the line closest to Taipei 101. It travels the furthest distance from central Taipei, to the beautiful northern districts of Tamsui and Beitou.

Bannan Line (Blue)

The Bannan (BLUE) Line is another busy line as it travels through the heart of the city and past many top attractions.

Songshan-Xindian Line (Green)

The Songshan-Xindian (GREEN) Line is not as busy as the red or blue lines but has a few attractions close to MRT stations.

Zhonghe-Xinlu Line (Orange)

The Zhonghe-Xinlu (ORANGE) Line forks into two lines on the outskirts of Taipei. However, you will probably only ever need to use 6 or 7 stations that run through the centre of the city.

Wenhu Line (Brown)

The Wenhu (BROWN) Line is the only line in central Taipei that's elevated above ground. When changing to or from the brown line, it will consequently take you longer to walk between the two lines.

Circular Line (Yellow)

The Circular (YELLOW) Line is the newest, runs through New Taipei rather than central Taipei, and is used mostly by commuters – so as a visitor you'll rarely need it.

Restrictions on Taipei MRT

  • There is strictly no eating, drinking or chewing gum once you've entered through a turnstile (not even water)
  • The dark blue seating is reserved for the elderly, disabled or pregnant passengers. You will receive many disapproving expressions from other passengers if you sit on these but don't fit this criteria
  • Always stand on the right when using escalators.

Taking Bicycles on the MRT

It is possible to take your bike with you on the MRT. However, there are some restrictions in place:

  • You can enter and exit at 85 of the stations. The entire Wenhu (brown) line is off limits, as are Tamsui, Taipei Main Station, Zhongxiao Xinsheng, Zhongxiao Fuxing, Nanjing Fuxing and Daan
  • Weekends and holidays are fine all day. On weekdays you're restricted to 10:00 - 16:00 and from 22:00 until the end of service

Folding bikes are exempt from all of that. As long as it's properly packed and no side is longer than 165cm, it counts as ordinary luggage – any station, any time, no extra fare.

Click here to see all the stations you are allowed to take a bike

There are extra wide turnstiles you can take your bike through when entering the MRT.

Go back to my Taipei Public Transport guide

title: Full Guide & Deals for Taiwan High Speed Rail (THSR)
excerpt: Travel to other parts of Taiwan in no time with the efficient High Speed Rail (HSR) train network.
content:
The Taiwan High Speed Rail (THSR) service is only for those who want to travel outside of Taipei. Opened in 2007, it travels almost the entire length of Taiwan (220 miles) at speeds in excess of 185 mph.

💡 The Quick Verdict: Booking THSR Tickets

  • Travelling as a pair? Check for Buy One Get One Free first. When this promotion is running it is far and away the cheapest option - about NT$1,266 for two adults Taipei to Kaohsiung, against NT$2,980 at full fare. It comes and goes in phases and you have to book two tickets, so check before you plan around it.
  • Foreign passport, visiting under 180 days? Book through Klook - one-way tickets, multi-day tourist passes, and the Taiwan PASS (HSR Edition) are all available, often with promotional discounts.
  • Combining HSR with day trips to places like Sun Moon Lake or Alishan? The Taiwan PASS bundles HSR with the connecting Tourist Shuttle buses - can be more convenient than buying separately.
  • Just need one journey with no frills? The THSR website, app, or station ticket machines all work fine too.

THSR Route

The high speed rail runs down the west coast of Taiwan, from Taipei in the north to Kaohsiung in the south, in under 100 minutes.

Note that it only serves the west coast. For Hualien, Taroko Gorge or Taitung you need Taiwan Railway (TRA) instead.

Trains generally run from 06:00 - 24:00 in intervals ranging from a few minutes to an hour (depending on the time of day). Unless you are catching a train at night, you won't need to wait long for a train.

The high speed rail is famously punctual - delays are rare and usually minor.

Click here for a Full Timetable of departures

There are only two lines - Northbound and Southbound - so you simply need to ensure you choose the right direction before boarding - and a total of 12 stations, 3 of which serve Greater Taipei (Banqiao is in New Taipei City):

  • Nangang
  • Taipei Main Station
  • Banqiao

For a more detailed look at the THSR route, visit the Destinations section below.

Carriages

THSR trains have 12 carriages:

  • 1 Business Class (carriage 6)
  • 11 Standard Class
    • Carriage 7 has wheelchair spaces
    • Non-reserved seating is usually carriages 10 - 12, but this is no longer fixed - follow the platform screens or staff directions, as THSR now opens extra carriages when trains are busy

The seats are comfortable with ample leg room, plus they recline and even rotate 180 degrees to facilitate passengers travelling in a group.

The Business Class carriage has more comfortable seating and fewer seats, whilst also giving passengers extra leg room. Additionally, there are complimentary drinks and cakes, a complimentary newspaper (in English if you require), with plug sockets, headphones and lights by each seat.

Toilets are in all odd-numbered carriages, and there are vending machines in some carriages selling drinks and snacks.

There are some great discounts for foreign travellers if ordering online (jump to discounts).

Klook.com

THSR Ticket Types

There are 3 classes of tickets you can purchase:

  • Standard Class (with reserved seat)
  • Standard Class (without reserved seat)
  • Business Class

If you choose not to reserve a seat in standard class, you can take your chances in the unreserved carriages (10 - 12) but if you find all the seats taken, you'll need to stand.

It is cheaper this way, but if you're travelling for a while, it's preferable to reserve one. The price difference between the two are between 3% - 5% depending on how far you travel.

The ticket will have the arrival and destination stations and times, along with the car and seat number. Obviously if you are reserving a seat, you must catch a specific train.

If you're not reserving a seat, you can catch any train on the date shown. One change to watch: THSR has announced that non-reserved tickets will stop being valid on any train during peak periods, so if you are travelling at a busy time it is worth reserving.

Prices

Which Discount Should You Use?

There are three different ways to pay less, and they do not stack. This is how they compare:

OptionSavingThe catch
Buy One Get One FreeAbout 50%You must book two tickets - no use travelling solo. Foreign passports only, and it runs in phases rather than all year, so check it is live.
Early-bird35%, 20% or 10%Book at least 5 days ahead, adult reserved standard seats only, limited numbers per train, and not sold at ticket counters or machines.
Klook one-way15%Foreign passport, visiting under 180 days. No date restrictions, so it is the reliable fallback.
Unlimited passDepends on useOnly pays off across several long journeys - see the pass prices below.

If Buy One Get One is running and there are two of you, it beats everything else by a wide margin: two adults from Taipei to Kaohsiung costs about NT$1,266 together, against NT$2,980 at full fare. Klook currently promotes it with the code GO2TAIWAN. (Promotion status last checked August 2026 - THSR and the Tourism Administration have re-run this campaign repeatedly, but each phase has an end date, so confirm it before counting on it.)

Early-Bird Tickets

Early-bird tickets are available if you are willing to book ahead. The booking window opens roughly a month ahead (THSR announces the exact date), and the last chance to buy one is 5 days before you travel.

Discounts of 35%, 20% and 10% are available for early-bird tickets, although these will not be offered on peak-time trains. Once the 35% tickets get sold, then the 20% tickets will become available and so on until all the discounted tickets are sold out..

35% discount tickets usually get snapped up on the first available booking day so you need to be very quick for these.

Early-bird tickets are applicable to standard adult reserved seating only.

Child Concessions

Children under the age of 6 years can travel for free, only if they do not require an extra seat.

Otherwise, children under 12 years can travel with a 50% discount (if your child is 12 years, you will need to pay the full fare).

The height that matters is 115cm. A child under 115cm and under 6 travels free provided they do not take a seat; from 115cm up to their 12th birthday they pay the concession fare, and staff may ask for ID to prove the age. There is a limit of 2 children per paying adult.

Group Tickets

Travelling as a group of 11 or more? THSR sells group tickets, with everyone booked on the same train and in the same car class. These can be booked from 29 days up to 1 day before departure, so unlike early-bird fares there is no last-minute cut-off five days out.

Fares From Taipei Main Station

All prices in New Taiwan Dollars (NT$300 is approximately US$10)

Click here for a full pricing matrix between every station

Click here to use the THSR fare-finder website

How to Buy High Speed Rail Tickets

There are a few ways you can purchase THSR tickets:

Purchase on Klook

This is the easiest option if you hold a non-Taiwanese passport and are visiting Taiwan for less than 180 days - though if you can book at least 5 days ahead, an early-bird fare at 35% off beats Klook's 15%. You can pre-order tickets online for the following offers:

  • One-way ticket between any two THSR stations
  • 2 or 3 day tourist passes
  • Taiwan PASS (HSR Edition)

The Taiwan PASS (HSR Edition) is worth a look if you're planning to combine the high speed rail with day trips outside the main stations - it bundles a 3-day HSR pass with MRT access and the Taiwan Tourist Shuttle (the bus network that connects HSR stations to nearby attractions like Sun Moon Lake, Alishan and other scenic spots that the railway itself doesn't reach). It's activated and used through the Taiwan PASS app, is valid for 7 days from activation, and is limited to short-term foreign visitors. If your itinerary includes stops that need a connecting shuttle bus anyway, it can work out more convenient than buying HSR and shuttle tickets separately.

Klook frequently runs promotional campaigns like buy-one-get-one-free (BOGO) for one-way tickets (especially for travel to central and southern stations). Since these promotions are seasonal and run for limited periods, check the active deals page to see what campaigns are running today!

Klook.com

You can also reserve seats for all tickets purchased on Klook

1. One-Way Ticket

The one-way ticket gives you 15% off the standard fare. Klook also runs a Buy One Get One Free package on some routes via a promo code - you have to book two tickets, but it works out at roughly half price each. You must select your origin and destination stations when purchasing the ticket. It is valid only for the selected direction of travel.

Click here to order discounted THSR One-Way Tickets on Klook

2. 2 and 3 Day Tourist Passes

The 2 and 3 day tourist passes will give you unlimited THSR travel, ideal if you want to do a tour of the major cities in Taiwan, or if you want to make use of the Tourist Shuttle Buses that depart from many THSR stations (see the Destinations section below for further details of these).

The 3 day pass must be used over 3 consecutive days.

The 2 day pass is more flexible, allowing you to travel within any 2 days of a 7-day period.

That is why the 2 day pass costs more than the 3 day one despite covering fewer days - you are paying for the flexibility of spreading those two journeys across a week rather than using them on consecutive days.

You must specify the date of your first journey when purchasing either of these. Klook vouchers are valid for 89 days from purchase, so you can book well ahead of a trip.

Prices

Klook shaves a little off the adult passes - about 5% on the 3-day and 3% on the 2-day. Child fares are the same either way.

Click here to order the Unlimited THSR 2-Day or 3-Day Pass on Klook

3. Taiwan PASS (HSR Edition)

The Taiwan PASS (HSR Edition) is a highly recommended 3-in-1 electronic joint pass for short-term tourists that includes:

  • An unlimited THSR 3-Day Pass
  • A Metro Travel Pass (choose from Taipei Metro 2-day, Taoyuan Airport MRT round-trip, Taichung Metro 48h, or Kaohsiung MRT 2-day)
  • A round-trip ticket for a Taiwan Tourist Shuttle route (choose from Alishan, Sun Moon Lake, Cingjing, or Kenting)

It requires using the Taiwan PASS App to activate the virtual card and redeem coupons.

Price: NT$2,800

Click here to order the Taiwan PASS (HSR Edition) on Klook

Important: anything bought on Klook is an e-voucher. It will not scan at the turnstiles - you have to turn it into a physical ticket first.

Redeeming a Klook voucher, in three steps:

  1. Once your booking is confirmed, find the 8-digit redeem code under Confirmation Details on the voucher in the Klook app.
  2. Reserve your seat on the official THSR booking portal. Click Manage, choose Sign in with redeem code, enter the code and your passport number, then Reserve and pick your train. You will be given a reservation number.
  3. Collect the physical ticket at a THSR ticket counter, bringing your reservation number and your non-Taiwanese passport with a valid short-term entry document.

You can skip step 2 and reserve at the counter instead, but doing it online first means you are not picking from whatever is left when you arrive.

Ticket Counter

These are located near the THSR entrances. It's pot-luck as to whether the person serving you will be able to speak English however. I find it preferable to use a Ticket Vending Machine instead.

Note: early-bird discounts are not sold at ticket counters. If you want one of those, book online, in the app, or at a convenience store.

You will need to tell them the departure date and station, then the arrival date and station if you're booking a return ticket, and also if you want to reserve seats.

You can pay by card or cash.

Ticket Vending Machine

These can be found near the THSR entrances and also within the MRT near the stations.

Note: like the ticket counters, the machines do not sell early-bird discounted tickets.

Note that some machines have trouble accepting cash payments. Just move to another machine and try again, or alternatively use your credit/debit card.

High Speed Rail Website

You can book tickets directly from the THSR website. English language can be selected from the top-right.

Click here to book tickets

You can also see if there are early-bird tickets still available using this method.

High Speed Rail App

Download the Taiwan High Speed ​​Rail T Express Mobile Ticketing Service App (Android / iOS).

Select the Booking tab and enter all the required information.

Tap Search and select the desired outbound journey, then the return journey if needed. You'll then need to enter contact information, including passport number and email address or phone number.

After you enter the payment details, you can choose to either collect your tickets from a ticket vending machine or service booth, or use an e-ticket directly on your phone (this option is better).

Convenience Stores

All convenience stores in Taiwan are equipped with machines where you can purchase THSR tickets from. However, these machines are in Chinese only.

Destinations

These are the main stations on the THSR route. I've included attractions and destinations that can be reached by the Tourist Shuttle Buses (TSB) which depart from most THSR stations. These will take you many top attractions around each county. The cost of these vary but they're around NT$100 - NT$300 per trip.

For more information about using these, please read my full Tourist Shuttle Bus guide.

There are also free shuttle buses that will take you from most THSR stations to the city centre. These are free for anyone with THSR tickets (so ensure you don't throw the stubs away!).

Click here for information about each station, including all the ways to travel from stations (TRA, TSB, buses, car hire, taxis) and locker availability.

Travel time from Taipei Main Station in brackets

Hsinchu (32 minutes)

The oldest city in northern Taiwan, and home to its largest Hakka community - worth stopping for the Hakka food and rice wine, here or in Miaoli.

The THSR station sits a few miles out of the city, but a free shuttle bus runs every 20 minutes.

Two Tourist Shuttle routes also leave from the station:

Click links for route, timetable and pricing

Miaoli (41 minutes)

Come in spring if you can: the county fills with blossom, and the climate is ideal for strawberries. The Dahu Strawberry Culture Park lets you pick your own and eat strawberry-flavoured everything.

Dahu isn't on the shuttle network though, so you'll need a taxi or car. Lion's Head Mountain Scenic Area is, and it's good hiking - also reachable from Hsinchu.

One Tourist Shuttle route leaves from Zhunan Station, a 15-minute bus ride from the THSR station:

Klook.com

Taichung (52 minutes)

Now Taiwan's second largest city. It has a metro - the Green Line - plus buses that are efficient and punctual, and both take EasyCard.

One Tourist Shuttle route loops the city's main sights, leaving from Taichung Train Station, a 20-minute bus ride from the THSR station.

There is another TSB that leaves from the THSR station, that will take you to one of the largest and most beautiful lakes in Taiwan - Sun Moon Lake. From there you can also take a cable car ride to visit the Formosan Aboriginal Culture Village, hire a bike to ride, or take a ride on one of the many boats.

Klook.com

Changhua (64 minutes)

Surrounded by mountains on three sides, Changhua is a great area to visit if you enjoy hiking and temples.

There are two Tourist Shuttle buses that depart from the THSR station:

Yunlin (70 minutes)

Much like Changhua, Yunlin County is one of the more rural areas of western Taiwan, with an abundance of temples and scenic areas.

There is a Tourist Shuttle bus that departs from the THSR station that will take you to some of the best temples in the area, along with the Glove Puppetry Museum:

Chiayi (79 minutes)

Chiayi is the gateway to Alishan - Taiwan's most popular national park, with its tallest mountain and waterfall.

Bus or train, both leaving from near the THSR station, about 2.5 and 2 hours respectively. Take the train if you can: the narrow-gauge mountain railway is largely unchanged since pre-war days. Only 3 run a day, all mornings (times here), plus two buses between 10:00 and 11:30.

There's also a Tourist Shuttle route from the station:

Klook.com

Tainan (88 minutes)

Taiwan's oldest city and its first capital, with over 500 Buddhist and Taoist temples - the Luerman Matsu Temple among them.

A free shuttle runs from the THSR station into the centre. Public transport isn't great once you're there, so plan on taxis or hiring a moped.

A Tourist Shuttle route covers the city's main sights, leaving from the North and South train stations:

Kaohsiung (97 minutes)

Kaohsiung is the third largest city and the largest port city in Taiwan. Like Taipei, it has its own underground MRT system which also accepts EasyCard. It's also a great city to cycle around, with many dedicated cycle paths.

Being in the south of Taiwan, it has a sub-tropical climate, so it's preferable to visit Kaohsiung (and Tainan for that matter) outside of summer months.

If you want to get up-close-and-personal with hundreds of Formosan Macaques, then Monkey Mountain is a fantastic hike where you'll also be rewarded with some awesome views.

Kaohsiung also has some of the best night markets in the country, including the Liuhe Night Market.

There is a Tourist Shuttle Bus that will take you to Kenting in the south, where you can enjoy the beautiful beaches and soak up the sun. This leaves from the THSR Station and takes around 2 hours.

You can also buy Kenting Express tickets on Klook for a more favourable rate:
