title: Taiwan Railway (TRA): Trains, Tickets & the East Coast
excerpt: How to use Taiwan Railway - the network that reaches Hualien, Taroko and the east coast, which the High Speed Rail does not. Train classes, EasyCard rules and booking.
content:
Taiwan has two separate rail networks and it is easy to confuse them. The High Speed Rail is the fast intercity line down the flat west coast. Taiwan Railway (TRA) is the older, slower network that goes everywhere else - and crucially, it is the only way to reach the east coast by train.

💡 The Quick Verdict: TRA

  • Use TRA for the east coast - Hualien, Taroko Gorge and Taitung have no High Speed Rail. Taipei to Hualien takes about 2 hours on the fastest trains.
  • Book ahead for the express trains. Taroko, Puyuma and Tze-Chiang 3000 are fully reserved and sell out at weekends and on holidays. The booking window opens 28 days before travel.
  • Do not tap an EasyCard onto a reserved express. It counts as travelling without a ticket and carries a fine. EasyCard is fine on Local trains.

TRA or High Speed Rail?

If you are heading to Taichung, Tainan or Kaohsiung, take the High Speed Rail - it is far quicker. Choose TRA when:

  • You are going to the east coast (Hualien, Taitung) - the HSR does not go there at all
  • You want Keelung, Ruifang or Yilan, which the HSR misses
  • You are doing a branch line day trip such as Pingxi
  • You would rather pay less and are not in a hurry

Train Types Explained

TRA runs several classes of train. The distinction matters, because it decides whether you can use an EasyCard or have to book a seat.

ClassSpeed and comfortSeatsEasyCard?
Taroko and PuyumaFastest; tilting trains built for the east coast curvesAll reservedNo - ticket required
Tze-Chiang 3000 (EMU3000)Newest and most comfortableAll reservedNo - ticket required
Tze-ChiangLimited express, air conditionedReserved, standing tickets soldStanding only
Chu-KuangSlower and cheaper limited expressReserved, standing tickets soldStanding only
Local and Fast LocalStops at all or most stationsUnreserved, sit where you likeYes - just tap

The EasyCard Mistake That Costs You a Fine

This one catches people out, so it is worth being blunt about.

You can tap an EasyCard or iPASS straight onto any Local or Fast Local train, exactly like the MRT. You can also use it to buy a standing ticket on a Tze-Chiang or Chu-Kuang.

But if you tap in and board a Taroko, Puyuma or Tze-Chiang 3000, you are treated as travelling without a valid ticket and can be fined - those services are fully reserved and your card is not a ticket for them. Buy a seat first.

Taipei to Hualien and the East Coast

This is the main reason a visitor uses TRA. Hualien is the gateway to Taroko Gorge, and the ride down the coast is scenic in its own right.

  • Journey time: about 2 hours on a Taroko, Puyuma or Tze-Chiang 3000; up to roughly 3 hours 45 minutes on the slower classes
  • Fare: around NT$440 each way on the fast reserved trains
  • Book early. These trains genuinely sell out at weekends, on public holidays and across Lunar New Year. If your dates are fixed, book the day the window opens

Pingxi Branch Line

The Pingxi line is a short branch off the main network and one of the easiest day trips from Taipei - it is the line for Shifen, where the sky lanterns are released, plus Houtong cat village and the old mining town of Jingtong.

An all-day pass costs about NT$52 and is sold at Ruifang, Houtong, Shifen, Pingxi and Jingtong. Single fares run from roughly NT$15 to NT$50, so the pass pays for itself once you make about four hops - which most people do, since hopping on and off is the whole point of the line.

How to Buy Tickets

  • Online at the Taiwan Railway booking site or its app - the window opens 28 days before departure
  • At any station, from a counter or a machine
  • Convenience store kiosks - the FamiPort machine in FamilyMart and the ibon machine in 7-Eleven both sell rail tickets
  • Nothing to buy for Local trains: just tap your EasyCard

Taipei Main Station is the hub, and the TRA platforms are in the same building as the High Speed Rail and the MRT. Follow the signs carefully - the three networks have separate gates and separate tickets.

title: Full Guide for Hiring and Riding a YouBike
excerpt: The Taipei Bike Sharing System, or YouBike, is a public bicycle sharing service in Taipei
content:
Found throughout the city are YouBike stations. A bike rental scheme set up by the government to help reduce traffic congestion and encourage people to get fit.

💡 The Quick Verdict: Renting a YouBike

  • No Taiwanese phone number? Download the YouBike 2.0 App, choose "Single Rental," and bind a credit card or Apple Pay - scan the QR code on the bike and go, no EasyCard or SIM needed.
  • Have a local number? Register your EasyCard once at a kiosk or in the app, then just tap to unlock every ride after.
  • Cost: standard YouBike 2.0 is free for the first 30 minutes then NT$10/30 min; electric-assist 2.0E is NT$20/30 min from the start with no free tier.

These are a good way to get around Taipei if you're feeling more energetic.

However, there are now electric-assist YouBikes available for those who are feeling less energetic!

How to Use a YouBike

Since January 2026, every rider – tourists included – has to register for free Public Bicycle Injury Insurance before their first ride. It only takes a couple of minutes in the YouBike app, and you can use your passport number if you don't have a Taiwanese ID.

How you hire a YouBike depends on whether you have a local Taiwanese phone number:

  • With a local phone number: You can register a physical EasyCard (at a kiosk or via the YouBike app) using your phone number to receive a verification SMS. Once registered, you simply tap your card on any bike to unlock it. This works for both standard YouBike 2.0 and electric 2.0E.
  • Without a local phone number (Tourists): You can download the YouBike 2.0 App, select "Single Rental" (單次租車), and bind a credit card (Visa/Mastercard) or Apple Pay. This allows you to rent a bike by scanning the QR code on the handlebars directly, without needing a Taiwanese SIM card or registering an EasyCard.

Most bike stations have a kiosk.

Select English language and simply follow the steps. You'll need to enter your Taiwanese phone number, and it will send you a confirmation code that you enter into the kiosk. Next, you place your EasyCard on the panel and you're registered.

You then need to hold your EasyCard against the panel on a bike docking station to release a bike.

Taipei operates both standard YouBike 2.0 bicycles and electric-assist YouBike 2.0E bicycles. Standard YouBike 2.0 is ideal for flat city riding, while YouBike 2.0E provides battery-assisted pedaling to help you tackle hills and bridges with ease. Note that there is a cost difference: standard 2.0 bikes are free for the first 30 minutes (then NT$10 per 30 mins), while electric-assist 2.0E bikes cost NT$20 per 30 minutes from the start with no free tier.

Both models have the card reader built directly on the bike's handlebars, so you simply need to press the green button near the handlebars and then hold your EasyCard next to the Sensor Zone.

Tourist Tip: If you do not have a local Taiwanese phone number to register your EasyCard, you can download the YouBike 2.0 App, choose "Single Rental", and bind a foreign credit card or Apple Pay to scan the QR code on the bike to unlock it instantly.

Make sure that when you return the bike to another station, you also place your EasyCard against the panel to confirm (otherwise you will be continually charged!)

Handy baskets at the front of the bike can be used to place any bags you have. The bikes also have three gears, a light that comes on automatically at night, and a bell. A lock has been placed in the basket should you need to secure your bike for a while.

Youbike 2.0 bicycles also let you secure the bike wherever you want. These have a lock you can put through the handlebars.

YouBike Cost

The charges for using a YouBike depend on the model you choose:

Standard YouBike 2.0

  • Free for the first 30 minutes
  • NT$10 per 30 minutes for the first 4 hours
  • NT$20 per 30 minutes between 4 to 8 hours
  • NT$40 per 30 minutes after 8 hours

Electric-Assist YouBike 2.0E

  • NT$20 per 30 minutes for the first 2 hours
  • NT$40 per 30 minutes after 2 hours

There are also transfer discounts if you hire a standard YouBike 2.0 within 60 minutes of using the MRT or city bus.

Taipei Cycle Routes

There are lots of cycle paths in Taipei with some next to pavements so always be aware of pedestrians. You will sometimes need to use the roads, which are usually very busy. It does though feel safe riding these in the city.

The following map lists all the cycle paths in Taipei and New Taipei City:

View Larger Map

Zoom in to see all the cycle paths in the city

Useful Information about YouBikes

Always check that the seat is adjustable and not wobbly before you release a YouBike. Once you've released a bike, you will need to wait 15 minutes until you can take another one.

Most main roads only have bike lanes on one side.

Some YouBike stations are shown on Google Maps. However, if you download the free YouBike app for you phone (Android / iOS), it will show all locations and also tell you if there are bikes available at specific stations.

Go back to Taipei Public Transport page

title: How to Find Every Michelin Food Stand at Raohe Night Market
excerpt: Every Michelin-listed stand at Raohe Night Market, plus what else is worth queuing for and how to reach it from Songshan MRT.
content:
One of the oldest night markets in Taipei, Raohe Night Market is probably the best one to visit if your primary objective is being fed.

Conveniently located next to the Songshan MRT station at the eastern end of the green line, it spans an 800m long road and side-streets, and is adjacent to the Keelung river.

I would argue that Raohe Night Market has a wider selection of food stalls than Shilin. Almost everything you can find at Shilin you can find here - and then some.

The official Michelin guide even recommends five stalls here, including Fuzhou Black Pepper Bun, located next to the main entrance and almost always with a large queue outside. Delicious buns filled with pork and spiced with black pepper.

These are all of the food stands recommended by the Michelin Guide. Four of these are recognised in the Bib Gourmand category, a special award for high quality yet cheap dishes.

Coloured dots match the pins on the map below.

  • Bib GourmandA Kuo Lu Wei

    Luwei style duck wings, crispy intestines, and baby corn

  • Bib GourmandBeef Noodles and Beef Entrails Soup

    Exactly as it sounds. Side dishes are also highly recommended here

  • Bib GourmandChen Tung Pork Ribs Medicinal Herbs Soup

    Herbal soup that contains pork ribs

  • Bib GourmandFuzhou Black Pepper Bun

    Black pepper bun filled with pork and spring onion

  • Mochi Baby

    Sweet gooey Japanese rice cakes with choice of fillings

Klook.com

Prefer to let a guide take the lead? Book the Taipei Michelin Bib Gourmand One-Day Food Tour on Klook

As per all night markets, it's the stalls with the queues that you should take note of. You'll find other stalls selling the imitations of their grub, but they will always be inferior. There is another black pepper bun stall right next to this one but always go to the original as it's worth the wait!

Another tasty snack to try is the potato pancakes, filled with cheese, ham, shrimp and an egg yolk. Topped with salad cream, crispy fish flakes and a side of wasabi. They're surprisingly light.

One of our favourites at Raohe Night Market is the battered shrimp, with a choice of sauces including sweet chilli and more traditional Taiwanese sauces.

Food from other Asian countries is well represented here too. The very Japanese Okonomiyaki, known as the Japanese Pizza in America, it's more like a savoury pancake filled with cabbage and a choice of meat.

To wash your food down, there are dozens of drinks stands selling the usual favourites such as bubble teas and watermelon juices, to the more unusual cactus juice.

A night market wouldn't be complete without a shaved ice place. There's a great one here towards the west of the market on the south side. Many varieties of shaved here can be found here, including some with the traditional Taiwanese 'pudding'.

There are gift shops and other more unusual places, such as the fortune telling canaries or places you can fish for small sea creatures to take them home.

At the east-end of Raohe Night Market is Songshan Ciyou Temple, one of the most ornate and beautiful temples in Taipei.

Raohe Night Market, while not having the wow factor or size as Shilin is still a great market to visit, especially if you want to try a variety of different but delicious food items.

Pros

  • Best night market for foodies
  • Close to MRT station and river

Cons

  • Gets very crowded

Traveller Tips

Bring some tissues with you as you'll no doubt get your fingers messy

Raohe Night Market Location

📍 Closest MRT: Songshan Station (green line - exit 1)

title: Fantastic Vietnamese Food at Wu Ding Yue Feng
excerpt: Vietnamese food that finally impressed after several disappointing tries elsewhere in Taipei. Five minutes from City Hall MRT.
content:
Having been to a few Vietnamese restaurants in Taipei, we've yet to experience one that really wowed us with it's food - until now. Wu Ding Yue Feng did just that.

Located about a 5 minute walk north of the City Hall MRT station, it's a very popular restaurant with ample seating available that quickly gets filled up.

Their menu comprises of the usual dishes you'll find in Vietnamese cuisine, with Pho and noodles featuring heavily, plus of course spring rolls. They also serve dishes that seemed to cater for Chinese tastes, with chicken curries and pork steaks on a bed of rice.

Being our first time here, we both opted for Phos. You can choose the type of the noodles you require for each - from rice noodles to udon. I opted for the medium sized noodles in the pork and shrimp pho.

The meat and fish were cooked perfectly, the shrimp very fresh although I would have perhaps preferred more that the two I got. The soup was fresh and fragrant and the noodles were exactly to my liking.

We also tried the seafood pho, with squid, shrimp and fish, this time with rice noodles. The broth was superb, with a nice kick to it. We could have happily just had a bowl of this, but with the fresh seafood soaking it up too, this was one to savour.

The Phos were easily enough to satisfy ones hunger. If we had know this beforehand, we probably wouldn't have ordered the accompaniments too.

The plate of water spinach, which is probably more of a Taiwanese dish.

We saw shrimp cake on the menu, although it would have been too much for two to share. However, they will let you purchase a half portion - which was just as well.

Definitely one of the best we've had in Taipei!

All in all, it was a great meal and we will certainly be making this a regular haunting spot. The cost of everything was well under NT$500 which was great value considering the quality.

Pros

  • The best Vietnamese restaurant we've been to in Taipei

Cons

  • No English menu available

Price: $$

Level of English: Low (No English on menu)

Traveller Tips

You are allowed to take in drinks from the outside.

Wu Ding Yue Feng Location

📍 Closest MRT: City Hall Station (blue line - exit 4)

title: Jimmy’s Hot Dog – Better Than Timeout?
excerpt: A newer Danish-style hot dog spot with wacky toppings including mac 'n' cheese. How it stacks up against Timeout's version.
content:
Jimmy's Hot dog is another danish style hot dog restaurant that's popped up in the last year.

they serve a variety of wacky hot dogs that have certainly been inspired by those in the USA.

Serving only a single size of hot dog, the fun toppings include mac 'n' cheese, teriyaki, chilli slaw and bbq sauce. They even serve a 'naked' dog, which comes with a selection of toppings you can add for your desired taste.

The Chilli Cheese dog, which comes with their homemade beef chilli cheddar cheese sauce, is delicious. Very moreish.

We also tried the New York Dog, which is cheaper than the chilli cheese at only NT$99, and comes with red onion sauce, sauerkraut and yellow mustard.

If hot dogs aren't really your thing, they have a range of burgers too, including pulled pork, BLT Beef burgers and the very American peanut butter and bacon burger.

They have a good selection of combos available, with various fries (including butterscotch), onion rings, nuggets and soft drinks that have unlimited refills. A satisfying meal for under NT$200.

If you find the toppings aren't enough, they have a few others to try, plus of course ketchup and mustard.

The walls are filled with pictures of (I assume) Jimmy, who is obviously very passionate about hot dogs. He's travelled across the USA wearing a crazy 'hat dog' to visit many different hot dog stands for inspiration.

Jimmy's Hotdog serves fantastic hot dogs. I'll need another couple of visits just to be sure though!

Menu

Pros

  • Nice combos available

Cons

  • Slightly off the beaten track

Price: $$

Level of English: Good (English menu available on request)

Traveller Tips

Make it a combo meal

Jimmy's Hot dog Location

📍 Closest MRT: Daan Station (red/brown lines - exit 5)

title: A Cosy Spot for Some Fine Ales at Beer Geek
excerpt: A cosy micro pub with seating for 25–30, a homely feel and friendly service.
content:
Being a Taiwan Travel Geek who appreciates a good beer, it seemed inevitable that a visit to Beer Geek was on the cards.

Described as a micro pub, although it is rather small, I was expecting Beer Geek to be much smaller. There's seating for around 25-30 people so there's ample space for a fair few Beer Geeks.

Run by an expat from the USA, the pub serves a good selection of Taiwanese and international ales, with many on rotation. There's a happy hour each night from 18:00 until 20:00, with many draught beers at a good discount, including Taiwan 18 days beer for only NT$100 per pint.

I opted for Taihu's Dessert Berliner Weisse, a white ale that was very sour but refreshingly so. For only NT$180 it was great value too.

They also serve a limited range of comforting food, with sausages featuring heavily. One thing I do really miss in the UK is a good home-cooked plate of sausage, beans and chips. It didn't disappoint!

The TVs are hooked into a music channel and mainly play classic rock, although they will play football games if there's a good match on.

Aside from the darts board, there's a small games machine in the corner with a selection of Nintendo games to play.

Beer Geek is a small but welcoming pub serving quality ales and good homely plates of grub. Size isn't everything.

Menu

Pros

  • Nice draft ales
  • Friendly service

Cons

  • Quite a walk from the closest MRT

Price: $$

Level of English: Excellent (English menu)

Traveller Tips

Happy hour every day from 18:00 to 20:00

Beer Geek Location

📍 Closest MRT: City Hall MRT (blue line - exit 1)

title: See the Wildlife at Guandu Nature Park
excerpt: A 57-hectare wetland nature reserve by the Tamsui river, off the beaten track and managed by the Wild Bird Society of Taipei since 2001. Worth it if you want nature away from the crowds.
content:
A little way out of the city and off the beaten track, the Guandu Nature Park is a great place for nature lovers. Spanning 57 hectares at the junction of the Danshui and Keelung rivers, it opened in 2001 after a decade of planning, and has been managed ever since by the Wild Bird Society of Taipei – the first NGO to be entrusted with running a park like this in the city.

Situated close to the Tamsui river and overlooking the Guandu Nature Reserve, a wetland area that offers a temporary home to many migrating birds, and also some grazing buffalo.

The many ponds and streams around the park attract large numbers of insects and reptiles such as dragonflies, cicadas, toads and mud-skippers, and many crabs can be found as you walk over the streams.

Located around the park are several bird-watching cabins overlooking the wetlands and the moon pond, the largest in the park.

Birds found here include many herons, grebes, moorhens, sandpipers, and if you're lucky, you may see a kingfisher or two. Over 280 bird species have been recorded here in total, and BirdLife International recognises the wetland as an Important Bird Area for the waterfowl and shorebirds it supports.

In the centre of the park is a nature centre detailing the ecosystem of the park and the migration routes of the birds.

Guandu Nature Park is one of the largest and best nature parks accessible from the MRT and is a great place for twitchers or nature lovers to walk around or simply sit for a while and enjoy the peace.

Price

NT$60

Opening Hours

09:00 - 17:00

Closed on Mondays and during National Holidays

Traveller Tips

See this on the way to a visit to Danshui. It's usually pretty quiet, though the NT$60 entry fee is a little steep by Taipei standards for what is essentially a walk around a wetland.

Guandu Nature Park Location

📍 Closest MRT: Guandu (red line - exit 1)
Then it's a 15 minute walk, or you can take a YouBike (stations next to MRT and the park)

title: Bowls of Syrupy Goodness at Eastern Ice Store
excerpt: A 20-year-old Da'an dessert institution known for handmade tapioca pearls, with two consumer awards to its name - serving soupy iced desserts from 11am to 11pm daily.
content:
One of the most established and famous desserts places in Taipei, the Eastern Ice Store (東區粉圓) has been serving up handmade tapioca pearls and other soupy iced desserts for over 20 years. The "Eastern" in the name refers to Dongqu, Taipei's East District around Zhongxiao Dunhua where the shop is based, and it's a genuinely decorated spot too, having picked up both the ROC Consumers' Association Golden Award and a Customer Satisfaction Gold Award over the years.

Open 11:00 to 23:00 every day, you'll usually find a large queue of locals waiting to be served and seated. With everything priced at only NT$60, you can choose up to four toppings to add to a syrupy soupy mix packed with ice.

The toppings available at Eastern Ice Store include many types of beans, softened and sweetened vegetables such as taro and sweet potato, tapioca, peanuts and jellies. You can just point to your desired choices from the many trays at the counter.

After you've paid, you can take the bowl to the seating area next door to consume it.

The small pieces of ice within will quickly begin to melt, which isn't really a problem since they'll still remain cold and tasty. You also have the option to top up with more ice from a table next to the counter.

If you've tried and liked the shaved ice dishes, then you'll no doubt like the deserts at Eastern Ice Store too. Refreshing and tasty treats that are very different to anything we have in the West.

Traveller Tips

Perfect way to cool down. There's no English spoken (though there's some English on the menu), so be prepared to point at your choices from the trays at the counter - a queue is likely, but it moves quickly and everything's priced the same regardless of what you pick.

Eastern Ice Store Location

📍 Closest MRT: Zhongxiao Dunhua (Blue line - exit 3)

title: Great Greek Pita Gyros at Taipei Souvlaki
excerpt: Fast-food style Greek souvlaki and gyros in Dunhua — follow your nose, the grilled meat gives it away before you see it.
content:
Taipei Souvlaki is a small Greek restaurant found within the Dunhua area. Best found with your nose rather than your eyes, the aroma of the grilled meat will draw you directly to it.

They offer two types of fast-food style Greek dishes.

  • Souvlaki, which is basically skewered meat
  • Pita Gyros, which is pita bread with meat, vegetables and sauces

So far we've only tried to Pita Gyros but I can safely say these were the tastiest pita dishes we've tried in Taipei. Coming wrapped in a cone-shaped pita and filled with a choice of meat, fish, mushrooms or falafel. They're also mixed with vegetables, chips and a Tzatziki sauce - a Greek yogurt sauce with dill, garlic, lemon and pepper to give the dish a lovely freshness and zing.

The succulence of the meat combined with the freshness of the vegetables and sauce and the warm freshly made pita are an absolute delight.

It's a small place with only a few tables. Although it's open to the Taipei heat, cooling fans will keep the heat at bay. The Greek owner/chef and his wife will make you feel very welcome and obviously enjoy feeding their customers some of their favourite Greek food.

Maybe the only criticism of Taipei Souvlaki is the time it can take for the meal to be cooked and prepared when it's busy here. It feels like they need two people cooking the food, although it must be difficult finding someone in Taipei with the skill and knowledge of Greek food the owner has.

Side dishes such a chips, falafel and calamari, and a small but nice selection of drinks complete the meal, including Mythos - a Greek lager.

With a good Greek meal difficult to find anywhere in this city, Taipei Souvlaki is one Greek place you should definitely sniff out!

Menu

Pros

  • Amazing aroma and taste to match

Cons

  • Limited seating

title: Enjoy an Outdoor Ale at Landmark Taihu
excerpt: A hole-in-the-wall Taihu taproom near Eslite in Xinyi, outdoor seating only. What's on tap and how it compares to the other branches.
content:
One of three Taihu taprooms located in Taipei, Landmark Taihu can be found close to the Eslite mall in the Xinyi Shopping District.

Functioning as a hole-in-the-wall pub with only an outdoor drinking area and no seating, it serves some fine craft ales to the many business people and shoppers in the area.

Although they mainly serve their own Taihu ales, other American brands such as Modern Times are also on the drinks menu. Ranging from IPAs, pale ales right through to the darker and heavier stouts. Their 'Grapefruitophraphy' ale also caters to those who prefer more sour ales.

Served in 300ml glasses, you can also purchase a 'flight' of four smaller sized glasses should you want to sample a range of their beers. These come in 150ml sized vessels and cost NT$400 for a tray of them plus a water to cleanse your palette between sips.

There's only snack food available here, with mixed nuts and chilli chips (which are actually fried chillis and not chips coated in chilli) among the options.

If you're in the Xinyi Shopping District and need a quick refreshing drink, then Taihu Landmark is undoubtedly your best bet!

Pros

  • Nice outdoor area to drink
  • Good selection of ales

Cons

  • Standing only
  • Not much food

Menu

Price: $$$

Level of English: Good (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

Even though it's outdoors, it's strictly a no smoking area.

title: Thrill Rides at Taipei Children's Amusement Park
excerpt: Cheap rides aimed at younger children, in northern Shilin. Ticket prices, which rides suit which ages, and how to get there.
content:
The Taipei Children's Amusement Park is located in the northern part of the Shilin district. While it's certainly no Disneyland, it's a great place to take children, being geared towards mainly younger kids.

With it's very cheap entry price (free on Saturday evenings), and the main rides costing only between NT$20 and NT$30, it's a fun and affordable way to keep kids entertained for a few hours.

You can also purchase a day ticket from Klook that gives you unlimited access to all the main rides.

See Price section below for details

Altogether, there are 13 main rides to choose from and a handful of smaller rides. The park is only a few acres in size but there's enough variety in rides to keep children of most ages entertained.

The Swing Ship, Drop Tower and of course the giant Ferris Wheel are the most popular rides, and serve up enough thrills to get pulses racing.

There's a large indoor section with many fun games machines and an activity play centre.

There's plenty of food options on site, and a large food hall serving Asian cuisine.

Located about 5 minutes walk from the Taipei Astronomical Museum and 15 minutes from Shilin Night Market, a visit to all of these would easily fill a whole day.

Taipei Children's Amusement Park doesn't ever get too busy, and a visit on a Saturday evening when the sun has gone down and entry is free is definitely the best time to visit.

Pros

  • Cheap large rides and entry
  • Great for young children

Cons

  • Certainly no Disneyland
  • Small rides are expensive

AdmissionNT$30NT$15NT$15Free

title: The Sky isn't the Limit at the Taipei Astronomical Museum
excerpt: The best museum in Taipei for children: three floors of interactive displays, IMAX and 3D theatres, and the Cosmic Adventure ride.
content:
The Taipei Astronomical Museum is the best Museum in Taipei for children. Not only does it have three floors full of fun and interactive displays, it also boasts IMAX and 3D theatres, and a unique Cosmic Adventure experience.

The main entrance hall gives you an insight of what to expect. A large hot air balloon that floats to the ceiling aided by controls. One great thing about the museum is that almost all of the information displays include English.

For just NT$40, you gain entry to the Main Exhibition Hall. With three floors featuring every aspect of space exploration. Astronomy, astrophysics, cosmology, Earth and planetary sciences all fully represented.

The floors are split up into the following categories:

  • 1st Floor
    • Kaleidoscope of the Universe
    • The Earth
    • Space Exploration
  • 2nd Floor
    • The Sun, Earth & Moon
    • The Solar System
    • Stars
    • The Milky Way
  • 3rd Floor
    • Galaxies
    • The Universe
    • The Search for Life
    • Observations
    • Astronomy in Taiwan

The Space Exploration section is one of the best thought out areas, with many interactive displays showing how problems in zero gravity were overcome, and even includes replica spacesuits.

There's a reconstruction of the lunar module, complete with a camera that displays your face on the helmet of the astronaut.

The Earth section includes a neat spinning representation of our planet, and even a simulated whirlwind.

All the sections in the Taipei Astronomical Museum are well designed and include many interactive displays and fun things for kids (and adults) to enjoy. There are well over 100 unique and interesting displays on the three floors.

They even have some fallen meteorites.

Outside the main exhibition hall, there are a few other activities you can enjoy, although these all cost extra (see Prices section).

On the 4th floor is Cosmic Adventure, which is a simulated adventure for kids to see what it would feel like to be in space, and features aliens and other surprises.

There are two theatres too, one IMAX and one 3D.

The 3D theatre rotates its programme every few months, so check the museum's website for what's currently showing.

The 'Cosmic' IMAX includes 'Mars: One Thousand One', a documentary about the issues involved in journeying to Mars.

Both theatres have screenings every hour on the hour from 09:00 until 16:00 (extended to 19:00 on Saturdays)

Being an Astronomical Museum, it is also equipped with two telescopes, although the larger of them is not open to the public.

The smaller one is open during the day, but is restricted to viewing sunspots. On Saturday evenings, it can be used to view stars and planets, and can be set to track anything in the night sky.

With the many attractions here, you could spend all day at the Taipei Astronomical Museum.

Pros

  • Great for kids
  • Packed with many fun and interactive displays

Cons

  • Not close to an MRT station

Prices

Closed on Mondays and public holidays

Traveller Tips

It's a great area to take children. Both the Taipei Children's Amusement Park and National Taiwan Science Education Center are located within the vicinity.

Come on a Saturday evening to take advantage of the telescope they have.

title: Taipei Markets: The Best Night and Day Markets to Visit
excerpt: A guide to Taipei's night and day markets - which night market to pick for food, crowds or local atmosphere, plus the morning markets and weekend halls where the city actually shops.
content:
Night markets are a national pastime rather than a tourist attraction, and Taipei has dozens of them – from vast tourist labyrinths to three-block affairs where you'll be the only foreigner in the queue. What far fewer visitors realise is that the city has a second, entirely separate market culture that runs while the night markets are shut: morning markets, covered halls and weekend flower sheds where locals actually do their shopping.

This guide covers both. Which night market to pick depends almost entirely on what you want from the evening, so that's how I've grouped them – and the day markets are worth an hour of your trip even if you have no intention of buying anything.

How Night Markets Actually Work

A few things worth knowing before your first one, because they're not obvious and they shape how much you enjoy it.

Most open around 17:00 or 18:00 and run to midnight. The sweet spot is roughly 18:00 to 20:00 – late enough that everything's open, early enough to avoid the worst crush. Arrive at 21:00 on a Saturday at Shilin and you'll spend the evening shuffling.

Bring cash. This is the one part of Taipei where your card is close to useless – the odd stall takes an EasyCard, but small notes are what you need. Nothing costs much: NT$50–100 buys most single items, and NT$300 is a very full evening for one person.

The right way to eat one is to share and keep moving. Buy one thing per stall, eat it standing up, walk on. Trying to have a sit-down meal in a night market is missing the point, and you'll fill up on the first thing you see.

One genuinely useful shortcut: the Michelin Guide lists street food stalls, and Taipei's night markets hold a lot of them. I've mapped every Michelin-listed stand across eight night markets, with the exact location of each, which takes the guesswork out of which of forty near-identical stalls is the good one.

The Night Markets, and Which to Pick

Shilin is the biggest, the most famous and the one every tour lands at. It's split between a warren of narrow alleys above ground and a sprawling basement food court, and it has the widest range of anything in the city – oyster omelettes and stinky tofu, but also claw machines, clothing stalls, shrimp fishing and games. If you're only doing one night market and you want the full spectacle, this is the correct answer. It is not the place to come for a quiet local evening.

Raohe is the one I'd send a food-first visitor to. It's a single straight street running between the Ciyou Temple gate at one end and the illuminated arch at the other, which makes it dramatically easier to navigate than Shilin's maze – you can walk the whole thing and genuinely try a lot in one evening. Five stalls here appear in the Michelin Guide. Join the queue for the black pepper buns at the temple entrance; it moves faster than it looks.

Ningxia is the connoisseur's pick. It's small, old-fashioned and almost entirely food – no clothes, no games, no distractions – with four Michelin-listed stalls packed into a couple of hundred metres. If Shilin feels like a funfair and you'd rather just eat very well for an hour, come here instead.

Tonghua – also called Linjiang Street – is the one a lot of locals name as their favourite, precisely because it still feels lived-in rather than curated. It's a few manageable streets a short walk from Taipei 101, which makes it the obvious evening if you've spent the afternoon in Xinyi.

If you want to go further off the trail, Nanjichang is the one to know about. It's a tight, scruffy, thoroughly local market out towards the Botanical Garden, and it punches enormously above its weight for Michelin-listed food – several of the city's best cheap eats are here, with almost no tourists. Opens 17:00. Yansan, north of the river near Dadaocheng, is similar in spirit and opens an hour later.

Two more with specific appeal. Gongguan serves the university district, so it's the cheapest of the lot and skews young, clothes and gadgets alongside the food, with a Michelin-recommended gua bao stall to anchor a visit. And Huaxi Street – the old Snake Alley – is these days more curiosity than dinner: a covered arcade beside Longshan Temple where a handful of vendors still serve snake and turtle alongside ordinary stalls. Worth twenty minutes for the strangeness, and it pairs naturally with the temple.

The Day Markets Nobody Tells You About

This is the half of Taipei's market culture that visitors miss entirely, and it's the more revealing one. Night markets are where the city goes out; morning markets are where it actually shops.

Shuanglian Morning Market is the one to start with, and probably my favourite market in the city. It runs along a narrow lane beside Zhongshan Linear Park, between Shuanglian and Minquan West Road stations, and it's a proper working market: fish, poultry, vegetables, flowers, pickles, and stalls doing breakfast to eat on your feet – fried oyster cakes, fish ball soup, hot soy milk with fried bread. There's a temple, Wenchang Gong, sitting incongruously in the middle of it. It trades from roughly 07:00 to 14:30, and you want to be there between 08:00 and 11:00; the seafood and the fried things are noticeably better before noon. Some stalls still offer wanmian, the traditional face-threading, which is worth watching even if you don't fancy it.

Nanmen Market is the grand indoor counterpart, and it's newly rebuilt – it reopened in October 2023 after four years in a temporary home, and all 254 original traders moved into a glass twelve-storey building near Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall. Founded in 1907, it's the place Taipei families come for the good version of everything: pork jerky, cured meats, dried fruit, Shanghai-style steamed sponge cake, and the zongzi that turn up on every table at festival time. Fresh produce and fish are in the basement, the dried goods and snack shops on the ground floor. Open 07:00–19:00, closed Mondays. Go hungry and expect to leave carrying things.

At weekends only, the Jianguo Flower and Jade Markets take over the covered space beneath the Jianguo expressway in Daan – two vast adjacent halls, one wall-to-wall flowers, orchids, bonsai and gardening kit, the other a maze of jewellery, antiques, carvings and a great deal of jade. Even with no intention of buying, the flower market on a Sunday morning is one of the most photogenic hours in Taipei.

Also weekends, the Expo Farmers' Market sets up in the greenery of Expo Park, selling produce, tea, honey and snacks direct from growers across Taiwan. It's the easiest of these to combine with something else – Maji Square is right there for lunch afterwards.

Two more that are really neighbourhoods rather than markets. Dihua Street in Dadaocheng is a whole street of dried goods, herbs, tea and mushrooms in restored Baroque shophouses, with the Yongle Fabric Market stacked above it – three floors of bolt cloth and tailors who'll make something up for you. It goes berserk in the fortnight before Lunar New Year, when the street becomes the city's festival shopping run. And near Yongkang Street, Dongmen Market is the everyday counterpart to the famous food street outside it – a traditional market a couple of minutes from the MRT, where the neighbourhood buys its fish.

So Which Should You Actually Go To?

If you have one evening: Raohe for the food, Shilin for the spectacle. If you have three, do Raohe, Ningxia and one local one – Tonghua or Nanjichang. If you're a serious eater, work from the Bib Gourmand list rather than wandering and hoping.

And give up one morning to a day market. Shuanglian if you want the living, breathing version; Nanmen if you'd rather browse in air conditioning and take food home. It's a completely different city from the one you see at 20:00, and it costs nothing to walk through.

Everything here is reachable on the MRT, most of it within a couple of minutes of a station.

Klook.com

title: Cool Jazz Vibes at Yuppy Bookstore Cafe
excerpt: A cafe that doubles as a live music and lecture venue, tucked on the third floor of a hotel near Zhongxiao Fuxing MRT.
content:
The Yuppy Bookstore Cafe, (aka Art Reading Cafe) is a restaurant/cafe that doubles as a live music venue and lecture/film screening room. Found close to Zhongxiao Fuxing MRT on the third floor of a hotel, it really does feel like you're entering into a world of films and literature.

The entrance has been styled to reflect the lobby in Wes Anderson's Grand Budapest Hotel. Certainly one of the best and more unique entrances in Taipei.

Walking into the long main room, you're greeted by the March Hare and many antique furnishings of all shapes and sizes imported from Europe. It's a very impressive room that teems with an opulence and richness rarely matched in Taipei.

Many elegant old lamps, clocks and other strange and wonderful objects adorn all parts of the room.

There are events here most nights, with lectures and film screenings, but it's the music you should come here for.

With mainly jazz bands playing, some coming from as far afield as Columbia and France, they attract some of the most talented jazz singers and musicians seen in Taipei.

Click here to see the live acts playing at Yuppy Book Store

The sets consist of jazz covers with some original songs thrown in. The three acts we've seen so far were all highly accomplished. The singers adept at many different styles of jazz, and all the musicians were masters of their instruments of choice.

When bands are playing, there's an entrance fee of around NT$400 each, and each person will also need to spend at least NT$400 on food and/or drinks. The food isn't the reason you should come here though. The pasta dishes we had were very hit and miss, although the seafood and Thai curry pastas were perfectly acceptable.

There are many wines available to drink. We're not really wine drinkers, but luckily they also have a great selection of Belgian beers.

You must arrive at 18:00 sharp to order and consume your meals before the acts start at around 19:30. The stage is obscured from some tables but they do have two large screens with a live feed of the stage.

The music normally lasts for 90 minutes with a break in the middle, and by the end of the night the performers we saw had the entire audience in the palms of their hands.

Booking well ahead is definitely advised, especially if you want a good table and avoid the ones behind the pillars. We've already booked the next act!

Pros

  • Delightfully decadent room
  • High class performers
  • Great selection of Belgian beers

Cons

  • Food is average at best
  • Stage not visible from all seats

Price: $$$$

Level of English: Good (English on menu)

title: Great Indian Restaurants in Taipei
excerpt: From homely Punjabi cooking to Michelin-recognised fine dining and dedicated vegetarian menus - the best Indian restaurants across Taipei.
content:
With dozens of Indian restaurants, Taipei isn't short of choice. However, many we've been to haven't exactly been memorable. Be it homely, fine-dining or vegetarian, these are some gems that really shine.

Click here to see all my 'best of' lists

Oye Punjabi

Found in the heart of Taipei, Oye Punjabi serves homely Indian dishes that will not only warm your belly, but your heart too. Their Naan bread is probably the best we've had in Taipei, while their Dal Tadkas are nothing short of sensational.

Click here to read more about Oye Punjabi

Saffron Fine Indian Cuisine

Although Saffron is a little out of the way in Tianmu, it worth the journey as their dishes are very fine indeed. Another Indian restaurant that has earned a place in the Michelin Guide, their spicing is a notch above most.

Click here to read more about Saffron Fine Indian Cuisine

A few more well-regarded options worth knowing about, based on strong local reviews rather than a visit of our own – worth trying and judging for yourself:

Balle Balle Indian Restaurant & Bar

A long-running Punjabi specialist in Songshan (open since well before 2014, and still going strong), known for tandoori chicken, murg malai kebab and baigan patiala – a smoky Punjabi-style eggplant curry. Portions are generous and a meal for two typically runs NT$600-800.

View Balle Balle Indian Restaurant & Bar on Google Maps

Mayur Indian Kitchen

A well-established chain with branches across the city, including a dedicated vegetarian/vegan location on Jinan Road. The menu spans both North and South Indian cooking, so it's a good option if you want dosa or samosas alongside the usual curries and tandoori.

View Mayur Indian Kitchen on Google Maps

Moksha Indian Restaurant

Rated among the best Indian food in the city by local reviewers, with an extensive vegetarian and vegan menu alongside the meat dishes. There are two branches – one in Da'an, and one in Shilin near Zhishan MRT, just around the corner from Zhishan Garden and the Traditional Theatre Centre.

View Moksha Indian Restaurant (Da'an) on Google Maps

Nataraj Indian Cuisine

The highest-rated of the bunch on local review sites, in Songshan. Some of the kitchen staff are from South India, so alongside the usual North Indian menu it's a solid option if you're after genuinely authentic South Indian dishes too.

View Nataraj Indian Cuisine on Google Maps

title: Lamigos at Taoyuan Baseball Stadium
excerpt: Home to the Lamigo Monkeys, one of only four teams in the Taiwan Baseball League. A first-timer's guide to watching a game.
content:
The Taoyuan International Baseball Stadium is the home ground for the Lamigo Monkeys, one of only four teams which form the Taiwan Baseball League.

Having never experienced a live baseball game before but watched many NBL games on TV, I thought it would be a good opportunity to take a trip to Taoyuan.

The league runs from March until about the end of September. The matches start in the evening when it's slightly more bearable temperatures, the times and dates can be found here (light blue denotes the Taoyuan games).

There are a few ways to travel to Taoyuan from Taipei. A cheaper but longer option would be to take the commuter train that runs along the Airport Express line, but I thought I'd give the HSR a try as trains only take 25 minutes or so from Taipei Main Station.

The baseball stadium is located about 2km from the Taoyuan HSR station, but there are YouBike stations handily placed near the station and the stadium, so this seemed ideal. It's about a 10 minute ride to reach the stadium.

Once there, you can easily purchase tickets (NT$400 for adults) which will allow you to sit in any of the public seating around there ground.

It took a while to find out how to actually get in though, as the entrance is towards the rear-right side of the ground.

Once inside, if you're feeling hungry, there are many booths selling food ranging from bento boxes, fried chicken and even a Pizza Hut. There's also a small convenience store selling snacks, soft drinks and thankfully beer, all at standard prices.

I opted for a Formosa Chang bento and it was very tasty!

The ground holds 20,000 although it was probably well less than a quarter full. Having said that, there were enough people for a great atmosphere.

On to the game. The standard was surprisingly good with the fielding very sharp, the hitting strong (with a couple of home runs), maybe the only slight letdown was the pitching - a little wild with a few free walks for batsmen being hit.

There are many activities to keep the crowd amused. The cheerleaders of course, sometimes dancing during the actual game. When the cheerleaders take a break, they open up the stages to give kids a try. There's even a rocket ship that takes off during the innings, and the cheeky Lamigo mascot makes a few appearances. The kids at the ground seem to love being there, as do the adults, with chants and dances occurring throughout the match.

In the end the Lamigos pulled through for a good win. I'll definitely be returning as it was a real blast and the baseball was of a high standard!

Pros

  • Fun for everyone
  • Lots of food stands
  • High standard

Cons

  • A bit of a trek outside Taipei city to get there

Prices

Adults: NT$400
Students: NT$300
Children: NT$250

Prices could vary for other matches

Dates

The baseball league runs from March until September.

Traveller Tips

Schedule found here.

Right outside Taoyuan HSR station is Gloria Outlets, and large shopping complex with many outlet stores.

Location

Take the HSR from Taipei Main to Taoyuan, then take a YouBike from there to the stadium.

title: Fine Craft Ales at Taihu Craft Beer Tasting Room
excerpt: The best of Taihu's three Taipei taprooms, pouring smoked, soured and barrel-aged beers from the brewery founded in 2013.
content:
Taihu is one of a best craft ale breweries in Taiwan. Founded in 2013, they've finely honed their beer making process and now make some excellent ales. Whether they're smoked, soured, barrel aged, steeped, or simply create a classic brew, there are many exotic and interesting flavours at play.

Taihu currently have three tap rooms based in Taipei, giving people a chance to sample some of their beverages. The best of which is the Taihu Craft Beer Tasting Room, found very close to the Zhongxiao Fuxing MRT station.

With over 20 different types of tap ales to choose from, these include IPAs, Stouts, Pale Ales, Amber and Golden Ales. Most are Taihu's own ales, while there's a small selection of beverages from other breweries including Modern Times. They serve some interesting cocktails/mocktails too, with more eclectic ingredients such as guava, lavender and sake.

All are served in 300ml or pint sizes Taihu glasses and generally cost between NT$200 and NT$250, with the pint glasses costing an extra NT$100. These are the best value, although if you prefer to try a selection then stick to the smaller ones.

The bar consists of two levels, with the first floor being a more casual affair. High wooden tables and stools, it's all nicely decked out.

Downstairs has a large bar and more comfortable seating. Probably a better option is you intend on staying a while.

They serve some bar food, including fried, wings, mac 'n' cheese and calamari fritters, but their speciality is burgers where you can effectively make your own, choosing size, condiments and toppings.

The Mini burger is just a single meat patty, while the Fat burger consists of three pieces. I decided to go down the middle - the Stack Burger, with two patties, it comes with sauces, pickles, cheese and onions. Others can be added (some for free), such as bacon, egg and jalapenos.

Coming wrapped in grease-proof paper, which is fully needed as these are messy affairs. They are serious burgers though. Proper gourmet burgers for sure, probably the best I've had in Taipei. The patty has a great texture and taste, and everything inside works well with the meat.

Great beers and fine burgers. What more could anyone ask for?

Taihu Craft Beer Tasting Room has a nice relaxed vibe, with friendly and super quick service. I will be getting another burger fix soon for sure!

Pros

  • Large selection of tap beers
  • Fantastic burgers

Cons

  • Pricey drinks

Price: $$$

Level of English: Good (English on menu)

title: Ancestral Houses with Charm in Abundance
excerpt: Step back in time with a visit to the most beautifully preserved ancestral houses in Taipei, with gardens to match.
content:
Some of the most beautiful and well-preserved ancestral houses found in and around Taipei – from a centuries-old Fujianese homestead to a baroque presidential guest house. All these homes have fantastic gardens to wander around too.

Click here to see all my 'best of' lists

Lin Family Mansion

Tucked away in the Banqiao district of Taipei, this hidden gem is a quintessential Chinese ancestral house, its 5 acre grounds centred on the Banyan Shade Pond, the largest of the three ponds on site.

Click here to read more about Lin Family Mansion

Chiang Kai-Shek Shilin Residence

Home to former military leader of Taiwan until his death in 1975, the Chiang Kai-Shek Shilin Residence is beautifully preserved and has many acres of fine gardens and outhouses, all free to wander around.

Click here to read more about Chiang Kai-Shek Shilin Residence

Lin An Tai Ancestral House

Dating to 1785, Lin An Tai is one of the oldest buildings in Taiwan – dismantled and rebuilt piece by piece at its current site after a 1978 preservation campaign that helped shape national heritage law. Step back in time and enjoy the buildings and gardens hidden behind the walls of the estate.

Click here to read more about Lin An Tai Ancestral House

Taipei Guest House

Built at the turn of the last century to house Japanese diplomats and officials, and only open on a select few dates each year, the Taipei Guest House is a grand baroque building that owes more to western architecture than other ancestral houses but this only adds to its uniqueness and charm.

Click here to read more about Taipei Guest House

title: Modern Mediterranean Grub at Gonna
excerpt: A Mediterranean restaurant built around healthy, vibrant dishes, now with three branches across Taipei. What to order and where to find them.
content:
Gonna is a popular Mediterranean-style restaurant that focuses on healthy and vibrant dishes.

Originally opened in the Daan distrinct of Taipei, this has proved so popular that it's since expanded and now has three city branches.

When you walk inside, you're presented with a playful yet modern setting, with amusing one-liners adorning the walls. "One Day I Am Gonna Make Onion Cry".

You'll be given the menu and a corresponding sheet to fill out your choices, of which they said you need to take to the counter to order and pay upfront, although they actually collected our order from the table. Some of the items on the menu were sold out unfortunately, although nothing we particularly desired.

The food menu at Gonna is divided into 7 sections:

  • Greens & Grains
  • Good Protein
  • Panini & Burger
  • Hearty Pasta
  • Snacks
  • Desserts

The menu headings are in English. However, their descriptions are not, so working out the ingredients is a bit of a guessing game if you don't read Chinese. Some pictures are at hand to help however.

The salad bowls looked too tempting not to try, so we opted for the Fattoush Salad with Grilled Halloumi as I've not seen many restaurants in Taipei serving Halloumi.

Containing sliced cucumber, tomato, radish, fennel and lettuce, it was exactly what the doctor ordered.

We've since been back to try another of their salads - the Char-boiled Chicken Caesar Salad, with iceberg lettuce, croutons, sun-dried tomatoes and quinoa. Another very fine salad.

There are plenty of interesting sounding pasta dishes at Gonna. The Macaroni with Chicken, Cauliflower and Broccoli sounded extremely tempting, but as we had already ordered chicken we opted for the Linguine Alla Puttanesca, which is actually tuna with olives, chilli and watercress in a tomato sauce.

Tuna pasta is something I've rarely seen in Taipei, so it was a nice change and tasted great.

They have some nice snack food a Gonna. The Sweet Potato Fries with Cranberry and Apple Sauce. Crispy on the outside, soft in the centre.

We had to try their soup too, which changes every so often. Today it was the Cream of Pumpkin Soup, thick and creamy and not too sweet like at other places we've tried it. It doesn't come with bread, so we ordered the Rosemary Garlic Bread, perfect for wiping the bowl clean.

To wash things down, we ordered the Guava & Cucumber and Beetroot & Berry juices. Combinations we've not tried before but former was cool and refreshing and the latter was very beetrooty! 100% natural pressed juice.

Gonna also has a range or beers and wines, including Buckskin on draft and large cans of Taihu, including bright ales, IPAs and Weisse, which I really like so had to try.

The service at Gonna is very quick, with all items coming within 5 minutes of ordering.

They also serve some tasty looking brunches, which are served until 14:00. These include omelettes and various super-food dishes.

Gonna is very popular. When we went, they didn't have a seat available for an hour but we decided to wait. It was definitely worth the wait though, and we will be back for sure!

Pros

  • Healthy and tasty
  • Nice selection of food that I've not seen elsewhere in Taipei
  • Pricing is reasonable
  • Quick Service

Cons

  • Not close to any other attractions
  • Descriptions on menu not in English

Price: $$

title: Deep Fried Cheesy Jackets at Prince Cheese Potatoes
excerpt: A Shilin Night Market stall selling jacket potatoes since 2004, on the corner near Jiantan MRT — one of the market's longest-running stands.
content:
Situated on the corner of Shilin Night Market near Jiantan MRT, Prince Cheese Potatoes is a stand selling jacket potatoes. One of the oldest stands in the night market, it's been around since 2004 and has gained a reputation for producing tasty spuds, having featured on a number of television programs.

They're not quite like the oven baked jacket potatoes you'd find in the UK, as these ones are coated in cheese, deep fried and topped off with a choice of toppings. The icing on the cake is a very generous helping of thick melted cheese, drowning the potato out of view.

When you join the queue, which is often quite long, you'll be given a pictured menu (see Menu section) to choose you desired toppings.

There are a few meat/fish options, with ham, German sausage, chicken, tuna or octopus. For vegetarians, there are plenty of choices too, with corn, egg or even pineapple.

We however chose the 'Club' potato, consisting of ham, corn, egg, tuna, broccoli and pineapple. Then drowned in cheese. At only NT$80 it's very good value.

You'll be asked if you want to takeaway or eat in the small room located behind the stand. If there's space, it's much better to eat sitting down due to the potential mess involved.

You're only given a plastic spoon, which I thought wouldn't be strong enough to get through the potato skin, but the potatoes are very soft and easy to eat. A very indulgent meal for sure.

There is another Prince Cheese Potato stand located in the Ximending District. While it doesn't reach the same heights as this one, it is still worth a visit if spuds are your thing!

Menu

Pros

  • Original and delicious

Cons

  • Queuing likely

Price: $

Level of English: Low (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

Come early to avoid excessive queues.

title: Fly Over Taiwan at i-Ride Taipei
excerpt: A 5D flying-theatre ride over Taiwan or the USA, on the 6th floor of Breeze Nanshan. Ticket prices and which film to pick.
content:
Located on the 6th floor within the newest Breeze Centre in the Xinyi Shopping District, the i-Ride Taipei is a 5D motion experience that takes you on a journey over either the USA or Taiwan.

You can choose between the two countries, or alternatively purchase a combo ticket where you can enjoy both. See Prices section for details.

The rides last for approximately 20 minutes. You'll sit on seats designed to move and sway to the movements of the large curved screen that takes up your full vision, with wind, mist and even scent effects bombarding your senses as you journey through the mountains and valleys. The music has been specifically composed to match the landscapes in each scene.

We only tried the Taiwan ride but it was as thrilling as it was intriguing to see this beautiful country from the air. You'll fly over the mountains in the centre, Taroko gorge, Taipei and many other beautiful parts of Taiwan that will give you a unique viewpoint of this beautiful island.

Klook.com

It's certainly something different from anything else we've experienced in Taipei, and will no doubt return for the USA experience too.

title: Take Your Laptop to Youmoutoohana Coffee
excerpt: A Japanese-themed cafe off Yong Kang Street, named for a real acoustic duo whose song became a Taiwan-Japan thank-you message after the 2011 earthquake.
content:
Situated just off the famous Yong Kang Street, Youmoutoohana Coffee (羊毛與花) is a great cafe that's perfect for a quick drink, but is also a great place to work for a while. It's one of several branches around Taipei, with others in Dongmen and at the Taipei Film House near Zhongshan.

With 20 or so tables available, and many plug sockets located throughout, it's a chilled and quiet cafe. It's walls are plastered with film and music memorabilia, mainly of Japanese origin, with many books and CDs and gentle Japanese music playing in the background.

The cafe takes its name and theme from Youmou to Ohana (羊毛とおはな), a gentle Japanese acoustic duo formed in 2004. Their song "Fuyu no Uta" was used in a Taiwanese TV commercial as a thank-you message from Japan after the 2011 earthquake, in recognition of Taiwan's huge outpouring of donations at the time – which likely explains the affection for them here. Vocalist Hana Chiba, one half of the duo, sadly passed away in 2015.

Their menu mainly consists of drinks, with tea, coffee, juices and smoothies. There is a small section for food, with some pies and brunch type dishes available.

We tried the green chicken curry pie and breakfast meal, which were both fine although nothing special.

They have a cabinet with delicious looking cakes too, and a fridge filled with premium beers. We'll try these next time we come for sure!

We went for the osmanthus sparkling water and the honey lemon smoothie, the latter being more like a sorbet but was very refreshing.

As with all the cafes on Yong Kang Street, the prices are slightly on the more expensive side, but if you're going to spend some time working here it's definitely worth it.

Traveller Tips

We wish we tried one of the cakes. There's lots of seating and plug sockets, making it a good place to work, although the food options are a bit limited – the drinks and desserts are the real draw. English is good, with English on the menu.

Location

📍 Closest MRT: Dongmen (red/orange lines - exit 5)

title: Wu Liu Shou - Izakaya in a Great Setting
excerpt: An izakaya in Dongmen with an authentic Japanese interior, serving small plates of meat and vegetables.
content:
The Dongmen area of Taipei has many Japanese restaurants to choose from, and one of the best here is Wu Liu Shou, an izakaya restaurant serving small places of meat and vegetable dishes.

The exterior is a very authentic Japanese style, as is the inside, with its predominantly wooden panels, floors and furnishings. The seating area is very narrow, especially next to the serving counter but this only adds to the authenticity and charm of the place.

If you're hungry, the minimum spend of NT$500 per person shouldn't be an issue, as you'll only need to order 4 or 5 small plates each. These are divided into sections - Cold Starters, Kebabs, Grilled, Stir-fried, Fried and Soups.

We tried the great looking spinach rolls for a starter, which were wrapped in seaweed and served with a sesame sauce. They tasted as good as they looked.

The lightly grilled scallop dish was another highlight, very soft in texture and melting in your mouth. Juxtaposed to that, the crispy fried chicken was exactly as described, very crispy.

The grilled baby corn was possibly the largest we've eaten - more like adolescent corn - but was perfectly cooked. The stir-fried vegetables with pork dish was crunchy and very moreish, we only wished there was more.

The kebab plates we tried were the shrimp wrapped in bacon and the pork cheek, the former being succulent and delicious, although the pork was slightly on the chewy side for us (maybe that's how it's meant to be).

To wash it all down, I ordered one of the draft beers, trying the Orion rather than the Asahi. It was suitably refreshing. They also have some bottled beers, plum liquors and of course Sake available, plus some soft drinks.

We were going to try the mochi dessert, but we'd eaten enough already.

The cost was just over NT$1,400 (with the 10% service charge) which was quite acceptable for the filling and delicious meal we enjoyed.

Pros

  • Very presentable and tasty food
  • Authentic Japanese style and cuisine

Cons

  • Booking ahead is advised

Price: $$$

Level of English: Ok (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

Minimum spend of NT$500 per person

Very popular place to dine, so booking ahead is strongly advised

title: Nice Western Food at Campus Cafe
excerpt: An American-style diner chain modelled on US college cafes, with several Taipei branches that vary noticeably in quality.
content:
Campus Café is an American inspired café/diner with a few branches in Taipei. As their name alludes, the cafes have been designed to reflect cafés in US college campuses.

Campus Café's branches do vary considerably in size and quality however. The Daan branch, which is very centrally located, is by far the best. This and the Neihu branches are the only ones I would recommend visiting. They're spacious, and have a good variety of seating perfect for either chilling or working.

If you have children, there is even a separate area where they can play alone, yet you'll still be able to keep your beady eyes on them. There's also a projector that will air any large US sporting events.

Campus Café's menu comprises of - you've guessed it - American-style food and drink, albeit with a number of Italian dishes including risottos, pasta, pizzas and paninis.

American dishes includes burgers, fried chicken, nachos, sandwiches and fries. Everything we have tried so far has been delicious.

A special mention goes to their salads, which come in two sizes (the large one ample for two people). The salmon salad is especially good, with a nice mix of vegetables and nuts, and a number of sauces to choose from.

Their drinks are very good also. Fruit juices are all freshly squeezed, and their ice blended drinks are packed with flavour. If you prefer something alcoholic, there are some bottled beers including some delicious fruity Belgian lagers.

The price is about par in Taipei for these western cafes, with a meal for two setting you back approximately NT$800.

Campus Café is a great place to enjoy a lunchtime meal. It's comfortable, relaxed and has a nice ambience.

Pros

  • Large and tasty salads
  • Very nice drinks

Cons

  • Branches vary in quality

I would only recommend the Daan and Neihu branches.

title: Freeze your Brain at Ice Monster (Permanently Closed)
content:
Permanent Closure Notice

Please note: Ice Monster has permanently closed.

Ice Monster is a Taiwanese dessert chain that's been serving shaved ice and other desserts for over 20 years. Garnering a number of awards along the way, including one of the top 10 desserts in the world by CNN.

It's a little on the expensive side compared to similar places in Taipei, with their shaved ice bowls costing between NT$200 and NT$250, although the portions are very large and easily big enough to share. They also come with a scoop of sorbet, some panna cotta and an extra portion of fruit on the side.

With three locations in Taipei, they are generally very popular and you'll often need to queue to get in, especially in the Dongmen restaurant.

The ice bowls come in a number of different flavours, with fruit based ones such as the popular mango, the melon and pineapple, or the more exotic lychee and kiwi. Their non-fruit based ice dishes are flavoured with peanut, coffee or pearl milk tea.

They also serve a variety of dessert soups filled with taro, red beans, sesame rice balls and sweet potato.

The ice dishes are a very tasty way to cool down amid the intense summer Taipei heat!

title: Buy an iPhone at the Modern Xinyi Apple Store
excerpt: Taiwan's first standalone flagship Apple Store, designed by Foster + Partners to look like a giant MacBook from above - two floors of the latest hardware.
content:
Opened on 15th June 2019, the Apple A13 store within the Xinyi Shopping District was Taiwan's first standalone, flagship-spec Apple Store, designed by Foster + Partners working alongside Apple's then chief design officer Sir Jony Ive. With a sleek ultra-modern exterior, it typifies the craftsmanship and attention to detail Apple are famous for.

Look up from above (or from a nearby rooftop) and the whole building reads unmistakably as a closed MacBook lid – metallic finish, rounded corners, logo centred on top. Those rounded corners aren't an accident either, deliberately echoing the curved edges of an iPhone or Macbook, and the roof itself is a razor-thin 23.4 metre carbon-fibre span, timber-lined underneath.

Featuring two floors selling the very latest Apple products and accessories, the minimal clean and bright interior perfectly complements their range of gadgets.

The ground level floor is dedicated to their products, with all the latest iPhones, iPads, Macs and Apple watches.

The basement focuses on accessories, with a projector and seating to showcase their latest tech.

There's a nod to Taiwan throughout the design too – the reflecting pool out front centres on a black boulder inspired by the basalt columns of Penghu, camphor trees (a native Taiwanese species) are planted around the plaza, and the pool's occasional mist is meant to evoke Taiwan's morning fog.

The staff here – around 155 of them, roughly half transferred in from other Apple stores, covering more than 10 languages between them – are all well-versed in Apple's product lines, and are eager to help with any queries you may have.

The Apple A13 store also offers a repairing service for any damaged or malfunctioning Apple products. You can pre-book a visit to their Genius Bar here to drop off your faulty goods. In some instances, they are even able to fix it in the same day.

Also, if you spend over NT$2,000 on Apple products, you are eligible for a tax rebate of 5% . Make sure you have your passport with you and ask them to complete a form after your purchase.

Click here to read more about the Taiwan Tax Refund scheme

For all you Apple aficionados, this is the store to visit in Taipei!

Xinyi Apple Store Location

title: Awesome Bento Lunches at Miss Energy
excerpt: Bento boxes with brown rice, vegetables and a choice of meat or fish, for around NT$100 — good value for a packed lunch.
content:
Miss Energy sells nourishing and delicious bento boxes ideal for taking on your travels.

The bento boxes come with warm brown rice, a selection of soft boiled vegetables, a boiled egg and meat or fish. All of the boxes cost only around NT$100 which is very good value for a tasty and filling meal.

Chicken, pork, beef or mackerel are the options available, cooked in a variety of ways to suit eastern and western tastes. The Boiled Tender Chicken Breast is succulent and moist.

The Boiled Chicken with Kimchi is a new addition that's not on this menu, and is probably the best box I've tried so far. Only slightly spicy, but the marinated chicken tastes delicious.

While the Marinated Pork Tenderloin Marinated with Kimchi has a nice spicy kick.

The Salt Roasted Mackerel had slightly more calories than the previous ones I tried. Thankfully, the bones had been removed too.

The boxes come wrapped, so they are ideal for taking away. The contents are warm but you could of course safe them for later and eat them cold should you wish. Otherwise, you can eat them on one of the stools within the small seating area.

Calories are shown for each box on the menu, which range from about 430 to 540, ideal for the calorie counters out there.

The original branch is located close to the Peace Park in the Zhongzheng district. Due to the resounding success of this branch, Miss Energy have since opened up at least 5 more branches - including one found very close to Daan MRT station and two in Gongguan. These too have proved very popular, so I'm sure they'll be opening more branches soon.

Catering mainly for local business people, Miss Energy's opening times reflect this, as it only tends to open during weekday lunch and evening times. If you come during peak lunch hours, they'll usually be a long queue of eager office workers.

They'll have many boxes pre-prepared though, so it doesn't take long to be served.

The popularity of Miss Energy is no fluke. Taiwanese people know their food, and they've voted with their stomachs for this great little bento place.

title: Visit the Lake at Dahu Park
excerpt: A tranquil lake park in Neihu with a famous Chinese 'Moon Bridge', egrets, and lotus flowers in late summer - 25 minutes out on the brown line.
content:
Situated away from the city centre in Neihu, and about a 25 minute MRT ride on the brown line, Dahu Park is a very tranquil park built around a lake, with the hills of Mt. Bailushi (Egret Mountain) rising behind it. The park opened in 1979 and covers around 13 hectares, roughly 10 of which are the lake itself – also known as Bailu Lake, or "Egret Lake", after the birds that gather there.

The park's best-known feature is its Chinese-style "Moon Bridge" – a graceful, semi-circular bridge that forms a full circle with its own reflection in the water, and one of the more photogenic spots in this part of Taipei. There are also a number of pavilions dotted around the lake, and it's close to several hiking trails that lead up into the surrounding hills.

Aside from the lake, the park also featured a pond, which, if you come during the right season (late August to September), will be covered in Lotus flowers.

The many trees will help to give you respite from the glaring sun should you need it.

On the edge of the park is a large outdoor swimming pool with a covered section for children.

It's a genuinely peaceful escape from the city, though it does take a solid 25-30 minutes on the MRT to get out here, so it's more of a half-day trip than a quick stop.

Traveller Tips

Ensure you have drinks as there are no shops nearby

Location

📍 Closest MRT: Dahu Park Station (brown line - exit 2)

title: How and What to Order at Jin Feng Braised Pork Rice
excerpt: Taiwan’s most famous braised pork rice, ten minutes from Chiang Kai-Shek Memorial Hall. What to order, what it costs and when to go.
content:
Jin Feng is one of the most famous and popular local restaurants in Taiwan, whose speciality is braised pork rice dishes.

Located just a 10 minute walk from the Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall, Jin Feng Braised Pork Rice is difficult to miss since there is almost always a large cluster of people on the street outside waiting to be seated.

However, we managed to time it well (Wednesday at 18:00), as it was the first time we've ever been able to walk straight in.

Otherwise, you could wait for up to 30 minutes.

The staff will find a table for you (often shared with others), and give you a small slip for you to fill in your order.

Unfortunately, this is in Chinese, but fortunately, you can ask for an English guide sheet with pictures (see menu section). You will still need to match the Chinese text next to the picture with that on the slip, although it's far easier to match the price first.

If you don't order the Braised Pork Rice dish (which we once didn't), they'll look at you strange! It's on the menu as Braised Ground Pork Rice and comes in three sizes (小 - small, 中 - medium, 大 - large). It's essentially a bowl of rice with some braised pork on top and a piece of bitter melon, but it is delicious. Make sure you mix it well before eating.

We find the best dishes to accompany this are the boiled vegetables, which is usually water spinach - on the menu as Cooked Veggie and/or Dried Bamboo Shoots.

We also normally go for the tea-stained boiled egg (Stewed Egg with Taiwanese Spice) and tofu (Oily Bean Curd). If you want to be more adventurous, you could opt for the pig brain/pig stomach soups. If not, then the Pork Thick Soup, with bamboo and coriander is absolutely delicious!

You can also substitute the rice for noodles at Jin Feng. The Ground Pork with Mushroom Dry Noodles is a great alternative.

The staff will work very hard in ensuring people enter, eat and leave in as little time as possible, although they won't press you to leave unless you just sit around talking.

A meal for two people at Jin Feng Braised Pork Rice will only set you back about NT$150 - NT$200, which is very good value, especially considering just how darn tasty the food is!

A Taipei Travel Geek Top Pick!

  • The best braised pork in Taipei
  • Very cheap
  • Long opening hours

Cons

  • Service can be abrupt

title: Contemporary Izakaya at Range Bistrokaya
excerpt: A bistro-izakaya hybrid near Taipei City Hall, serving cocktails and small plates from an open kitchen.
content:
Range Bistrokaya, as the name suggests, is a cross between and bistro and izakaya restaurant, serving cocktails and small plates of food.

Situated close to the Taipei City Hall, the establishment is cosy and nicely fitted out, with an open kitchen where you can watch the skilled chefs preparing and cooking one of the many dishes available.

You'll typically need to order 5 or 6 dishes for two people. They have a number of beef dishes available, with the more premium Wagyu beef or Diced Beef Premium, which we tried and was succulent and one of the best beef dishes we've tried in Taipei.

Their fish dishes are equally as nice, with the mouthwatering Prawns, squid, salmon, scallop and cuttlefish, or you could opt of a seafood combo comprising of all of the above.

We also tried the mozzarella sticks with pork - they too were exceptional. In fact, all the dishes we tried looked and tasted amazing.

You'll probably need to order 5 or 6 dishes to satisfy two people's hunger. We chose the Pork Shoulder and Smoked Salmon Salad, with a lovely yellow mustard sauce.

You can often tell how good the cocktails are likely to be be the choice of spirits behind the bar, and Range Bistrokaya have only high quality spirits - not a Bell's whiskey or Gordon's gin in sight. Their House Special Cocktail, which is a mixture of beer, vodka and gin was very strong but with a deep multi-layered flavour.

My girlfriend isn't much of a drinker, so she tried the refreshing Grapefruit Spritzer.

You'll pay more than your average bar in Taipei, but I would definitely say it's worth the extra as the food really is top-drawer, especially the meat and fish dishes.

We shall be returning to Range Bistrokaya to sample some of their other dishes.

Pros

  • High quality meat and fish dishes

Cons

  • Not clear if you can book ahead

Price: $$$

Succulent beef is a must!
