title: Munch on Authentic Neapolitan Pizzas at Pizzeria Oggi (Permanently Closed)
content:
Permanent Closure Notice

Please note: Pizzeria Oggi has permanently closed.

Pizzeria Oggi serves the most authentic Italian pizza in Taipei. That's not just me saying it - they have an "Italian Napoli Pizza Association Certification", meaning they use the ingredients and process to create authentic Neapolitan pizzas.

Using mozzarella buffalo cheese, Italian top-grade virgin olive oil, homemade fresh tomato sauce and natural sea salt. Most importantly, they use flour imported direct from Italy. To cook the Pizza to the strict standards, they have imported an Italian sloping volcanic rock kiln for each restaurant.

And it really does show in their final product. The pizzas, which come in either 9" or 12" sizes, are exactly how they taste in Italy. Thin chewy elastic bases with a crisp crust, the cheese and tomato sauce are divine, and the toppings heavenly.

One option that's not on the menu below lets you choose your base and two pizzas and they'll put half on each side. A very good option if you have difficulty deciding on a pizza, although it is limited to specific pizzas.

Alternatively, you can create your own pizza, choosing from either Napolitano, Romano or Taiwan Wheat dough, Tomato Sauce, Pesto or Cream, and four toppings (two meat, two veg).

Pizzeria Oggi serve calzones, pasta dishes and other mains too although we'll probably never try these as the pizzas are so delicious. We did however opt for a salad to make us feel less guilty about the calories - the Caesar salad with salmon, and very nice it was too.

They've done a good job on the interior (at least in the Daan branch we went to). Playing some great Italian/Spanish music that (coupled with the food) really does make you feel like you're dining in the Mediterranean.

Drinks-wise, Pizzeria Oggi have a very good selection of beers, ciders, wines and soft drinks. The Cokes and 7-Ups having unlimited refills.

Will we be returning to Pizzeria Oggi? Heck yes!

Pros

  • We've not found a more authentic Italian pizza in Taipei

Cons

  • None of the branches are close to an MRT station

Price: $$$

Level of English: Good (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

If you have difficulty deciding on a pizza, go for the half and half one.

If you add them on Line, you can get 1 point per NT$250 spend. 3 points equates to a free dessert, while 12 points will get you a free pizza!

title: Fresh and Tasty Hawaiian Bowls at Yu Poke
excerpt: A Hawaiian poke bowl stall inside Gongguan Night Market — a fresher option than the market's usual fried food.
content:
Yu Poke is a small Hawaiian restaurant located within the Gongguan Night Market. If you're tired of the abundance of fried food found in night markets and want to opt for something altogether fresher and healthier, then Yu Poke is worth a visit.

For those not familiar with poke dishes, they're bowls of rice and vegetables usually topped off with raw fish and a sauce. Here, you get to customise your bowl with the following options:

  • 1 Fish/Meat
    • Chicken / Octopus / Shrimp / Salmon / Tuna
  • 1 Base
    • White Rice / Brown Rice / Salad / Half & half
  • 4 Mixes
    • Egg / Mushrooms / Corn / Cucumber / Broccoli / Edamame / Black Beans / Tomato / Carrot / Seaweed
  • 1 Sauce
    • Sesame / Ponzu / Teriyaki / Sriracha Spicy Mayo
  • 1 Topping
    • Coriander / Spring Onion / Black or White Sesame / Masago

You can add further mixes for an additional NT$15

The final bowls are some of the freshest and tastiest dishes we've tried in Taipei, and cost only NT$160.

You'll need to mix them well before devouring, as the sauces are placed at the bottom of the bowl. If you're not keen on raw fish, they have cooked chicken as an option too.

You can upgrade to add a drink or a small dessert similar to a panna cotta.

If you come here during peak hours, the queue often extends outside of the restaurant, and the lack of seating means you will need to wait a while but it's definitely worth the wait.

Yu Poke is a fantastic fresh alternative to the abundance of fried food found in the nearby night market. Thoroughly recommended!

Yu Poke Menu

Pros

  • Very fresh and tasty bowls

Cons

  • Not much seating

Price: $$

Level of English: Good (English on menu)

Avoid peak dinner hours

title: Enjoy a 'Crap' Meal at Modern Toilet
excerpt: Taipei's toilet-themed restaurant is now Shilin-only after the Ximending branch closed. Is the novelty worth the mediocre food?
content:
Modern Toilet is probably the only restaurant of it's kind. A toilet themed restaurant. I'm not sure who had the bright idea of combining these two rather disparate things, but for amusement factor, it scores highly.

Reopened

The Ximending branch closed for over three years during the pandemic, but reopened in 2024. It has moved to 2F, No. 7, Lane 50, Xining South Road – about seven minutes from Ximen MRT exit 6, inside the Lane 50 food alley.

Let's get one thing straight. The food here is mediocre at best, and I would definitely not have included this if it wasn't for the novelty factor. They've actually done a rather fine job of bringing the humour from the bathroom into the dining room.

Toilets as seats, poo shaped food, or meals served in a miniature toilet. A button on each table you can 'flush for service'.

Even the toilet sink is a cherub peeing into a toilet!

If your stomach and brain can handle the concept of eating out of a toilet, or drinking out of a urinal bottle (although glasses are also provided), then it's certainly worth checking out Modern Toilet. Even though the food isn't amazing, it's a decent enough meal.

One thing you must try though it the Swirly Poop Ice Cream, especially if you're with kids.

There are two restaurants left, both in the very touristic areas of Ximen and Shilin – and they are now the only two Modern Toilets anywhere in the world, after the chain’s other branches shut. We only went to the Ximen one, which I hear is much better than the other.

For humour factor alone, Modern Toilet is one to visit, especially if you have kids.

Menu

Pros

  • You won't find another restaurant like it

Cons

  • Food is average

Level of English: Good (English on menu)

Price: $$ (mains NT$290–350, ice creams NT$100–270)

Klook.com

Traveller Tips

Why drink out of a glass, when you can upgrade to a drink out of a urinal bottle?!

Upgrade your meal to include poo shaped/coloured ice-cream.

title: Exquisite Chinese Gardens in Taipei
excerpt: From a calligrapher-inspired retreat by the National Palace Museum to a century-old family estate in Banqiao - the best Chinese gardens in and around Taipei.
content:
Some of the best examples of Chinese gardens found in and around Taipei – from a museum-side retreat modelled on the writings of a famous calligrapher, to a private family estate that still feels like stepping back a hundred years.

Zhishan Garden

Located next to the National Palace Museum, this 5 acre garden is laid out around eight scenic spots inspired by the writings of the famous calligrapher Wang Xizhi, with three carp-filled ponds threaded together by bridges and pavilions. It's a great place to unwind after a visit to the museum, and is free to enter with a museum ticket.

Click here to read more about Zhishan Garden

Lin Family Mansion

This ancestral house lives and breathes within its 5 acre grounds of beautifully landscaped gardens, ponds, caves and trees – centred on the Banyan Shade Pond, the largest of the three ponds on site – and is definitely worthy of an MRT ride to Banqiao.

Click here to read more about Lin Family Mansion

Shuangxi Park and Chinese Garden

Named for the two creeks that meet nearby ("Shuangxi" literally means "twin streams"), this compact garden packs in rockeries, a moon bridge and a thundering waterfall between two busy roads in Shilin – a little oasis you should definitely check out if you're in the area.

Click here to read more about Shuangxi Garden

Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall Gardens

The 24 hectare Liberty Square where the huge Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall sits also contains some of the most beautifully landscaped gardens in Taipei, plus a trail full of the trees found in other parts of Taiwan – and if you time it right, the Changing of the Guard ceremony too.

Click here to read more about Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall Gardens

title: Visit the Idyllic Shuangxi Park and Chinese Garden
excerpt: A compact but richly detailed Chinese garden in Shilin - rockeries, a moon bridge and a thundering waterfall, named for the twin creeks that meet nearby.
content:
If you have a penchant for beautifully landscaped gardens, Shuangxi Park and Chinese Garden will be right up your alley. The name comes from the confluence of the Wai Shuangxi (Outer Twin Creek) and Nei Shuangxi (Inner Twin Creek) rivers nearby – "Shuangxi" literally means "twin streams" – and despite what the name suggests, it's a proper Chinese garden, not open parkland.

Built in 1974 and laid out by landscape architect Hu Guoli in a southern Chinese courtyard style, it packs a lot into just 2 hectares (about 5 acres): rockeries, zigzagging pathways, caves, ponds, a moon bridge and a thundering waterfall. Look out for the grey octagonal Orchid Pavilion near the entrance, modelled on the original Orchid Pavilion in Shaoxing, China – the same pavilion that inspired the design of Zhishan Garden across town.

It's a 15-minute walk from Shilin MRT, which keeps it well off the typical tourist route – you'll usually have the winding paths mostly to yourself.

Its only real drawback is that it straddles two busy roads, so some traffic noise is unavoidable. Aside from that minor quibble, the landscaping is second to none – Shuangxi Park and Chinese Garden is without question one of the nicest gardens to visit in Taipei.

Opening Hours

Open 24 hours a day, admission is free

Traveller Tips

Take some drinks with you – there's little in the way of amenities inside the garden itself.

Shuangxi Park and Chinese Garden Location

309 Fulin Road, Shilin District

📍 Nearest MRT: Shilin (red line - exit 2)
15 minute walk from here, or you could take a YouBike next to the MRT and leave your bike next to the entrance for a while

title: Enjoy the Peace and Beauty at Zhishan Garden
excerpt: A 5-acre Chinese garden at the foot of the National Palace Museum steps, styled after the Sung and Ming dynasties, with carp-filled ponds.
content:
Zhishan Garden is a beautiful Chinese garden at the base of the steps leading up to the National Palace Museum in Shilin. It was designed and built by the Taipei Fine Arts Museum specifically to bring the feel of a traditional Eastern garden closer to the public.

Reflecting the styles of the Sung and Ming dynasties across around 5 acres (1.88 hectares), it's laid out around eight named scenic spots inspired by the writings of Wang Xizhi, the famous Chinese calligrapher – among them the Orchid Pavilion, Songfeng Pavilion and Pen Washing Pool. Three ponds filled with carp are threaded together by bridges and pathways, with three wooden pavilions dotted around for you to sit and take it in.

If you find yourself at the National Palace Museum, Zhishan Garden is a must-visit – especially since it's free to enter with a museum ticket.

Price

NT$20 (you'll need two NT$10 coins handy)

Free to enter with a National Palace Museum ticket

Opening Hours

08:30 - 18:30

Closed on Mondays

Traveller Tips

Drinks machines are located within the garden. It's not situated near an MRT station, so it's really only worth the detour if you're already visiting the Palace Museum.

Location

title: Delicious Western Breakfasts at The Diner
excerpt: Taipei's oldest western brunch spot, now with four branches. What to order, what it costs, and which location to pick.
content:
The Diner is the oldest western style brunch place in Taipei. With the original branch in Daan, it has since expanded with the addition of three branches, one located in the heart of the Xinyi Shopping District while another is in Nangang near the exhibition centre. The forth branch is in Hsinchu City, quite a way from central Taipei.

Over the years it has established itself as one of the best brunch spots in Taipei, and consequently you'll often find a large gathering of people waiting to be seated, especially over the weekend mornings at the Daan branch.

Tables can however be reserved for each branch via Inline (see Traveller's Tips section).

Their brunch menu is quite extensive, with the usual English/Australian style fry-ups, eggs done many ways including omelettes and benedicts, plus more health conscious options like fruit or veg bowls. Or if you're feeling unhealthy, they have American style pancakes with a variety of waist-bulging toppings.

Not on the main menu, we spotted a nice sounding dish from their super-food menu. The Super Perfect Salad with grilled salmon, with roasted nutty couscous, a boiled egg, a nice selection of vegetables and a dijon sauce. A spectacular bowl and a salmon fillet cooked to perfection.

The Smoked Salmon Scrambled Breakfast, with nicely cooked scrambled eggs on an artisan bread, and soft avocado. All the salmon at The Diner is sourced from Norway, and it really does shine.

Both dishes amounted to a couple of the best brunches we've had in Taipei.

We've since tried a couple of The Diner's sweet brunch offerings (in the Xinyi branch). The Special K Acai Bowl, a very nicely presented bowl packed with fresh seasonal fruit and mixed nuts, and a side of special K cereal was another great tasting dish.

I was also keen to sample one of their pancakes - The Caramel, Banana and Walnut Pancake, with a small jug of moreish butterscotch sauce. It was much larger than I imagined it to be, and struggled to finish it even though it perfectly sweet and soft.

The drinks are equally excellent. The avocado smoothie and the strawberry yogurt drink both exceeding our expectations. With coffees, teas, milkshakes, fizzy drinks, slushies and freshly squeezed juices also available there's plenty of choices.

Breakfasts are served all day, while they also have a large range of non-brunch food, with salads, sandwiches, pasta and vegetarian options available.

The Diner's burgers, of which you can effectively build-you-own, are absolute beasts (probably too big for my liking). You can even substitute the beef patty for chicken, and swap-out other ingredients to suit your needs.

The Diner also has some smaller plates, of which you can purchase individually for NT$180, or purchase as a set of three for NT$480.

The Fried Mozzarella Sticks, Loaded Potato Skins and Grilled Cheese Fries we tried here were all perfectly adequate, although I much prefer the brunch items here.

The original Daan branch of The Diner is also the best rated, but is a little out of the way from central Taipei.

The interior is well decked out and the service is friendly, although when it's busy it can take a while for your food to arrive.

The Xinyi branch has the most convenient location, found on 1F of ATT for Fun within the Xinyi Shopping District. Although it's a large restaurant, it will still be packed over weekends. The only downside to this branch is that it has no toilets, so you need to trek to the nearby mall.

The Diner, with such a huge menu, will take many visits to get a full understanding of their menu. What we've tried so far has been great, especially their breakfasts/brunches. Service is efficient and they generally speak good English.

Pros

  • Many brunch options
  • Food generally delicious

Cons

  • Will normally need to queue at brunch times

Price: $$$

Level of English: Excellent (English on menu)

title: The Best Places to Keep Kids of All Ages Amused
excerpt: It's sometimes difficult to find good spots to keep kids amused. Here are some of the best places in Taipei to let them run riot.
content:
Taipei has many fun attractions that can be enjoyed by children of all ages. These are the best places to let them run riot, keep them quiet, or help them inadvertently learn about science and the world around them.

Click here to see all my 'best of' lists

Taipei Astronomical Museum

The best museum in Taipei for children, not only does it have three floors packed with interactive exhibits, but there's also an IMAX and 3D theatre, a cosmic adventure area and a telescope where they can explore the night sky. As a bonus, the museum is also very close to the next two attractions in this list.

Click here to read more about Taipei Astronomical Museum

National Taiwan Science Education Center

Situated opposite the Taipei Astronomical Museum, the National Taiwan Science Education Center is a huge building whose primary objective is to help educate children in science. There are several floors packed with interactive rides, a sky-ride bike, and a number of theatres including one that simulates earthquakes. There's also a dinosaur-themed restaurant in the basement.

Click here to read more about the National Taiwan Science Education Center

Taipei Children’s Amusement Park

The third attraction within very close proximity of each other, the Taipei Children’s Amusement Park is certainly no Disneyland, but it is a good value and offers enough rides and thrills to keep more younger children amused for an evening, although there are a handful of rides aimed at more older children too.

Click here to read more about the Taipei Children’s Amusement Park

Klook.com

Taipei Zoo

Taipei Zoo is one of the best in Asia, with animals from all over the globe including penguins, meerkats, elephants, koalas and of course giant pandas. The new Pangolin Dome is a fantastic walk-through where they can see tropical wildlife up-close. There are a few opportunities for kids to interact with the animals too. The Maokong Gondola, a fantastic cable-car ride into the mountains, also has a station in the zoo.

Click here to read more about Taipei Zoo

National Taiwan Museum

One of the best museums in Taipei, it's also very accommodating to children of all ages, with a large dinosaur exhibition and lots of interactive displays for them to have fun while inadvertently learning.

Click here to read more about National Taiwan Museum

Maji Square

Found within the Taipei Expo Park, Maji Square has plenty of attractions for younger children, with a bouncy castle and other rides, plus you can rent out small vehicles for them to ride around in the large covered area in the square.

Click here to read more about Maji Square

Miramar

The Miramar shopping centre in Neihu not only has the largest Ferris wheel in Taipei, but has numerous games machines and toy shops. Miramar also boasts the largest IMAX screen in Taipei should you need a couple of hours peace.

Click here to read more about Miramar

Miniatures Museum

Another museum that's perfect for both kids and adults, the Miniatures Museum has dozens of miniaturised worlds that will keep children fascinated for at least a couple of hours.

Click here to read more about the Miniatures Museum

Klook.com

Modern Toilet

Yes that's right. A toilet themed restaurant that is guaranteed to keep kids amused while feeding them too. Toilets as seats, poo-shaped food and a child friendly menu.

Click here to read more about Modern Toilet

i-Ride Taipei

Fly over Taiwan or the USA on this unique 5D experience ride. With seats that move while you watch a giant screen, and wind & mist effects, children will love it.

Click here to read more about i-Ride Taipei

Shilin Night Market

The best night market to visit with kids, there are dozens of games of all shapes and sizes, toy shops, and even a place to go fishing for shrimp. You'll be able to feed them easily too.

Click here to read more about Shilin Night Market

Wooderful Life

The exquisite Wooderful Life, Taiwan's very own wooden toy brand, has created many unique and charming music boxes and accessories since it's inception in 2012. The Wooderful Life pop-up store, located with the Huashan 1914 Creative Park, features a 'wooden playground' with many educational, interactive and brain training facilities to keep younger children fascinated for a few hours.

Click here to read more about Huashan 1914 Creative Park

Yu Kids Island Kids Playground

Another place ideal for younger children up to 7 years, this famous Japanese indoor children's playground has a branch found on the fifth floor of Shin Kong Mitsukoshi A8 mall in Xinyi. With rooms full of balls, a balloon house, a mini play-supermarket and toys whichever way you look, this is a sure-fire way to get children away from their games consoles and do something more active instead.

Klook.com

Locations

title: Delightfully Sticky Korean Food at Taebak (Permanently Closed)
content:
Permanent Closure Notice

Please note: Taebak has permanently closed.

Taebak is an authentic Korean restaurant with a well located restaurant near the centre of Taipei.

We've walked past these many times and often seen people queuing to get in. There was no queue when we went, but it was full so we still needed to wait 30 minutes to be seated. Fortunately, they took our number so were able to call us when ready.

The dining area is brightly lit and simple, with nods to Korean culture adorning the walls.

Taebak specialises in sharing dishes, which come in two sizes that can be shared between 2 or 3 - 4 people depending on the size.

These dishes are representative of different parts of Korea - we chose the Traditional Korean Fried Chicken, a very cheesy dish containing vegetables and rice cakes, and what looked like a sprinkling of cornflakes on top.

Attempting to extract the food without leaving pieces of gooey cheese over everything was an almost impossible task. It was however incredibly tasty and comforting food with a bit of a kick of spice.

As with most Korean restaurants, you'll get four small sharing dishes too, with kimchi, pickled radish and a selection of others.

No Korean restaurant would be complete without serving one of their most well know and delicious dishes - the Bibimbap. Served in either a normal or a piping-hot cast-iron bowl, and filled with rice, meat, vegetables, and topped off with a fried egg. I simply adore these.

Stirring immediately after receiving it is essential, otherwise the rice will quickly start to burn and stick to the bowl. I'll normally stir it for a good couple of minutes until the heat from the bowl starts to dissipate.

I've had many a bibimbap in the last few years, and this one was up there with the best. Packed with flavour and a nice sticky texture that went down a treat. The only criticism I have was that it could have had a bit more beef.

Another Korean speciality are their Seafood Pancakes - a doughy mix of seafood and vegetables.

Found within this one were shrimp, squid and clams, with peppers, scallion and other veg. It was probably not the best we've ever tried but it was nice nonetheless.

For drinks, you can purchase one of their make-your-own style cocktails, with rice wine, sprite and optional Korean beer combined to give a unique Korean twist. Since they're self made, you can choose your own desired strength.

There is even have a free coffee machine which pours surprisingly good (sweet and creamy) coffee.

Taebak is a great place to come, especially if you're in a group, although two people can easily find something to tuck in to and enjoy.

Pros

  • Authentic Korean dishes
  • Interesting cocktails

Cons

  • Menu only in Chinese and Korean

Price: $$

Level of English: OK (English not on menu)

Traveller Tips

Very good free coffee is available from a machine.

If you enjoyed Taebak, I would heartily recommend visiting Broccoli Beer also.

Location

title: Vegan Goodness at Miss Green
excerpt: A vegan restaurant using farm-sourced organic ingredients for salads, wraps, paninis and handmade vegan burgers.
content:
Miss Green is a vegan restaurant that serves farm sourced organic ingredients to create dishes that look and taste great.

Serving salads, wraps, paninis and handcraft vegan burgers, they also have a few pasta and risotto dishes. The salads come in two sizes, most containing quinoa and chickpeas and topped off with locally sourced Taiwanese vegetables like asparagus, mushrooms and a variety of beans.

We opted for the power green salad, with avocado and edamame and a homeade smoked vegan cheese and was delicious.

There are a number of side dishes you can order to compliment the salads of whatever you choose. We chose the sweet potato chips and cauliflower dishes, both of which were excellent. The chips were crispy on the outside and fluffy in the middle. The cauliflower was light and crispy and packed with flavour.

Drinks available range from coffees and teas to smoothies and detox juices. The Detox Me drink we chose consisted of beetroot, lemon, ginger and apple, while the smoothie contained a variety of wild berries. Thoroughly enjoyable they were!

If you add them on Line, they'll even give you a free vegan gluten-free cake! In our case, a moist chocolate cake with plenty of gooey cream that we felt less guilty eating because of everything that preceded it.

You can book ahead if needed, as the restaurant does get busy during weekend brunch periods. It's a relatively small place, although there is extra seating in the basement. It's a relaxed place to enjoy a delicious vegan meal.

Miss Green is one of the best vegan restaurants we've been to in Taipei. Everything we tried here was well thought out and above all, tasty and (mainly) healthy.

Pros

  • Very nice vegan food

Cons

  • Menu is a little confusing

Price: $$$

Level of English: Good (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

If you add them on the Line app you'll receive a free cake!

Miss Green Location

📍 Closest MRT: Xinyi Anhe (red line - exit 2)

title: Stunning Seasonal Dishes at Sugar Pea Cafe
excerpt: A cafe built around seasonal, wholesome bowls — rice, quinoa or grains topped with fresh, simple ingredients.
content:
The Sugar Pea Cafe's tag line is "Wholesome, Seasonal, Simple Cuisine", which perfectly encapsulates what this cafe/restaurant is about.

Serving seasonal salads and bowls of goodness with rice, quinoa, grains or legumes as their base, the dishes are healthy and fresh without compromising on the taste. For more in the same vein, see our quick and healthy meals round-up.

Although they have a couple of dishes geared towards evening meals, most of them are aimed at brunch time - which is when they are most busy, so it's advised to book ahead.

Sugar Pea Cafe have a nice selection of market bowls. With a base of rice, grains and legumes, they're topped off with vegetables and sauces. Some come with fish or meat, or you can choose to add these.

The Korean Pork Bowl (which is similar to a bibimbap) included marinated pork bulgogi, lots of crunchy vegetables, and a sunny-side egg and optional chilli paste to give the dish an extra kick. It was divine.

While there are only two salad dishes on their menu, the Avocado and Shrimp Salad, which was their take on a Caesar salad, looked too good to ignore. With homemade garlic croutons and creamy parmesan, the avocado was so soft and delicious and it was another dish to savour.

Sugar Pea Cafes brunch menu has recently seen the addition of another great sounding dish. The Smoked Salmon & Spinach Frittata, an Italian omelette with capers, feta, red onion and dill.

Avocado can also be added for an extra NT$60. Seeing as we love it here, we had to add it.

Another recent addition to their market bowls section is the Pomodoro Shrimp Pasta. With cherry tomatoes, spinach and basil, with toppings of prosciutto breadcrumbs, parmesan and chili. The falafel pasta, combined with the lovely tomato sauce and everything else, was heaven. It looked the part too.

Sugar Pea Cafe have a couple of sweet brunch options also. Two types of pancakes, including Blueberry Pancakes - with a blueberry lemon compote, vanilla whipped mascarpone and maple syrup. Another very elegant plate of food, and another great tasting dish.

I have to give a special mention to the smoothie drinks at Sugar Pea Cafe.

The Green Piña Colada, with pineapple, spinach, coconut milk, lime, and the Tea Berry, with mixed berries, earl grey, house made yogurt and honey. Vibrant colours, silky smooth textures and a fruit taste-sensation.

Aside from their delicious food and drinks, another enticing selling point of Sugar Pea Cafe is their lovely conservatory. Located at the front of the building, it's a wonderful place to eat, although there is only room for 4 or 5 tables in here.

The rear room is much larger, and although it's no match for the conservatory, it's still a very pleasant environment to dine in.

Prices at Sugar Pea Cafe are on the expensive side, with two meal and two drinks costing upwards of NT$1,300 (with the 10% service fee) but, like they say, you get what you pay for.

One of my Top Picks!

Pros

  • Food tastes as good as it looks
  • Lovely place to dine in

Cons

  • Away from all the attractions

Level of English: Excellent (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

Definitely advisable to book ahead at the weekend but can easily do so from here.

title: 30 Best Things to Do in Ximending: Food, Culture & Nightlife
excerpt: The 30 best things to do in Ximending, from Michelin noodles and blow-torched beef to a 300-year-old temple, Japanese-era ruins and Taipei's best street art.
content:
Perfect For

  • Street Food & Night Market Snacks
  • Shopping and Gifts
  • Street Art & Performers
  • Bars & Bubble Tea
  • Cinemas & Arcades
  • Japanese-era History

Overview

Ximending is where I send anyone who has one evening in Taipei and wants to feel the city at full volume. It sits in Wanhua, Taipei's oldest district, and the comparison you'll read everywhere is Tokyo's Harajuku or Shibuya – pedestrianised streets, neon, crowds, street performers and more bubble tea shops per square metre than anywhere else in Taiwan. It's also one of the most convenient areas to stay in Taipei.

What most guides miss is that all of this is built on top of something much older. The gate the district is named after was demolished over a century ago. There's a 300-year-old temple wedged between the clothes shops, the ruins of a Japanese temple complex five minutes from the MRT, and the hall where Japan formally handed Taiwan over in 1945. You can walk past all of it without noticing.

So rather than a list of shops, here are 30 things worth actually doing here, grouped so you can eat your way through in order, or skip straight to the history. Everything is within about a 15-minute walk of Ximen MRT station.

When to Go and How Long to Spend

Ximending gets extremely busy on Friday and Saturday evenings. If you can, come on a weekday evening instead – it's still lit up and buzzing, but you can actually move. Most shops open around 11am and the district doesn't really wake up until early afternoon, so mornings are quiet.

Give it three to four hours for the food, shops and street art. Add another hour or two if you want the temples and Zhongshan Hall as well. If you're doing it as part of a wider plan, it slots neatly into our 3-5 day Taipei itinerary.

Street Food & Snacks

The stalls here are scattered through the lanes off the main pedestrian streets rather than lined up in one strip like a traditional night market, and several of the best are on wheels. Treat this as a list of things to look out for rather than a route – almost all of it is within a few minutes of exit 6. These are the ones worth queuing for.

1. Ay Chung Flour Rice Noodles

Ay Chung is the most famous food stand in Ximending and probably in Taipei – a standing-room-only counter that has been selling one thing since 1975. Bowls of thin, thickened mee sua noodles with pig intestine, eaten on the pavement with a plastic spoon. Around NT$60–75 and open from mid-morning until about 10.30pm. Delicious, though not for the faint of heart.

2. The Lane 50 Food Alley

The densest run of street food in Ximending is Lane 50 (open in Google Maps), a covered alley two or three minutes from exit 6 that cuts through between Emei Street and Wuchang Street. Around twenty stalls are packed into it, most opening from early afternoon and running late into the evening. If you only have time for one stop, make it this one – it's as close as the district gets to a proper night market strip.

Start with the torched beef dice, right on the corner where the lane meets Emei Street – cubes of beef seared in front of you with a blow torch, so they pick up a barbecue char while staying rare in the middle. You'll smell it before you see it, and there's usually a knot of people around it.

Directly next door is a Korean cheese tteokbokki counter, with two big trays of rice cakes simmering away in chilli sauce. Chewy rice cakes in a thick sweet-spicy sauce with melted cheese over the top, handed over in a paper cup you can carry off down the street.

A few doors along, Prince Cheese Potatoes does deep-fried jacket potatoes buried under cheese with a choice of toppings. Absurdly rich, and easily a meal on its own.

3. Stinky Tofu and Grilled Mochi

Two of the best snacks here are on wheels. If you catch a smell you'd describe as drains, you've found the stinky tofu cart – it tastes far better than it smells, and it's one of the most Taiwanese things you can eat. The mochi cart sells warm, gooey rice cakes rolled in peanut powder or sesame.

Both move around, but they tend to set up near Ay Chung to take advantage of the queue.

4. Monga Fried Chicken

Taiwan takes its fried chicken cutlets seriously, and Monga is the Ximending name to know – a plate-sized boneless fillet, fried to order, with around ten seasonings to choose from. Cheap, enormous, and the ideal thing to eat while walking.

5. Lao Tian Lu

A proper Ximending institution on Wuchang Street, trading for around 60 years. Lao Tian Lu does dry-braised luwei – soy-braised snacks sold cold, by weight, in a bag to take away. Duck tongues and duck wings are what it's known for, with braised tofu, chicken wings and eggs for anyone less adventurous. Locals stock up here on the way to the cinema, which is exactly what you should do with it.

Sit-Down Meals

6. Lao Shan Dong Homemade Noodles

The best-kept secret in Ximending is in a basement. Lao Shan Dong has been making noodles by hand since 1949 and holds a Michelin Bib Gourmand, and it's tucked into the food court under the Wannian Building. Beef noodles and sesame noodles are the order. If you only sit down for one meal here, make it this one.

7. The 24-Hour Beef Noodle Strip

Kunming Street has four beef noodle shops almost next to each other – Fuhong, Caihong, Jianhong and Xiaowu – and between them they're open around the clock. Fuhong is the best known. Taiwan's national dish, available at 4am, which is exactly the sort of thing Ximending is good for.

8. Sanwei Shokudo

A famously chaotic Japanese place where the draw is portion size – sashimi cut thick and piled high, at prices that don't make sense for what arrives. Expect roughly NT$430–490 a head and expect to queue. Worth it if you like raw fish and don't mind sitting elbow to elbow.

9. Modern Toilet

Modern Toilet is exactly what it sounds like: toilets for seats, food served in miniature toilets, a bell on each table to flush for service. It closed for over three years during the pandemic and reopened in 2024, and the Ximending and Shilin branches are now the only two left anywhere in the world. The food is average and the point is entirely the novelty – but with kids, it's unbeatable. You'll find it on the second floor at No. 7, Lane 50, Xining South Road, with mains around NT$290–350.

10. Breakfast: Grilled Toast or Soy Milk

Two very different options. Golden Flower Grilled Toast does gloriously messy charcoal-toasted sandwiches – the cheese and peanut butter is the one. For something more traditional, Yong He Soy Milk serves Chinese doughnuts, turnip cake and soy milk, sweet as a drink or savoury as a soup, and stays open almost around the clock.

Sweet Things

11. Snow King Ice Cream

Open since 1947 and still family-run, Snow King makes around 70 flavours of ice cream, and a good number of them are things no one else would attempt – pork floss, sesame oil chicken, basil, wasabi. You can taste before you commit, which you should. Scoops run about NT$80–150. Genuinely one of the most interesting things to eat in Taipei, not just in Ximending.

12. Ximen Mango Shaved Ice

Ximending is one of the best places in the city to try Taiwan's signature dessert, and this shop on Hanzhong Street is the one to pick – a whole mango's worth of fruit over fine, soft shaved ice. Best in summer when mangoes are actually in season, though other fruits are available year round. Avoid mid-afternoon, when tour coaches arrive and service slows to a crawl.

13. Mammy Pancake

Hong Kong-style bubble waffles, crisp outside and soft in the middle, in a long list of flavours. They held a spot in the Michelin Guide's street food selection for six years running, from 2016 to 2021. Find them on Wuchang Street Section 2, a few minutes from Ximen exit 6.

14. Mr Brownie

If you want something less Taiwanese and more chocolate, Mr Brownie near the Red House does the best brownies in Taipei. No further explanation needed.

Bubble Tea, Coffee & Bars

15. The Bubble Tea Shops

Nobody should leave Ximending without a bubble tea. It's the cheapest place in Taipei to drink them and there are dozens of shops, so the only hard part is choosing.

Xing Fu Tang is the one to go for, and this branch is the brand's flagship. Their brown sugar tea with fresh cream is excellent and they torch the sugar in front of you. It's also the one with the enormous queue.

If you can't face waiting, there are two good alternatives within a couple of minutes. Tiger Sugar does an equally good brown sugar version, hot or cold, so it works in winter too. Sharetea has shorter queues and a much longer flavour list, and lets you swap the tapioca for grass jelly, coconut jelly or even pudding.

16. Fong Da Coffee

The perfect antidote to all that sugar. Fong Da opened in 1956, is credited with introducing iced coffee to Taipei, and still roasts its beans on the original machine in the window. The interior hasn't changed in decades. Sit in, order a siphon coffee and a walnut pastry, and it's hard to believe the neon is thirty seconds away.

17. The Red House Outdoor Drinking Area

There is no better place in Ximending for a drink in the open air than the Ximen Outdoor Drinking Area, directly behind the Red House – a row of bars sharing one big outdoor seating area under umbrellas. It's the heart of Taipei's LGBTQ+ scene and everyone is welcome. Look for the rainbow crossing painted on Hanzhong Street outside exit 6 on your way in.

18. Driftwood

Driftwood on Kunming Street is run by Taihu, Taiwan's best-known craft brewery, and done out like a tropical beach cabin. Around NT$200 a goblet for some genuinely good beer.

19. Hanko 60

One of the coolest bars in Taipei, let alone Ximending. Hanko 60 is a speakeasy hidden behind a cinema front, serving cocktails with real imagination – including one that arrives inside a bag of popcorn. Hard to find, which is the point.

20. Geography Bar and Ximen Beer Bar

Two smaller places worth knowing, a few minutes apart.

Geography Bar is up on the fourth floor at No. 92-2 Kunming Street – look for the brightly painted stairwell – and builds eight cocktails entirely from Taiwanese fruit, tea and spirits. Open 7pm until 3am.

Ximen Beer Bar at No. 83 Wuchang Street Section 2 is a compact, unpretentious pub with six rotating Taiwanese craft taps at around NT$200–250 a glass. Open from 6pm, or 5pm at weekends.

For more across the city, see our pick of the best cocktail bars in Taipei.

History & Landmarks

This is the part of Ximending almost everyone walks straight past. All four of these are free.

21. The Red House

Calling the Red House a shop does it a disservice. Built in 1908 during the Japanese era, it's a beautiful octagonal red-brick market hall and worth seeing for the building alone. Inside are some of the best crafts and gifts you'll find anywhere in Taipei, and at weekends a creative market fills the courtyard with stalls.

22. Nishi Honganji Relics

Five minutes from the MRT are the remains of a large Japanese Buddhist temple complex, including a bell tower from 1922 and several restored wooden buildings set around a lawn. It was largely destroyed by fire and has been turned into a small public park. Almost no visitors find it, which is exactly why it's worth the detour.

23. Taipei Tian Hou Temple

A working temple to Mazu, goddess of the sea, roughly 300 years old and now surrounded on all sides by clothes shops on Chengdu Road. Step through the door and the noise drops away completely. The contrast with what's outside is the whole appeal.

24. Zhongshan Hall and the Old City Gates

Zhongshan Hall, a short walk north, is where Japan formally surrendered Taiwan in 1945 and where Chiang Kai-shek later gave his inaugural speech. It's still a working concert venue with a cafe, and the steps outside are a long-standing skateboarding spot.

Nearby, look for the Ximen Gate itself – or rather where it was. The West Gate that gave the whole district its name was pulled down in 1905, and a modern metal sculpture now traces its outline in the middle of a traffic island.

One gate did survive, and it's worth the short walk out of the district to see. The North Gate, or Cheng'en Gate, is the only one of Taipei's five city gates still in its original form – the other three that are left were remodelled in 1966. It opened in 1884 as the main entrance to the walled city and came close to being demolished for an overpass, until the expressway was routed around it instead. It has been a protected historic site since 1983 and now stands in its own plaza.

Strictly speaking this isn't Ximending – it's about ten minutes north on foot, next to Beimen MRT – but it's close enough to fold into the same afternoon, and it's the best surviving piece of the old walled city.

Street Culture

25. Street Art, America Street and the Performers

The best street art in Taipei is here, with over 25 pieces ranging from full building-side murals to sprayed-over utility huts. The densest concentration is around America Street (Lane 96, Kunming Street), where painting is legal and the walls change constantly. Most of the rest is tucked down side alleys, so I've mapped the main ones below – it's worth an hour of wandering.

Click on a marker to see the art for each location.

Street art is an ever-changing medium, so expect some of these to have been painted over by the time you arrive.

The same streets have some of the best street performers in the city – dancers, musicians and spray-can artists who'll produce a finished piece in a few minutes using nothing but stencils and aerosols. If you like one, you can usually buy it on the spot.

Entertainment & Shopping

26. Cinema Street

There are no fewer than seven cinemas inside a single square kilometre here, most of them along Wuchang Street – I've never seen anything like it. The best are the Ambassador, with a huge screen and D-Box seats that move with the film, and In89, for fully reclining seats. Films are shown in their original language with Chinese subtitles, so English-language releases need no planning at all.

27. The Wannian Building, Arcades and Claw Machines

Ximending is awash with arcades, and Taiwan has a particular obsession with claw machines – those impossible games where the grabber has roughly the grip strength of a wet tissue. Whole shopfronts are given over to nothing else.

The one to seek out is the Wannian Building, a wonderfully dated mall stacked with gashapon machines, model kits, retro toys and comic shops, plus that Michelin noodle shop in the basement. There's also a VR arcade in the district if you'd rather fight ninjas than win a plush toy.

28. Pop Mart, Donki and the Themed 7-Elevens

Ximending is Taipei's youth shopping district, and while the main streets are chain stores, the interesting shops are down the alleys – small fashion labels, gift shops and accessory stalls.

Three modern ones are worth singling out: Pop Mart has a four-storey flagship devoted to blind-box collectibles, Don Don Donki is open 24 hours for Japanese snacks and cosmetics, and there are several themed convenience stores here, including Hello Kitty and Lay's branded 7-Elevens. There's also an underground mall running from the MRT station, full of K-pop and anime shops. For the wider picture, see our guide to the best shopping areas in Taipei.

29. Tattoo Street

Ximending is where Taipei comes for tattoos and piercings, and there's a covered lane off Hanzhong Street lined with well-regarded studios doing both. I can't claim any expertise here, but it has a strong reputation and plenty of people travel specifically for it.

30. Hire a Private Cinema Room

Taiwan hung on to a format that died out almost everywhere else: the MTV, where you book a whole room instead of a seat, choose a film from a library of a few thousand, and watch it on a big screen with sofas, a phone on the wall for ordering, and your own food and drink if you'd rather. U2 has a branch on the ninth floor of the Wannian Building, a few steps from the arcades, at roughly NT$200–240 a head.

There are no showtimes either. You turn up whenever you like and the film starts when you're ready, which makes it a rare thing in Ximending that doesn't involve queueing for something.

Also Worth a Look

Things that didn't quite make the thirty but are very Ximending:

  • KTV – Party World has a large branch here, and private-room karaoke is a Taiwanese institution. See our Taipei nightlife guide.
  • Korean photo booths – self-service studios with themed sets and props, currently everywhere in the district.
  • Cat and maid cafes – several of both, mostly on upper floors near exit 6.
  • Taipei Cinema Park – a 1930s gas works turned public space, now a skate and legal graffiti spot.
  • Eighty-Eightea Rinbansyo – a tea house in a 1924 wooden building, closed for renovation with a reopening expected around 2026, so check before making the trip.

Practical Tips

  • Come on a weekday evening if you can. Weekend nights are shoulder-to-shoulder.
  • Bring cash. Many stalls and the older shops don't take cards – see our Taipei money guide.
  • Most shops open around 11am, so don't arrive early expecting much.
  • The pedestrianised streets are genuinely traffic-free, but scooters still use the surrounding roads, so watch the crossings.
  • It rains a lot in Taipei. The cinemas, arcades, malls and underground shops make Ximending one of the better rainy day options in the city.
  • Plenty here is free: the street art, the performers, the temples and the Red House exterior all cost nothing. More ideas in Taipei on a budget.

Virtual Tour

Getting There

📍 Closest MRT: Ximen Station on the blue and green lines. Exit 6 puts you straight onto the main pedestrianised crossing, next to the rainbow crossing and a short walk from the Red House. For the North Gate, use Beimen Station instead.

Everything in this guide is inside about a 15-minute walk of that exit, so there's no need to plan a route – the district is small and almost entirely traffic-free.

Click here for the map of Ximending's street art

title: Tamsui Guide: 20 Best Things to Do, Plus Taiwan's Best Sunset
excerpt: A local's guide to Tamsui: the 20 best things to do, what to eat (A-gei and iron eggs were invented here), the ferries, and where to watch the best sunset in Taiwan.
content:
Perfect For

  • Walking and relaxing
  • Street Food & Snacks
  • Historical buildings
  • Gifts and souvenirs
  • The best sunset in Taiwan

Overview

Tamsui sits at the mouth of the Tamsui river in New Taipei City, and it's where the city goes to slow down: a long riverside walk, an old street full of food stalls, a Spanish fort on the hill, and a sunset that is genuinely one of the best I've seen anywhere.

You'll also see the name written as Danshui, and older guides and street signs still use it. It's the same place – just an older romanisation of the same two characters – and the MRT calls it Tamsui, so that's the one to look for.

Although it's outside Taipei proper, it is one of the easiest trips in the city to make. Tamsui is on the Taipei MRT – the last stop at the northern end of the red line – so it's a single train with no changes, roughly 35 to 40 minutes from Taipei Main Station, and your EasyCard covers it. There's no bus, no tour and no planning needed to get here.

I lived in Tamsui for a year, so this guide is built on local knowledge rather than a day trip. Every place in it is pinned on the map at the end.

When to Go and How Long to Spend

Come on a weekday if you can. Locals pour in at weekends and on public holidays, and the historic buildings up by the fort are mostly closed at weekends anyway. Allow two hours for the old street alone, half a day with Fisherman's Wharf, and a full day if you want the fort and the temples as well.

Whatever else you plan, be here for sunset.

Because the sunset anchors the end of the day, Tamsui pairs beautifully with Xinbeitou and its hot springs. Both are on the red line – Xinbeitou is a short branch off it, changing at Beitou station – so you can spend the morning and early afternoon in the hot springs, get back on the line north, and be on the Tamsui riverbank in time for the light to go. It's one of the easiest full days in Taipei to put together, and you never leave one MRT line.

The Riverside and Old Street

1. The Riverside Walk

The 1.5km walk along the water between the MRT station and Fort San Domingo is the heart of a day here, and it's where most of your time will go. Wide, flat and pedestrianised, it's lined the whole way with souvenir and gift shops, food stalls, arcades, tea shops and restaurants, one after another, with the river and the township of Bali in view on the far bank.

There's more than enough on this stretch alone to fill an afternoon – you can do your present shopping and eat your way from one end to the other without ever leaving the water.

2. Tamsui Old Street

The riverside is only half of it. One street back from the water, running parallel, is a second dense run of shops and stalls – narrower, busier and more local in feel, with a small night market towards the MRT end. Most visitors walk the promenade and never turn inland at all, which is a mistake.

3. Love Lane and the Painted Steps

Behind the old street the ground rises steeply, and a set of narrow lanes climbs the hill towards the fort. Love Lane, off Chongjian Street, is a slice of old Tamsui that the promenade has passed by – crumbling houses, murals, and almost nobody on it. On the way up you'll pass a staircase painted as a 3D mural, which is worth the detour on its own.

4. Fuyou Temple

Wedged in among the shops on Zhongzheng Road, Fuyou Temple is the oldest of Tamsui's four major temples – finished in 1796 and dedicated to Mazu, goddess of the sea, which tells you what this town used to do for a living. During the Sino-French War in the 1880s locals credited Mazu with protecting Tamsui, and the Emperor sent a plaque saying as much; it still hangs in the main hall. Free, ten minutes of your time, and almost everyone walks straight past the door.

5. The Riverside Park

Between the MRT and the start of the old street is a stretch of grass and paving where street performers set up and you can hire a YouBike. It's the best place to sit with something bought from a stall, and where you'll end up waiting for the light to go.

Tamsui's Own Food

Tamsui invented two dishes that you'll find all over Taiwan, and the versions here are still the best. Get these before you touch a restaurant menu.

6. A-gei

A-gei is the one thing to eat here. Fried tofu is hollowed out, stuffed with glass noodles and sealed shut with fish paste, then steamed and served in a thin, sweet-savoury sauce. It was invented in Tamsui in 1965 and it exists nowhere else in this form. Several vendors near the MRT and up towards the fort do it; the queue tells you which is which.

7. Fish Ball Soup

The traditional partner to A-gei, and locals order them together. A light broth with springy fish balls, cheap and warming, and the thing to have in winter. In summer, a cold soy milk does the same job.

8. Iron Eggs

Iron eggs also come from Tamsui. Quail or chicken eggs are braised in soy and spices for hours, air-dried, then braised again – repeated daily for about a week – until they shrink to dense, dark, chewy little things that taste far more intense than an egg has any right to. They come plain, garlic, spicy, mala or black pepper, sold in bags, and they are the edible souvenir to take home.

9. The Fried Seafood Stalls

Along the promenade, stall after stall sells fried squid, shrimp, cuttlefish and whole small fish, cut up with scissors into a paper cup with pepper salt. It's the smell of the riverside walk.

10. Tower Ice Cream and the Turkish Stand

A summer speciality here is the absurdly tall ice cream, stacked so high you need to work fast. The Turkish ice cream stand near the harbour has been running for years and comes with the full routine of snatching the cone away as you reach for it – a performance as much as a dessert.

Sit-Down Places

11. La Villa Danshui

The best restaurant on the riverbank. La Villa Danshui is a superb Italian with a large outdoor seating area facing the water – the place to book if you want to eat properly rather than from a paper cup.

12. Monini

Another Italian, directly next door to La Villa, and a good fallback when it's full. Which, at sunset on a weekend, it will be.

13. Between Tea House

A lovely vegetarian place just off the old street, and a genuinely calm room in a district that doesn't have many. Worth knowing about if you're avoiding meat, since the stalls outside are almost entirely seafood and pork.

14. BritShake

Set up by a British expat, and about as authentic as British food gets in Taiwan – scones, pies, and fish and chips. An odd thing to find at the end of the red line, and all the better for it.

Fisherman's Wharf

15. Fisherman's Wharf

At the river mouth about 3km from the old street, Fisherman's Wharf is a working harbour turned promenade, with seafood restaurants, shops and bands playing in the evening. It's more touristy than the old street but the setting is better – open water on three sides.

16. Lover's Bridge

The white cable-stayed footbridge across the harbour, lit up after dark and the most photographed thing in Tamsui after the sunset itself. Walk out to the middle for the view back down the coast.

17. Lover's Tower

A 100m revolving observation tower next to the bridge, giving a slow 360-degree turn over the river mouth and out to sea. I haven't been up it myself. Expect somewhere around NT$200 with a discount for EasyCard, though it's worth checking the current price on the operator's page before you go.

Beyond the Old Street

18. Fort San Domingo and the Historic Buildings

Up the hill at the end of the riverside walk is Fort San Domingo, a hilltop fort begun by the Spanish and later the British consulate. NT$80 gets you in, and the same ticket covers several other historic buildings scattered around the hill. Opening hours vary between them and most close at weekends, so read my full guide before you go.

19. Cloud Gate Theatre

Cloud Gate are Taiwan's internationally acclaimed contemporary dance company, and their theatre is here in Tamsui. Worth checking whether anything is on while you're in town – the building and its grounds are lovely even when it's quiet.

20. Tianyuan Temple in Cherry Blossom Season

Up in the hills behind Tamsui, Wuji Tianyuan Temple is a striking round, multi-tiered temple surrounded by hundreds of cherry trees. For a few weeks in February and March it becomes one of the best blossom spots anywhere near Taipei, and it gets extremely busy at weekends because of it. Outside blossom season it's a quiet and rather odd building; during it, it's the reason to come to Tamsui at all.

This one is not walkable – it's up in the hills and you'll need a bus or a taxi. Buses 875, 876, 877 and 866 all run there from Tamsui Station, leaving from just to the right of exit 2, and cost around NT$15. 875 is the one to aim for, as it stops directly in front of the temple. They run from roughly 05:00 to 21:00, and during peak blossom season the temple also puts on a shuttle from the MRT station.

The Ferries

Ferries run from the harbour about halfway along the old street, and tickets are sold from the booths beside it – cash or EasyCard.

Tamsui to Bali

Bali is a quieter mirror of Tamsui, with its own old street and riverside walk. The Shihsanhang Museum of Archaeology is there too, though you'll need a bus or taxi from the wharf to reach it.

Tamsui to Fisherman's Wharf ferry suspended

This service is currently not running while the vessels are under maintenance, and no restart date has been announced. Use the light rail or bus R26 instead, and check before you plan around it. When it does run, the crossing takes 12 to 15 minutes and costs about NT$60 for an adult.

For something more scenic, the Blue Highway river cruise runs from Dadaocheng Wharf all the way to Tamsui Wharf on weekends only (day sailings at 10:00 and 13:30, plus evening "night flight" departures), taking about 60 minutes for NT$300 (NT$150 concession). It's more of a tour than a practical ferry, but a nice option if you have a free weekend afternoon – see the official Blue Highway page for current sailing times.

The Sunset

The one thing you absolutely must witness in Tamsui is the sunset.

The riverbank fills with locals and visitors all angling for the best spot, and it earns the crowd – not just one of the most beautiful sunsets in Taiwan, but one of the best we have ever seen anywhere.

Tamsui Sunset Times
Summer: between 18:00 and 18:45
Winter: between 17:00 and 18:00

If you can, get one of the riverside seats at the Water Front restaurant – the best spot to watch it from, with a cold drink in hand. Fisherman's Wharf and Lover's Bridge are the other classic vantage points, and being further out at the river mouth they get a cleaner horizon.

Getting Around

  • Tamsui Station is the end of the red line, exit 1. Note that only every second train runs the full distance – check the destination on the front before boarding.
  • The Danhai Light Rail connects Tamsui to the newer districts, and its coastal branch reaches Fisherman's Wharf and Shalun Beach. This is the fallback while the ferry is suspended.
  • Bus R26 runs from the MRT to Fisherman's Wharf in about 16 minutes.
  • You can cycle the riverside to Fisherman's Wharf in around 15 minutes, and there are YouBike stands by the station.
  • Shalun Beach is reachable on the light rail if you want sand, though there are no facilities to speak of.

Practical Tips

  • Weekdays over weekends, both for the crowds and because the historic buildings shut at weekends.
  • Bring cash. Stalls and the ferry booths take it; some also take EasyCard – see our Taipei money guide.
  • Work backwards from sunset when planning the day, not forwards from lunch.
  • Museum entry is included with the Taipei Fun Pass, though the ferry crossings are no longer covered and need paying for separately.
  • It's noticeably windier and cooler at the river mouth than in central Taipei, especially in winter.

Virtual Tour

Tamsui Map

📍 Closest MRT: Tamsui Station, the end of the red line, exit 1. Everywhere mentioned in this guide is pinned below, including the temples up in the hills.

title: Xinyi Shopping District: All 13 Malls Compared
excerpt: If you want to spend the whole day shopping, by far the best area to visit is Xinyi (near Taipei 101). There are no less than 13 malls here connected by walkways, and no shortage of restaurants and bars.
content:
Perfect For

  • Shopping
  • Restaurants
  • Bars and Clubs
  • Walking

Overview

I've been to the Xinyi shopping district dozens of times, and I still get lost. It's a maze of malls, walkways and department stores connected both above and below ground – but that's also why it's by far the best area in Taipei for a full day of shopping. Xinyi has the highest density of shopping malls in the world, with no less than 13 malls packed into about 1km next to Taipei 101, and it's a strong choice of where to stay if shopping is your priority.

There's also no shortage of restaurants, bars and clubs in the district. It is however one of the most expensive places to shop and dine in Taipei, although there are still bargains to be had if you know where to look. It can also be quite daunting if you don't know your way around, which is where the walkways below help.

You can choose your starting point from either the south, at the Taipei 101 MRT station (red line) or the north, at the City Hall MRT station (blue line).

There are walkways above or below ground connecting the entire 1km area, and most of it is pedestrianised.

The best time to visit the Xinyi Shopping District is during a weekend evening, as it's a lot more vibrant and there are loads of street performers. Also, the district looks beautiful when it is lit up.

Map

Xinyi Shopping Malls

The shopping malls located in the Xinyi shopping district are (from South to North):

* Recommended; ** Essential

Click here to find out more about the Essential malls

Some malls also have Tax Refund Desks which can be used to claim 5% back on purchases over NT$2,000.

Probably the only store not located inside a mall is Apple's new ultra-modern flagship store.

Click here for my full guide on the Ximending Shopping District

Food & Drink

Most of the malls have their own food courts (see table above), and there are restaurants, cafes and bars found inside the malls - a few with outdoor seating.

Food Courts are a good choice if you're not sure what to eat or if you're on a budget. You'll mainly find Asian food in these, but they're cheap and usually a good standard.

The Taipei 101 and Shin Kong A11 food malls are my personal favourites – inside the Taipei 101 food hall, look out for Chung Ching Shrimp Rice, a small stall with a strong local following – although the Bellavita mall also has some great places (albeit slightly more expensive).

The Shin Kong A13, which opened in December 2019, also has a nice dining area on 3F.

If you want to try some Taiwanese food, then I would recommend going to Din Tai Fung, the world renowned restaurant chain.

There are now three located in this area - one in the basement of the Taipei 101 mall, and the other 2 located inside the Shin Kong Mitsukoshi A4 & A13 malls. These branches are usually less busy than the 101 branch.

If you're here early and looking for some breakfast/brunch, look no further than The Diner - one of the best breakfast spots in Taipei, located within the ATT For Fun mall.

If you're in need of something sweet, I recommend KaiKai Dessert, which serves delicious Hong Kong-style sweet soups that can be found on the Michelin Guide.

Many restaurant chains can be found here, including Jamie's Italian, Miacucina (for vegetarians), Gordon Biersch, Texas Roadhouse and TGI Fridays Songgao which is a really cool retro version of their chain with a different menu to the other branches found in the city.

Two Xinyi restaurants have also been recognised in the Michelin Bib Gourmand: Sinchao Rice Shoppe, near City Hall MRT, for its inventive takes on fried rice, and Open Smile, near Taipei 101 MRT, for its braised pork rice and pork belly.

For more variety, there's also a scattering of good independent restaurants tucked away from the malls themselves. Range Bistrokaya, a short walk from City Hall MRT, is a cosy bistro-izakaya hybrid serving cocktails and small plates around an open kitchen. A few minutes further north, Thai Elephant does surprisingly cheap, authentic Thai food, and Wu Ding Yue Feng is one of the better Vietnamese restaurants in the city, though it fills up fast. For dim sum, Dim Dim Sum is a well-regarded Hong Kong chain that's featured in the World Chefs Global Diet Guide.

A large cluster of restaurants can be found near the ATT for Fun mall, some with outdoor seating including Lobster Foods, which also serves a great pint of Guinness.

Beyond what's covered on this site, Xinyi has plenty of other well-known names worth being aware of. Fine dining options include Morton's The Steakhouse and Smith & Wollensky, both inside the Shin Kong Mitsukoshi towers, and Pearl Liang for Cantonese. For hotpot, Haidilao (the mainland Chinese chain known for its theatrical table-side service) and JJ Friend Spicy Hotpot are both popular in the district, and Lao A Bo is worth knowing for home-style Taiwanese cooking. I haven't personally reviewed any of these, so it's worth checking recent reviews before making a special trip.

For a nice refreshing Taiwanese ale, Landmark Taihu serves some great craft ales close to the Taipei 101 MRT exit.

Found on the 10th floor of the ATT for Fun mall is Frank, one of the best clubs in Taipei with a fantastic rooftop bar, although it has a dress code and does get very busy at weekends. Located within the W Taipei hotel is the excellent Woobar, mixing some of the best cocktails in Taipei.

For skyline views to match, CÉ LA VI Taipei, on the 48th floor of Breeze Nanshan, is one of the best rooftop lounges in the city for a Taipei 101 view, and WAT Bar pairs a bottled-cocktail counter out front with a hidden speakeasy through a velvet curtain.

For late-night clubbing, Xinyi's other well-known venues include Myst, M Taipei and IKON Taipei, all a short walk from the ATT for Fun cluster. For something quieter, The Sipping Room is a good standing bar for cocktails.

Entertainment

If you've not visited it, then the Taipei 101 Observation Deck has spectacular views. If possible, try to time your visit an hour before sunset.

If you're travelling with kids, then the ATT for Fun mall is the best place to take them. Found within is Vie Show, is one of the best cinemas in Taipei. Most of the shops here are also aimed at kids and teenagers, plus there's VR+ room found on the first floor towards the east and an arcade near the food hall on 2F.

There's another virtual reality ride of sorts found in the southern Breeze Centre. i-Ride Taipei is a fantastic 5D experience that takes you on a journey over Taiwan or the USA.

There are also a few street performers and artists situated around Xinyi Shopping District, and if you're visiting over the weekend there are many markets and other promotional events.

In the centre of the district is the Xiangti Avenue Plaza. There will often be a stage erected here over the weekend, where they'll be live musical performances or even events like B-Boy competitions.

Xinyi isn't cheap, and it isn't easy to get your bearings on a first visit – but it rewards the effort. It's one of the best areas to visit when it's raining, since you can cross most of the district without ever going outside, and unlike Ximending it rarely feels overcrowded, even though you may need to queue for the more popular restaurants.

If you want the widest possible spread of shops, restaurants and nightlife under one mostly-connected roof, this is where to spend your day.

Opening Hours

The general opening hours of all the malls are:
11:00 - 21:30 (extended to 22:00 on weekends)

If you find yourself in a mall at the start or end of the day, it is customary for all staff to stand and bow to everyone.

title: Eat, Drink and be Merry in Maji Square
excerpt: One of the few places in Taipei to eat and drink outdoors under cover, inside Expo Park. A dozen restaurants and bars to choose from.
content:
Found within the Taipei Expo Park, Maji Square is one of the few large areas in Taipei where you can drink and eat outdoors.

Covered by the roof of the Expo centre and protected from the elements, there are a dozen or so restaurants and bars, plus some nice craft shops.

The best bars and restaurants in this area are

  • The Three Lions Inn
  • Blue Rooster Bistro
  • British Oysters Seafood Shed
  • Triangle
  • Gaucho
  • Casa Bar
  • Crafted - Beer & Co.

There's also a large area with many small food stalls selling traditional Taiwanese food, and some with Western styles including Mexican and burgers.

Adjacent to this area are some nice craft shops and a great little deli-style supermarket selling both local and international produce.

Also located within Maji Square is a stage that will have Taiwanese musicians playing over the weekend.

The square will often host events, including Latin dancing, and is one of the best places in Taipei to watch big sporting events such as the Football World Cup - they'll erect 3 large screens showing matches live.

Click here to see what's on at Maji Square

Most places are open during the day, and the Triangle bar opens late in the evening and sometimes has very good bands playing. The Three Lions Inn serves traditional English-style food and drink with a nice outdoor seating area.

Click an image to find out more about each

For kids, there is a small fairground that includes a merry-go-round, lots of inflatables and games machines.

One of the more fun things for the smaller children to enjoy here are the many child-size vehicles that can be rented out. They can be driven around in the vast area near the expo centre, although unbeknownst to the children, they're actually controlled remotely by their parents following frantically behind.

With so few options to drink outside in Taipei, Maji Square is a great place to go to if you prefer a less stuffy environment to enjoy a drink. It can be quiet here during the week but at the weekend it has a much better atmosphere.

Pros

  • Lots of bars and restaurants
  • A few rides for kids

Cons

  • Some of the restaurants are a bit sub standard
  • Toilets aren't great here

Traveller Tips

Come at the weekend when the Farmer's Market is at the Expo and it's livelier.

Location

📍 Closest MRT: Juanshan Station (red line - exit 1)

title: Daan Walking Route
excerpt: A 4–6 hour weekend walk from the Jianguo flower market through Daan Forest Park and Yongkang Street to Chiang Kai-Shek Memorial Hall.
content:
A walk to be taken at the weekend, that begins in a weekend only flower market, through the largest park in Taipei, Yongkang Street for food and finish off at the Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall. The walk will take 4 - 6 hours.

It's best to get to the flower market in the morning when it's less busy (it opens at 09:00).

Perfect For

  • Markets
  • Flowers and parks
  • Food and cafes
  • Historical buildings

Suggested Walking Route

Step-By-Step

  • [A] Arrive at the north entrance of Jianguo Flower Market from either Zhongxiao Xinsheng or Zhongxiao Fuxing MRTs (alternatively you can go to the south entrance near [B] that's close to Daan Park MRT)
  • Walk through the flower market
  • [B] Take a look at the Artists Corner market
  • [C] Walk into Daan Forest Park
    • Make sure you visit the lake to the north west to see the heron, turtles and carp
    • There's a nice Louisa cafe with outdoor seating within the north of the park near Daan Park MRT
  • [D] Exit the park via the north-west exit, cross the main road and walk towards Yongkang Street
    • Enjoy the many restaurants, cafes, desserts shops and cafes
    • [optional] Visit the original Din Tai Fung. Note that it does get very busy, but if you get a numbered ticket from them first, you can check the current ticket number on their website (Xinyi Branch) and can explore the area while you wait
    • [optional] Alternatively, try the Scallion Pancake stand, Toasteria or visit the Yaboo Cafe for refreshments
    • You must also try some shaved ice dishes here, Smoothie House is a popular choice
  • [E] Continue 10 minutes west along the main road until you reach the Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall
    • Visit the museum and galleries at the base of the Memorial Hall
    • Visit the Performance Halls
    • Walk through the gardens and trail
    • See both ceremonies (see Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall post for more details)
  • [F] Walk to the Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall MRT station
  • Optional Extra: Visit Jin Feng Braised Pork Rice, one of the most popular local restaurants in Taipei, only 5 minutes walk from the MRT station

title: Tasty Scallion Pancakes at Lin's Chinese Pizza
excerpt: Scallion pancakes, not pizza despite the name, right next to Shilin MRT — handy before the night market opens.
content:
You've probably guessed already that these aren't pizzas – they're scallion pancakes, a doughy mix with scallion, filled with egg and flavoured with fresh basil. Lin's is one of the best stalls in the area to try them, and sits right next to Shilin MRT station, making it a handy stop if the night market hasn't opened yet and you're feeling peckish.

The pancake is cooked fresh to order on a flat griddle right at the stall – a quick, satisfying thing to watch while you wait, especially if it's your first time seeing one made. They don't serve many varieties, but you can add cheese and chilli sauce for a bit of heat, and it's cheap enough that it's worth getting two if you're hungry.

It's a small, no-frills operation – the kind of stall that's clearly aimed at locals rather than tourists – and it's rated 4.4 stars on Tripadvisor, one of the better options in the wider Shilin area for this kind of quick street food.

Traveller Tips

You can add cheese for NT$10 extra.

Location

📍 Closest MRT: Shilin - red line exit 1

title: New Orleans Inspired Seafood at Shrimp Daddy
content:
Shrimp Daddy is a great little restaurant near Songshan Cultural Park serving shrimp and lobster dishes.

Inspired by restaurants from New Orleans, it has many different takes on Shrimp dishes but their most popular ones are the seafood bowls, containing shrimp or lobster marinated and mixed with clams, crab, mussels and octopus, with a choice of vegetables and sauces.

You can choose the spiciness too, from mild the very spicy - we tried the shrimp, clams and mussels and chose a medium spiciness, which was at the upper echelons for the levels we can ensure!

The bowls are packed with seafood, and the marinated shrimp are deliciously juicy and flavoursome. There is plenty to get through for 2 people, but be prepared to get your fingers very messy. They provide loads of napkins and have a large sink if the mess gets too much.

For a little extra, you can purchase add ons such as a small salad and soup, although these were nothing special.

If you don't fancy one of these bowls, there are plenty of other choices - Gumbos, buns, even mac 'n' cheese with shrimp, and lots of side dishes. We opted for some onion rings, which in hindsight was probably a bad idea due to the amount of food we already needed to consume.

If you fancy something particularly fresh, you can choose from one of the live lobsters they keep in the tank.

I wouldn't say it's the fanciest place we've ever dined in, and it does feel almost like a local place, but it's all about the food here.

We had a great meal and will definitely return at some point. Shrimp Daddy is on the expensive side however, with the meal costing us NT$1,700, although we did pig-out rather!

Pros

  • Juicy shrimp
  • Nice selection of dishes

Cons

  • Expensive
  • Very messy

Price: $$$

Level of English: Good (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

Bibs are provided to help contain the mess

Location

📍 Closest MRT: Sun Yat-Sen Memorial Hall Station (blue line - exit 1)

title: Stunning Dishes at BON Meingerda & Dumpling
excerpt: A Taiwanese restaurant known for meingerda, a slippery, tricky-to-eat local take on gnocchi, alongside classic dumplings.
content:
BON Meingerda & Dumpling is a Taiwanese restaurant serving local dishes such as dumplings and Taiwanese pasta.

The dishes they are most famous for however, are meingerda - a Taiwanese take on gnocchi. Slightly more slimy in texture than gnocchi and consequently very difficult pick using chopsticks.

The mushroom meingerda and pepper sauce is one of the most beautiful looking local dishes we've tried in Taipei, vibrant in colour and sitting pristinely within the fine bowl it's served in. Even though it's a vegetarian dish, the meingerda and mushrooms give it a meaty texture. The dried chilli sitting atop adds some zing.

The Tom-Yam meingerda with seafood and pork is the most expensive dish on their menu but there are many delightful textures and tastes at play, giving the dish a surf 'n' turf feel.

The clams meingerda with rice wine is another of our favourites. The dishes may look small but the bowls are deep, with many pieces of pasta hidden underneath.

The meingerda dishes come in soup form too (although we've yet to try these) and have seafood, pork, vegetarian or chicken variations.

The dumplings also come on their own or in a soup. The non soup versions can be purchased in quantities of 10, 15 or 20, and are filled with pork and either leek or cabbage. I can just about handle 15.

There are a number of soups and side dishes too, with cucumber, vegetables, radish and many others.

It's a small but popular place to dine. The walls are adorned with dried flowers and there's the usual paraphernalia scattered around.

If you come during peak hours you'll probably need to wait for a while. Outside is a board where you'll need to write your phone number and wait for them to ring you, but it's definitely worth the wait.

BON Meingerda & Dumpling is a hidden gem worthy of being found.

Menu

Pros

  • Consistently high quality
  • Beautifully presented
  • Tasty

Cons

  • Usually a queue to get in

Price: $$

Level of English: OK (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

Opening Hours:
11:30 - 14:00
17:30 - 20:30

Add soup for an extra NT$50
Add soup and a basic drink for an extra NT$80
Add soup and a special drink for an extra NT$130
