📍 Closest MRT: Jiantan (red line - exit 3)

title: Taipei East District: Where to Shop, Eat and Drink
excerpt: The East District area of Taipei is packed with independent shops, cafes, restaurants and bars.
content:
Perfect For

  • Independent Shops
  • Cafes
  • Bars and Restaurants

The East District (known as Dongqu by the locals), located only slightly east of the centre of Taipei, is a vibrant and popular area to visit during the night or day.

Before Ximending was developed into the shopping district it is today, the East District was the place to go for independent shops, cafes, restaurants and bars. In fact, while it doesn't have the flashing lights or pedestrianised streets of Ximending, I believe it has a much wider range of shops, restaurants and bars.

These are all located both north and south of Zhongxiao East Road between the Zhongxiao Fuxing and Sun Yat-Sen Memorial Hall Stations on the blue line.

There are loads of cool independent shops selling everything from fashion, cosmetics, gadgets and gifts.

As for restaurants, there are dozens to choose from, with a wide range of cuisine available. Italian, Spanish, Greek, Mexican, French, lots of great vegetarian/vegan places, and a wealth of Asian cuisine.

These won't be too busy during the week, but during weekend evenings there will often be queues to dine in popular restaurants.

See my Places of Interests section at the end of this post to view all the places I recommend here

Some of the best bars in Taipei can also be found in the East District. Expat bars, cocktail bars, and even hair salons which double as bars.

The district also has a metro mall that covers the length of the main road between the MRT stations, ideal if it's too hot or rainy outside. There are also three large SOGO malls in the district if you prefer something more high-end.

The East District is great alternative to both the Xinyi and Ximending shopping districts. While it's less crowded here, it's still vibrant and offers many choices when to comes to shopping, eating or drinking.

Places of Interest

The places I'd actually point you to in the East District:

Eat

  • Kobayashi Noodle Restaurant – cheap, no-frills Taiwanese dishes: pork rice, noodles, oyster omelettes.
  • Little Creatures – an Australian-inspired restaurant and bar, built around its own craft ales.
  • Chamonix – higher-end teppanyaki, six courses around a huge circular grill.
  • Shrimp Daddy – New Orleans-inspired shrimp and lobster dishes.
  • Taipei Souvlaki – fast-food style Greek souvlaki and gyros.
  • Ducky Restaurant – European-leaning, with duck done properly. A short walk further out, near Zhongxiao Xinsheng.
  • Home's Thai – the Fuxing Road branch is more formal than their Songshan one.
  • Oye Punjabi – small, authentic Indian, run by Indian expats.
  • Eastern Ice Store – one of Taipei's most established dessert shops, open 11am–11pm daily.

Cafes

  • Cafe Costumice – relaxed, good for working or socialising, with an outdoor drink option too.
  • Coffee Lover's Planet – serious single-origin coffee and gourmet sandwiches.
  • Unicofa Coffee – some of the cheapest coffee and tea in the city.
  • Ray Cafe – small, good-value cafe known for its coffee and waffles with quirky toppings.
  • Yuppy Bookstore Cafe – cafe, live music and lecture venue in one, on the third floor of a hotel near Zhongxiao Fuxing.
  • Campus Cafe – an American-diner chain modelled on US college cafes. Quality varies by branch.
  • Mr Brownie – what might be Taipei's best brownies, with a big range of toppings.

Bars

  • Taihu Craft Beer Tasting Room – the best of Taihu's three Taipei taprooms.
  • A Train, B Line, C Park, D Town – four related cocktail bars, same owners, same high standard.
  • On Tap – billed as Taipei's only real British pub, draft ales and pub food.
  • Indulge Experimental Bistro – terroir-driven craft cocktails from a fixture on Asia's 50 Best Bars list.
  • Bar Mood Taipei – a standing taproom up front, a moody cocktail lounge behind it.
  • Draft Land – craft cocktails served on tap, no waiting around.

East District Location

📍 Closest MRT: Zhongxiao Dunhua Station (blue line)

title: A Technophile's Delight at Syntrend Creative Park
excerpt: A 12-storey tech shopping mall in the Technology District, floors organised by theme from exhibits to higher-end electronics.
content:
Located within the Technology District, Syntrend Creative Park is a modern 12 story building selling technology related products.

Aimed at the higher-end market, it's floors are categorised into different areas:

  1. LOOK - Exhibits and promotions changing weekly
  2. TOUCH - Computers and accessories / IOT / Gifts
  3. CLICK - Photography / Outdoor / VR / Drones
  4. HOME - Appliances / Kitchenware / Exercise / Relaxation
  5. LISTEN - Audio/Visual
  6. GAME - Games / Toys / Anime / Comics / E-Sports
  7. PLAY - Books / Toys / Games

The other floors have lecture theatres, cafes, restaurants and a creative space, while there's a good food hall in the basement.

Click here for a complete floor guide

Many of the largest technology brands can be found at Syntrend Creative Park, including Apple, Samsung, HTC, Dyson, Sharp, Bose, HP, B&O, Canon, GoPro to name just a few.

On the third floor there's an area where you can try the HTC Vive and play in a virtual reality space against others.

The second floor has a large area selling some nice gifts and accessories.

While the open space on the first floor has temporary exhibitions, usually aimed at video gaming, films, toys or cartoons.

For technology buffs and geeks, Syntrend Creative Park is a great place to find some of the latest tech. Even if you have no intention of buying anything, there's still plenty of things to see and do here, and there are many other tech shops located in the technology district.

Pros

  • Best place to shop for branded technology goods
  • Plenty of food options

Cons

  • Can be expensive

Traveller Tips

If you spend over NT$2,000, you are eligible for a tax rebate. Make sure you have your passport with you and ask them to complete a form after your purchase. This can be claimed at either airport when departing.

Syntrend Creative Park Location

📍 Closest MRT: Zhongxiao Xinsheng (blue/orange lines - exit 1)

title: Craft Beer Cafe - the Best Selection of Bottled Ales in Taipei? (Permanently Closed)
content:
Permanent Closure Notice

Please note: Craft Beer Cafe has permanently closed.

Situated in the Fuxing area, Craft Beer Cafe is a bar with probably the largest collection of bottled ales in Taipei.

Featuring no less than 10 fridges all packed to the brim with ales from around the world, including Belgium, UK, USA, Germany and some from the Asian regions, including Japan and of course Taiwan.

They also have a few tap beers, with white ale, pale ale, fruit ales and more. These can be purchased in 330ml or 500ml, costing NT$220/NT$290 respectively, although there's a 30% discount before 8pm.

The bar has a modern looking interior and a large screen showing sports, and they serve fried snack food and pizzas.

But it's the ales you should come here for, with hundreds of bottles to choose from, including pale ales, IPAs, Trappist, sour, stouts and fruity beers.

Pros

  • Nice selection of tap beers
  • Huge number of bottled beers

Cons

  • Food is average

Price: $$$

Level of English: Good (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

30% off tap beers until 8pm

Location

📍 Closest MRT: Zhongxiao Fuxing (blue/brown lines - exit 4)

title: Be Gulliver at the Miniatures Museum of Taiwan
excerpt: Over 200 miniature exhibits collected from across the globe over two decades, including the museum's famous through-the-window scenes.
content:
The Miniatures Museum of Taiwan is dedicated to all things miniature. With over 200 miniaturised exhibits, it's a mightily impressive and varied collection.

The museum is located in the basement of a modern office building, which is easy to miss as there's only a poster on the wall giving away it's whereabouts.

For over 20 years, the Miniatures Museum of Taiwan has been collecting these miniature works of art from across the globe, with large proportion originating from Europe.

Some of the best and most detailed pieces are the Through-the-window scenes. A voyeuristic peek into the lives of others.

The level of detail on everything is staggering. The furnishings, the working lights, and most impressively, even the postage-stamp sized paintings have been expertly hand painted.

You can barely even tell just by looking at some the pictures that they are in fact tiny versions.

The majority of the exhibits here are of Buildings, from Tudor and Victorian English architecture, right through to castles and ruins of ancient Rome.

Almost all of the pieces here are of a scale of 1:12.

Fantasy and Fairy Tales are well catered for, with Pinocchio, Jack and the Beanstalk and fantastical scenes with dinosaurs.

There's also a section devoted to dolls and toys, including toy cars. Maybe not strictly miniatures, but impressive nevertheless.

You can even purchase miniature bottles of booze from the museum's gift shop!

The Miniatures Museum of Taiwan is a great museum for both adults and kids. Many of the miniature models have been crafted with incredible skill, care and precision, and truly deserve people's attention.

Pros

  • Great for kids
  • Great variety of miniatures

Cons

  • More expensive than other museums

Price

Adults: NT$200
Juvenile (13 to 18 years): NT$160
Children (6 to 12 years or above 110 cm): NT$120
Other children are free to enter

Klook Price: NT$180

Click here to order a Miniatures Museum of Taiwan ticket

Opening Times

10:00 - 18:00
Closed on Mondays, Chinese New Year’s Eve and Chinese New Year’s Day

Traveller Tips

There is a gift shop selling all things miniature

Location

📍 Closest MRT: Songjiang Nanjing Station (green/orange lines - exit 5)
Located on floor B1 of the office building.

title: Ximending Outdoor Drinking Area: Bars & Prices
excerpt: One of the few places in Taipei to drink outdoors. Which bars are worth it, what drinks cost, and when the area gets busy.
content:
Taipei doesn't have many areas where you can eat of drink outside, probably due to the heat, rain and mosquitos, but if you do want to brave the elements and enjoy a drink in the open, the Ximending outdoor drinking area is the best place to go in Taipei.

Located directly behind the Red House, the area includes several bars and a shared seating area, and is a popular hangout for the LGBT community.

The bars in this area include

  • Karen Bar
  • Sol Bistro
  • Commander
  • G-Paradise
  • Casa Bar

Some pink neon lighting and rainbows will give hints at the campness of the area, but for straight people it never feels like you're unwelcome. In fact, the opposite is largely true, as the bar staff are generally friendly, and not pushy like bar areas in other Asian countries.

Drinks served here include standard lagers, and slightly more camp ones such as Hoegaarden Rose. Many cocktails can be purchased here and they're actually not too bad.

You can also rent shishas in some of the bars, which come with flavoured tobacco.

Many of the bars also serve food, although I would recommend eating in the main Ximending area before you come here. You'll find far more interesting food there.

During the summer months, the area has fans and vapour sprays to cool people down if the temperature is up.

The Ximending Drinking Area is a vibrant place over the weekend, and is the best place in Taipei to enjoy a drink outside.

Pros

  • Best area for outdoor drinking
  • LGBT friendly

Cons

  • Food isn't great here

Traveller Tips

Ensure you have some mosquito spray handy

Ximending Outdoor Drinking Location

📍 Closest MRT: Ximen Station (green/blue lines - exit 1)

title: 25 Best Things to Do on Yongkang Street: Food, Gifts & Old Taipei
excerpt: The 25 best things to do on Yongkang Street, from the original Din Tai Fung and sixty-year-old beef noodles to mango shaved ice, gift shops and the Japanese-era lanes behind it.
content:
Perfect For

  • Street Food & Snacks
  • Desserts & Shaved Ice
  • Cafes & Craft Beer
  • Gifts and Souvenirs
  • Japanese-era Architecture

Overview

Yongkang Street runs for about a kilometre through Daan, and it packs more good eating into that distance than anywhere else in Taipei. TimeOut named it the 4th coolest street in the world in 2022 – and the coolest in Asia – which is a lot to live up to, but the mix earns it: the original Din Tai Fung at one end, sixty-year-old beef noodles, shaved ice, tiny gift shops, and lanes of Japanese-era wooden houses just behind.

It isn't pedestrianised, so the pavements get tight at weekends, and the best of it isn't on the main street at all – the alleys running off it, mostly to the west, are where the cafes and small shops hide. Yongkang Park sits in the middle as somewhere to sit down with whatever you've bought.

So rather than a wander, here are 25 things worth stopping for, grouped so you can eat your way along in order or skip to the shops and the old streets. Everything is within about ten minutes' walk of Dongmen MRT.

When to Go and How Long to Spend

Come Tuesday to Friday if you can. A lot of Taipei closes on Mondays, and weekends bring queues at every place worth queueing for. Give it two hours for food and shops alone, or half a day if you're adding Qingtian Street and Rongjin Gorgeous Time.

Street Food & Snacks

1. Tian Jin Onion Pancake

Tian Jin Onion Pancake is the one unmissable thing on the street. Flaky scallion pancakes cooked to order for around NT$30–60, with an egg or cheese if you want, handed over in a paper bag. The queue regularly turns the corner but it moves fast, and it's the cheapest genuinely great thing you'll eat here.

2. Din Tai Fung, the Original

The corner of Yongkang Street and Xinyi Road is where Din Tai Fung began, and it's the reason a lot of people come. One important change though: the original branch is now takeout only. There's no seating, so order your xiaolongbao at the counter and carry them to Yongkang Park or Daan Forest Park.

For a table, cross the road to the Xinsheng branch – four floors and several hundred seats, and the queue moves rather better than the old flagship's ever did. Our full guide has the tricks for getting seated faster.

Klook.com

3. Yongkang Beef Noodles

Yongkang Beef Noodles has been making the same deep, dark braised broth for around sixty years, and it's still one of the best bowls in the city. Order the beef noodle soup, add a plate of braised side dishes, and don't be put off by the plain dining room.

4. Dongmen Dumplings

Trading since 1963 and mostly full of locals rather than visitors. Pot-stickers are the order, along with an unusually long list of cold side dishes you pick from a counter. A good answer when the Din Tai Fung queue defeats you.

Sit-Down Meals

5. Hao Kung Tao

A Michelin Bib Gourmand dumpling house on the street itself, which is remarkable for somewhere this unassuming. Xiaolongbao are the order, alongside the fried chicken it's equally known for, and they arrive in a bamboo steamer at a fraction of what the famous name on the corner charges. Plain room, mostly locals, no queue worth speaking of.

6. James Kitchen

Old-school Taiwanese home cooking in a room that hasn't been redecorated for the cameras – General Tso's chicken, clams with loofah, lamb tripe. Anthony Bourdain ate here, which has done nothing to spoil it. Book, or go early.

7. Wu Liu Shou

Taiwan's Japanese colonial period left the city with a serious appetite for Japanese food, and this neighbourhood has some of the best of it. Wu Liu Shou is a narrow izakaya serving small plates in a lovely setting. Busy at both lunch and dinner.

8. Toasteria

Toasteria, right next door to Din Tai Fung, started with toasted paninis and has grown into a proper Mediterranean and Middle Eastern menu. Open all day, modern room, and a reliable break from Taiwanese food.

9. Gusto Pizza

One of the best pizzas in Taipei, from a place that started in London. Handmade artisan bases with authentic Italian dough, and a short menu done properly.

Sweet Things

10. Smoothie House

Yongkang Street is often credited as the birthplace of mango shaved ice, and Smoothie House is the bright yellow shop that made it famous. A mountain of shaved ice under fresh mango and condensed milk, at around NT$250 for the full version – best in summer when the fruit is actually in season. There's a second branch just off the main street if the first is full.

11. Taro King

Less famous, less busy, and very good. Taro is the speciality, served over ice or in a warm soup depending on the weather.

12. Douhua, Two Ways

Douhua is soft tofu pudding in sweet syrup, and it's the Taiwanese dessert most visitors skip. Two places here do it properly: one makes it with spring water from the Xueshan range, the other is known for red bean, tapioca and peanut toppings. Cheap, warm in winter, iced in summer.

13. Ciao Ciao Scone Cafe

An unlikely thing to find on a Taipei food street: proper English-style scones with clotted cream, at around NT$65–80 each. Tiny, and they sell out.

Klook.com

Coffee & Beer

14. Youmoutoohana and Yaboo

There are dozens of cafes in the alleys here and these two are our favourites. Youmoutoohana is the one to take a laptop to, and Yaboo is the one to sit in with a book.

15. Saturn Landing Turkish Coffee

Coffee brewed in hot sand at the table, plus baklava and other Turkish sweets. As much a piece of theatre as a drink, and there's nowhere else in the city doing it like this.

16. Zhang Men Brewing

Taiwanese craft beer has come a long way, and Zhang Men is one of the names leading it. The Yongkang taproom pours more than twenty of its own beers, which is a rarity in a city where most bars stick to imports.

17. A Bubble Tea for the Walk

No serious ceremony required – there's a branch of one of Taiwan's big chains on the street, and a cup of milk tea for well under NT$100 is the correct way to walk off a bowl of beef noodles.

Gifts and Shops

18. Lai Hao

Lai Hao is the best of the gift shops here, and there are a lot of them – hundreds of small, genuinely Taiwanese things rather than airport tat. This is the street to do your present shopping on.

19. ORINGO

Handmade shoes and leather goods from a Taiwanese label that has won design awards for them. Not cheap, but they're made here and they last.

20. Ma Ma Umbrella

A shop selling colourful umbrellas and stationery, overlooking Yongkang Park. In a city this rainy, an umbrella is the most useful souvenir you can buy.

21. Pineapple Cake and Nougat Crackers

Yongkang Street is one of the best places in Taipei to buy edible presents. Pineapple cake is the classic, and the local speciality worth seeking out is the green onion nougat cracker – salty, sweet and much better than it sounds, sold by the box for around NT$220. Some of these small shops are cash only.

Parks and Old Taipei

This is the part of Yongkang almost everyone misses. All four of these are free.

22. Yongkang Park and the Weekend Market

The park in the middle of the street is where you take your scallion pancake and your takeaway dumplings. At weekends it and the surrounding street turn into a market with stalls, street performers and live music, which is the best time to be here if you don't mind the crowds.

23. Qingtian Street

Five minutes east and the noise stops completely. Qingtian Street is a grid of quiet, tree-shaded lanes lined with wooden houses built for Japanese academics in the 1930s, and several have been restored. One of them is open as a tea house and restaurant where you can sit on the tatami. It's the single best reason to walk away from the food.

24. Rongjin Gorgeous Time

The old Taipei Prison officials' dormitories, Japanese-era wooden buildings that sat empty for decades, reopened in 2022 as a small park of shops, tea rooms and cafes. Sections of the original prison wall still stand nearby. Very new, and still mostly full of locals.

25. Dongmen Market

A traditional market a couple of minutes from the MRT, and the everyday counterpart to the tourist street outside. Produce and butchers at the front, a handful of very old food stalls tucked inside. Go in the morning, when it's actually working.

While You're Here

Yongkang Street is within a quarter of a kilometre of both Daan Forest Park and Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall, or one MRT stop either side of Dongmen. It also sits on a walking route we've put together for the area.

Practical Tips

  • Tuesday to Friday beats the weekend, and a lot of Taipei shuts on Mondays.
  • Bring cash. Several of the stalls and smaller gift shops don't take cards – see our Taipei money guide.
  • The street isn't pedestrianised, so watch for scooters on the pavement.
  • The alleys off to the west are where the good cafes are. Don't just walk the main road.
  • Eat before you shop – the food places queue up at lunch and dinner, the shops stay open later.

Virtual Tour

Getting There

📍 Closest MRT: Dongmen Station on the red and orange lines. Take exit 4 or 5 and walk south down either Yongkang Street or Lishui Street – both drop you straight into the food.

Everything in this guide sits within about a ten-minute walk of that exit, so there's no route to plan. Daan Forest Park and Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall are each a quarter of a kilometre away, or one stop either side on the MRT.

title: Go Bargain Hunting at Gongguan Night Market
excerpt: A student-area night market with a Michelin-recommended gua bao stall among its evening food scene. What else is worth trying.
content:
The Gongguan area during the daytime has many shops and restaurants, and during the evening the night market adds loads of great food stalls and other stands selling an abundance of gifts, jewellery and clothes.

While the market itself isn't huge, the combination of this and the established shops make this a great area to come for people looking for bargains or food.

There are three food stands I would strongly urge you to try here:

  • Lan Jia Traditional Taiwanese Snack serves delicious Gua Bao – a soft bun filled with a mixture of pork belly. It's even recommended by the Michelin Guide
  • Ho's Sweet Potato Balls are by far the best we've tried in Taipei - so light and crispy, they melt in your mouth

Click each image to found out more

You'll be hard pressed to miss these, since there are always long queues extending from each stand.

A couple of other nice food stands I would recommend at the Gongguan Night Market are the Korean Topokki (found close to Ho's Sweet Potato Balls), and the multi-coloured dumpling stand.

If you've never tried it, Topokki is a spicy stir-fried rice cake dish with egg and cheese, and the ones here are divine. The dumpling stand serves a large selection of many types of sweet and savoury dumplings filled with shrimp, curry, custard and many others.

There are many other great restaurants and food places in the Gongguan area that are not part of the night market.

Please visit this post to find out more

The market extends the area's bargain shopping into the evening too, with dozens of stalls selling clothes, jewellery and accessories at similarly good prices – see the Gongguan area guide for the daytime shops and malls.

Some of the alleys at the Gongguan Night Market are quite narrow, so consequently you may find it difficult to walk around freely, especially during weekend evenings. But for bargains and food, it's one of the best areas to visit in Taipei.

Pros

  • Great for bargain hunters
  • Many nice food stalls and restaurants

Cons

  • Alleys and streets can be confusing to navigate

Traveller Tips

Recommended stalls found below

Location

📍 Closest MRT: Gongguan Station (green line - exit 1)

title: Wander the Winding Alleys of Gongguan
excerpt: Gongguan has many cheap shops and restaurants, and comes alive during the evening when the night market opens
content:
Perfect For

  • Bargain hunters
  • Restaurants and food stalls
  • Live music
  • Kids

Located on the green line in the Southern part of Taipei, Gongguan is situated close to Taiwan's largest university - NTU, and as such has the largest population of students in Taipei.

Due to this, Gongguan benefits from having some of the cheapest shops and restaurants found in Taipei. There are many clothes shops, with a huge number of sportswear shops selling trainers at far cheaper prices found in shopping malls.

For kids, there are plenty of amusement arcades, and a water park called Road Castle with water slides and pools.

There are also a few music venues, The Wall Live House being the best of these, with live international underground acts of high calibre.

The James Joyce Irish Pub also usually has bands playing over the weekend, or you could just go for one of the best pints of Guinness in Taipei.

The streets and winding alleys at Gongguan make it easy to get lost, especially at night when Gongguan Night Market brings in many more visitors.

Many of the night market stalls are open during the day. If you visit the above post, there are three really great stands I would urge you to visit.

Alternatively, there are a couple of small restaurants to grab some quick meals. Yu Poke has some fresh and tasty Hawaiian poke dishes.

If the hustle and bustle of the streets becomes too much, you have the option of escaping to either the huge NTU campus or the Taipei Water Park, which features a museum and nice areas to walk, and leads to Treasure Hill Artists' Village.

Click an image to read more about each area

Gongguan Location

📍 Closest MRT: Gongguan Station (green line)

title: Try a Delicious Bao at Lan Jia Traditional Taiwanese Snack
excerpt: A 30-year-old Gongguan Night Market institution serving Bib Gourmand-listed gua bao, or 'tiger bites pig' - a lucky Taiwanese bun with a history behind its name.
content:
Found within the Gongguan Night Market, Lan Jia (藍家割包) serves gua bao (割包) - a soft bun filled with pork belly and other delights. It's been running for around 30 years, starting out as an unassuming little cart in a lane off Roosevelt Road before building a loyal following among National Taiwan University staff and students, and workers from the nearby Taipower Building.

The stand is extremely popular as these are arguably the best gua bao found in Taipei - they've even found a place on the Bib Gourmand Selection in the Taipei Michelin Guide.

Recommendations don't come much higher than that.

Gua bao itself has a name that literally means "cut bun" in Hokkien, referring to how the flat steamed dough is folded over into a pocket. It's also known as "tiger bites pig" (虎咬豬), since the folded bun resembles a mouth biting into the pork – a shape that traditionally made it a lucky food to eat at the Lunar New Year, resembling a gold ingot.

A soft, warm bun stuffed with marinated pork belly, peanut powder and coriander. I was initially sceptical about the presence of the peanut powder, but it adds a nice sweetness that gives the bun a deep and rich flavour. The pork belly has obviously been marinated for some time as it melts in the mouth.

I'm not usually a fan of fatty meats, but the fat here has been cooked and rendered down to a texture that's palatable even for my mouth.

You can even ask for your preferred ratio of fat to lean meat, if you have a preference. For only NT$60 it's a cheap and delicious snack that's worth every penny. They also serve soups if you want something to go alongside it, including a corn and pork rib soup and a traditional four-herb soup.

If you're in Gongguan, Lan Jia Traditional Taiwanese Snack is certainly worth queuing for, as their Bao's are succulent and complex and will perfectly fill that hole in your stomach.

Traveller Tips

There are normally two queues, one for eating inside and one for takeaway (which is much quicker).

Location

📍 Closest MRT: Gongguan- green line exit 4

title: Delicious Snacks at Tian Jin Onion Pancake
excerpt: Widely considered Taipei's best scallion pancake stall, on Yongkang Street - the name literally means 'scallion grab-cake', for how the dough is torn while frying.
content:
Tian Jin Onion Pancake (天津蔥抓餅) is a food stall that's found on the famous Yongkang Street, just down the lane from Yong Kang Beef Noodles – and widely considered the best scallion pancake stall in Taipei, if not all of Taiwan.

They're not actually onion pancakes though, as the translation is lost slightly here. There are scallion (similar to spring onions) pancakes - a fried doughy mix infused with scallion, a very popular dish especially at breakfast time.

The Chinese name, cong zhua bing, literally means "scallion grab-cake" – a reference to how the dough is scrunched and torn by hand as it fries, which is what gives it those flaky, chewy layers. The pancakes are fried to a golden crisp and then beaten to make them as light as possible, all prepared by a team of experienced aunties who keep the long queue moving quickly.

You can have them on their own, although you'll find them a bit dry without any fillings, of which you have a few choices - egg, cheese, sweetcorn and ham or a mixture of these. Prices run from around NT$25 for a plain one up to NT$60 for the works. We opted for the corn, cheese and egg one and it was very tasty!

You'll need to find a good spot to eat them as there are no tables here, and they are very messy things. They don't supply napkins so make sure you have something to wipe your hands after!

Queuing is likely here, but you won't need to queue long as they are quite efficient. But it's worth queuing for as they are delicious gooey delights!

Menu

Traveller Tips

Come early to avoid afternoon queuing, and make sure you have something to wipe your hands. English on the menu is limited, but you can point at the pictures if needed.

Location

📍 Closest MRT: Dongmen - red/orange lines exit 5

title: Traditional Desserts at Shaved Ice Huaxi
excerpt: A shaved ice stall in Huaxi Night Market dating back to around 1920, serving locals and TV crews alike for over a century - no English menu, all charm.
content:
Tucked into Huaxi Night Market, this local shaved ice and fruit smoothie stall is one of the oldest of its kind in Taiwan, established around 1920. Wanhua is Taipei's oldest district, and Longshan Temple has been drawing crowds here for centuries – shaved ice vendors have been setting up nearby to serve temple-goers and market crowds for just as long, and this is one of the few still going from that era.

Very popular with the locals, it made its name over the years, featuring on many TV shows to help spread the word of its shaved ice desserts.

The menu is only in Chinese, so it's difficult to identify the many variations of shaved ice available, but we opted for their signature dish, which features a couple of types of beans, taro and glutinous rice and costing only NT$120. You'll probably need to point and hope you pick something you like – there's no English on the menu or among the staff, but that's part of the charm.

They also offer blended fruit drinks which are equally as nice. If you're in Huaxi Night Market or indeed Longshan Temple and are in need of some light and delicious refreshment, then look no further!

Location

📍 Closest MRT: Longshan Temple - blue line exit 1

The restaurant is not on Google Maps but it's located on the left side as you're walking from Longshan Temple, somewhere around here.

title: Shaved Ice Heaven at Snow Bro
excerpt: A Da'an shaved ice spot worth going back to - classic and milky shaved ice, tonnes of toppings, and a Taiwanese peanut soup worth trying too.
content:
Snow Bro (秘方雪人兄弟) is a Taiwanese dessert place in Da'an serving a variety of shaved ice dishes – the kind of spot people go back to more than once on the same trip.

I'm only aware of a couple of branches located in the Daan district but there could well be more. You can buy either classic shaved ice or a milky version mixed with condensed milk that is more fattening but delicious.

There are tonnes of toppings available, with the classic mango or other fruit toppings such as berries, or a variety of beans, lotus seeds or even Oreo, plus a few syrup options – including the more traditional longan syrup alongside the milkier condensed-milk version. If you're after something warm instead, their Taiwanese peanut soup is also worth trying, from NT$65 with one topping up to NT$85 with three.

You just need to make sure you don't eat them too quickly, as brain-freeze will often kick in!

Snow Bro's shaved ice dishes are some of the best we've tried in Taipei.

Menu

It's not a big place, so seating can be limited at busy times, but the shaved ice more than makes up for it – a large selection, very tasty, and mid-range priced. English is spoken reasonably well and the menu has English on it too.

Traveller Tips

Mango shaved ice is a must try!

Location

📍 Daan Branch (closest MRT: Daan - red/brown line exit 5)

title: 7 Shopping Malls with that 'Wow' Factor
excerpt: Seven Taipei malls worth a visit, including the Xinyi district that packs 13 into one neighbourhood. What each is good for, and where to eat inside.
content:
Taipei isn't short on shopping malls, with dozens spread across the city. In fact, the Xinyi Shopping District has the highest density of shopping malls in the world, with 13 of them!

Finding food while shopping isn't an issue, as many shopping malls have their own food hall in the basement and restaurants on the lower and upper floors.

Malls generally open and close late, with usual hours between 11:00-21:30 (22:00 at weekends). It's traditional for staff to stand by their shop and bow to everyone who passes when the mall opens and closes.

Don't forget to take your passport while shopping. You'll need this if you want your 5% VAT rebate on any purchased goods valued over NT$2,000.
Click here to read more about the Taiwan Tourist Tax Refund

Below are what I consider to be the best shopping malls in Taipei.

Taipei 101 Mall (Xinyi)

Located within the Xinyi Shopping district, and undoubtedly the most luxurious shopping mall in Taipei, the Taipei 101 mall is housed within the first five floors of the Taipei 101 building.

With many high-end brands to choose from, it also caters for more mid-range shoppers with brands such as H&M and Zara.

The forth floor features a huge open area with cafes and premium shops, with escalators leading to the Taipei 101 tower.

Click here to read more about the Taipei 101 observation deck

There's also a tax refund booth located on the 1st (ground) floor should you spend above NT$2,000.

Best For

  • Luxury
  • Wow factor

Breeze NanShan (Xinyi)

One of the newest shopping malls in Taipei, the Breeze Centre in the southern part of Xinyi Shopping District is also one of the best.

Featuring many shops, restaurants and cafes not found anywhere else in Taipei, this striking building also has an open-air walkway in the third floor that offers great views of Taipei 101 (which is right next door).

The mall also features a nice immersive ride called i-ride, which has a large IMAX-like screen and seating that moves and has wind effects, taking you on a virtual flight over Taiwan or the USA.

Click here to read more about i-ride Taipei

Best For

  • Original shops
  • Modern interior

Sogo (Fuxing)

Located right next to Zhongxiao Fuxing MRT, the Sogo mall is a good place for high-end brands that has a popular cosmetics floor and two decent food halls, one with a Din Tai Fung.

It's one of the busier malls in Taipei, especially on weekends, and offers a lot in the way of female shoppers, with many clothing outlets and cosmetics.

The mall is located either side of Fuxing road, and is linked by underground walkways.

If you want to venture outside, the are many shops, restaurants and cafes found to the East of the mall in the Dunhua district. There's also another Sogo mall in this area.

Best For

  • High end
  • Female shoppers

Miramar (Neihu)

Located on the outskirts of Taipei, Miramar is worth checking out if you're in the area. It's quite easy to spot - just look for the huge Ferris Wheel!

Miramar is the best mall if you have kids, as it includes a large amusement arcade and a great cinema complex with an IMAX screen.

As per all malls, there a huge food hall in the basement, and many other restaurants on the ground and upper floors

Best For

  • Kids
  • Something for everyone
Klook.com

Q Square (Taipei Main)

Attached to the Taipei Main station, Q Square is a busy but diverse mall, with shops of all types, from high-end to budget.

Q Square has a large cinema complex on the highest level, and many restaurants on the ground and upper floors. The newly renovated food hall is one of the best in Taipei.

With 7 floors, the lifts usually require a wait, so you'll find the escalators more convenient.

Best For

  • Dining
  • Variety

Mega City (Banqiao)

Located a few stops down the blue line in Banqiao, Mega City is a huge mall packed with shops and restaurants, plus an IMAX cinema.

The upper restaurant floor has an Italian themed section with some good restaurants, while the basement has a large food hall with a Din Tai Fung.

With 12 floors, each devoted to selling different products or dining, there's plenty for everyone.

Best For

  • Variety
  • Food

Syntrend (Zhongzheng)

If you're shopping for tech, then look no further than Syntrend. Located in the heart of Taipei's technology district, this futuristic building has several floors dedicated to everything tech related, and has shops for all the top tech brands.

The ground floor will usually have some cool promotional events, and there's a nice VR area that promotes Taiwan's own HTC VIVE headsets. Syntrend sells some nice non-tech gifts too.

Additionally, there's a huge building directly adjacent to Syntrend which has some fantastic tech bargains. In fact, the entire square kilometre area is a technophile's dream.

Best For

  • Tech
  • Gifts

Locations

title: Navigate the Campus at National Taiwan University
excerpt: Taiwan's most prestigious university, founded in 1928 as Taihoku Imperial University - its campus, open to the public, is home to Royal Palm Boulevard and the famous Fu Bell.
content:
The National Taiwan University (NTU) is the largest and most prestigious University in Taiwan. It has a huge campus that's open to the public to walk around.

It was originally established by the Japanese while they were occupying Taiwan during the early 20th century - founded in 1928 as Taihoku Imperial University, the seventh Imperial University in the Empire of Japan - so there are many buildings that have Japanese architecture. It was handed over to Chinese administration and renamed National Taiwan University on 15 November 1945.

To walk around the entirety of the roughly 115 hectare (1.15 km squared) campus at the National Taiwan University takes a good few hours so you'll need your walking boots on, but it has many beautiful buildings and areas of natural beauty, plus there are a number of museums to visit:

  • NTU Agricultural Exhibition Hall
  • NTU Museum of Anthropology
  • NTU Herbarium
  • NTU Heritage Hall of Physics
  • NTU Geo-specimen Cottage
  • NTU Museum of Zoology
  • NTU Insect Museum

They have differing visiting hours but generally open between 10:00 - 16:00 (some close for any hour at midday).

Most of the area is pedestrian only, so you'll not be bothered by the noise of traffic, and it's generally a very tranquil area to walk around, with lots of shaded areas and cafes to escape the sun for a while. Look out for the Fu Bell along Royal Palm Boulevard, the campus's tree-lined main artery - it's rung 21 times between classes, a tribute to former president Fu Ssu-nien's famous saying that a day has only 21 hours, with the remaining three reserved for reflection.

The National Taiwan University campus is a huge place that's ideal for walking or taking in a museum or two.

Traveller Tips

Visit one of the many museums found on site. It's a huge area with lots of cafes to explore, though it's about 10 minutes' walk from the nearest MRT exit.

A map of the campus can be found here.

Location

📍 Closest MRT: Gongguan Station (green line - exit 3)

title: Enjoy the View of Taipei 101 at Lobster Foods
excerpt: Lobster dishes with outdoor seating and Taipei 101 views, in the Xinyi shopping district.
content:
Located within the Xinyi shopping district, Lobster Foods serves a variety of interesting lobster dishes. With plenty of outdoor seating available and with great views of Taipei 101, it's one of the best places to dine in the area if you prefer sitting outdoors.

Their main dishes are Lobster Rolls, for which you can buy with either a half or a full lobster's worth of meat. Coming served in a soft brioche roll and topped off with some tangy salsa, they're a delight.

For slightly extra, you can order a set, which comes with either chips or quesadillas, salad and a very good lobster chowder.

Alternatively, you can get a lobster risotto, lobster pizza, lobster pasta or a lobster burger.

Lobster Foods also serves one of the best pints of Guinness in Taipei - they even have a certificate from Guinness as proof. A very full bodied pint with the trademark creamy white head and black body. I too can certify that it was a damn good pint, easily up there with the James Joyce Guinness we tried in Gongguan!

Lobster Foods is in a very good location, situated in a nice part of Xinyi with plenty of outdoor seating, and is a nice place to relax for a while. It's location does make Lobster Foods even more expensive than it would normally be however. It's certainly not cheap here, with a meal for two and drinks costing well in excess of NT$1,400.

Pros

  • Nice lobster
  • Outdoor seating
  • Great Guinness

Cons

  • Expensive

Price: $$$$

Level of English: Good (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

Try the Guinness!

Lobster Foods Location

📍 Closest MRT: Taipei 101 Station (red line - exit 4)

Note that Lobster foods in not on Google maps but it's directly adjacent to this place.

title: A Great Pint of Guinness at James Joyce Irish Bar
excerpt: An Irish chain bar with what might be the best pint of Guinness in Taipei — full-bodied with a proper creamy head.
content:
A capital city wouldn't be complete with an Irish bar. James Joyce is an Irish chain you've probably heard of, and of course serves pints of Ireland's most famous drink - Guinness.

And it's a damn good pint of Guinness, full in body with a creamy head that goes down very smoothly.

If Guinness isn't your thing, they have a few other tapped beverages, including the very Irish Magner's Cider and the not so Irish Carlsberg and Taiwan beer.

Their shelves are also stocked to the brim with Irish whiskeys, plus a large selection of other spirits from which they can make some basic cocktails. They have a nice selection of gins available too and make a mean Gin 'n' Tonic.

They do however serve no food, although a pint of Guinness could almost pass as a liquid meal.

James Joyce Irish Bar is cosy place with a few small tables by the bar and some some seating at the back, plus they have three tables outside. All in all, they is seating for around 40 people and it does get very busy after 8pm.

In the corner is a small stage where they'll have bands playing genres such as folk (Irish probably) and country. The bands usually only play on a Saturday evening.

James Joyce Irish Bar is a small but great little pub that serves one of the best pints of tap Guinness in Taipei.

Menu

Pros

  • Very good pint of Guinness
  • Live music at the weekend

Cons

  • Small
  • No food available

Price: $$

Level of English: Good (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

Come for the Guinness

Location

📍 Closest MRT: Gongguan (green line - exit 3)

title: Be Inspired at the Museum of Contemporary Arts
excerpt: A contemporary art museum inside a red-brick 1921 Japanese-era schoolhouse that later served as Taipei's City Hall - two floors of changing exhibitions near Q Square.
content:
Otherwise known as MOCA, the Museum of Contemporary Art shows temporary art exhibitions, with a heavy emphasis on modern audio/visual art.

Situated close to the Q Square shopping mall, the red-brick building with its distinctive central clock tower dates back to 1921, when it was built as Jiancheng Elementary School under Japanese colonial rule – designed by Kondō Jūrō, the same government architect behind several of the era's official buildings. After 1945 it served as Taipei's City Hall until the city government moved to Xinyi in 1994, before being restored and reopening as a museum in 2001. Unusually, it still shares its site with a working junior high school next door.

There are usually a couple of exhibitions at any one time across its two floors, often with screens showing multimedia or interactive artwork – the art is interesting and often carries a strong message, though some of the audio doesn't come with English subtitles.

The main room on the second floor usually hosts some impressive larger exhibits. The first time we went, they had a number of large projections that told a story from a different perspective on each screen. The most recent exhibition featured many interactive displays, one which painted your image as you moved and swayed.

Located on the first floor are other exhibits, a cafe and a gift shop with some eclectic items on sale.

Price

NT$50

Child under 6 years and senior citizens over 65 years enter free of charge

Opening Times

10:00 - 18:00

Closed on Mondays and national holidays

Traveller Tips

All bags must be left in lockers for the cost of NT$10

See here for a list of their current exhibitions

Location

📍 Closest MRT: Zhongshan (red/green line - exit 6)

title: Tasty Drinks at Yaboo Cafe
excerpt: A quiet, student-friendly cafe tucked off Yongkang Street near Dongmen - pricier than most in the area, but a lovely spot to work or unwind.
content:
Yaboo (鴉埠咖啡) is a popular student friendly cafe tucked down a side street off Yongkang Street near Dongmen, founded by sisters Emily and Tina Tsai back in 2010.

As with most cafes in the area, you'll pay above the average for beverages and food, but it's a nice place to unwind or work. It has a mellow vibe and is very quiet, while they provide indoor and outdoor seating (plus a basement floor for extra room), as well as the obligatory free WiFi.

They have a selection of teas and coffees available, including more unusual offerings such as banana tea, while some of their coffees have an alcoholic twist.

Yaboo have their own coffee bean grinder outside with many exotic beans to choose from.

There's a selection of pasta dishes, otherwise you can opt for one of their very good cakes. The house cat can usually be found sleeping in it's comfy bed.

Yaboo Cafe is a nice place to chill with a drink while you are in the Dongmen area – just be prepared to pay a bit more than at other cafes nearby for the privilege.

Traveller Tips

If it's too busy here, their sister cafe YABOO II is a few minutes' walk away on Lishui Street – a brighter, more work-friendly space, though I've not been myself.

Location

📍 Closest MRT: Dongmen (red line - exit 5)

title: See the Dinosaurs at the National Taiwan Museum
excerpt: Taiwan's oldest museum, founded 1908, with dinosaurs and natural history across three buildings by 228 Peace Park. Tickets, layout and what to see.
content:
Established in 1908, the National Taiwan Museum is the oldest museum in Taiwan. The museum's main focus is in four areas of science:

  • Anthropology
  • Earth sciences
  • Zoology
  • Botany

The museum consists of three buildings, two of which are located close to the 228 Peace Park, with the third building a 15 minute walk (or 1 MRT stop) away.

Main Building

The Main Building sits right on the edge of the park and is where all the newest and best temporary exhibitions are.

The most impressive of the three buildings, the main lobby area features Renaissance-style windows, huge columns and dome shaped roof.

There are four floors in the main building, although 1 or 2 are sometimes closed while they prepare for new exhibitions.

The lower floors are where you'll find the temporary exhibitions, while the third floor has a permanent one.

When I visited, there was a very good exhibition on insect life and plants that featured a number of interactive exhibits which are ideal for children.

More recently, the National Museum of Australia lent the museum a collection of Aboriginal bark paintings.

Click here for the current temporary exhibitions in the Main Building

The permanent exhibition on floor three focuses on the natural history of Taiwan.

Discovering Taiwan: Re-visiting the Age of Natural History and Naturalist of Taiwan, has exhibits on the most important naturalists during the early and mid 20th century, along with many of their findings.

Land Bank Exhibition Hall

The Land Bank Exhibition Hall is just across the road from the Main Building. Formally home to the state-owned Land Bank of Taiwan, it was later restored and renovated into the museum.

Although there are four floors, only the ground and first floor have exhibitions.

Both floors contain permanent exhibitions.

The first focuses on the history of the Land Bank building, from its origin as the Kangyo Bank during the Japanese colonial period to the establishment of the Land Bank after the war, and includes a section on the restoration of the building.

The large Evolution Hall contains an impressive dinosaur exhibition, featuring both real and artificial bones/skeletons, with many displays of fossils and bones.

The exhibition also includes fossils and stuffed animals from the periods before and after the dinosaurs.

The second floor of the hall also has a nice cafe with an outdoor terrace should you need to rest your legs for a while.

Locomotives

Located between the Main and Land Bank buildings within a transparent enclosed structure are two old Locomotives.

Used in the late 19th and early 20th century, the steam engines are two of the oldest examples left in Taiwan.

Nanmen Park

The third building is just one stop away south on the red line.

The Red House building was originally the camphor warehouse, while the Little White House was used as a warehouse to store the finished products.

The museum here focuses on the history of the camphor industry, and the medicinal products harnessed from the camphor.

The Red House building contains models of the factory and the equipment used.

Camphor was also used in the production of opium.

The site also has a courtyard area with what remains of the cistern, the wasted water generated from the manufacturing process that was used by the fire department. The white house building can be found next to this.

While I would only recommend visiting the Nanmen Park site if you have a particular interest in this industry, the buildings close to the park contain some great exhibitions, many of them child-friendly.

The National Taiwan Museum is one of the best places to visit for kids and adults alike. Why not visit this as part of a walking tour I've devised?

Pros

  • Lots for kids
  • Very cheap
  • Impressive buildings

Cons

title: Music Festivals with Class Acts
excerpt: Taipei has a number of music festivals each year, with some being completely free of charge
content:
Some fantastic music festivals to appreciate first rate musicians in the parks or mountains.

Click here to see all my 'best of' lists

Taipei Jazz Festival at Daan Park

Spanning two months each year, the Taipei Jazz Festival culminates with a fantastic concert lasting three October evenings at the Daan Forest Park pavilion. With four acts each evening, it's popularity has surged year-on-year. For jazz lovers, there no excuse not to come as it's also completely free.

Click here to read more about Taipei Jazz Festival

Taiwan World Music Festival

The best annual music event in Taipei, the Taiwan World Music Festival in October is a chance to listen to some world class performers from musicians and groups across the globe. Spanning 3 days, the festival has two large stages, a tent and many stalls and activities throughout each day. The World Music Festival is one event that music lovers shouldn't miss out on.

Click here to read more about Taiwan World Music Festival

Tiger Mountain Ramble

For just one December day a year, Tiger Mountain will host a small but fantastic music festival. Curated by expats, the Tiger Mountain Ramble has two stages and some brilliant acts playing Americana and other styles. The atmosphere and musicians here are first rate.

Click here to read more about Tiger Mountain Ramble

Honourable Mention - Daniel Pearl Music Festival

Daniel Pearl was a journalist and accomplished musician who devoted his life to helping others and improving the world. He was kidnapped and murdered in 2002, and ever since, concerts have been set up in many countries to celebrate his life. For just one September day each year, the Hakka Cultural Park hosts a small festival, with local, expat and some international bands playing, along with some food and gift stalls.

title: Take a Steamy Tour of the Beautiful Xinbeitou
excerpt: Xinbeitou is an area of natural beauty found in Beitou, and is most famous for its Hot Springs.
content:
Perfect For

  • Walking
  • Relaxing
  • Nature
  • Hot Springs

Xinbeitou is an area of natural beauty found in the northern Beitou district of Taipei. Due to the high amount of volcanic activity deep below the ground, it is most famous for its Hot Springs.

Having it's own dedicated MRT line, you can catch the Xinbeitou MRT train by changing via the Beitou station on the red line. It's just a 5 minute journey and a single stop away from here.

Steaming streams and pools run through the whole area, and the sulphur in the air is the first thing you'll notice stepping off the train.

The walk from Xinbeitou station to Thermal Valley will take you past many beautiful buildings and through the lovely Beitou Park.

The Beitou Hot Spring Museum and Beitou Library are just two of the fine buildings you'll walk past, and both are open most days.

There are numerous hotels around the streets, all taking advantage of the hot springs, many with private baths filled with the thermal spring water.

Klook.com

If you fancy a dip in the spring water yourself, there are many foot spas located around Xinbeitou. They are however quite strict on what you can wear, so ensure you take some appropriate swim wear with you!

Alternatively, you can find one of the hot spring sinks to test the waters for free.

Beitou Hot Spring Museum

Set on the edge of Beitou Park, the museum explains how the springs formed and how the town grew up around them. Do it first and the rest of the walk makes a lot more sense.

Ideally situated on the edge of Beitou park, and on the route to Thermal Valley, the Hot Spring Museum offers a great insight into the history of the Xinbeitou area and the formation of the hot springs.

Before you enter, you must replace your shoes with a pair of provided slippers. The two floors have a good variety of things to see.

The Tatami lounge is a place to sit and relax for a while.

Examples of the baths used to bathe in the hot spring water. Beitou was actually used as a place of relaxation for US soldiers during the Vietnamese war.

Downstairs has (which was thought) the largest hot spring public bath in East Asia at that time. Wind chimes attached to blue ribbons over the bath and on the ceiling fans adds a meditative and soothing feeling to the room.

Displays detailing every aspect of the springs, from the formation, to how they were used recreationally and culturally.

Beitou was a hot location during the 40s and 50s to shoot movies. The Guitar in the Hot Spring Town a classic Taiwanese film shot in Beitou.

I would recommend you making the Beitou Hot Spring Museum one of your first stops during your visit to Xinbeitou to help you gain an understanding of the area before you walk around.

The museum is free and open 09:00–17:00, closed on Mondays and national holidays unless they fall at a weekend. You'll swap your shoes for a pair of provided slippers at the door. It's a ten-minute walk from Xinbeitou MRT (exit 4).

Thermal Valley

From the museum it's another ten minutes uphill through the park to Thermal Valley – the largest hot spring lake in the area, and the reason the rest of Xinbeitou is here at all.

The valley was formed from a volcanic eruption hundreds of years ago and covers an area of 3,500 sq meters. The hot spring water comes from deep inside the volcano underground and rises to mix with the surface water to form the hot spring.

The rising steam gives off a heavy sulphuric smell as it condenses with the air. If you come during the winter months, the difference in temperatures will cause the steam to become much more visible.

Access to the lake isn't possible, and it's definitely not advised to climb over the fence, as water temperatures can range from 60°c to almost 100°c.

There's a gift shop and toilets just before you enter the site, and a small temple that offers a good vantage point for views of the lake.

Thermal Valley is a must visit attraction if you're in the Xinbeitou area.

Thermal Valley is also free, open 09:00–17:00 and closed on Mondays and over Lunar New Year. It's about fifteen minutes on foot from Xinbeitou MRT. Come in the colder months if you want to see it at its steamiest — though the sulphur is strong enough that some people don't last long.

Done at a gentle pace, the walk from the station up to Thermal Valley and back takes a half day, and Xinbeitou is one of the most beautiful places in Taipei you can reach on the MRT. You could even combine your visit with a trip to Danshui (at the end of the red line) to catch the stunning sunset there.

Xinbeitou is also located close to the Yangmingshan National Park, another beautiful spot located in the mountains. This isn't easily accessible, but you can combine a trip to Xinbeitou and Yangminshan with a day tour.

title: Fine Crafts and Gifts at The Red House
excerpt: A 1908 Japanese-era landmark next to Ximending, now housing craft stalls, a tea shop and a music venue. What to see and buy.
content:
Located right next to the Ximending Shopping district, The Red House is a striking building that contains numerous gift shops, a tea shop and music venue.

Constructed in 1908 by the Japanese, it's name comes from the bricks used to build it, and it's Western design and octagonal shape is certainly quite unique in Taipei.

It's the most well preserved class III building in Taiwan and although it was originally built as a public market hall, it's since been used as a cinema and theatre before being opened to the public to look around.

If you like quirky and unique gifts, this is one of the best places in Taipei to visit.

The Creative Boutique features two floors of stalls selling all manor of gifts, such as flattened glass bottles, temporary tattoos, jewellery, fragrances and clothes. All the gifts found here are of an exceptional standard.

Also located within the structure is a nice tea house and the Riverside Live House, a music venue that plays mainly Taiwanese music styles.

There's usually a market outside during the weekend, with over 20 tents selling similar items to those found inside.

Directly behind the building is a large outdoor drinking area that opens in the evening and is very popular with the LGBT community.

Click to read more about the Ximen Outdoor Drinking Area

The Red House is one of the best places to shop for unique and interesting gifts in Taipei, and is a must visit if you're in the Ximending area.

title: Huaxi Street Night Market: Taipei's Snake Alley Today
excerpt: Once famous for live snake shows, Huaxi Street Night Market near Longshan Temple is now a Michelin Bib Gourmand food street - the snake vendors closed for good in 2018.
content:
Right next to Longshan Temple in Taipei's oldest district, Wanhua, sits Huaxi Street Night Market – better known by its old nickname, Snake Alley. It was Taiwan's first market built specifically for tourists, opening in 1951, and for decades it earned its name honestly: vendors would skin and kill live snakes on the street to draw a crowd, selling snake meat, snake wine and snake gallbladder as health tonics.

That's all history now. Snake performances were banned under Taiwan's Animal Protection Act in the 2000s, and the last snake restaurant on the street, Asia Snake Meat Store, closed for good in May 2018. If you've come hoping to see snakes, you're a few years too late – but what's replaced them is arguably more worth the trip.

What's There Now

Much of the market runs down a long, covered indoor section – unusual for a Taipei night market, and a nice option if you're caught out by rain. Alongside the usual night market food, you'll find dozens of cheap massage and nail treatment stands, a holdover from the street's earlier days as a red-light district before prostitution was outlawed in Taiwan in 1991.

The whole market was awarded a Michelin Guide Bib Gourmand in 2019, and one stall in particular has its own individual recognition: Yuan Fang Guabao, which has been selling gua bao (steamed buns stuffed with marinated pork belly, pickles and ground peanuts) for over 60 years, earned its own Bib Gourmand in 2020. You'll find it at No. 17-2 Huaxi Street, open from 12:00 to 22:00.

For dessert, Shaved Ice Huaxi is one of the oldest shaved ice shops in Taiwan, dating back to around 1920, with a good range of fruit and bean toppings to choose from.

One practical warning worth taking seriously: some stands don't post prices, and foreign customers have been known to get quoted more than locals. If a stall has no visible price list, it's worth asking the cost before you order.

Traveller Tips

The market starts right at Longshan Temple, so it's easy to combine the two into one visit – see the temple first, then walk straight into the market as evening sets in.

title: Visit the Magnificent Longshan Temple
excerpt: Taipei's most famous temple, built in 1738 and rebuilt after wartime bombing. Over 100 deities, how to pray now incense is banned, and the best time to visit.
content:
Longshan Temple is one of the oldest temples in Taiwan, founded in 1738 by settlers from Fujian and dedicated to Guanyin, the Goddess of Mercy. It's been rebuilt more than once since – earthquakes have damaged it over the centuries, and it took a direct hit from US bombing during WWII, destroying much of the main hall.

Despite all that, it remains one of the most popular and impressive temples in Taipei, drawing large crowds throughout the day. Under one roof you'll find over 100 deities from a mix of Buddhist, Taoist and Chinese folk traditions – alongside Guanyin, look out for Mazu (goddess of the sea), Wenchang Dijun (god of literature, popular with students before exams), the red-faced Guan Gong (god of war and business), and Yue Lao, the matchmaker god. Yue Lao in particular draws a steady stream of visitors praying for love, both local and foreign.

How to Pray

One thing worth knowing before you go: Longshan Temple banned incense burning by visitors back in March 2020, on top of stopping the burning of paper "joss" money a few years before that (Taipei's then-mayor announced the change at the temple in 2017, when the number of incense burners was also cut from seven to three). Both moves were about air quality – the temple sits in a dense, built-up part of the city. These days, worshippers pray with their hands rather than lit incense, on the idea that a sincere prayer counts for just as much without the smoke.

If you want to try the temple's other traditions, look for the jiaobei – two crescent-shaped wooden blocks used to ask the gods yes/no questions, thrown on the ground to read the answer – and the numbered fortune sticks (qian), which you match to a corresponding printed fortune. Both are free to use. There are also chanting ceremonies three times a day, at 06:00, 08:00 and around 16:00, each lasting about 45 minutes (the evening one usually runs longer) – worth timing your visit around if you'd like to hear one.

A few points of etiquette: dress reasonably modestly, keep quiet and stand to the side near anyone actively praying, don't use flash photography close to worshippers, and don't eat or drink inside. The cushions set out around the temple are for kneeling to pray, not for sitting down to rest.

I'd recommend visiting in the evening – the temple looks fantastic lit up after dark, and you can combine it with the Huaxi Street Night Market right next door. Entry is free.

Traveller Tips

Come at night when the temple is lit up, and pair it with the adjacent night market.

Location

title: Cheap Drinks and Snacks at Yolo's Cafe
excerpt: A cheap and cheerful Taiwanese cafe chain named for YOLO - good wifi, plug sockets, and a black tea for as little as NT$35.
content:
Yolo's Cafe is a Taiwanese chain named after the acronym YOLO ("You Only Live Once"), with a good selection of food and beverages at very reasonable prices – a black tea can cost as little as NT$35.

The cafes are well decked out, with cool and funky styling, and are a good place to work as the WiFi is generally good and they have plug sockets at most seats.

Serving mainly sandwiches, they have toasties, bagels, toasts and also burgers and hot dogs – the German hot dog burger with cheese and the cheese croissant with beef are among the more popular picks. They also have something called a mochi crispy sandwich, which I've not tried but I'm guessing is a dessert as it's filled with red beans, matcha or sweet potato.

Drinks include milk-based coffees such as lattes and mochas, drip coffees from around the world, and of course tea, with many fruit teas, Twinings teas (their brown sugar milk tea is a favourite) and the usual green/black teas.

Yolos Cafe is one of the cheapest and best places to visit for a nice drink or snack. Just be aware some of the seating isn't the comfiest if you're planning to stay a while.

Along with Louisa, probably the best value for money cafe chain in Taipei

title: Travel Back in Time at the Lin Family Mansion
excerpt: An overlooked 19th-century mansion and garden once owned by one of Taiwan's wealthiest families — one of the best-preserved of its kind in Taipei.
content:
Often overlooked by visitors to Taipei, the Ben-Yuan Lin Family Mansion is a beautiful and tranquil property with stunning gardens.

Formerly owned by a wealthy Taiwanese businessman, this is one of the few (and probably the best) garden/mansions in Taipei that has still retained many of it's original features.

Set behind a wall, stepping into the 5 acre property is like stepping into a time machine taking you back a hundred or so years. The buildings and gardens are all in exquisite condition, with many doors, corridors and paths leading you to areas even more beautiful than the ones before.

The Banyan Shade Pond at the front of the property is the largest and most impressive of the three, with paths and bridges winding around it, and turtles, ducks and carp also enjoying the peacefulness.

Over the years, the roots of the trees have become entwined with the walls and rocks within the property, giving you an ethereal and other-worldliness feeling as you walk around, while some out-buildings and paths have been cleverly built into the surrounding landscape.

The beautiful grounds are a popular destination for wedding photography, and it's easy to see why. Stunning gardens, pavilions, terraces, ponds and buildings which would make a great backdrop for any photo.

The three-house courtyard to the east is largely a private property. Ancestors of the the original Lin Family still live there, but you can pre-book a guided tour to see this. You must book 30 minutes prior, and it is limited to 30 people at a time. The tour will be given in Chinese however.

The Lin Family Mansion is one of the most exquisitely preserved and serene properties I have visited anywhere in the world. If you only have time to visit one ancestral home in Taipei, this hidden gem would be the one I would recommend.

  • Lots to see and explore

title: Trendy and Tasty Brunches at Kuang's Bistro
excerpt: A brunch spot in Banqiao, 15 minutes from Taipei Main by MRT, in a cluster of a dozen or so brunch places worth the trip.
content:
Kuang's Bistro is located in Banqiao near a cluster of brunch and breakfast places.

Although it's a 15 minute MRT ride from Taipei Main, it's worth the journey as they provide one of the best brunches in Taipei. Even if you don't get a space here, there are at least a dozen other very good brunch options within walking distance.

Focusing on salads, panini, brioche and smørrebrød (a traditional Scandinavian open-faced sandwich), they also have some smaller bruschetta bites available. The dishes can be vegetarian, or come with a choice of meat (pork, beef, salmon, crab, duck). They're immaculately presented and taste just as good, although the salad we had was slightly on the greasy side.

The Crab Meat Brioche, served on a bed of fresh vegetables and a side of crispy thyme potatoes and a dollop of creme fraiche. It looked stunning and tasted equally as good.

Being huge avocado fans, we opted for the Avocado Salad, with lettuce, radish, tomato and black olives, and a side of warm toasted fingers. Although it was slightly greasy for our liking, all the ingredients were fresh and most importantly, the avocado was soft and delicious.

We also chose a Smoked Salmon Bruschetta to share. The Bruschetta dishes are much smaller so it's advised not to get one of these as your only dish. Simple but tasty with the salmon being the star.

The drinks also look the business, the cold drinks very refreshing and the hot ones comforting. The hot Caramel Latte and the ice Fruit Tea were both superb.

Due to its fairly remote location, Kuang's Bistro is great value for money, with many of the main dishes costing sub NT$200.

Kuang's Bistro is highly recommended if visiting Banqiao, and certainly merited a visit in it's own right!

title: Find the Surprise in Ay Chung Flour Rice Noodles
excerpt: A single-dish stall in Ximending famous for its flour rice noodles and a queue that rarely lets up. Is the wait worth it?
content:
Found within the Ximending (Ximen) district, Ay Chung is a famous and extremely popular stall that serves only one thing - Flour Rice Noodles.

It's tucked away down one of the alleys in Ximending, but it's difficult to miss as there's almost always a huge queue of people, while others hang around to consume them.

The good news is the staff have a very efficient production line, so the queue moves rapidly.

Coming in two sizes (costing NT$60 or NT$75), the noodles are very silky and the mixture runny. It's difficult to eat with the supplied plastic spoon, but the taste is deep and strong. The hint of basil adds a nice freshness to the taste.

You can also order these via Klook for only NT$54 and NT$70 respectively

Klook.com

Hidden within the mix is a surprise - salty cured pig intestines, which are very chewy and I found difficult to swallow. If you want to add a bit of spice or extra flavour, there are three condiments to choose from:

  • Pureed Garlic
  • Chilli Sauce
  • Vinegar

As there are no tables, it's advised to eat them close to the store (it's considered rude to take them away). There is a food bin to dispose of leftovers, and other bins for the bowls and spoons.

If you're in in the Ximen area and want to give a local delicacy a try, Ay Chung Flour Rice Noodles is a must visit!

title: See the History of the Taipei Story House
excerpt: Taiwan's only Tudor-style heritage building - a 1913 guesthouse turned prison turned legislator's home, now a small free museum next to the Fine Arts Museum.
content:
The Taipei Story House is a small faux-Tudor house and museum right next door to the Fine Arts Museum – and it's the only Tudor-style heritage building in Taiwan, which alone makes it an odd, interesting little detour.

It was built in 1913–1914 during the Japanese colonial era by Chen Chao-chun, a wealthy tea merchant, as a guesthouse for dignitaries and business associates. Its history since has been anything but quiet: it was used as a prison and detainment centre in the later years of Japanese rule, then became the private residence of Huang Kuo-shu, a speaker of the Legislative Yuan, in the 1950s. It was named a heritage site in 1998, restored by the Taipei Fine Arts Museum from 2000, and reopened as a small museum in 2003.

Inside, look out for the two original fireplaces and art nouveau tiles featuring natural and floral patterns. It now hosts rotating exhibitions, workshops and occasional traditional tea ceremonies, so what's actually on show will vary by the time you visit.

It's not really worth a special trip on its own, but it sits near a few other attractions worth combining it with, or you could see it as part of a walk I've devised.

title: Visit the Zones of the Collective Botanical Garden
excerpt: Officially the Future Pavilion, a leftover greenhouse from the 2010 Taipei International Flora Expo - smaller than the main Botanical Garden, but a wider range of plants indoors.
content:
The smaller of the two botanical gardens located in Taipei, the Collective Botanical Garden does however have a much wider range of plants, since it's mainly located inside, with climate controlled zones featuring flora from around the world. It's officially known as the Future Pavilion (未來館), one of the buildings left over from the 2010 Taipei International Flora Exposition, and now sits inside Xinsheng Park within the wider Taipei Expo Park – the same park that's home to Maji Square. It's also certified as a diamond-level green building, the highest tier in Taiwan's green building rating system.

The zones found inside are

  • Tropical
  • Subtropical
  • Temperate
  • Succulents
  • Alpine

As you walk through the huge greenhouse, you'll start off in the tropical climate and walk through each of the zones.

Tropical - high temperature, high humidity with mainly flora found in rain-forests.

Subtropical - Making use of Taiwan's native trees and shrubs to create a rich plant ecology.

Temperate - grasses, conifers, deciduous trees and temperate fruit trees

Succulents - Desert plants, with over 500 succulent plants including many cacti.

Alpine - plants found over 3,500 meters in altitude able to withstand cold temperatures

There's also a beautiful outdoor section devoted to native flora, with flowers, plants and a pond full of lilies.

The Collective Botanical Garden was virtually empty when I looked around, so I was able to wander around at will. With no entry cost, and hundreds of plants to see, it's certainly worthy of a visit – just be aware it's noticeably smaller than the Taipei Botanical Garden proper, and it's usually pretty quiet.

title: Visit the Beautiful Lin An Tai Ancestral House
excerpt: One of Taiwan's oldest buildings, dating to 1785 - dismantled and rebuilt at its current site after a preservation campaign that helped shape national heritage law.
content:
An exquisite and very well maintained house and gardens found in the northern part of the city, the Lin An Tai Ancestral House dates back to 1785, making it one of the oldest buildings in Taiwan. The Lin family named it "An Tai" in honour of their ancestral home, Anxi County in Fujian, and Rong Tai, the family business that paid for it.

There are five buildings within the grounds, built in the southern Fujian courtyard style with distinctive upturned swallowtail roof ridges, and you're free to explore inside the houses (although there was a wedding reception during my visit so I never got to see inside). A useful English guide to the buildings can be found here.

The beautiful landscaped gardens and pond look stunning, and there are walkways and pavilions to explore. Look out for the large weathered rocks scattered around the front courtyard too – they started out as ballast on Chinese merchant ships and were repurposed once they'd served their purpose at sea.

The house hasn't always stood here. It originally sat on Siwei Road in Da'an District, but was threatened with demolition in 1978 to make way for the widening of Dunhua South Road. The campaign to save it drew in scholars and local artists, and is widely credited as a catalyst for Taiwan's 1982 Cultural Heritage Preservation Act. The whole building was carefully dismantled and rebuilt piece by piece at its current riverside site, reopening to the public in 1987.

Although Lin An Tai Ancestral House's location is quite a walk from the closest MRT, there are a few other attractions nearby, and it's worth seeing this as part of a walk I've devised. It's free to enter, and the grounds alone are worth the trek – the 20 minute walk from the MRT is really the only downside.

Closed on Mondays and during national holidays

Free

title: Taipei Fine Arts Museum: Tickets & What's On
excerpt: Taiwan's first modern art museum, opposite Expo Park. Current exhibitions, ticket prices and how long to allow.
content:
Located just over the road from the Expo Park, the Fine Arts Museum is the best place to visit if contemporary/modern art is your thing. Opened in 1983, it became the first modern art museum in Taiwan - and is arguably still the best.

Showcasing contemporary Chinese and international art, the building itself is a striking piece of geometric art.

There are four levels, with the 2nd floor dedicated to Chinese art and sculptures, and the basement and 3rd floor rotating a number of exhibitions each year.

The collections span many art-forms and styles, from traditional paintings, sketches and sculptures, to photography, installations and multimedia works.

Click here to see their current exhibitions

The second floor is where you'll find the majority of the Taiwanese exhibitions. Works span the Japanese rule period to the present day, and include contemporary art and those in more traditional styling.

The 3rd floor also had many interesting and unique art works and sculptures, featuring both local and international artists.

Including some slightly more surreal concoctions.

During my visit, there was a great audiovisual installation in the basement that involved the use of not only sound, but light and movement.

Many people come here just to work, as there's a library in the basement and a few areas to sit.

The Fine Arts Museum is a must visit attraction for any art lovers, especially as it's ridiculously cheap to gain entry to the museum - at only NT$30.

Pros

  • Very cheap
  • Lots of interesting exhibits

Cons

  • A bit out of the way
