title: National Palace Museum: What to See & How Long to Allow
excerpt: Nearly 700,000 imperial Chinese artefacts spanning 8,000 years. Which galleries to prioritise, how to skip the queues, and how long you actually need.
content:
If it's a wealth of imperial Chinese history and cultural treasures you seek, the National Palace Museum (國立故宮博物院) in Taipei is an absolute must-visit. Housing nearly 700,000 rare artifacts spanning over 8,000 years of Chinese history—from Neolithic jade carvings to Qing Dynasty imperial porcelain—it ranks alongside the Louvre, the British Museum, and the Metropolitan Museum of Art as one of the world's premier cultural institutions.

History & Imperial Origins

The story of the National Palace Museum is as dramatic as the treasures it houses. The collection originally belonged to China's emperors and was housed within the Forbidden City in Beijing. In the 1930s, as war broke out across East Asia, the Chinese government embarked on a heroic 16-year evacuation, packing thousands of crates of priceless relics and transporting them across mountains and rivers to prevent their destruction or looting.

In 1948–1949, amidst the Chinese Civil War, nearly 3,000 crates containing the finest, rarest pieces of the imperial collection were safely transported across the Taiwan Strait to Taipei. The museum in Shilin opened its doors in 1965 to preserve and showcase these magnificent cultural treasures to the world.

Famous Masterpieces & Must-See Artifacts

Because the collection is so vast, only around 3,000 to 5,000 items can be displayed at any given time, with exhibits rotating every three to six months. However, several famous iconic treasures are almost always on display and draw visitors from across the globe:

  • The Jadeite Cabbage (翠玉白菜): Perhaps the museum's most celebrated masterpiece, this 19th-century Qing dynasty carving was crafted from a single piece of half-white, half-green jadeite. The artisan ingeniously used the natural color flaws of the jade stone to carve a vivid head of Chinese bok choy, complete with a tiny locust and katydid perched on the leaves symbolizing fertility and purity.
  • The Meat-Shaped Stone (肉形石): Carved from natural banded jasper stone, this uncanny piece of art looks precisely like a glistening, juicy piece of slow-braised Dongpo pork belly (東坡肉). The craftsman carved, polished, and stained the stone layers to mimic tender layers of fat, lean meat, and even tiny pores on the crispy rind.
  • The Mao Gong Ding (毛公鼎): A prized bronze ritual vessel from the Western Zhou Dynasty (circa 800 BCE). Inside its bowl is an intricate 500-character inscription—the longest ancient bronze inscription in existence—recording royal decrees and historical court events.
  • Ivory Dragon Balls & Carvings: Intricately carved ivory spheres containing up to 24 concentric, independently revolving inner balls carved out of a single solid piece of elephant tusk without any seams.
  • Rare Ru Ware & Imperial Porcelain: Featuring priceless sky-blue Ru kiln porcelain from the Song Dynasty—of which only around 80 intact pieces survive worldwide—as well as vibrant Ming and Qing enamel vases.

With a strictly no cameras policy in certain delicate galleries (though general non-flash photography is allowed in most areas), you can also take a virtual preview tour via Google Maps below:

Museum Architecture & Exhibit Layout

The main exhibition hall is designed in traditional northern Chinese palace style, featuring yellow-tiled roofs, green glazed cornices, and majestic archways set against the green hills of Yangmingshan in Shilin District. The main building spans four primary exhibition floors:

  • 1st Floor: Religious sculptures, furniture, special rotating exhibitions, audio guide desk, and museum gift shop.
  • 2nd Floor: Ancient Chinese ceramics, calligraphy masterpieces, classic landscape paintings, and rare books.
  • 3rd Floor: Famous jade carvings (including the Jadeite Cabbage), bronzes, jades, and decorative court objects.
  • 4th Floor: Sanxiantang Tea House offering traditional tea sets and panoramic mountain views.

Zhishan Garden & Silks Palace Dining

Adjacent to the museum building is Zhishan Garden (至善園), a peaceful 1.5-hectare classical Chinese garden constructed according to Song and Ming Dynasty landscape aesthetics. It features winding stone pathways, koi-filled ponds, wooden pavilions, and shaded bamboo groves—making it one of the finest traditional gardens in Taipei.

Click here to read about Zhishan Garden

When you get hungry, there are several dining options on-site. The most unique is Silks Palace (故宮晶華), operated by the Regent Hotel group. Located right next to the exhibition hall, Silks Palace offers a high-end imperial banquet experience featuring edible replicas of famous museum artifacts—such as a savory dish modeled after the Jadeite Cabbage and Dongpo pork crafted like the Meat-Shaped Stone!

Their official website has a useful map and exhibit guide should you wish to plan your route in advance.

Tickets, Visitor Tips & Getting There

Pros

  • World's largest and most complete collection of imperial Chinese artifacts
  • Stunning traditional palace architecture and scenic mountain backdrop
  • Includes entry to the peaceful Zhishan Garden next door

Cons

  • Not directly connected to an MRT station (requires a short 15-minute bus ride from Shilin MRT)
  • Popular galleries get very busy with tour groups during peak midday hours

Price & Tickets

Standard adult entry is NT$350 (or NT$500 with a multimedia audio guide device rental).

Click here to purchase a ticket from Klook

Tickets for the museum are also fully included in the Unlimited Taipei Fun Pass.

Opening Times

Open daily from 08:30 to 18:30 all year round. (Note: On Fridays and Saturdays, evening hours are often extended until 21:00).

Traveller Tips

  • Free English Tours: Free guided tours in English are offered daily at 10:00 and 15:00 (online booking required in advance). Alternatively, audio headphone guides can be rented in multiple languages for NT$200.
  • Locker Storage: Large bags, backpacks, cameras, and drink bottles are not permitted inside exhibition halls. Free coin-operated storage lockers (NT$10 deposit returned upon retrieval) are located near the main entrance.
  • Photography: Non-flash photography is allowed for general exhibits, but flash and video recording are strictly prohibited.
  • Beat the Crowds: Arrive right at opening time (08:30) or during late afternoon to view famous items like the Jadeite Cabbage with minimal wait times.

Location & How to Get There

By MRT & Bus: Take the Taipei Metro Red Line to Shilin MRT Station (Exit 1). Walk forward to the bus stop on Zhongzheng Road and take bus R30 (Red 30), 255, 304, or 815 directly to the National Palace Museum. Bus journey time is approximately 15 minutes.

Click here for a full list of bus services to the National Palace Museum

This is also one of the featured stops on the official Taipei Sightseeing Bus tour.

Alternatively, YouBike stations are available nearby (such as this location near the museum grounds).

title: Heavenly Desserts at Mr Brownie
excerpt: What might be Taipei's best brownies - moist and gooey with a big range of toppings, from banana to cotton candy, at two central branches.
content:
Mr Brownie (or Mr Brownies) is the best place in Taipei for a proper brownie fix. Moist, gooey and thoroughly chocolatey, with a huge range of toppings to choose from – expect flavours like banana, cotton candy and strawberry alongside the classics.

Beyond the brownies themselves, they do a wide range of brownie-adjacent treats – crêpes, ice cream and drinks all built around the same base. If you're after something savoury instead, the cheesy toasties are also worth trying.

Both branches are small, and reviews mention they can get crowded and a little slow to serve at peak times – worth bearing in mind if you're in a rush, but not enough to put you off. Brownie heaven, basically.

Traveller Tips

Buy a selection of six brownies for a nice saving.

Locations

📍 Ximen Branch (closest MRT: Ximen blue line exit 1)
Dunhua Branch (closest MRT: Zhongxiao Dunhua blue line exit 2)

title: Grab some Grub at Ningxia Night Market
excerpt: One of Taipei's oldest and most compact night markets, with 200+ stalls packed into 170 metres, four Michelin-recommended food stalls, and a surprise 2019 visit from Will Smith.
content:
One of the smallest night markets in Taipei, Ningxia Night Market tends to specialise in food. It's a compact pedestrian street just 170 metres long, yet somehow crams in over 200 stalls, tracing its roots back to Jiancheng Roundabout (建成圓環) a short walk away – a recreational park built by the Japanese colonial government in 1908 that drew food vendors from the start. When the roundabout later declined after a fire, Ningxia Road took over as the neighbourhood's go-to night market. Because of its size, it's a night market not visited by many tourists but is very popular with the locals.

In fact, because it doesn't tend to attract huge crowds, Ningxia Night Market was the one Ang Lee chose to bring Will Smith to in October 2019, while the pair were in Taipei promoting their film Gemini Man. Smith tried sesame oil chicken and a papaya and watermelon milk, declared bitter melon juice "不好喝" (not tasty) in Mandarin, and even had a go on one of the BB gun balloon game stalls.

All the locals favourite food can be found here, such as oyster omelettes, fried chicken, or the braised pork and rice, it's a night market you should visit if you want have a more authentic foody experience.

There are four Michelin recommended food stalls found within Ningxia Night Market, locations of which can be found below:

Coloured dots match the pins on the map below.

  • Fang Chia Shredded Chicken on the Rice

    Shredded chicken rice and caramelized onions

  • Liu Yu Zi

    Deep-fried taro balls with choice of fillings including egg yolk & pork floss

  • Rong's Pork Liver

    Pig liver with egg yolk, mushrooms and sticky rice balls wrapped in bamboo leaves

  • Yuan Huan Pien Oyster Egg Omelette

    Omelette with oysters drizzled in sweet homemade hot sauce

Ningxia Night Market does still has a few other stalls selling crafts and clothes, plus games that you'll find at other night market, but it's the food you should come here for. It was also one of the first night markets in Taipei to go eco-friendly, banning disposable styrofoam dishes in favour of reusable stainless steel chopsticks and bowls, and investing around NT$14 million in underground grease-trap and waste collection systems to cut down on the mess and smell that can plague older markets.

Traveller Tips

Come to this night market if you're mainly after food. It's a compact space so queues can build up around the most popular stalls, but the variety on offer more than makes up for it.

Location

📍 Closest MRTs:
Shuanglian Station (red line - exit 1)
Zhongshan Station (red line - exit 5)

title: Tonghua Night Market - The Locals' Favourite Night Market
excerpt: Tonghua Night Market has five Michelin-recommended food stalls — where to find each one, and what else is worth eating.
content:
As night markets go, Tonghua Night Market certainly isn't the biggest but its still got a very wide selection of food and stalls.

Known as Linjiang Street Night Market to the locals, it's the most south-easterly night market in Taipei, although it's easily accessible via the MRT and not too far from Taipei 101. Most locals rate this as their favourite night market in Taipei because it still offers a good variety of quality food.

Tonghua Night Market also has five food stalls that are recommended by the Michelin Guide (listed below).

With one long road containing most of the stalls, it has a cross-roads in the middle with some small restaurants. If you come during a week night, you'll find it far less crowded than Shilin Night Market, and you will generally find items much cheaper than Shilin.

Boasting a large variety of local food stalls and restaurants, there's everything you would expect from a night market.

Shops selling clothes, trainers, jewellery and even some artwork.

There are 5 food stands recommended by the Michelin Guide. Four of these are recognised in the Bib Gourmand category, a special award for high quality yet cheap dishes.

Coloured dots match the pins on the map below.

  • Bib GourmandLiang Chi Lu Wei

    Dishes include braised cow stomach, duck wings, seaweed, and dried tofu

  • Bib GourmandLo Chi Hsiao Chao

    Stir-fried dishes including fried lamb, beef, and clams

  • Bib GourmandTien Hsiang Stinky Tofu

    Fried and very pungent tofu

  • Bib GourmandYu Pin Yuan Iced and Hot Tangyuan

    Hot and sweet glutinous rice dumplings served on shaved ice

  • Golden Fried Chicken

    Tempura chicken fried to order

Alternatively, if you're just looking for snacks, there are loads of stands selling just that. The deep fried quail eggs for instance, with 6 to a stick, just cover them with a sauce to your liking and devour.

The edamame beans, coated in spices and oils will get your fingers very messy and are probably best eaten elsewhere.

There are some really good dessert places at Tonghua Night Market too. Why not try some Hong Kong style bubble waffles?

Also amongst the many stalls you'll find a great shaved ice place, selling one of the nicest mango shaved ices in Taipei, with sticky rice balls filled with peanut powder and sesame. Just one of many dishes to try.

As per with other night markets, there are massages and an abundance of games to play.

While Tonghua Night Market doesn't quite have the wow factor that Shilin has, it still has enough stalls to keep you engaged. If you want to avoid the hustle and bustle of busier night markets, Tonghua is a great night market to visit.

Pros

  • Not as busy as some night markets
  • Good variety of food

Cons

  • Not that big

Traveller Tips

Why not come here after visiting Taipei 101

Location

📍 Closest MRT: Xinyi Anhe Station (red line - exits 3 or 4)

title: Jazz, Funk and Blues at Sappho Live Jazz
excerpt: A basement jazz, funk and blues venue in Xinyi that's picked up the slack since Brown Sugar closed. Usually an entrance fee.
content:
With the closure of Brown Sugar, watching some good live jazz in Taipei is becoming increasingly difficult, but Sappho Live Jazz is one place you can go that usually delivers.

Located in Xinyi, after walking down some steps into the basement, you'll usually need to pay an entrance fee between NT$100-300 before you can enter, although if there's no band playing it's free.

They don't just play jazz here though, as the live music can take the form of blues, funk or even ska and reggae. Bands usually start at 21:30 although it's best to get there 30 minutes before to have a better chance at getting a good seat, especially at the weekend.

Sappho Jazz has a cosy feel with a nice ambience. Once the band kicks off, the atmosphere will grow into one of the most electric in Taipei, especially when there's a popular act playing. Dancing in front of the stage is also welcomed.

So far we've seen a ska/funk band from Tainan, and a four-piece jazz band. Both were great at turning on the style and getting the crowd involved.

They'll put up the current month's acts of their upcoming bands on their website. On Mondays they're closed and Tuesdays are normally reserved for the house band (and it's free to enter), but every other night they'll have a different band on.

There is some bar food available, although we've yet to try any. The drinks consist of beers, spirits, wines and cocktails, although I've had much better cocktails elsewhere.

However, for music and atmosphere, Sappho Jazz delivers in buckets.

Pros

  • The best jazz venue in Taipei
  • Great atmosphere

Cons

  • Cocktails not great

Price: $$$

Level of English: Good (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

Check out which bands are playing from their events page.

Location

📍 Closest MRT: Xinyi Anhe Station (red line)

title: Amazing Brunches at The Antipodean Specialty Coffee
excerpt: An Aussie-style brunch spot with what might be the best western breakfast in Taipei, now with several branches beyond its original in Neihu.
content:
The Antipodean Specialty Coffee is a great Aussie-style breakfast/brunch restaurant which serves (IMHO) the best western breakfast in Taipei.

The original branch, a little way out from the centre of Taipei in Neihu, has proved so popular that they've since opened another one closer to the city.

Although not actually run by Aussies, the Taiwanese owners spent many years in Melbourne, Australia and grew to love the delicious breakfasts and brunches the city had to offer.

With it's modern a clean interior The Antipodean has a relaxed ambience and very friendly and polite waiters who speak good English.

The Antipodean Specialty Coffee's prize dish is their Queen's Breakfast Platter.

A huge board that's shared between two, it comes with 'the works'. Salmon, halloumi, 2 eggs, avocado, mushroom, ham, baked beans, toast, cherry tomatoes and two greek yogurt muesli topped with seasonal fruits.

Definitely a dish fit for a queen, and one of the best breakfast plates we've had anywhere in the world. At NT$890, it's one of the most expensive breakfast's we've had too, but it's easily enough for two to feast on.

Actually, we did opt for their Crispy Hash Browns and Scrambled Eggs too, as these are the best we've had in Taipei.

If you don't like some of the ingredients on the Queen's Breakfast, you can even make your own 'brekkie', choosing any of the ingredients (and more) from this dish.

If sharing isn't your thing, then The Antipodean Big Breakfast is another great dish. Served with delicious homemade pork sausages, bacon, the aforementioned hash browns, mushrooms, scrambled eggs and baked beans. The best fried breakfast plate in Taipei!

Another stunning looking and tasting dish is their Smoked Salmon Avo Toast, with Norwegian smoked salmon, avocado mash on a thick cut of grilled sourdough toast, with baby leaves and shredded parmesan.

We've yet to try their Bircher Muesli or Acai Bowls, but we had to try their Wild Berry Porridge, as porridge is something you don't often find in Taipei.

It's another stunning looking and tasting dish. The fruits will change depending on the season, but there's a great variety of these, along with nuts, seeds and raisins. The warm porridge, with a sprinkling of cinnamon, tastes divine and is easily enough to fill you up.

You can probably tell we've been here a few times now. One more dish that I would thoroughly recommend, even if you're not a vegetarian, is their Avocado Breakfast Plate.

With grilled halloumi, sauteed mushrooms, delicious cherry tomatoes and their trademark scrambled eggs on some grilled sourdough bread. Many of our favourite things all on one plate!

They of course have a great selection of coffees here too. Almost any type of espresso based coffee, and many single origin coffees from Africa and South American. Tea Lattes, Hot Chocolates and Lemonades too.

Their tea pots can be shared between two, and come served in a very cute tea set which can also be purchased.

The Antipodean Specialty Coffee delivers on all fronts and is easily worth the short journey to Neihu to experience their incredible plates. Even though it's location isn't the best, brunch hours are still very busy so I would strongly recommend booking a table here.

We have yet to find a better breakfast/brunch spot in Taipei. Without question, a Taipei Travel Geek Top Pick!

Pros

  • Probably the best western breakfast in Taipei
  • Great service

Cons

  • Quite Expensive
  • Short ride on the brown line required

Price: $$$

Level of English: Very Good (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

Booking a table here is recommended and quite straight-forward. Breakfasts are served until 16:30.

The Hippest Brunches in Taipei

title: Watch an Artist at Work at Treasure Hill
excerpt: A hillside artists’ village of rickety huts and studios above the river, with some of the best city views in Taipei. Free to wander.
content:
If you don't mind steps, Treasure Hill Artists' Village is a culturally rich little wonderland set on the side of a hill, offering great views of the city at it's peak.

With dozens of huts and rickety buildings located on the different levels of the hill, many of which are studios to the local and international artists who work and live here.

The maze-like steep paths and alleys are decorated with street art and installations, with a surprise seemingly around each and every corner.

If you peer through some of the windows, you can even see some of the artists busy with their creations.

There are usually a few exhibitions on show, some being free, while others requiring a small entry fee. A list of the current ones can be found here.

If you do manage to make it to the top of the village, you'll be rewarded with some great views of the city.

There are a few cafes located in the artists village, although when we visited it was difficult to get a table. There are however one or two small shops selling drinks and snacks.

Treasure Hill offers a unique experience in Taipei, and is a great place to walk around and explore. It doesn't get overly busy here, especially if you visit during a weekday.

Pros

  • Cultural experience like no other

Cons

  • The few cafes on site get busy
  • Many steps to climb

Price

Free to walk around. Some galleries have an entrance fee.

Opening Hours

11:00 – 21:00

Closed on Mondays

Traveller Tips

Check out which exhibitions and art galleries are currently running by visiting their events page.

If you're visiting the Water Park first, then you can gain entry to Treasure Hill from here. This is the best way to save your legs since you'll enter at the peak and walk downhill.

Not suitable for the elderly, as there are many steps to climb.

Treasure Hill Location

📍 Closest MRT: Gonguan Station (green line - exit 1)

title: Songshan Cultural and Creative Park: Full Guide
excerpt: A Japanese-era tobacco factory turned cultural hub: galleries, design shops, a baroque garden and the Eslite flagship. What to see and how long to allow.
content:
Songshan Cultural and Creative Park is another great place to walk around and enjoy the outdoor and indoor spaces. Formally a Japanese built tobacco factory, it has since been converted into a cultural hub packed with galleries, exhibitions, design spaces and shops.

Also found within the park is a large pond area, a baroque garden and the Eslite Spectrum Mall.

Although there is plenty to see here during the week, it's best to visit over a weekend, when there are usually markets selling gifts and food, or other themed events.

The Songshan Cultural and Creative Park is comprised of the following areas:

Tobacco Factory

In the centre of the cultural park is the Tobacco Factory building. A huge building with 2 floors and many long corridors leading to spaces filled with cafes and craft shops.

Also found within the Tobacco Factory is the Taiwan Design Museum, with many rooms dedicated to showcasing some of the best local and international designs. Most of the exhibitions here do require payment.

Click here for the current exhibitions at the Taiwan Design Museum

A couple of other nice areas found within the Tobacco Factory are Not Just Library, which has over 20,000 books on modern and contemporary design, and Design Pin, a craft shop selling exquisitely designed crafts that have won prizes both in Taiwan and overseas.

The Tobacco Factory hosts a number of annual art and design events, including the Taipei Illustration Fair, which is one of the best annual art exhibitions in Taipei.

Baroque Garden

The Tobacco Factory surrounds a small but beautiful baroque garden. At it's centre, a large fountain and many garden ornaments.

As the garden is completely surrounded by the walls of the tobacco factory, it feels cut off from the city, giving it a certain 'secret garden' feel.

Warehouses

Five large warehouses will often have temporary exhibitions, many of which tend to focus on art or design, but there will usually be one or two based on cartoons or anime.

The exhibitions tend to stay for around a month each, with some being free and other costing up to NT$400. There are usually a couple that are worth visiting at any one time.

Click here for a list of current exhibitions within the warehouses

Pond and Seating Area

Towards the east of the park is a large pond with plenty of outdoor shaded seating. Drinks can be purchased from nearby cafes or vending machines. The pond attracts a large number of birds and frogs, while you'll usually find the resident ducks waddling around.

Eslite Spectrum Mall

Dominating the skyline around the park is the Eslite Spectrum Mall.

The upper-most floors are reserved for guests staying at the Eslite Hotel, but the first few floors are filled with shops, with a very good food court in the basement. The crafts shops especially are worth looking around, with some places giving you an opportunity to make your own jewellery or other gifts.

Also located in the basement is the Eslite Art House, probably the best independent cinema in Taipei, and the Eslite Performance Hall, which hosts some fine jazz and classical concerts.

The third floor of the building is also worth a visit, as there is a large bookstore (of which Eslite is famous for) with many books and magazines in the English language.

The Songshan Cultural and Creative Park has many delightful cafes, shops and creative spaces to keep your visit enlightened and inspired. Even if you have little interest in art or design, it's still a great place to walk around.

  • Nice area to walk around
  • Lots of stalls and exhibitions
  • Eslite building adds a lot more value

Cons

  • No convenience stores

Free

There are usually a few exhibitions and art galleries at any one time. For a list, visit their events page.

Visit the Sun Yat-Sen Memorial Hall after, just 10 minutes walk from the cultural park.

If you enjoyed it here, why not check out the Huashan 1914 Creative Park too?!

There are some nice cafes and shops if you leave the park to the east (near the lake).

title: Huashan 1914 Creative Park: What's On & Full Guide
excerpt: A 1914 wine factory turned arts complex: galleries, craft shops, an independent cinema and live music. What is on, and how to get there.
content:
Built in 1914, Huashan 1914 Creative Park is an old wine factory and grounds which was converted into a creative space in 2007.

A number of the old factory warehouses now hold temporary art or other exhibitions, while the park is also home to craft shops, an independent cinema and live music/theatre venues.

The park is a great place to walk around, especially if the sun isn't too intense and the rain stays at bay. The 4 hectare area has been well converted, seamlessly mixing the modern areas with the traditional buildings.

There are a few nice cafes and restaurants on the site should you need to escape the heat for a while. Trio is a cosy cafe located at the front of the park with some nice outdoor seating, while Piccola Botega is a nice Italian.

You'll also find many street performers as you walk around the park, with dancers, statuesque characters and comedy routines that kids will love.

A map of Huashan 1914 Creative Park

Park Areas

Huashan 1914 Creative Park has two park areas, a small one at the front and a large open park space at the rear.

Both parks will have special events during most weekends and sometimes during the week. These include markets, concerts, dance shows or promotional events advertising trips abroad or beverages.

The quality of these does vary a lot, but they're all free.

Click here to see what events are on at Huashan

Warehouses

Several of the old wine production buildings at Huashan 1914 Creative Park have been converted into warehouses and show a number of great exhibitions every year.

These are marked as 2, 3, 6, 15 on the map above

There are normally between two and five exhibitions at any one time in the warehouses. Sometimes they're free to enter, but the better ones will cost between NT$200 and NT$400.

They're usually art or character based, sometimes from world renowned artists. Many of the best exhibitions I've visited in Taipei have been at Huashan, so it's worth checking out to see if there's anything good showing.

Click here to their current exhibitions

Both the Jason Freeny toy anatomy and the exhibit of miniature works by Japanese artist Tatsuya Tanaka were outstanding.

The Art of the Brick, an excellent exhibition created entirely by lego, was also at Huashan in 2017.

Craft Shops

There are a number of shops selling unique and interesting merchandise. Many are pop-up style shops that will come and go, but most sell highly original and well crafted gifts and accessories.

Click here to see the current pop-up shops at Huashan

A special mention goes to the Wooderful Life store, a Taiwanese craft shop selling magical wooden toys. It also has a play area for kids to construct (and destruct) their own creations.

Cinema, Theatre and Music Venue

One of the best independent cinemas in Taipei is located in Huashan 1914 Creative Park. The Spot shows films from around the world, and hosts a number of film festivals each year.

Click to find out what's on at the The Spot Huashan

Making good use of one of the large warehouses at Huashan, which has been converted into one of the best music venues in the city. Legacy hosts some of the biggest indie and rock acts in Taipei, with the likes of Mumford & Sons and Foster the People playing here.

Click to find out what's on at Legacy

Another venue found here is the Umay Theatre, a small but very functional theatre which mainly shows Taiwanese plays and dance acts.

Click to find out what's on at the Umay Theatre

Huashan 1914 Creative Park is one of the best spots in Taipei to walk around. If you come here during the week, it's usually not too busy, although you'll miss out on the weekend events in the park areas. Weekends can be crowded, but there's always quieter places within the park you can escape to.

Virtual Tour

Pros

  • Many things to do here
  • Has some great exhibitions and events

Cons

  • Toilets not so nice

Traveller Tips

Try to time your visit with an exhibition you may be interested in. A list of them can be found here.

Just over the road from Huashan is the Technology District, with hundreds of shops selling computer equipment and electronic devices.

If you enjoyed it here, why not check out the Songshan Cultural and Creative Park too?!

Huashan 1914 Creative Park Location

title: Taipei Zoo - Guide and Tips to Make the Most of Your Visit
excerpt: Full guide, including map, tips on when to visit, and suggested route for the Maokong Gondola
content:
Taipei Zoo is the largest and one of the best zoos in Asia. Not only does it have a huge variety of animals, the zoo has been well designed and offers many nice walking areas.

Most importantly, the animals seem well looked after and their enclosures are large and suitably made to match their native habitats.

Costing only NT$100 for entry, it's a cheap but fantastic day out which you can combine with a trip on the Maokong Gondola, a cable car ride high into the mountains. One of the stations for this is inside the zoo.

Tip: Try to visit Taipei Zoo from Tuesday to Friday. See my Traveller Tips section below for reasons.

The newest addition to Taipei Zoo, the Pangolin Dome, is a NT$390 million, 1.5 hectare structure filled with the flora and fauna of rainforests.

With a total area of 165 hectares, if you intend to visit all of the enclosures, it would take you most of the day. A shuttle train is available to quickly take you to another area, including the Maokong Gondola station.

Tickets can be purchased at the entrance to the zoo. However, you can use your EasyCard directly at the turnstile, which in turn will also give you a discount if you decide to ride in a Maokong Gondola on the same day.

Free entry to the zoo also comes as part of the Taipei Fun Pass.

Taipei Zoo Map

Zones

I've grouped the zones into 3 areas. North (near the main entrance), Centre and South.

North

The area closest to the main entrance is the best place to take children, as it features a children's zoo where they can interact with the animals, an insectarium, and also the koala house.

If you're interested in seeing some of Taiwan's native animals, the Formosan Animal Area includes their elusive Black Bears, Formosan Rock Macaques and Wild Boars.

The black bears are especially endearing to Taiwanese people, and were voted the wildlife most representative of Taiwan by the general public.

The Children's Zoo features farm animals, alpacas, ponies, camels and meerkats. Some enclosures allow you to walk through them, while others will give you a chance to pet the animals.

Next to this is the Koala House, featuring a couple of the cuddly marsupials.

Don't miss out on the Flamingos and White Handed Gibbons found in the centre of the north area.

Two of the zones I would only recommend if you have a keen interest in these areas:

Insect Valley is which is probably the most forgotten and neglected part of the zoo, although it does feature an Insectarium with a nice butterfly walk-through.

The Animal Ecology and Dinosaur Museum is a large 2-floor building which has many stuffed animals, a nice dinosaur section and an area detailing the history of Taipei Zoo. This costs extra to enter (NT$20).

Klook.com

Centre

The Tropical Rainforest zone is one of the best areas to visit in Taipei Zoo, while the Giant Panda House is a must-visit.

The Giant Panda House is the first place you should visit in this section (the earlier you go, the quieter it will be).

If you're visiting over a weekend, you will need to get a free panda-visiting ticket at the zoo entrance. This will give you a fixed time slot to see them, which isn't ideal. If you're here in the week, you can normally see them without issues (if they decide to show themselves!).

There is both an indoor and outdoor section, and of course a gift shop selling all things panda.

The Tropical Rainforest zone features the brand new Pangolin Dome, which in my opinion is the best attraction in the zoo.

The glass dome structure, which gets its name from the shape of the endangered pangolin, features a huge water tank filled with fish, many tropical birds flying around, a nocturnal animals section, and many mammals including monkeys and the star attractions - two-toed sloths.

The remaining areas of the rainforest zone are also great, and includes Orangutans, Indian Elephants, Malayan Tapirs and Bengal Tigers. Also look out of the largest flower in the world, the Rafflesia Arnoldii, which can grow to be 3 feet across!

When you leave this area to the south, there's a nice Garden area.

Next you'll walk past the Desert zone, which features camels and some wild asses.

The Australian zone is probably the most disappointing in the zoo. I honestly don't think they have kangaroos anymore, while the koalas are best viewed in the koala house. There are some Cassowarys here (similar to emus). I'd give this a miss however.

South

The Africa Animal zone features many star attractions, while the Bird World has a huge netted aviary with many species of birds.

Many of the enclosures in the African Animals zone are very large, which is obviously great for the animals, but you'll sometimes only get to view them from a distance.

Taipei Zoo has all the main African beasts - Elephants, Hippos, Rhinos, Giraffes, Lions, Zebra, Gorillas and other primates can all be found here.

The Temperate Zone has Bison, a Brown Bear and some cute Red Pandas. Many of the animals in this zone, however, were either hiding or on holiday.

This area also includes the Penguin House, which was a bit of a disappointment during my visit as the penguins weren't very active. It's a shame they don't give you feeding hours as I'm sure it would be great during these times.

There are two types of penguin here. The King and Jackass penguins.

The Reptile & Amphibian House was actually the busiest area of the entire zoo, partly because it's relatively small, but also because of the specimens they have here. These include many lizards, frogs and snakes, including a huge Boa Constrictor.

Outside this, you'll also find an Aldabra Giant Tortoise, the largest tortoises in the world. I could almost feel the ground vibrating.

Finally, Bird World is a huge netted space you can walk around, with birds flying, eating, roaming, and doing whatever else birds do. With two sections, it includes many species of Flamingos, Pelicans, Peafowl, Ibises, Cranes and almost anything else with wings!

Fruit and feeding bowls are found throughout, to encourage birds closer to the walkway.

Also found near Bird World is one of the Taipei Zoo Shuttle Train Stations.

Shuttle Train

The Taipei Zoo Shuttle Train is a quick way to travel between the zones in the north and south. It also travels to the Maokong Gondola South Station.

There are 3 stations found in Taipei Zoo:

  • Koala House
  • Maokong Gondola South Station
  • Bird World

The Maokong Gondola South Station is closed on Mondays

It costs only NT$5 per ride, which is easiest to pay with your EasyCard.

It travels in an anticlockwise direction only, so if you wish to travel from Bird World to the Maokong Gondola South Station, you'll need to stay on it when you arrive at the Koala House.

Food & Drink

There are many vending machines and free water fountains found throughout the zoo.

Near the entrance is a convenience store and a McDonalds. However, the best food areas are near the Desert and African Animals zones (both on the main walkway about 3 minutes from each other).

These include Ireland's Potato (honestly), Street Churros and Mos Burger, along with ice creams and drinks.

There are a few other huts selling snacks and drinks around the zoo.

Suggested Route for Gondola

If you plan on taking advantage of the Maokong Gondola ride after a visit to Taipei Zoo, I would recommend visiting the following zones in this order.

  1. Formosan Animals
  2. Children's Zoo
  3. Koala House
  4. Giant Panda House
  5. Tropical Rainforest
  6. African Animals
  7. Temperate Zone
  8. Bird World

Then catch the Shuttle Train from Bird World to the Maokong Gondola South Station.

Of course you could visit more/less zones dependant on your time available, but this is the most convenient order to see them. This would take about 5 hours.

Tip: You could instead take the Maokong Gondola to the South Station when you arrive at the zoo, and do the above in reverse. This will mean you'll mainly be walking downhill. You will also still get your discount for the gondola.

Virtual Tour

Pros

  • Very large and good selection of animals
  • Animals seem content and well looked after
  • Very cheap

Cons

  • Gets very busy, especially during weekend
  • Some attractions closed on Mondays

Prices

You can pay for tickets with an EasyCard. General EasyCard users get an automatic NT$20 discount on weekdays if transferring to the Maokong Gondola on the same day.

  • Adults: NT$100
  • Taipei City Residents: NT$60 (with valid ID)
  • Discount Fares: NT$50
    • Students with valid ID
    • Foreign students with an International Student Identity Card (ISIC)
  • Preschool children: Free
  • Seniors (65+): Free (valid for domestic seniors and domestic seniors with Taipei City resident senior cards)
  • Handicapped (with certification): Free

Internal Shuttle Train

  • Single Ride: NT$5
  • Preschool children: Free
  • Handicapped (with certification): Free

Animal Ecology and Dinosaur Museum

  • Adults: NT$20
  • Discount Prices: NT$10

Klook Deals

You can also purchase combo tickets for both the Zoo and Maokong Gondola from Klook

Klook.com

Opening Times

09:00 to 17:00 daily (Last entry 16:00)

Some enclosures are closed on Mondays

This rotational Monday closure schedule affects the indoor exhibits, which includes the Giant Panda House, the Penguin House, the Pangolin Dome, and the Amphibian & Reptile House.

Closed on Chinese New Year's Eve

Traveller Tips

Definitely try to avoid weekends as it gets very busy, especially the panda enclosure.

I would also avoid Mondays. Enclosures are sometimes closed during this day. For instance, the panda house is closed during the first Monday of each month. Also, the Gondola Shuttle Train is closed every Monday (and the Moakong Gondola itself if often closed on a Monday too).

If you have to visit over a weekend, I would recommend arriving early and getting a free panda-visiting ticket from the zoo entrance, which will give you a time to visit the house.

Smoking is not allowed anywhere within the zoo.

Take an umbrella and mosquito spray.

Location & Getting There

Taipei Zoo is accessible from the MRT. If you're travelling from Taipei Main Station, just take the Blue line to Zhongxiao Fuxing MRT station and change to the Brown line. Take the MRT that travels south to Taipei Zoo and it's the final stop after a 20 minute ride.

📍 Closest MRT: Taipei Zoo Station (end of brown line - exit 1)

title: Fine Dining at Saffron Fine Indian Cuisine
excerpt: Michelin Bib Gourmand North Indian food in Tianmu - aromatic curries, tandoori and fresh naan, worth the trip even if you're not staying nearby.
content:
Saffron is a great option if you happen to find yourself in Tianmu, in the northern part of Taipei – and it's earned a Michelin Guide Bib Gourmand for doing it well. The restaurant leans North Indian, with unique spice blends and a couple of signatures worth ordering specifically: murgh Nawabi (chicken curry) and gosht Lahori (mutton curry), both made with meat charred in the tandoor. The masala lamb shank, tandoori chicken and kebabs also come recommended, alongside the usual naan and saffron rice, with roti as an alternative.

The dining room has a genuine fine-dining feel – terracotta floors, textured walls, burgundy lanterns and dark wood furniture – with elegant cutlery and plating to match. It's rated 4.5 stars on OpenTable for consistent cooking and warm service.

It's a fair way from any MRT station, so it's really one for those already staying up that end of the city, or willing to make the trip for Michelin-recognised North Indian food. Expect to pay accordingly – this isn't a cheap meal, but the naan bread alone might be some of the best in Taipei.

Traveller Tips

The naan bread is some of the best in Taipei.

Location

📍 Closest MRT: Mingde (red line)

title: Tajine Moroccan - Authentic Moroccan Meals
content:
Tajine Moroccan is one of only a handful of Moroccan restaurants in Taipei, but it's also one of the best.

The owner and chef of Tajine Moroccan is himself Moroccan, and it shows in the authenticity of the dishes. Specialising in tajines, they come served with a choice of either saffron rice, couscous or pitta bread.

Since lamb is the meat often associated with Moroccan food, I had to try the Traditional Lamb Tajine. My girlfriend, being a seafood lover chose the Lemon Seafood Tajine.

The lamb meat must have been stewed for some time, as it was very tender. I also loved the soft potatoes in my tajine and the kick from the spices.

The prawns and fish in the seafood tajine were also perfectly cooked and tasted very fresh. The restaurant no doubt benefits from the Taipei fish market, which isn't too far from the Songshan restaurant.

The warm pitta bread and couscous were a perfect accompaniment to the tajines, allowing us to soak up the delicious sauces.

We paid NT$120 each to get a drink and dessert, which is especially worth getting if you want a drink, as these cost at least this amount on their own. We chose the Moroccan Mint Tea and Mint Lemon Juice.

For desserts, we chose the Orange Blossom Yogurt and Almond Cake. While they were both quite small, they were both delicious.

In fact, everything we tried at Tajine Moroccan was delicious. We've yet to try another Moroccan restaurant in Taipei so I cannot compare this to others. It will be tough to top this one though. The owner and his Taiwanese wife were perfect hosts, and the meal we had was authentic and first rate.

Pros

  • Authentic Moroccan food
  • Friendly service

Cons

  • Not many seats in the restaurant

Price: $$

Level of English: Good (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

Great value lunch menu available during the week (see menu section)

Tajine Moroccan Location

📍 Da-an Branch (Closest MRT: Xinyi Anhe Station)

title: Matcha Saro - Green Tea Desserts to Savour
excerpt: A matcha dessert chain with branches across Taipei's mall food halls, serving Taiwanese-Japanese green tea sweets.
content:
108 Matcha Saro (一〇八抹茶茶廊) started life in 2013 as a passion project among friends in Asahikawa, Hokkaido, before matcha dessert expert Yamamoto-san brought the brand to Taiwan in 2014. It's since become a fixture in Taipei's shopping mall food halls, with several branches serving up its Kyoto-sourced matcha desserts and ice-cream.

As the name suggests, most of the menu is flavoured with matcha (green tea), a favourite among locals, though hojicha (roasted tea) versions show up too.

There are many different ice-creams to choose from (all containing matcha of course), with red beans, jellies and other delights carefully placed inside or on top.

Their other speciality is the matcha pancake – really an imagawayaki, a Japanese filled cake cooked in a special mould rather than a flat pancake, warm and stuffed with matcha custard or red bean. They're all freshly made and ooze goodness.

Matcha Saro is a must for addicts of green tea. It's slightly on the expensive side and the English level among staff is low (though the menu does have English on it), but they deliver on quality and flavour across all three of their locations.

Traveller Tips

The imagawayaki pancakes are a must!

Locations

📍 Taipei Main Q Square Basement (Closest MRT: Taipei Main)
Xinyi Eslite (Closest MRT: Taipei City Hall)
Shilin Mall Basement (Closest MRT: Mingde)

title: Chiang Kai-Shek Memorial Hall: What to See & Guard Times
excerpt: The changing of the guard times, what to see across Liberty Square, and how long to allow. Free to enter, and one of the few Taipei sights worth timing.
content:
The Chiang Kai-Shek Memorial Hall is a shrine to the former President of the Republic of China.

Situated within Liberty Square, a huge open expanse covering over 24 hectares, it also boasts the National Performance Halls, along with the Gate of Integrity and some beautiful gardens and trails.

Two ceremonies are performed on the Memorial Hall site. Both the Changing of the Guards and the Flag Ceremony come highly recommended.

Chiang Kai-Shek

Chiang Kai-Shek was a Chinese military leader and politician who served as the leader of mainland China between 1928 and 1949, and then of Taiwan until his death in 1975.

A highly divisive figure in Taiwan, Chiang Kai-Shek is both hated and revered here.

On the one hand, he helped China overcome the Japanese threat in 1945. But his authoritative rule spanning almost 40 years (known as the 'white terror'), plus his apparent role in the 28 February massacre, have left many with a very bitter taste in their mouth.

Memorial Hall

The huge memorial hall was erected in Chiang Kai-Shek's honour a year after his death, in 1976. Constructed using mainly concrete and marble, the 89 steps leading up to the Bronze Statue Hall represent the number of years he was alive.

The hall features a large statue of the former leader and is guarded by two military personnel.

Changing of the Guards

Every hour between 09:00 and 17:00, the changing of the guards ceremony will take place. The current guards, who have been stood completely motionless for the previous hour, will be replaced by two new guards (much to their relief!).

If you come over the weekend, it is recommended to arrive at least 15 minutes prior to the ceremony, otherwise you'll have to watch it over the crowds. It will be much more manageable during the week however.

While the changing of the guard ceremonies at the Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall and the Martyr's Shrine are also highly accomplished spectacles, I believe the best military personnel are saved for the ones here. The one-handed rifle spinning routine is especially impressive.

Within the base of the Memorial Hall are a number of exhibition rooms, including a museum documenting the history of Chiang Kai-Shek.

The museum has several rooms, each focusing on different aspects of Chiang Kai-Shek's life, including his ascension to power and his presidency in Taiwan.

There are many of Chiang Kai-Shek's possessions found here, including furniture and even a couple of the Cadillac's he owned.

There is also a reconstruction of his office, complete with original desk and chairs.

Also found within the memorial hall are four exhibition halls.

Three of them can be found on the ground floor, and usually have some great exhibits. They're usually free to enter, and will have both local and international artwork.

You will have to pay for entry into some of the more recognised artist's work however. Recent exhibitions here have included Andy Warhol and Japanese anime from Studio Ghibli.

Click here to see the current exhibitions within the Chiang Kai-Shek Memorial Hall

Performance Halls

Two large performance halls face each other on either side of Liberty Square.

The National Theatre and National Concert Hall, collectively known as NTCH, are two striking buildings that share very similar architectural aesthetics.

Featuring red pillars and classic pagoda-style roofs, both are free to enter and have some galleries, cafes and gift shops inside. The National Concert Hall also has a branch of Chun Shui Tang, the brand that created the first Bubble Tea.

NTCH are two of the best venues in Taipei for watching international music, theatre and dance acts.

The National Concert Hall is the music venue, hosting classical, jazz, choirs and traditional Taiwanese concerts. It boasts a huge pipe organ, which was the largest in Asia for a number of years.

The National Theatre shows theatrical and dance performances, with Taiwan's world famous contemporary dance group Cloud Gate often performing. It also hosts some world class ballet productions, with the St. Petersburg ballet recently performing here.

The halls also have an experimental theatre and a recital hall. There are usually a few performances each day in either these or the main halls.

Many performances are easy to get tickets for - these can be purchased on site or via their website (tickets can be collected here too).

Click here to find out what's on at the Performance Halls

Democracy Boulevard & Square

A large open area in the centre is a great place to relax or take pictures, and will often host many activities and events throughout the year.

The Gate of Integrity is the impressive main gate that sits to the west of the square.

The square will often host concerts, markets or other events, and is a focal point for pro-democracy rallies.

Click here to see the upcoming events in the square

Flag Ceremony

In the centre of the square is a long pole with the Taiwanese flag raised high into the sky. If you are here during early morning or evening, you can witness the raising/lowering of the national flag, an impressively well-drilled and rehearsed ceremony.

1st April to 30 September: Flag Raised: 06:00 / Flag Lowered : 18:10
1st October to 31st March: Flag Raised: 06:30 / Flag Lowered : 17:10

Again, there will usually be a large crowd gathered for this, but there's more space for people to get a good view. The flag is expertly lowered and carefully folded into a neat roll. The guards will then march off back towards the hall.

Tip: If you stand between the flag pole and the memorial hall, you'll get some great pictures as they march past.

Gardens and Trail

Around the edges of the grounds are some beautiful gardens and tree-lined avenues.

The Chinese-style gardens have been exquisitely landscaped, and feature bridges, rock formations and many plants and trees. Guanghua Pond and Yunhan Pond are a haven for wildlife, with koi, turtles, squirrels and many species of heron and other birds found here.

The gardens are connected by the Araucaria Trail, a long tree-lined path that goes around the back of the memorial hall. It features dozens of species of trees, including those found in southern and central Taiwan, and also ones found on Orchid Island.

If you have time, I would recommend walking through the gardens and trail here as they've been beautifully landscaped.

It goes without saying that the Chiang Kai-Shek Memorial Hall is a must see attraction. Since it's such a huge area, it will never feel overcrowded, although if you wish to see the changing of the guards, it's best to avoid the weekends.

Virtual Tour

Traveller Tips

Make sure you're there for the guards to troop and raise/lower the Taiwan flag:

1st April to 30 September: Flag Raised: 06:00 / Flag Lowered : 18:10
1st October to 31st March: Flag Raised: 06:30 / Flag Lowered : 17:10

The changing of the guards ceremony takes place every hour on the hour from 09:00 until 17:00.

Try Chun Shui Tang inside the National Performance Hall, the brand that created the first Bubble Tea.

See the Memorial Hall as part of a walk I’ve devised. The Daan route is a weekend walk with a flower market and park, while the Zhongzheng route would be preferred by architecture and history buffs.

Opening Hours

Memorial Hall: 09:00 - 18:00 (closed on Mondays) 
Memorial Park: 05:00 - midnight

Closed for February 28th anniversary day, Chinese New Year's Eve and New Year's Day

Location

📍 Closest MRT: Chiang Kai-Shek Memorial Hall (green/red lines - exit 5)

title: Healthy and Tasty Brunches at Tamed Fox
excerpt: A healthy, easy-on-the-waistline brunch spot with a large communal sharing table. Come outside peak hours for a table to yourselves.
content:
If you're in need of a brunch that's appetising yet easy on the waste-line, Tamed Fox is one of the best places to visit in Taipei.

The dining area is very spacious although there are only a few tables here, including a large sharing table. Consequently you may need to wait to be seated.

Their food menu, while only consisting of 15 or so dishes, has enough variety to cater for most people's needs.

Their 'snacks' consists of yogurt bowls, French toast, an open sandwich and quiche. We've yet to try any of these, but their yogurt bowls especially we will come back to try.

The main dishes have a heavy emphasis on vegetables. Their Smoked Salad Roasted Vegetable Salad, with mixed greens, pumpkin and mushrooms, and a semi-soft boiled egg. A well executed and light dish that went down well.

You can also choose one of three vegetable bowls, with a pick of organic brown rice or quinoa (or half of each).

We decided on the Signature Chicken Bowl, with pan fried honey soy rosemary chicken, scrambled eggs, broccoli, roasted mushrooms and sweet potatoes - it was certainly a combination I've never tried before but most the ingredients were cooked with precision. Maybe the eggs looked a bit lost but they were soft and delicious.

Their dishes include a wide range of vegetables, with pumpkin, sweet potato, avocado, edamame and radish. If you need something heartier, they have the Tamed Fox 'Hangry' Breakfast Plate. American sausage meat that's accompanied by a selection of vegetables. As original as it was tasty!

Drinks-wise, they have a wide range of coffees, including some single-origin, teas and of course smoothies. If you order a meal, they'll give you NT$40 off any drink.

It's a pet-friendly restaurant, and have their own in-house cute dog that lives in a wigwam in the corner. Or maybe it's a tamed fox?!

Tamed Fox's location isn't the best, which is probably why you can usually find a table here. I'm sure if they were more centrally located, people would be queuing to try the delicious and healthy dishes they have to offer.

Menu

Pros

  • Amazing salads
  • Great healthy options

Cons

  • Not the best location
  • Not many tables

Price: $$$

Level of English: Ok (English menu available)

Traveller Tips

Get NT$40 off a drink when you order a main.

Location

📍 Closest MRT: Xinyi Anhe (red line)

title: Authentic Thai Cuisine at Home's Thai
content:
Home's Thai have a couple of branches in Taipei which serves some great authentic Thai food.

With two branches in Taipei, the Songshan branch is a lot less formal than the Fuxing Road branch - which is aimed at the many businesses in this area.

We often try the Shrimp Pancakes as a test for the authenticity and tastiness of a Thai restaurant. The ones at Home's Thai are juicy and packed with shrimp flavour.

If you like your Thai food especially spicy, Homes Thai will not disappoint, as most of their dishes do not hold back on the heat. Even the vegetable dishes are infused with chilli heat.

The Tom Yam soups are especially spicy, while the Pad Thai is very authentic, being exactly as they are in Thailand.

They have all the usual Thai dishes, and include some nice fish dishes on the menu - the lemongrass sea-bass is probably the most popular, while the tempura-like soft-shell crab with lemongrass is a complex flavour sensation.

The crispy chicken, with soy sauce and infused with garlic, chillis and spring onion is another great dish.

The service is also very good, with friendly staff and a nice atmosphere. Home's Thai is one of our favourite places for Thai Food and is one to try especially if you love spicy food.

Menu

Visit their website menu page.

Pros

  • Very spicy (although you can ask to tone it down)
  • Generally no waiting to be seated
  • Authentic

Cons

  • Slightly expensive

Price: $$$

Level of English: Ok (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

The Songshan branch is less formal and a good option after a visit to Songshan Cultural Park or Sun Yat-Sen Memorial Hall.

Although it wasn't busy while we were there, you can book a table online.

If you prefer slightly less spicy Thai food, why not give Very Thai a try?

Locations

Songshan Branch
Fuxing North Road

title: Huge Western Menu at Gordon Biersch
excerpt: A German-inspired American chain with four branches in central Taipei, known for its craft ales alongside a big western menu.
content:
Gordon Biersch is a German inspired American restaurant chain with four branches in the Taipei city centre. Originally based in California, it has since expanded around the globe and is known for creating some fine craft ales and delicious western food.

As far as I'm aware, Gordon Biersch have never opened a branch in the UK so I was unfamiliar with their brand, and keen to sample some of the ales and food.

Gordon Biersch have a range of beers, from light to very dark and includes hoppy, fruity and malty variations. If you want to try one of each without getting too tipsy, they have flights which can be purchased together.

Food-wise, Gordon Biersch have one of the largest range of western dishes in Taipei, with many salads, burgers, pasta, pizza, seafood, tacos, ribs and steaks.

As with all the western chains in Taipei, you will tend to pay more than you would normally in the west, but their burgers, steaks and pasta dishes especially as some of the best I've had in Taipei.

Gordon Biersch also have one of the best dessert menus I've seen in Taipei, which includes cheesecakes, brownies, ice-cream and a selection of other fine cakes. These are rich and indulgent and are ideal for those with an especially sweet tooth.

If you're visiting during October, Gordon Biersch has their own Oktoberfest which includes discounted food and drinks menus.

Menu

Visit their extensive menu pages on their website.

Pros

  • Nice variety of tasty beers
  • Very large and diverse selection of western food

Cons

  • Expensive

Price: $$$

Level of English: Excellent (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

If you visit during lunchtime, you can purchase a drink and one of a selection of dishes for a good saving.

Locations

📍 Xinyi Branch (Closest MRT: Betweeen Taipei 101 and Taipei City Hall)

title: Very Thai - Refined and Delicious Thai Dishes
excerpt: An upmarket Thai restaurant chain with several branches, related to the cheaper Thai Town and the noodle-focused Very Thai Noodles.
content:
Very Thai is an upmarket Thai restaurant chain with a number of conveniently located branches that serves some of our favourite Thai food in Taipei.

The same company also owns the Very Thai Noodles chain (also very good) and the slightly cheaper Thai Town, but it's worth the extra money to come here instead.

A starter we always enjoy here is the Shrimp Pancakes with sweet chilli sauce. They advertise it as their number one signature dish, and with reason. A perfect start to any Thai meal.

It's difficult for us to eat at any Thai restaurant without trying the Pad Thai, on the menu as Thai-style Fried Rice Noodles - and Very Thai do a great one. Very Pad Thai!

Another of their signature dishes is the Tom Yam Soup. Juicy pieces of shrimp in a hot and sour soup, it's very spicy but just as delicious.

Thai curries are another of our favourites, and it's sometimes difficult to choose between the red, green and yellow variants. This time we chose the Green Curry, again laced with chilli heat but creamy and rich.

Their selection is very large, and very authentic. The Thai style Shrimp Fried Rice dish, with spring onions and egg is as delicious as it sounds.

Dishes generally cost between NT$200 and NT$350, although the sea-bass will set you back around NT$600. They also have a number of beverages, both alcoholic and non-alcoholic. Their beer selection is extensive and includes a number of Belgian beers.

Very Thai is our favourite Thai restaurant in Taipei. We've yet to find another Thai restaurant that matches the quality and consistency here. Highly recommended.

Menu

Their large menu is best viewed from their website.

Pros

  • Many dishes are of a high standard
  • Great service

Cons

  • Slightly expensive

Price: $$$

Level of English: Ok (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

I would also recommend their other chain, Very Thai Noodles.

Locations

Shilin Branch
Nangang Branch

title: Refined Indian Cuisine at Joseph Bistro (Permanently Closed)
content:
Permanent Closure Notice

Please note: Joseph Bistro has permanently closed.

Joseph Bistro is an Indian Restaurant with a touch of class. Established and run by an Indian chef, it's a fine-dining restaurant that's found a place in the Michelin Guide.

Taipei isn't a great city for Indian cuisine, but this great little Indian restaurant ranks up there with the very best.

While I wouldn't say Joseph Bistro's menu is extensive, they tend to focus on a small number of quality dishes rather than bombarding you with everything you can imagine. Many of the items on the menu are rotated every few weeks to keep dishes fresh for regular diners.

Of course, they have curries and tandoori dishes found in any Indian restaurant, but unusually, they also have salads. Being lovers of salads, we were keen to find out what they were like.

With greens, cucumber, radish, nuts and mushrooms, and a raita sauce bringing everything together, it was a great looking and tasting salad with an Indian twist. If this is what all Indian salads are like, I only wish more Indian restaurants would subscribe to them.

The grilled options on the menu include many tandoori, and a spicy Indian steak which sounded interesting, although it was a little out of our price range. We opted instead for a couple of curries. The Palak Paneer, an Indian cheese braised in a mild spinach curry, along with a Shrimp Rogan Josh.

We're not huge fans of rice, so we went for a couple of their Naan breads to help devour the curries. Both curries were exceptional and we were left highly satisfied.

We still had room for a bit more however, and their desserts looked intriguing.

The Pan and Rose Kulfi, a traditional Indian ice cream, and the Chocolate Mouse, which came with coffee jelly and a rasmalai panna cotta. Again, fabulous looking and tasting desserts that were a great way to finish any meal.

Joseph Bistro's service is with a smile, and the Indian chef will ensure you have a great meal - although you will pay that little bit more than most Indian restaurants in Taipei. It is definitely money well spent though, and we will be returning to see what other dishes will be added to their menu.

Pros

  • One of the best Indians in Taipei
  • Salads are sublime

Cons

  • Expensive

Price: $$$

Level of English: Good (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

11:30 - 14:00 (13:00 last orders)

Dinner

title: Very Thai Noodles - Comforting Bowls of Goodness
excerpt: A quick-service spin-off of Very Thai, serving Thai and Vietnamese-inspired noodle dishes for a fast, hearty meal.
content:
Very Thai Noodles is a spin-off restaurant of the excellent Very Thai restaurants, with an aim to bring quick and hearty food.

They specialise in Thai/Vietnamese inspired ramen-style dishes but offer dry noodles and rice dishes too. Service here is fast, so if you're in a hurry but looking for something delicious, this is a good option.

The standard and consistency of the dishes is very good., with the broths being deep and rich in flavour and the accompanying meat or fish cooked nicely.

The Tom Yam Kung Noodles, with a choice of pork, seafood or both is rich with a bold taste. The Thai Style Curry Noodles with chicken drumstick is hearty, creamy and delicious.

The only issue you'll have is the mess you will no doubt make, attempting to eat them with spoon and chopsticks. They do however provide bibs to contain any splash-back.

You could also choose a safer option - the minced pork on a bed of rice with a deep-fried and battered egg on top and plenty of chilli. Splash-back free!

They also have ice-cream to take away which comes in two flavours - matcha and sesame - both excellent.

There are many locations dotted in and around Taipei, one is right before the security check at departures in Songshan airport.

Very Thai Noodles is a great choice whether you're in a hurry or just fancy something comforting yet delicious!

Pros

  • Many locations
  • Quick service

Cons

  • Limited choice

Price: $$

Level of English: Ok (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

They can be messy to eat but bibs are available if required!

Locations

Near Taipei Arena
Taipei Main Q Square
Shilin

title: Get Wooed by the Cocktails at Woo Taipei (Permanently Closed)
content:
Permanent Closure Notice

Please note: Woo Taipei has permanently closed.

Woo Taipei is a stylish and popular bar and restaurant that specialises in wines and cocktails, while serving some great western dishes.

The large main room is decked out with old wooden furniture, cast-iron stoves and many filament light bulbs which are the only light-sources in this dimly lit environment. With the sounds of smooth cool music and the buzz of chat, Woo Taipei has a great atmosphere.

The wine list is extensive, and there are many fine cocktails to choose from, each with their own twist. Their "We'll Make You Woo" cocktails are precisely crafted alcoholic works-of-art.

The food choice is also good, with English style pub food like fish and chips, plenty of pasta options, and a variety of food to share such as tapas and seafood platters. We particularly enjoyed their Garlic Shrimp & Mushrooms in Taiwan Beer.

Woo Taipei is a great bistro style bar that usually gets busy over the weekend. You may need to queue to get in, but you'll have a great time once inside.

Pros

  • Great atmosphere
  • High quality cocktails

Cons

  • Quite expensive
  • Expect to queue to get in during peak hours

Price: $$$

Level of English: Good (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

The food platters are great sharing options

Location

📍 Closest MRT: Zhongxiao Dunhua (blue line)

title: Watch the Footy at The Brass Monkey
excerpt: An established western bar popular with American expats, built around watching live sport on a projector and multiple screens.
content:
One of the more established western bars in Taipei, The Brass Monkey is a popular destination for American ex-pats and tourists.

It's one of the best venues to watch live sport, with a projector in the back room and numerous TVs, and show a very wide range of sports including:

  • Premier & Champions League Football
  • F1 and Moto GP
  • Boxing and UFC
  • NBA & AFL

The Brass Monkey also has a good selection of draft lagers and real ales, and have a couple of great happy hour deals.

From 11:00 - 20:00 each day, you can get draft lagers, beers, bottles and spirits from around NT$100. They also have a new Monkey Hour between 17:00 and 18:00, where many of these are reduced to NT$90 including house wines.

Brass Monkey serve largely portioned western dishes that are some of the best in Taipei. I've not had better pies or Fish & Chips anywhere else in Taipei. This is the smaller sized version which is plenty for me but they have a large portion too.

If you're visiting over the Christmas period, this is the place to come for a great meal. Turkey, stuffing, mash, veg, sausages, gravy and cranberry sauce. Probably the best Christmas meal in Taipei.

The room towards the rear also has a large pool table that's free to play, and for large sporting events they'll pull down a screen here for the projector.

Brass Monkey is usually a lively place to enjoy a drink, especially when Taipei plays host to large business events.

Pros

  • Large portions
  • Great for live sport
  • Pool table

Cons

  • Quite pricey, as with most western bars

Price: $$$

Level of English: Excellent (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

Check out their lunchtime specials between 11.30am - 2pm Mon to Fri

Check the schedule for a full list of offers, sports events and special nights.

They offer one of the best Christmas meals in Taipei.

Brass Monkey Location

📍 Closest MRT: Nanjing Fuxing (green/brown lines)

title: On Tap - The Most Authentic British Pub in Taiwan
excerpt: Billed as Taipei's only authentic British pub, with draft ales and walls covered in British memorabilia. What's on tap and the vibe.
content:
Billed as Taipei's only real pub, On Tap is the most authentic British style bar in Taipei, serving draft lagers and ales, plus a variety of pub food.

The walls are plastered with British memorabilia, with Union Flags, London buses and numerous icons from British pop and film culture. It's probably the closest you'll come to feeling like your drinking in an English pub in Taipei.

Consisting of two levels, the ground level includes plenty of outdoor seating (only until 22:00 though), while the basement has a free pool table, darts and other games such as Jenga.

If you're after live sport, On Tap is the best place to come in Taipei.

With no less than 14 screens, 3 of them projectors, they have the ability to show multiple sporting events simultaneously. Although, much like other venues, they will only turn the sound up for the largest events such as the Football World Cup or the Wimbledon final.

The beer selection at On Tap is very good, and includes a few very British Badger Ales and some Belgian lagers, and they have some decent tap ales, including Taiwan's own Redpoint. The drinks menu is extensive to say the least, with bottled and canned beers/ciders as well as the drafts ones, wines, whiskeys, cocktails, shots, bombs and soft drinks.

There is a wide variety of pub food to choose from, and it's generally of a good standard. Almost everything you'll find in a pub in Britain can be ordered from On Tap's extensive menu. Burgers, pies, salads, pasta and of course a couple of English favourites - Fish 'n' Chips & Bangers 'n' Mash!

On most days there's a great offer on a selection of the food (see Traveller's Tips below).

There's usually a great atmosphere at On Tap, especially over the weekend, where locals, expats and holiday makers will all come to enjoy a very British experience.

Pros

  • Plays some great music
  • Free pool table
  • Authentic British feel

Cons

  • No sound during most live sports screenings

Price: $$

Level of English: Excellent (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

Happy Hour Drinks every day until 20:00, with draft ales costing as little as NT$150 during this time!

For each day of the week, there's also a very good offer on food and/or beverages:

On Tap also co-own another British-style pub in Taipei. The Three Lions Inn is located in Maji Square and includes a large outdoor seating area.

title: Perfect English Afternoon Tea at Smith & Hsu
excerpt: The most authentic English afternoon tea in Taipei, according to a Brit who's had plenty of the real thing back home.
content:
If you crave an afternoon tea whilst in Taipei, look no further than Smith & Hsu.

They serve the most authentic afternoon tea in Taipei. This is coming from a Brit who has had many an afternoon tea in the English towns around the country. Smith & Hsu is a match for many I've had.

You can purchase a Tea Set for One, which consists of a tea and scones with clotted cream and jam. The scones are without question the best I've tried in Taiwan. Soft and moist on the inside with a firm exterior, although perhaps I'd like a larger portion of cream and jam.

If you're here as a pair, then I'd recommend going for the Lady Smith Afternoon Tea Set or the Queen Victoria Afternoon Tea Set. These come with the scones and tea, with the addition of 6 sandwiches, one jelly each and cake (the queens will come with 2 cakes and cookies).

When we were there, the sandwiches consisted of

  • Ham Salad
  • Smoked Salmon and Capers
  • Beef and Tomato

All were delectable and worthy of any English tea set.

We chose the Earl Grey Cheesecake, which was soft and creamy, with the taste of tea to match our beverages.

You can choose from around 30 teas, which they'll bring samples for you to sniff at your table. These range from fine English teas, fruit teas, Oolong, and more unusual ones such as Black Chocolate Mint Tea.

At a cost of just over NT$1,100 with the service charge, the Lady Smith is probably a similar pricing to the UK so it's pretty good value considering.

Smith & Hsu is our go-to place whenever we are in need of an afternoon tea. If there's a better place for this in Taipei, we've yet to find it!

Pros

  • Sandwiches and scones are both first class
  • Excellent tea selection

Cons

  • Stingy on the jam and cream

Price: $$$

Klook.com

Level of English: Ok (English on menu)

Traveller Tips

Go for one of the larger afternoon tea sets
