title: Michelin Bib Gourmand Taiwanese Small Eats in Taipei: The Complete Guide
excerpt: Explore the top Michelin Bib Gourmand awarded Taiwanese small eats (Xiao Chi) in Taipei City, featuring iconic fried rice, scallion pancakes, pork belly bao, and traditional broths.
content:
Taipei is world-famous for its vibrant food culture and iconic Xiao Chi (小吃, small eats)—bite-sized delicacies packed with centuries of culinary heritage. The prestigious Michelin Guide honors the very best of these wallet-friendly eateries with its coveted Bib Gourmand designation, awarded to places offering exceptional food at moderate prices.

In this guide, we break down all 16 Michelin Bib Gourmand Taiwanese Small Eats establishments in Taipei City (excluding New Taipei), giving you essential details on signature dishes, pricing, locations, and insider tips for visiting.

1. Sinchao Rice Shoppe (心潮飯店)

A stylish spinoff of Kaohsiung's Old & New Taiwanese Cuisine, Sinchao Rice Shoppe elevates traditional street fried rice into a glamorous dining experience. Famous for creative dishes like bottarga with seared scallop fried rice and red yeast fried chicken, the kitchen marries rich local flavors with modern flair. Set inside a chic 1920s Art Deco dining room, Sinchao also pairs its meals with Taiwanese tea-infused cocktails and natural wines.

  • Type of Cuisine: Taiwanese (Modern Taiwanese Small Eats & Fried Rice Specialties)
  • Price: ££ (Moderate, approx. NT$300 – NT$600 per person)
  • Location & Map: 2F, Breeze Xinyi, No. 68, Section 5, Zhongxiao East Road, Xinyi District, Taipei City (Google Maps / near MRT Taipei City Hall Station Exit 3)

2. Open Smile (開囍滷肉專賣店)

Living up to its joyful name, Open Smile (開囍滷肉專賣店) is a bright, modern eatery in Xinyi District specializing in Taiwanese comfort food classics. Famous for its rich braised pork rice (Lu Rou Fan) and tender braised pork belly, the kitchen slow-simmers fresh local pork with traditional spices to deliver deep, savory perfection. Paired with house-pickled vegetables and steaming broths, it offers a clean, elevated take on humble street food.

  • Type of Cuisine: Taiwanese (Braised Pork Rice & Traditional Small Eats)
  • Price: £ (Budget-Friendly, approx. NT$100 – NT$250 per person)
  • Location & Map: No. 441, Zhuangjing Road, Xinyi District, Taipei City (Google Maps / near MRT Taipei 101/World Trade Center Station)

3. Jin Shang Hsuan (金賞軒)

Tucked away in Songshan District with just six tables and a private dining room, Jin Shang Hsuan (金賞軒) is a cozy neighborhood gem celebrated for its refined Taiwanese home-style cooking. The chef-owner crafts flavor-packed classics with immaculate technique, including signature stir-fried beef with coriander and crispy garlic, home-style poached chicken, and fragrant bottarga fried rice. Due to its intimate seating capacity, advance reservations are highly recommended.

  • Type of Cuisine: Taiwanese (Refined Taiwanese Small Eats & Stir-Fries)
  • Price: ££ (Moderate, approx. NT$300 – NT$600 per person)
  • Location & Map: No. 111, Lane 155, Dunhua North Road, Songshan District, Taipei City (Google Maps / near MRT Taipei Arena Station)

4. Yu Yu 1969 (有有1969)

Originally established in 1969 and now helmed by its third-generation owner, Yu Yu 1969 (有有1969) blends nostalgic vintage charm with warm, modern wooden booth seating. Situated near Liaoning Night Market, this beloved eatery specializes in high-fire Taiwanese stir-fries infused with powerful wok hei. Must-try dishes include their signature fried rice, tender braised pork, and flavorful seafood stir-fries, making it a staple destination for authentic family-style dining.

  • Type of Cuisine: Taiwanese (Traditional Wok Stir-Fries & Small Eats)
  • Price: ££ (Moderate, approx. NT$300 – NT$600 per person)
  • Location & Map: No. 48, Liaoning Street, Zhongshan District, Taipei City (Google Maps / near MRT Nanjing Fuxing Station)

5. Ching Jiao (晴郊)

Featuring a bright, light-filled interior with traditional Chinese window screens, Ching Jiao (晴郊) offers a tranquil setting in Zhongzheng District. Run by a passionate husband-and-wife duo, the menu revolves around slow-simmered, nourishing chicken broths and artisan Taiwanese small eats. Highlight dishes include their signature chicken soup, savory rice cakes, and marinated braised sides, offering comforting home-style cooking with exceptional depth.

  • Type of Cuisine: Taiwanese (Nourishing Chicken Broths & Small Eats)
  • Price: ££ (Moderate, approx. NT$300 – NT$600 per person)
  • Location & Map: No. 9, Section 2, Jinan Road, Zhongzheng District, Taipei City (Google Maps / near MRT Shandao Temple Station Exit 2)

6. Soft Power (軟食力)

Located in a charming alley near Xingtian Temple, Soft Power (軟食力) is a beloved modern breakfast spot famous for its southern Taiwanese-style egg crepe rolls (Dan Bing). Made with freshly poured batter, these signature crepes feature a crispy golden exterior wrapping a soft, chewy core packed with fillings like pork chop, sweet potato, or cheese. Pair them with freshly ground soy milk for an iconic local breakfast.

  • Type of Cuisine: Taiwanese (Traditional Breakfast & Egg Crepe Rolls)
  • Price: £ (Budget-Friendly, approx. NT$100 – NT$200 per person)
  • Location & Map: No. 21, Alley 30, Lane 135, Section 2, Minquan East Road, Zhongshan District, Taipei City (Google Maps / near MRT Xingtian Temple Station Exit 3)

7. Chi Chia Chuang (雞家莊 長春路)

A Taipei institution operating for decades on Changchun Road, Chi Chia Chuang (雞家莊) is renowned for its obsession with premium Taiwanese chicken dishes. The owner selects only young 5-to-6-month-old pullets to ensure exceptionally tender meat. Signature dishes include their fragrant three-cup chicken, poached salted chicken, and chicken rice cooked in rich poultry broth, finished with their legendary complimentary egg caramel pudding.

  • Type of Cuisine: Taiwanese (Classic Poultry & Home-Style Dishes)
  • Price: ££ (Moderate, approx. NT$300 – NT$600 per person)
  • Location & Map: No. 55, Changchun Road, Zhongshan District, Taipei City (Google Maps / near MRT Zhongshan Station Exit 3)

8. Shuang Yue Food / MoonMoonFood (雙月食品社 青島東路)

Situated near Shandao Temple, Shuang Yue Food (雙月食品社) is famous across Taipei for its deeply restorative, slow-simmered Taiwanese soups. Their signature clam and chicken soup features generous chunks of free-range chicken and fresh clams in a rich, cabbage-infused broth. Complemented by lu wei (braised delicacies) and oil rice, this warm, family-friendly shop draws constant queues of locals seeking wholesome comfort food.

  • Type of Cuisine: Taiwanese (Health-Conscious Soups & Braised Delicacies)
  • Price: ££ (Moderate, approx. NT$200 – NT$400 per person)
  • Location & Map: No. 6-2, Qingdao East Road, Zhongzheng District, Taipei City (Google Maps / near MRT Shandao Temple Station Exit 2)

9. Hsiao Cho Chih Chia (小焯之家)

Founded in 1995 and boasting over 40 years of culinary mastery, Hsiao Cho Chih Chia (小焯之家) is an intimate five-table eatery on Jilin Road. The chef prides himself on preparing pure, additive-free Taiwanese classics with uncompromising precision. Signature dishes include steamed fish with tree seeds, seasoned pork intestine, and stir-fried squid, delivering clean, deeply authentic home-style flavors that keep loyal patrons returning for decades.

  • Type of Cuisine: Taiwanese (Additive-Free Home-Style Cooking & Seafood)
  • Price: ££ (Moderate, approx. NT$300 – NT$600 per person)
  • Location & Map: No. 420, Jilin Road, Zhongshan District, Taipei City (Google Maps / near MRT Zhongshan Elementary School Station)

10. Huang Chi Lu Rou Fan (黃記魯肉飯)

A celebrated neighborhood fixture in Zhongshan District, Huang Chi Lu Rou Fan (黃記魯肉飯) has built a cult following purely through word of mouth. Their iconic braised pork rice features melt-in-your-mouth pork belly slow-cooked in rich soy sauce and aromatic spices, served over piping hot rice. Complemented by thick braised pork soup, stuffed cabbage rolls, and stewed tofu, it represents quintessential Taiwanese street food at its finest.

  • Type of Cuisine: Taiwanese (Braised Pork Rice & Traditional Street Eats)
  • Price: £ (Budget-Friendly, approx. NT$80 – NT$200 per person)
  • Location & Map: No. 28, Lane 183, Section 2, Zhongshan North Road, Zhongshan District, Taipei City (Google Maps / near MRT Zhongshan Elementary School Station Exit 1)

11. Inn's+ (英斯 雙城街)

Hidden in a quiet alley near Shuangcheng Street, Inn’s+ (英斯) is an elegant culinary hideaway run by a former bistro chef. Reinterpreting traditional Taiwanese dishes with modern wellness in mind, the kitchen reduces oil and sodium without sacrificing robust flavor. Signature offerings include scallion chicken, braised pork ribs, and seasonal vegetable stir-fries, making it a refined choice for health-conscious food lovers.

  • Type of Cuisine: Taiwanese (Health-Conscious Modern Taiwanese)
  • Price: ££ (Moderate, approx. NT$300 – NT$600 per person)
  • Location & Map: No. 8, Lane 28, Shuangcheng Street, Zhongshan District, Taipei City (Google Maps / near MRT Zhongshan Elementary School Station)

12. Da-Qiao-Tou Tube Rice Pudding (大橋頭老牌筒仔米糕)

Dating back to 1973 on Yanping North Road, Da-Qiao-Tou Tube Rice Pudding (大橋頭老牌筒仔米糕) is a famed third-generation stall open from dawn till dusk. Their signature steamed glutinous rice is cooked in cylindrical bamboo tubes with savory pork and spices, resulting in a delightfully chewy texture. Served with your choice of lean or fatty pork and topped with sweet chili sauce, it pairs perfectly with pork liver soup.

  • Type of Cuisine: Taiwanese (Tube Rice Pudding & Traditional Soups)
  • Price: £ (Budget-Friendly, approx. NT$60 – NT$150 per person)
  • Location & Map: No. 41, Section 3, Yanping North Road, Datong District, Taipei City (Google Maps / near MRT Daqiaotou Station Exit 1)

13. Yi Jia Zi (一甲子餐飲)

Now managed by its third generation, Yi Jia Zi (一甲子餐飲) is legendary in Wanhua District for its mouthwatering Tainan-style street food. Their signature stewed pork belly rice (Kong Rou Fan) features melt-in-your-mouth pork with perfectly rendered fat layers, served alongside house-pickled cucumbers. Paired with savory Gua Bao (lotus leaf buns) and pork blood soup, it draws endless lines of devoted foodies daily.

  • Type of Cuisine: Taiwanese (Stewed Pork Belly Rice & Tainan Street Eats)
  • Price: £ (Budget-Friendly, approx. NT$60 – NT$150 per person)
  • Location & Map: No. 79, Kangding Road, Wanhua District, Taipei City (Google Maps / near MRT Longshan Temple Station Exit 3)

14. Wang's Broth (小王煮瓜)

Operating in Huaxi Street Night Market for over 45 years, Wang's Broth (小王煮瓜) has evolved from a humble street stall into a Michelin-starred favorite. Renowned for its signature "Black Gold" braised pork rice, the kitchen slow-simmers pork belly in dark soy sauce until glistening and gelatinous. Equally famous is their steamed minced pork soup with pickled cucumber, offering a comforting, aromatic broth steeped in tradition.

  • Type of Cuisine: Taiwanese (Black Gold Lu Rou Fan & Steamed Pork Soups)
  • Price: £ (Budget-Friendly, approx. NT$80 – NT$180 per person)
  • Location & Map: Stall 153, Huaxi Street Night Market, No. 17-4, Huaxi Street, Wanhua District, Taipei City (Google Maps / near MRT Longshan Temple Station Exit 1)

15. Su Lai Chuan (素來川)

Celebrating over 70 years of heritage in Wanhua District, Su Lai Chuan (素來川) is a beloved Taiwanese small eats stall famous for its traditional Ba-Wan (meatballs). Third-generation owners prepare the steamed and poached Ba-Wan from scratch daily, featuring a translucent, chewy rice-flour casing wrapped around spiced pork and bamboo shoots. Pair it with their savory steamed taro cake and pork ball soup.

title: Songshan Airport (TSA): Getting To and From Taipei
excerpt: Songshan Airport (TSA) is Taipei's smaller, closer-to-the-city airport - here's how to get to and from the centre by MRT or taxi, and when you'd use it over Taoyuan.
content:
Songshan Airport (TSA) is Taipei's smaller, much more central airport – just three MRT stops from the middle of the city, compared to almost an hour from Taoyuan. If your flight lands here, you'll be in the city centre faster than almost any other capital airport in Asia.

💡 The Quick Verdict: Getting To and From Songshan

  • MRT (NT$20–30, ~15–25 min): the best option almost every time – the station sits right under the terminal, on the brown line.
  • Taxi/Uber (roughly NT$150–250, ~15–20 min): worth it late at night, with heavy luggage, or if your final stop isn't near an MRT station.
  • Landed at the wrong airport for your trip? See the comparison with Taoyuan Airport further down this page.

Overview

Songshan Airport has two terminals, but only Terminal 1 handles international flights – Terminal 2 is domestic-only. Songshan mainly serves domestic routes (Kaohsiung, Taitung, Kinmen, Penghu and more), plus a handful of international city-to-city routes to nearby airports such as Tokyo Haneda, Seoul Gimpo and Shanghai Hongqiao.

It has far fewer services than Taoyuan. If you need to purchase a SIM card, your only option here is a Chunghwa Telecom SIM – see the SIM Card guide for details.

For details and maps of all services, shops and booths, take a look at the Songshan Airport passenger guide.

Songshan Airport to Taipei

Songshan Airport is located just three stops from the centre of Taipei on the brown line of the MRT, with the station sitting directly beneath the terminal.

Should you wish to travel to Taipei Main Station, change at Zhongxiao Fuxing and take the blue line in the Dingpu direction. The journey time from Songshan Airport to Taipei Main Station is approximately 25 minutes.

You don't need an EasyCard to ride the MRT anymore – a contactless Visa/Mastercard or your phone (Apple Pay, Google Pay, Samsung Pay) taps directly at the gate, no ticket machine required. An EasyCard is still worth getting if you'll be riding a lot, since it works out slightly cheaper and doubles as payment at convenience stores. You can buy one from a machine located just outside the MRT entrance.

See the EasyCard guide for further details

Taipei to Songshan Airport

Make your way to the brown line and travel north to the Songshan Airport MRT station. The airport is a 5 minute walk from here (or you can walk straight up from the station concourse to the terminal).

Any money left on your EasyCard can be refunded at the MRT information desk immediately after leaving the MRT station – minus a small handling fee.

Check to see if your flight is on time from their flight departure web page.

Taxi and Uber

A taxi or Uber is a reasonable option given how close Songshan is to the city centre. Using the standard metered rate (NT$85 for the first 1.25km, then NT$5 per 200m), a typical trip into central Taipei works out at roughly NT$150–250 and takes around 15–20 minutes depending on traffic and your exact destination – treat this as an estimate rather than a fixed price.

Taxis and Uber pick-up points are outside the arrivals hall at Terminal 1. It's worth having your destination written in Chinese or shown on Google Maps, since English isn't guaranteed.

Songshan vs Taoyuan Airport

Most visitors to Taipei will land at Taoyuan Airport, Taiwan's main international gateway, roughly 40km west of the city. Songshan is the one to know about if you're flying in on a domestic connection, arriving from one of the small number of international routes it serves (mainly nearby Northeast Asian cities), or catching a connecting domestic flight onward to somewhere like Kinmen or Penghu at the end of your trip.

The trade-off is straightforward: Taoyuan has far more flights, shops and services, but takes closer to an hour to reach the city by Airport MRT. Songshan has a fraction of the facilities, but can have you in central Taipei in well under half an hour.

title: Taiwan Tourist Shuttle Bus: Routes, Cost & How to Use It
excerpt: How Taiwan's Tourist Shuttle Bus network works - cost, timetables, how to pay, and the most popular routes from Taipei to places like Yehliu, Pingxi and Beitou.
content:
Taiwan's Tourist Shuttle Bus network has over 60 routes covering all the major scenic and cultural spots around the island, including many of Taiwan's outlying islands. They're a nice middle ground if you don't want to fork out for a private driver or guided tour – the cost is only a fraction of a tour coach.

💡 The Quick Verdict: Tourist Shuttle Buses

  • Cost: NT$50–1,000 per day depending on the route, though most fall between NT$100–250.
  • From Taipei: 4 routes run directly off the MRT system (see below); another ~25 run from Taiwan High Speed Rail stations.
  • Already have a Taipei Fun Pass? The Unlimited and Transport variants include 6 popular routes for free – see below.

Some routes are designed so the final stop of one is close to the starting point of another, letting you effectively hop from one bus onto the next. Other routes circle back around to your starting location.

If you've brought a bicycle, around 30 routes are specifically designed for cyclists (it needs to be a foldable bike). There are also around 15 routes aimed at senior citizens or people with disabilities, with seat reservations possible and easy access on and off the bus.

Popular Routes from Taipei

Six routes run directly from Taipei and are covered free by the Unlimited and Transport Taipei Fun Passes:

  • Jiufen – Jinguashi (965)
  • Beitou – Zhuzihu
  • Muzha – Pingxi
  • Crown North Coast
  • Gold Fulong
  • Coastal Keelung

The Beitou – Zhuzihu route travels the shortest distance (to Yangmingshan National Park), so it's a good option if you want to see the rural side of Taiwan without travelling very far. Other destinations along these routes include waterfalls and more of Yangmingshan National Park.

For the Gold Fulong and Coastal Keelung routes, you'll need to take a train first, to Keelung Train Station or Ruifang Train Station respectively. Since their start and end points are close to each other, you can combine the two into one trip.

The Jiufen – Jinguashi (965) route is the most useful addition – it runs direct from Ximen MRT (the stop is about 160m from Exit 2) all the way to Jiufen Old Street and the Gold Museum, so you avoid the usual change onto a local bus at Ruifang. It's frequent too, every 10–15 minutes at peak times.

Alternatively, the Crown North Coast route runs from Tamsui MRT to Yehliu Geopark – from there, a local bus or taxi gets you to Waimushan in about 15 minutes.

Around 25 further routes run from Taiwan High Speed Rail stations rather than Taipei directly – I've listed the best of these, station by station, in my High Speed Rail guide.

How to Use the Tourist Shuttle Buses

  • Choose your preferred route. You can do this from their website, or if that's too confusing then there's a nice PDF file with all the routes
  • Timetables for all buses can be found by locating your route on their website (or by scanning the QR Code on the PDF) and selecting the Fare & Timetable button
  • The departing bus stop can also be found using the above method. Look out for the Taiwan Tourist Shuttle Bus Stop sign when you arrive (pictured above)
  • You can pay for the ride using your EasyCard. You must tap it when you get on and off the bus each time
  • Most buses operate similar to the Sightseeing Buses in Taipei, so when you get off at a stop, the bus will depart and you'll need to wait for one of the next buses. However, there are some cruise-style buses that will wait for you, meaning you'll remain on the same bus throughout

Cost & Timetables

You can either pay for a day pass to use a route for the entire day, or on some routes it's possible to pay per stop if you only want to travel part of the way – this is calculated automatically when you tap your EasyCard.

The cost of using a Tourist Shuttle Bus per day varies between NT$50 and NT$1,000 depending on the length of the route, although most fall between NT$100 and NT$250 per day. It's also possible to get two or three day passes on some routes.

Frequency varies a lot by route too, from as often as every 20 minutes to as little as every 3 hours, and from as few as 4 buses a day to as many as 28. Some routes only run on weekdays, others only on weekends and holidays – all detailed on their website or the PDF file.

title: Taroko National Park Day Trip from Taipei: Full Guide
excerpt: Everything you need to visit Taroko Gorge from Taipei - how to get there, what's currently open after the 2024 earthquake, and the marble canyon scenery that makes it worth the trip.
content:
Perfect For

  • Marble canyon scenery
  • A dramatic scenic drive
  • Wildlife spotting
  • Combining with Hualien

Taroko Gorge (太魯閣) is Taiwan's most famous natural landmark outside Taipei – a roughly 19km marble-walled canyon carved by the Liwu River (立霧溪) through the eastern edge of the Central Mountain Range, with cliff faces rising as high as 1,100 metres in places. It sits within the wider Taroko National Park (太魯閣國家公園), a 920 km² protected area established in 1986 and named after the Truku people, an Indigenous group who have lived in the region for generations and only gained official recognition as a separate tribe (previously classified under the Atayal) in 2004. It's roughly 2 hours from Taipei by express train to Hualien, making it one of the most spectacular – if ambitious – day trips from the city, though plenty of visitors prefer to stay a night or two nearby to see more of it properly.

Current Access Notice (2026)

Taroko National Park suffered severe damage in the magnitude-7.4 earthquake that struck Hualien on 3 April 2024, followed by several typhoons through 2024 and 2025 that caused further landslides. Recovery is ongoing, and several of the gorge's most famous trails – including Swallow Grotto, Eternal Spring Shrine, Zhuilu Old Trail, Shakadang Trail and Baiyang Trail – remain closed to foot traffic at the time of writing, though most can still be seen from the road. Tianxiang and part of Lushui are open for walking. Always check the official Taroko National Park website or your tour operator for the latest status before you go – this changes month to month as repairs continue.

How to Get There

Taroko is a genuine trek from Taipei – there's no direct train to the gorge itself, and since the 2024 earthquake, the road through it only opens to private vehicles in short timed windows. There are four main ways to do it.

By Guided Day Tour (Easiest)

Given the current access restrictions, a guided day tour is by far the simplest way to visit right now – it handles the train journey, the timed road access, and knowing which viewpoints are actually open, all in one booking. This Taroko Gorge Day Tour from Taipei by Train departs from Taipei with hotel pick-up included, takes the scenic train ride up the east coast, and also stops at Qixingtan Beach. It's rated 4.9/5 from reviewers and multilingual guiding (Chinese/English/Japanese) is included.

Check availability and book on Klook

By Train + Shuttle Bus

Take the Taroko Express or Puyuma Express from Taipei Main Station to Hualien – around 2 hours, roughly NT$440 one-way (regular, non-express trains take 3-4 hours). For a shorter final leg, stay on to Xincheng Station instead, which is only about 5km from the park's Visitor Center, versus a longer ride from Hualien itself. From either station, Taroko Bus Co. route 302 or TaiwanTrip Bus 310 runs to the Visitor Center (7-8 minutes from Xincheng). An all-day shuttle bus pass covering the main stops inside the gorge costs around NT$250 and can be bought near Hualien Station.

By Rental Car or Self-Drive

Since the earthquake, the highway through the gorge only opens to private vehicles during a handful of short daily windows – historically something like 06:30-08:00, 10:00-10:05, 12:00-13:00, 15:00-15:05 and 17:00-17:30, though these are adjusted regularly as repairs progress, so check the current release-time schedule on the official park website before you set off. Miss a window and you'll be waiting for the next one, which makes self-driving considerably less relaxing than it used to be.

By Taxi or Private Driver

Hiring a taxi or private driver for a half or full day from Hualien or Xincheng gives you more flexibility than the shuttle bus timetable without needing to navigate the timed road access yourself, and is a solid option for small groups splitting the cost.

What's Currently Open

Given how much this has shifted since 2024, here's a rough snapshot of where things stand:

  • Open for walking: Tianxiang Recreation Area (including the Tabido and Xiangde Temple trails), part of the Lushui Recreation Area (reopened in stages from February 2026), the Visitor Center and entrance archway.
  • Viewable from the road, closed to foot traffic: Swallow Grotto, Eternal Spring Shrine, the Tunnel of Nine Turns.
  • Closed, long-term repair: Zhuilu Old Trail, Shakadang Trail, Baiyang Trail and the Water Curtain Cave – some of these are expected to take years to fully reopen.

Swallow Grotto (燕子口)

Swallow Grotto takes its name from the swallows that once nested in the small pockmarked holes riddling the marble cliff face above the trail – look closely at the rock and you can still see them dotted across the surface.

Before the 2024 earthquake, this was arguably the single best short walk in the gorge – a narrow path carved directly into the cliff, ducking through a series of tunnels with the Liwu River rushing turquoise far below. It's currently closed to walkers, but the stretch is still one of the most dramatic sections to pass through by car or tour bus, with the marble walls closing in tight on both sides.

Eternal Spring Shrine (長春祠)

A small red pagoda shrine set into the cliffside with a waterfall running beneath it, built to honour the workers who died constructing the Central Cross-Island Highway through the gorge in the 1950s and 60s. It's currently closed to visitors and, according to the park authority, isn't expected to reopen until 2029, but the pagoda is still clearly visible from the road as you drive past – it's one of the most recognisable images of the gorge even from a distance.

The Marble Gorge & Liwu River

What makes Taroko worth the journey is the canyon itself – huge slabs of white and grey marble, tumbled boulders the size of houses, and the Liwu River running a startling turquoise-green through the middle of it all, mineral-rich rather than glacial but no less striking for it. Mist regularly rolls through the upper reaches of the gorge, softening the peaks above and giving the whole place a slightly otherworldly feel.

The scale of it is hard to appreciate in photos – cliff faces here rise as much as 1,100 metres above the riverbed in places, carved out of rock that's taken around 4 million years to be pushed up and cut through since the Philippine Sea Plate first collided with the Eurasian Plate.

Tunnel of Nine Turns (九曲洞)

Named for the nine bends the original road once wound through as it was carved into the cliff (the modern road has since been realigned with fewer turns), this stretch tunnels directly through the marble rather than around it. It's reopening in stages with visitor numbers capped per time slot, so check current booking rules on the official site before planning a walk through – but even just driving through it, with the rock pressing in on both sides and glimpses of the river below, is one of the more memorable parts of the journey.

Wildlife

Keep an eye out for Formosan rock macaques – Taiwan's only wild monkey species, and endemic to the island – which turn up fairly regularly around the gorge's viewing platforms and roadside pull-offs. They're generally unbothered by people, but resist the urge to feed them; it's both bad for them and occasionally makes them a bit too comfortable approaching visitors for food.

Combining with Hualien

Most visits to Taroko are combined with Hualien city or the coastline just north of it – Qixingtan Beach, a long pebble beach with the mountains as a backdrop, is a common add-on and features on several of the guided day tours. If you're staying overnight rather than doing it as a day trip, Hualien itself makes a relaxed base with a night market of its own.

See my full guide to day trips from Taipei for more ways to spend a day (or more) outside the city.

Guided Day Trip Tour Options

Given the current access restrictions inside the gorge, a guided tour is the option I'd recommend for most visitors right now – it takes care of the train journey, the timed road access, and knowing which stops are actually worth making.

This Taroko Gorge Day Tour from Taipei by Train covers the marble gorge, a scenic train ride along Taiwan's east coast, and a stop at Qixingtan Beach, with hotel pick-up included and guiding available in Chinese, English and Japanese.
